Course roadmap

CS336 follows the life-cycle of a language model: understand the building blocks (tokenizer → architecture), make them fast (GPU → kernels → parallelism), decide how big to go (scaling laws), serve and measure the result (inference, evaluation), feed it (data), and finally turn the base model into an assistant or reasoner (post-training), extending to images (multimodality). Click any node to jump to the lecture.

A short timeline of the models referenced

2017 Transformer, Adam/AdamW, MoE (Shazeer), PPO.
2018–19 BERT, GPT-2, T5, Megatron-LM, ZeRO, GPipe, RMSNorm.
2020 GPT-3, Kaplan scaling laws, The Pile, linear attention.
2021–22 Switch Transformer, RoPE, Gopher/PaLM, InstructGPT, Chinchilla (20 tokens/param), muP.
2023 LLaMA 1/2, Mistral 7B, GQA, FlashAttention-2, DPO, vLLM/PagedAttention, LLaVA, GPT-4.

2026 DeepSeek-V4-style attention, Kimi K2.5, GLM-5, MiniMax M2.5, Mamba-3, OLMix.

Course overview, the LM landscape, and tokenization

lecture_01.py course overview logistics syllabus tokenization BPE scaling laws
TL;DR. CS336 teaches language models by building them. Frontier models are closed and too expensive to replicate, so the course focuses on what transfers: mechanics, mindset (efficiency and scaling), and a few intuitions. The lecture then walks through the LM landscape from n-grams to open-weight models, outlines the five assignments (basics, systems, scaling laws, data, alignment), and begins the first unit: tokenization. It covers Unicode, character, byte and word tokenizers, then byte-pair encoding (BPE) run in full on a small string, with the compression ratio as the efficiency measure throughout.

Why this course exists

The lecture opens with a diagnosis: researchers are becoming disconnected from the underlying technology. The source traces three eras.

2016 Researchers implemented and trained their own models.
2018 Researchers downloaded pretrained models (e.g., BERT) and fine-tuned them.
Today Researchers prompt API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini).

Each step up the abstraction ladder boosts productivity, but the abstractions are leaky, unlike programming languages or operating systems. Fundamental research still requires tearing up the stack, and that needs full understanding of the technology. The course's philosophy follows from this: understanding via building.

The industrialization of language models

The obstacle is cost. Frontier models are very expensive to build:

  • 2023: GPT-4 was reported to cost about $100M to train (a Wired article quoted by the source).
  • 2025: xAI built a cluster with 230K GPUs to train Grok (a post by Elon Musk quoted by the source).

There are no public details on how frontier models are built. The GPT-4 technical report, for example, discloses nothing about data or architecture beyond headline results.

The consequence is that frontier models are out of reach for us. A class can build small models (under 1B parameters), but the source warns they may not be representative of large ones. Two examples show why scale changes the picture:

Example 1: FLOPs shift with scale. The fraction of FLOPs spent in attention versus the MLP changes as models grow. The OPT setups table (from a post by Stephen Roller) shows MLP (FFN) share rising from 44% at 760M to 80% at 175B, while attention falls.

Example 2: emergent behavior. Some abilities appear abruptly as scale grows, which is why small-model experiments can mislead (Wei et al., emergent abilities).

What transfers to frontier models?

The lecture separates three kinds of knowledge:

KindMeaningExampleTransfers across scale?
MechanicsHow things workWhat a Transformer is; how model parallelism worksyes
MindsetSqueezing the most out of hardware; taking scaling seriouslyMeasuring FLOPs and bytes before runningyes
IntuitionsWhich data and modeling decisions give good accuracyWhich activation to use; learning-rate scheduleonly partially
Intuitions? Some choices are not justified yet.

Some design decisions are simply not (yet) justifiable and just come from experimentation. The source's example is Noam Shazeer's paper that introduced SwiGLU. Its conclusion attributes the success of these architectures "to divine benevolence" (the figure below is the source's illustration for this point).

Shazeer (2020), GLU Variants Improve Transformer

The bitter lesson and efficiency

The "bitter lesson" is often misread. The wrong reading is that scale is all that matters and algorithms do not. The right reading is that algorithms that scale are what matter. The lecture frames it as:

\[ \text{accuracy} = \text{efficiency} \times \text{resources} \]

Efficiency matters more at larger scales, because at that point you cannot afford to be wasteful. The source cites a result showing 44x algorithmic efficiency on ImageNet between 2012 and 2019 (arXiv 2005.04305).

Framing for the course

What is the best model one can build given a certain compute and data budget? In other words, maximize efficiency.

The current LM landscape

The lecture tours the field chronologically. Each entry below is a paper the source links in the same order.

Pre-neural (before the 2010s)

  • Shannon's language model to measure the entropy of English (1950).
  • N-gram language models used in machine translation and speech recognition (Brants et al., 2007).

Neural ingredients (2010s)

  • LSTM (1997).
  • First neural language model (Bengio et al., 2003), a feedforward net over the last n words.
  • Sequence-to-sequence for machine translation (2014).
  • Adam optimizer (2014).
  • Attention for machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015).
  • Transformer architecture for machine translation (Vaswani et al., 2017).
  • Mixture of experts (Shazeer et al., 2017).
  • Model parallelism: GPipe (2018), ZeRO (2019), Megatron-LM (2019).

Early foundation models (late 2010s)

  • ELMo: pretraining with LSTMs; fine-tuning improves downstream tasks (2018).
  • BERT: pretraining with a Transformer; fine-tuning improves downstream tasks (2018).
  • Google's T5 (11B): casts everything as text-to-text (2019).

Embracing scaling

  • GPT-2 (1.5B): fluent text, first signs of zero-shot (2019).
  • Scaling laws give predictability (Kaplan et al., 2020).
  • GPT-3 (175B): in-context learning (2020).
  • PaLM (540B): massive scale, undertrained (2022).
  • Chinchilla (70B): compute-optimal scaling laws (Hoffmann et al., 2022).

Early open attempts (replicating GPT-3)

  • EleutherAI: The Pile dataset (825GB) and GPT-J (2021).
  • Meta's OPT (175B): GPT-3 replication with many hardware issues (2022).
  • Hugging Face / BigScience's BLOOM (176B): focused on data sourcing (2022).

Credible open-weight models (weights + paper)

  • Meta's Llama: Llama 1, Llama 2, Llama 3.
  • Mistral: Mistral 7B, Mixtral.
  • DeepSeek: 67B, V2, V3, R1, V3.2.
  • Alibaba's Qwen: Qwen 2.5, Qwen 3.
  • Moonshot's Kimi: Kimi 1.5, Kimi K2.5.
  • Z.ai's GLM: GLM 4.5, GLM 5.
  • MiniMax M2.5 (announcement) and Xiaomi MiMo v2 (announcement).

The source says these are approaching closed models (GPT, Claude, Gemini).

Fully open (weights + paper + code + data)

  • AI2's Olmo: Olmo 1, Olmo 2, Olmo 3.
  • NVIDIA's Nemotron: 15B (2024), Nemotron 3.
  • Marin (open development): 8B retro, 32B retro.

The source argues openness matters for trust and innovation (arXiv 2403.07918), and that ideas from open models are what make it possible to teach CS336.

What is a language model, over time?

2018 (BERT) Something you fine-tune.
2020 (GPT-3) Something you prompt.
2022 (ChatGPT) Something you talk to. The source links an example conversation.
2026 (agents) Something that acts autonomously. The source links an example trace.

The fundamentals are the same (attention, kernels, optimization). The specs are different: longer context, and inference efficiency matters even more.

What this program is: an executable lecture

Its execution delivers the lecture content, which makes it possible to view and run code (since everything is code), and to see the hierarchical structure of the lecture. Course logistics

  • Everything is on the course website. This is a 5-unit class.
  • Spring 2024 evaluation comment, quoted in the source: the entire assignment was approximately the same amount of work as all 5 assignments from CS 224n plus the final project.
  • Lectures from the 2nd offering (Spring 2025) are on YouTube. This is the 3rd offering. New this year: more coverage of modern ingredients (mixture of experts, long context, agents), and the same from-scratch philosophy.

Why take it

  • You have an obsessive need to understand how things work.
  • You want to build up your research engineering muscles.

Why not

  • You need research done this quarter (talk to your advisor).
  • You want the hottest new techniques (multimodality, RAG). A seminar fits better.
  • You want good results on one application (prompt or fine-tune an existing model).

Following along at home

All lecture materials and assignments are posted online. Lectures are recorded via CGOE.

Assignments, AI policy and compute

  • Five assignments: basics, systems, scaling laws, data, alignment. There is no scaffolding code, but there are unit tests and adapter interfaces. Implement locally for correctness, then run on the cluster for accuracy and speed benchmarks. Some assignments have leaderboards (minimize perplexity given a training budget).
  • AI policy. Coding agents can solve all the assignments, but you will not learn anything that way. AI is very useful for answering questions and tutoring. Students must use the provided AGENTS.md, which asks the AI to be pedagogically minded. Read the AI policy guide.
  • Compute is provided by Modal. See the access guide linked in the source.

Syllabus: five units

The lecture previews every assignment, because the course's efficiency theme runs through all of them. Each tab below summarizes one unit as the source presents it.

Goal: be able to train a basic language model. Components: tokenization, model architecture, training.

Model architecture. Start from the original Transformer (2017), then refine:

  • Activations: ReLU, SwiGLU (Shazeer 2020).
  • Positions: sinusoidal, RoPE (2021).
  • Normalization: LayerNorm (2016), RMSNorm (2019), QK-norm (2023), pre-norm vs post-norm (2020).
  • Attention: full, sparse/local (Sparse Transformer 2019), grouped-query (GQA, 2023), multi-head latent attention (MLA, 2024).
  • Recurrent / state-space / linear attention: linear attention 2020, Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-3.
  • MLP: dense, or mixture of experts (2017, Switch Transformers 2021).
  • Shape: hidden dimension, depth, number of heads, number of experts.

Training. Loss (multi-token prediction, 2024); optimizer (Adam, 2014; AdamW, 2017; SOAP, 2024; Muon, 2024); initialization (Xavier, 2010; muP, 2022); learning-rate schedule (cosine, 2017; WSD, 2024); regularization (dropout, weight decay); batch size (critical batch size, 2018); MoE load balancing (aux-free, 2024).

Assignment 1: implement the BPE tokenizer, Transformer, cross-entropy loss, AdamW and the training loop, and do resource accounting. Train on TinyStories and OpenWebText. The leaderboard minimizes OpenWebText perplexity given 45 minutes on a B200.

The principle behind all of it balances three things: expressivity (represent complex dependencies), stability (keep parameter and gradient norms in a goldilocks zone), and efficiency (runs fast, both training and inference).

Goal: squeeze the most out of the hardware (GPU or TPU). Components: kernels, parallelism, inference.

Resource accounting. The lecture's first worked number: training a 70B model on 1T tokens costs 6 * 70e9 * 1e12 = 4.2e23 FLOPs. Parameters must move from HBM to the SMs, and the B200 example is 2.25 PFLOP/s (bf16) against 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. Roofline analysis says whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound. Profiling (nsight) shows what happens in practice. The calculator in the next section reproduces these numbers.

Kernels. A kernel is a function that runs on the GPU. PyTorch launches one standard kernel per primitive op. Custom kernels can fuse work. The principle is to minimize data movement: a naive sequence reads and writes HBM after each op, while a fused kernel reads once and writes once. Strategies include operator fusion (matmul + activation) and tiling (FlashAttention). The source lists low-level concerns such as warp divergence, memory coalescing, bank conflicts, occupancy and asynchronous bulk transfers. You can write kernels in CUDA, Triton, CUTLASS, or ThunderKittens.

Parallelism. With 1024 GPUs, inter-GPU data movement is even slower, but the same principle holds. Use collectives (gather, reduce, all-reduce). Shard parameters, activations, gradients and optimizer states. Split computation as data, tensor, pipeline, sequence or expert parallelism.

Inference. Two phases. Prefill processes known tokens all at once and is compute-bound, like training. Decode produces one token at a time and is memory-bound. Ways to speed decoding: a cheaper model (pruning, quantization, distillation), speculative decoding (a cheap draft model proposes tokens that the full model scores in parallel, exact in distribution), and systems tricks (fused kernels, continuous batching).

Assignment 2: implement a fused RMSNorm kernel in Triton, distributed data parallel training, and optimizer state sharding, then benchmark and profile. Recommended reading: How to Scale Your Model (Google, TPU-focused, same concepts).

Setting. Suppose you have 1e25 FLOPs. Which hyperparameters give a good model? Hyperparameter tuning at full scale is too expensive.

Key shift. Think of a scaling recipe: a map from FLOPs to hyperparameters. Run experiments at smaller scales (up to 1e24 FLOPs), fit a scaling law, and predict the loss at the target scale (1e25) before running it. This lets you optimize the recipe using small experiments, and predict the loss in advance. Scaling laws do not happen automatically; they need a carefully constructed recipe. Parameterize the model to get hyperparameter transfer (muP). The source's slogan: predictability is at least as important as optimality.

Question. Given a budget C = 6 N D, should you use a bigger model (N) or more tokens (D)? Classic answers: Kaplan et al. 2020 and Chinchilla 2022, using ISOFLOP curves (for several small budgets, find the optimal N, then fit a law to extrapolate). The TL;DR: D ≈ 20 N, so a 70B model should see about 1.4T tokens. The caveat is that this ignores inference cost, which favors a smaller model.

The source also shows a live example from Marin, where a preregistered loss prediction was to be checked against the finished run (post).

Assignment 3: you define a training API (hyperparameters to loss) based on previous runs, submit training jobs under a FLOPs budget, fit scaling laws to the data points, then submit extrapolated hyperparameters and loss predictions. The leaderboard minimizes loss given a FLOPs budget.

Start with the question: what capabilities should the model have? Multilingual? Good at conversation? Agentic coding?

Evaluation. Internal evaluations guide development (smoothness across scales; relative performance matters). External evaluations measure absolute quality on a real use case (ecological validity matters). Examples: perplexity on private documents not on the Internet (to avoid contamination), and advanced benchmarks such as GPQA, HLE, SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench. LMs are general-purpose, so they need a diverse set of evaluations.

Data curation. Data does not fall from the sky. Sources include crawled webpages, books, arXiv papers and GitHub code. Legal questions remain (fair-use arguments, arXiv 2303.15715; licensing deals such as Google with Reddit). Raw data is HTML, PDF and directories, not text.

Data processing. Transformation (HTML/PDF to text, extracting main content); filtering (classifiers that keep quality data and remove harmful content); deduplication (saves compute and avoids memorization, via Bloom filters or MinHash); data mixing (how much to up- or down-weight each source; RegMix, Olmix); rewriting and synthetic data (WRAP).

Types of data. Pretraining (large and diverse), mid-training (high quality, includes long context), post-training (supervised fine-tuning on conversations and agentic tool-use traces).

Assignment 4: convert Common Crawl HTML to text; train classifiers for quality and harmful content; MinHash deduplication. The leaderboard minimizes perplexity given a token budget.

So far the model is trained on full supervision (predict the next token). Once the model is reasonable, it can improve from weak supervision. That is most useful when it is easier to critique than to generate.

Basic template. (1) Generate responses. (2) Score them with a human, a verifier, or an LM judge. (3) Update the model to prefer the better responses.

  • PPO from reinforcement learning (2017), used for InstructGPT (2022).
  • DPO, for preference data, simpler (2023).
  • GRPO, which removes the value function (DeepSeekMath, 2024).

Challenges. RL algorithms are unstable and hard to tune. At scale they need new infrastructure (async rollouts). You constantly trade off systems efficiency against on-policyness.

Assignment 5: implement DPO and GRPO.

The efficiency thread

The remark that ties the syllabus together: remember it's all about efficiency. Resources are data plus hardware (compute, memory, communication bandwidth). The question is how to train the best model for a fixed set of resources. Today we are compute-constrained, so design decisions squeeze the most out of given hardware. Tokenization is one example of the trade-off: working with raw bytes is elegant but compute-inefficient with current architectures. Tomorrow we will become data-constrained.

Tokenization: the atoms of the model

This unit was inspired by Andrej Karpathy's video on tokenization. The question is: what are the atoms the model operates on?

Formally, a tokenizer converts between raw inputs (bytes or Unicode strings) and sequences of integers (tokens). The source defines an abstract interface:

class Tokenizer(ABC):
    """Abstract interface for a tokenizer."""
    def encode(self, string: str) -> list[int]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def decode(self, indices: list[int]) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

Tokenization examples

The source suggests trying an interactive tokenizer. Observations:

  • A word and its preceding space form one token (e.g., " world").
  • The same word is tokenized differently at the start versus the middle of text ("hello hello").
  • Numbers are split into chunks of a few digits.

The source then loads OpenAI's tokenizer through tiktoken (o200k_base, called the GPT-5 tokenizer in the source), round-trips a test string, and reports the compression ratio.

def get_gpt5_tokenizer():
    # Code: https://github.com/openai/tiktoken
    return tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")

tokenizer = get_gpt5_tokenizer()
string = "Hello, 🌍! 你好!"
indices = tokenizer.encode(string)
reconstructed_string = tokenizer.decode(indices)
assert string == reconstructed_string

compression_ratio = get_compression_ratio(string, indices)   # 2.5 bytes per token
vocabulary_size = tokenizer.n_vocab                          # 200019

Measured on this string: 20 UTF-8 bytes become 8 tokens, a compression ratio of 20 / 8 = 2.5. The vocabulary has 200,019 entries. The source notes that the ratio grows with vocabulary size (more possible tokens means each token can cover more text), but a bigger vocabulary makes the embedding and output matrices sparser.

Compression ratio

\[ \text{compression ratio} = \frac{\#\text{UTF-8 bytes}}{\#\text{tokens}} \]

A larger ratio means a shorter sequence, which is good because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length.

def get_compression_ratio(string: str, indices: list[int]) -> float:
    """Given `string` that has been tokenized into `indices`, return the number of UTF-8 bytes per token."""
    num_bytes = len(bytes(string, encoding="utf-8"))
    num_tokens = len(indices)
    return num_bytes / num_tokens

Character tokenizer

A Unicode string is a sequence of characters. Each character maps to a code point (an integer) via ord, and back via chr. The source checks: ord("a") == 97, ord("🌍") == 127757, chr(127757) == "🌍".

class CharacterTokenizer(Tokenizer):
    """Represent a string as a sequence of Unicode code points."""
    def encode(self, string: str) -> list[int]:
        return list(map(ord, string))

    def decode(self, indices: list[int]) -> str:
        return "".join(map(chr, indices))

On "Hello, 🌍! 你好!" this gives 13 tokens (one per character). The vocabulary is at least max(indices) + 1 = 127758 (the source calls this a lower bound). The source's two problems:

  1. The vocabulary is very large (there are roughly 150K Unicode characters).
  2. Many characters are rare (like 🌍), which wastes vocabulary.

The compression ratio is 20 / 13 = 1.54. The source's verdict: the worst of both worlds (large vocabulary, low compression).

Byte tokenizer

Unicode strings can be represented as bytes, integers from 0 to 255, via UTF-8. A character like a takes one byte. Others take several: bytes("🌍", encoding="utf-8") == b"\xf0\x9f\x8c\x8d".

class ByteTokenizer(Tokenizer):
    """Represent a string as a sequence of bytes."""
    def encode(self, string: str) -> list[int]:
        string_bytes = string.encode("utf-8")
        indices = list(map(int, string_bytes))
        return indices

    def decode(self, indices: list[int]) -> str:
        string_bytes = bytes(indices)
        string = string_bytes.decode("utf-8")
        return string

The vocabulary is nice and small: 256 values. But the compression ratio is exactly 1, so sequences are far too long. Since a Transformer's context is limited and attention is quadratic, this "is not looking great".

Why bytes are not enough

The encoding is lossless and tiny, but it spends one attention position per byte. That makes long text expensive. The next section and the BPE section are about spending positions more efficiently.

Word tokenizer

The classical NLP approach splits strings into words. A regular expression keeps alphanumeric characters together:

import regex

string = "I'll say supercalifragilisticexpialidocious!"
chunks = regex.findall(r"\w+|.", string)
# ['I', "'", 'll', ' ', 'say', ' ', 'supercalifragilisticexpialidocious', '!']
compression_ratio = get_compression_ratio(string, chunks)   # 44 bytes / 8 chunks = 5.5

The good news: each token is meaningful, since humans invented words, and the compression ratio is high. The bad news is the vocabulary: it is the set of distinct chunks in the training data, which can be huge. Moreover:

  • Many words are rare, so the model learns little about them.
  • It has no fixed vocabulary size.
  • Unseen words need an UNK token. That is ugly and distorts perplexity.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE)

BPE was introduced by Philip Gage in 1994 as a data-compression algorithm. It was adapted to NLP for neural machine translation by Sennrich et al. (2016), and GPT-2 used it (2019). Before this, papers used word-based tokenization.

Idea. Train the tokenizer on raw text to build a vocabulary suited to the data. Common byte sequences become one token; rare ones take many. Sketch: start with each byte as a token, then repeatedly merge the most common adjacent pair.

The source gives the original 1994 reference: Gage's article.

Training: the merge loop, in full

The source's merge helper replaces every non-overlapping occurrence of a pair, scanning left to right:

def merge(indices: list[int], pair: tuple[int, int], new_index: int) -> list[int]:
    """Return `indices`, but with all instances of `pair` replaced with `new_index`."""
    new_indices = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(indices):
        if i + 1 < len(indices) and indices[i] == pair[0] and indices[i + 1] == pair[1]:
            new_indices.append(new_index)
            i += 2
        else:
            new_indices.append(indices[i])
            i += 1
    return new_indices

The trainer counts adjacent pairs, picks the most frequent one, merges it, and repeats:

def train_bpe(string: str, num_merges: int) -> BPETokenizerParams:
    indices = list(map(int, string.encode("utf-8")))
    merges: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}          # index1, index2 => merged index
    vocab: dict[int, bytes] = {x: bytes([x]) for x in range(256)}  # index -> bytes

    for i in range(num_merges):
        # Count the number of occurrences of each pair of tokens
        counts = count_adjacent_pairs(indices)
        # Find the most common pair
        pair = max(counts, key=counts.get)
        # Merge that pair
        new_index = 256 + i
        merges[pair] = new_index
        vocab[new_index] = vocab[pair[0]] + vocab[pair[1]]
        indices = merge(indices, pair, new_index)

    compression_ratio = get_compression_ratio(string, indices)
    return BPETokenizerParams(vocab=vocab, merges=merges)

def count_adjacent_pairs(indices: list[int]) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    """Return a dictionary mapping each adjacent pair of tokens in `indices` to the number of times it occurs."""
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    for index1, index2 in zip(indices, indices[1:]):
        counts[(index1, index2)] += 1
    return counts

Two details matter for the walkthrough below. First, max(counts, key=counts.get) returns the first maximal key in dict insertion order, so ties go to the pair that appears earliest in the text. Second, the code merges all non-overlapping occurrences of the chosen pair in one pass.

Interactive: BPE training trace on "the cat in the hat"

Use the stepper below. Each step shows the real token sequence, the top adjacent pairs with their counts, and the pair merged. The last step encodes "the quick brown fox" with the three learned merges. The trace is computed in the widget from the same algorithm as the source's train_bpe, with the same tie-breaking.

Using the tokenizer

Given new text, encode applies the learned merges. The source's BPETokenizer stores the vocabulary (index to bytes) and the merges (pair to new index). Its encode loops over all merges in the order they were learned. The source notes this is slow and is an exercise for Assignment 1.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BPETokenizerParams:
    """All you need to specify a BPETokenizer."""
    vocab: dict[int, bytes]              # index -> bytes
    merges: dict[tuple[int, int], int]   # index1,index2 -> new_index

class BPETokenizer(Tokenizer):
    """BPE tokenizer given a set of merges and a vocabulary."""
    def __init__(self, params: BPETokenizerParams):
        self.params = params

    def encode(self, string: str) -> list[int]:
        indices = list(map(int, string.encode("utf-8")))
        # Note: this is a very slow implementation
        for pair, new_index in self.params.merges.items():
            indices = merge(indices, pair, new_index)
        return indices

    def decode(self, indices: list[int]) -> str:
        bytes_list = list(map(self.params.vocab.get, indices))
        string = b"".join(bytes_list).decode("utf-8")
        return string

Decoding is the easy direction: look up each id's bytes, concatenate, then decode UTF-8 once at the end. This is why decoding the whole sequence is safe even though a single token may hold a partial character in other tokenizers.

Playground: BPE with a merge budget

Pick a string and the number of merges k. The widget trains BPE on that string (the same loop as train_bpe), keeps the first k merges, and encodes the string. The chart shows how the token count falls as merges are added.

Things to try in the playground

Set the string to the cat in the hat and step the merges from 0 to 3. Token counts fall 18, 16, 14, 12, matching the stepper. Then switch to the emoji string. It has 20 bytes, and the early merges only compress its ASCII part.

Compression on real tokenizers

The same measure, bytes per token, on a range of strings. These counts come from running tiktoken with the gpt2, cl100k_base and o200k_base encodings on the strings shown. Treat the exact values as measurements from one tiktoken install, since tokenizer releases can change them.

A few lessons from the table. The English sentence compresses well in every encoding because common words are single tokens. Non-Latin scripts depend heavily on vocabulary size: the 200K encoding gives Hindi 6.9 bytes per token, while GPT-2's 50K vocabulary falls back to byte fragments (many tokens are invalid UTF-8 halves). That is the "sparsity" trade-off the source mentions.

Vocabulary size vs. sequence length: the trade-off

The source's efficiency lens: a larger compression ratio shortens sequences (1000 bytes become about 250 tokens at ratio 4), which saves attention compute. The price is a larger vocabulary, which grows the embedding and output layers. The calculator below treats this as a formula. Its defaults are the source's numbers: 1000 bytes, o200k's 200,019 vocabulary, and a width of 4096.

Tokenizer-free alternatives: the dream

The dream is architectures that operate directly on bytes and skip the tokenizer entirely. The source cites several attempts, none yet scaled to the frontier:

  • ByT5 (2021): a byte-level variant of T5.
  • MEGABYTE (2023): a multiscale model that splits bytes into patches.
  • BLT (2024): byte latent Transformer, with dynamically sized patches.
  • T-FREE (2024): tokenizer-free embeddings.
  • H-Net (2025): hierarchical networks that learn chunk boundaries.

The source's summary wants any solution to satisfy two properties: (1) the model operates on chunks (abstractions) of the sequence, whether text, video or DNA; and (2) the chunks are variable, so more capacity can go to interesting parts of the input. BPE is an effective data-driven heuristic that meets neither property perfectly, which is why tokenization is still a separate step.

Unit summary

Key takeaways
  • A tokenizer converts between strings and integer sequences. The model only sees the integers.
  • Character tokenization has a huge vocabulary and low compression. Byte tokenization has a tiny vocabulary (256) but compression ratio 1, so sequences are too long.
  • Word tokenization gives meaningful tokens but a huge, open-ended vocabulary with UNKs.
  • BPE trains on data: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair. Ties go to the earliest pair. It balances vocabulary and compression.
  • Compression ratio (bytes per token) sets sequence length, which sets attention cost. Vocabulary size sets the embedding cost. The trade-off is explicit.
  • Tokenizer-free models (ByT5, MEGABYTE, BLT, H-Net) are promising but not yet at the frontier.
  • Efficiency frames the whole course: maximize accuracy per unit of compute, and predict before you spend.

Compute, roofline and scale: the numbers in the syllabus

The syllabus preview quotes several numbers that the course returns to. The calculator and chart below reproduce them from formulas.

Roofline for a B200

A kernel's arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved from HBM. Attainable performance is min(peak, bandwidth × intensity). The source's numbers are 2.25 PFLOP/s (bf16) and 8 TB/s. The ridge point is 2.25e15 / 8e12 = 281.25 FLOP per byte. Below it a kernel is memory-bound (decode is an example); above it, compute-bound (prefill is an example).

Kernel fusion: two memory traffic patterns

The source's principle: organize computation to minimize data movement. Compare the two sequences below, one per row. Each arrow is an HBM transfer or a compute step.

Why does the stepper say the first merge is (t, h) rather than (h, e) or (a, t), since all three occur twice?
All of them tie at count 2. The source's max(counts, key=counts.get) returns the first maximal key in dict insertion order. Scanning "the cat in the hat" from left to right, the pair (t, h) appears first, so it wins. The JS widget uses the same rule with a Map, which keeps insertion order too.
Compute the compression ratio for "the cat in the hat" after 3 merges.
The string is 18 bytes. After 3 merges it has 12 tokens (ids 258, 99, 97, 116, 32, 105, 110, 32, 258, 104, 97, 116). So the ratio is 18 / 12 = 1.5 bytes per token.
Why is the byte tokenizer's compression ratio exactly 1, and why does that matter?
Each token is one UTF-8 byte, so the number of tokens equals the number of bytes, and the ratio is 1 for any input. Attention cost grows with the square of the sequence length, so a ratio of 1 makes long inputs expensive. BPE raises the ratio by spending a larger vocabulary on common byte sequences.
Why does the GPT-2 tokenizer need several tokens for the globe emoji 🌍, and why does o200k do better on Hindi?
🌍 is four UTF-8 bytes (f0 9f 8c 8d). GPT-2's vocabulary has no merge that covers the whole character, so the bytes become several partial tokens (the tiktoken output shows pieces like ' �'). The o200k vocabulary is about four times larger and includes many non-Latin sequences, so Hindi and Chinese compress to 6.9 and 4.3 bytes per token.
Using the source's 1000 bytes at ratio 4, how much attention work does ratio 8 save?
Ratio 4 gives 250 tokens, so attention is proportional to 250² = 62,500. Ratio 8 gives 125 tokens, so attention is 125² = 15,625. That is 1/4 of the work. Attention cost falls as 1/r², so doubling the ratio quarters the cost.
What is the B200 ridge point, and what does it imply for prefill versus decode?
The ridge is 2.25e15 / 8e12 = 281.25 FLOP per byte. A kernel with intensity below this is memory-bound (its speed is limited by bandwidth), and one above it is compute-bound. Prefill processes many tokens at once, so its intensity is high and it is compute-bound. Decode produces one token per step and reads the weights each time, so it is memory-bound.
Reproduce the source's 4.2e23 FLOPs and the Chinchilla token count for a 70B model.
C = 6 · 70e9 · 1e12 = 4.2e23 FLOPs. The Chinchilla rule gives D ≈ 20 · 70e9 = 1.4e12, which is 1.4T tokens. The source's caveat is that this ignores inference cost, which favors a smaller model trained on more data.

Resource accounting: tensors, precision, FLOPs, memory

lecture_02.py PyTorch einops dtypes FLOPs MFU roofline AdamW checkpointing
TL;DR. Everything in deep learning is an operation on tensors: data, parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations. Efficiency means knowing before running anything how many bytes and how many FLOPs a computation costs. Key numbers: a training step costs \(6\,N\,D\) FLOPs for \(N\) parameters and \(D\) data points; mixed-precision AdamW needs \(2+2+4+4=12\) bytes per parameter before activations; matrix multiplies are compute-bound while elementwise ops and matrix-vector products are memory-bound, judged against the H100 ridge point of about 295 FLOP/byte; gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing trade time for memory.

Where we are, and the napkin-math mindset

Lecture 1 was the overview and tokenization. Lecture 2 is the systems prerequisite. The guiding question is: given fixed resources (compute and memory), what is the best model one can train? That is a question about efficiency, so we first have to be able to account for the resources a computation consumes.

The lecture states three take-aways for itself:

Mechanics

Two motivating questions

Both questions are answered on the back of an envelope using the formulas this lecture builds toward.

def motivating_questions():
    # Q1: How long to train a 70B model on 15T tokens on 1024 H100s?
    total_flops = 6 * 70e9 * 15e12                  # 6.3e24 FLOPs
    h100_flop_per_sec = 1979e12 / 2                 # 989.5e12 dense bf16 (1979e12 is with sparsity)
    mfu = 0.5
    flops_per_day = h100_flop_per_sec * mfu * 1024 * 60 * 60 * 24   # 4.377e22 FLOPs/day
    days = total_flops / flops_per_day              # ~143.9 days

    # Q2: Largest model you can train on 8 H100s with AdamW?
    h100_bytes = 80e9
    bytes_per_parameter = 2 + 2 + (4 + 4)           # params (bf16) 2, grads (bf16) 2, optimizer state (fp32 m and v) 8
    num_parameters = (h100_bytes * 8) / bytes_per_parameter   # ~5.33e10 = 53.3B (activations ignored: upper bound)

Q1 as a calculator: training time = 6ND / (peak × MFU × GPUs)

The first answer comes from three multiplicative factors. Change any slider to see how the answer moves; the chart shows how the time falls as you add GPUs at the same MFU.

Defaults (70B parameters, 15T tokens, 1024 H100s, MFU 0.5) reproduce the lecture: \(6.3\times10^{24}\) FLOPs at \(4.377\times10^{22}\) FLOPs per day gives about 144 days. MFU (model FLOPs utilization, defined later) enters multiplicatively. At MFU 0.25 the run takes twice as long.

Q2 as a calculator: how large a model fits?

The bound is \(N_\max = \dfrac{\#\text{GPUs}\times\text{memory per GPU}}{\text{bytes per parameter}}\). It ignores activations, which depend on batch size and sequence length, so the result is an upper bound. The bytes per parameter depend on the dtypes and the optimizer, which you can change below.

With the lecture's defaults (8 × 80 GB, bf16 parameters and gradients, AdamW state): \(80\text{ GB}\times 8 / 12 \approx 53.3\)B parameters. The lecture's own caveat is that activations are not included, so 53B is a ceiling. The lecture calls this "a rough back-of-the-envelope calculation, but it gives you the flavor of napkin math".

Tensors and their memory

Tensors store data, parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations. The lecture's example is the parameter set of DeepSeek-V3.2 (paper; the safetensors index on Hugging Face maps every parameter tensor to the file that stores it). A tensor's rank is its number of dimensions:

x = torch.zeros(4)          # rank 1: vector
x = torch.zeros(4, 8)       # rank 2: matrix
x = torch.zeros(4, 8, 2)    # rank 3
# In Transformers you see rank 4: (batch, sequence, heads, dim per head)
B, S, H, D = 32, 16, 16, 64
x = torch.zeros(B, S, H, D)

Memory = number of values × bytes per value

Memory is determined by the number of values and by the data type of each value. The lecture checks this with assertions:

x = torch.zeros(4, 8)                          # @inspect x
assert x.dtype == torch.float32                # default dtype
assert x.numel() == 4 * 8                      # 32 values
assert x.element_size() == 4                   # fp32 is 4 bytes
assert get_memory_usage(x) == 4 * 8 * 4        # 128 bytes  (numel * element_size)

# One feedforward matrix of GPT-3 (d_model = 12288, d_ff = 4 * 12288):
assert get_memory_usage(torch.empty(12288 * 4, 12288)) == 2304 * 1024 * 1024   # shown as "2.3 GB"

The GPT-3 check is 2304 MiB, which is \(2.416\times10^9\) bytes, or 2.25 GiB. The lecture's "2.3 GB" is that number rounded.

At the default shape there are \(32\cdot16\cdot16\cdot64 = 524\,288\) values, which is 2 MiB in fp32. Halving the bit width halves both the memory and the bandwidth needed to move the tensor, which is why precision is the first lever.

CPU memory vs GPU memory

Tensors are stored in CPU memory by default. A GPU has its own DRAM and many streaming multiprocessors, and the PCI bus between CPU and GPU is slow. The rule is to move data to the GPU once and keep it there.

x = torch.zeros(32, 32)
assert x.device == torch.device("cpu")   # default: CPU memory
device = cuda_if_available()
x = x.to(device)                         # copy to GPU memory (crosses the PCI bus)

with torch.device(device):               # or create the tensor directly on the GPU
    x = torch.zeros(32, 32)
    assert x.device == device

Floating-point formats: fp32, fp16, bf16, fp8, fp4

A floating-point number stores a sign bit \(s\), an exponent field \(E\) (with \(e\) bits and a bias), and a mantissa (fraction) field \(M\) (with \(m\) bits). For a normal number

\[ x = (-1)^{s}\cdot 2^{E-\text{bias}}\cdot\Bigl(1+\frac{M}{2^{m}}\Bigr). \]

When \(E=0\) the number is subnormal: \(x=(-1)^{s}\cdot 2^{1-\text{bias}}\cdot\frac{M}{2^{m}}\). The main idea is that exponent bits buy dynamic range, and mantissa bits buy precision.

Interactive: bit-layout explorer

Pick a format, then click any bit to flip it and watch the decoded value change. Or type a number and see how it is rounded in each format. The table encodes the same number in every format, so you can see underflow (\(10^{-8}\) is 0 in fp16 but not in bf16) and overflow (70000 is infinity in fp16).

Dynamic range and resolution

Two charts make the trade-off concrete. The first is the largest finite value and the smallest normal and subnormal values of each format. Those three numbers are computed from the bit layouts. The second is the spacing between adjacent representable numbers (the unit in the last place, ULP) as a function of magnitude. The spacing is \(2^{\lfloor\log_2 |x|\rfloor - m}\), so it is set by the mantissa width.

formatbits (s / e / m)biasmax finitemin normalmin subnormalmachine epsilon 2-mH100 peak in the lecture's code
fp321 / 8 / 231273.4 × 10381.2 × 10-381.4 × 10-451.2 × 10-767.5 TFLOP/s
fp161 / 5 / 1015655046.1 × 10-56.0 × 10-89.8 × 10-4989.5 TFLOP/s (dense)
bf161 / 8 / 71273.4 × 10381.2 × 10-389.2 × 10-417.8 × 10-3989.5 TFLOP/s (dense)

The H100 column uses the numbers hard-coded in the lecture's get_promised_flop_per_sec. The fp8 values are not in the lecture's code; the table gives them only for comparison with the bit layouts. fp32, fp16 and fp8 E5M2 follow IEEE-style conventions (with infinities). fp8 E4M3 follows the OCP FP8 variant, which has no infinities. bf16 is Google's format.

Underflow in code

x = torch.zeros(4, 8, dtype=torch.float16)
assert x.element_size() == 2                 # half the memory of fp32

x = torch.tensor([1e-8], dtype=torch.float16)
assert x == 0                                # underflow: 1e-8 is below the smallest fp16 subnormal (~6e-8)

x = torch.tensor([1e-8], dtype=torch.bfloat16)
assert x != 0                                # no underflow: bf16 has fp32's 8-bit exponent
Why underflow matters

Small gradients or activations that flush to zero silently remove learning signal, and the resulting instability is hard to debug. fp16 training therefore usually needs loss scaling. bf16 has enough range that it usually does not. The price is precision: bf16 keeps 7 explicit mantissa bits, so \(\varepsilon = 2^{-7} \approx 0.8\%\), while fp16 keeps \(2^{-10} \approx 0.1\%\).

Mixed precision, fp8 and fp4

The implications for training:

  • Training everything in fp32 works but needs a lot of memory (and gives low throughput).
  • Training everything in fp16, or even bf16, is risky: you can get instability.

The standard answer is mixed precision training (Micikevicius et al., 2017). The lecture's version of the recipe:

Low precision (bf16)

Parameters, activations and gradients. These dominate the matmuls and the memory traffic.

High precision (fp32)

Optimizer states. They accumulate averages over powers of many steps, so rounding error would build up.

PyTorch has an automatic mixed precision library (AMP docs). It casts to bf16 where that is safe (matmuls) and leaves other ops (such as exp) in higher precision:

with torch.amp.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    x = torch.zeros(4, 8)       # ops inside the context run in bf16 where safe
Two accounting conventions

The lecture counts 2 bytes for parameters, 2 for gradients and 4+4 for Adam state, a total of 12 bytes per parameter. The original Micikevicius recipe also keeps an fp32 master copy of the weights (another 4 bytes) so that small updates are not lost when added to bf16/fp16 weights. The lecture does not include this term; the Q2 calculator above lets you add it.

fp8

In 2022 fp8 was standardized, motivated by machine-learning workloads (NVIDIA Transformer Engine fp8 primer; reference paper FP8 Formats for Deep Learning, 2022). The H100 supports two variants:

  • E4M3: 4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits, range \([-448, 448]\). More precision, less range.
  • E5M2: 5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits, range \([-57344, 57344]\). More range, less precision.

The lecture shows the NVIDIA figure of these two formats; it is a remote image, so use the explorer above (select fp8 E4M3 or fp8 E5M2) to see the bit layouts. E4M3 reaches its 448 maximum because it has no infinities: the all-ones exponent is used for ordinary values, and only the all-ones pattern is NaN.

fp4 (NVFP4)

In 2025 NVIDIA developed NVFP4: only 4 bits per value. The representable values are \(\{\pm6,\pm4,\pm3,\pm2,\pm1.5,\pm1.0,\pm0.5, 0\}\) (the lecture lists them; that is the E2M1 grid). To get more dynamic range, each block of values has a separate scale factor, so values within a block cannot vary freely from their neighbors but different blocks can sit at very different magnitudes. Nemotron 3 Super was trained in NVFP4 (technical report, 2026). The lecture notes that some of this is done inside NVIDIA libraries outside the user's control.

With one scale for the whole tensor, a 4-bit grid cannot cover both tiny and huge numbers. With a scale per block, the same 15 values cover whatever magnitude that block has. (The real NVFP4 stores the scale in fp8 with additional tensor-level scaling; this widget is a simplified illustration of the principle, not the NVFP4 specification.)

Einops and einsum

Traditional PyTorch code makes it easy to mess up dimensions. What does transpose(-2, -1) do to which axis?

x = torch.ones(2, 2, 3)      # batch seq hidden
y = torch.ones(2, 2, 3)      # batch seq hidden
z = x @ y.transpose(-2, -1)  # batch seq seq ... but what are -2, -1?

Einops is a library for manipulating tensors with named dimensions. It is inspired by Einstein summation notation (Einstein, 1916).

einsum: generalized matmul with bookkeeping

x = torch.ones(3, 4)    # seq1 hidden
y = torch.ones(4, 3)    # hidden seq2
z = x @ y                                                       # old way
z = einsum(x, y, "seq1 hidden, hidden seq2 -> seq1 seq2")       # einops way

x = torch.ones(2, 3, 4) # batch seq1 hidden
y = torch.ones(2, 3, 4) # batch seq2 hidden
z = x @ y.transpose(-2, -1)                                                          # old way
z = einsum(x, y, "batch seq1 hidden, batch seq2 hidden -> batch seq1 seq2")          # new way
# Dimensions not named in the output are summed over.
z = einsum(x, y, "... seq1 hidden, ... seq2 hidden -> ... seq1 seq2")                 # '...' broadcasts over any leading dims

Because the inputs are all ones, every entry of z here equals hidden = 4. The rule is simple: any index that appears in the inputs but not in the output is summed over, and indices appearing in several inputs are multiplied elementwise.

The last three specs in the walk-through are exactly the forward, input-gradient and weight-gradient matmuls used later in the backward-pass accounting. They all have the same cost \(2BDD\).

reduce

Reduce one tensor along some dims with sum, mean, max, min.

x = torch.ones(2, 3, 4)                        # batch seq hidden
y = x.sum(dim=-1)                              # old way (which dim is -1?)
y = reduce(x, "... hidden -> ...", "sum")      # einops way; result is a (2, 3) tensor of 4s

rearrange: split and merge dimensions

Sometimes one dimension is really two (for instance total_hidden = heads × hidden1) and you want to operate on one of them. Split with parentheses on the input side, merge with parentheses on the output side:

x = torch.ones(3, 8)    # seq total_hidden, where total_hidden = heads * hidden1
w = torch.ones(4, 4)    # hidden1 hidden2

# Break total_hidden into (heads, hidden1)
x = rearrange(x, "... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden1", heads=2)       # (3, 2, 4)
# Apply w to the hidden1 axis, independently per head
x = einsum(x, w, "... hidden1, hidden1 hidden2 -> ... hidden2")             # (3, 2, 4)
# Merge heads and hidden2 back together
x = rearrange(x, "... heads hidden2 -> ... (heads hidden2)")                # (3, 8)

FLOPs, FLOP/s and MFU

A floating-point operation (FLOP) is a basic operation such as an addition \(x+y\) or a multiplication \(x\cdot y\). Two terribly confusing acronyms that are pronounced the same:

  • FLOPs: floating-point operations, a measure of the amount of computation done.
  • FLOP/s (also written FLOPS): floating-point operations per second, a measure of hardware speed.

Intuitions about scale

at peak dense rate
h100_flop_per_sec = 1979e12 / 2                          # dense: half of the with-sparsity number
total_flops = 8 * 2 * (60 * 60 * 24 * 7) * h100_flop_per_sec    # 8 GPUs x 2 weeks x peak = 9.575e21

So 8 H100s running at 100% for two weeks do \(9.6\times10^{21}\) FLOPs, which is only 3% of GPT-3's budget. Training GPT-3 on a single such node would need over a year even at perfect efficiency. The H100 peak numbers are from the NVIDIA tensor-core datasheet (and the H100 datasheet).

A linear model: counting the FLOPs of a matmul

B, D, K = 16384, 32768, 8192            # points, input dim, outputs (the GPU branch; CPU fallback is 1024, 256, 64)
x = torch.ones(B, D, device=cuda_if_available())
w = torch.randn(D, K, device=cuda_if_available())
y = x @ w

For each \((i,j,k)\) triple there is one multiplication x[i][j] * w[j][k] and one addition into y[i][k]. Hence

\[ \text{FLOPs}(x\,w)=2\,B\,D\,K .\]

actual_num_flops = 2 * B * D * K                          # 2 * 16384 * 32768 * 8192 = 8.796e12  (= 2^43)
actual_time = benchmark(lambda: x @ w)                    # seconds, averaged over 5 trials, with cuda synchronize
actual_flop_per_sec = actual_num_flops / actual_time
promised_flop_per_sec = get_promised_flop_per_sec(x.dtype)   # depends on GPU and on dtype
mfu = actual_flop_per_sec / promised_flop_per_sec

The numbers measured in class depend on the GPU used, so they are not hard-coded here; the formulas are what to remember. At the GPU defaults the matmul is \(2^{43}\approx8.8\times10^{12}\) FLOPs, which an H100 at 100% of dense bf16 peak would finish in about 8.9 ms (in fp32 with the 67.5 TFLOP/s peak, about 130 ms). Benchmark note: torch.cuda.synchronize() before and after is essential because CUDA kernels launch asynchronously.

Model FLOPs utilization (MFU)

\[ \text{MFU}=\frac{\text{actual FLOP/s}}{\text{promised FLOP/s}}\quad(\text{ignoring communication and overhead}). \]

The lecture's rule of thumb: MFU of at least 0.5 is quite good. The promised numbers depend heavily on dtype, and the lecture's table is:

GPUfp32bf16 / fp16 (dense)bf16 (as quoted, with sparsity)
A10019.5 TFLOP/s312 TFLOP/s(n/a)
H10067.5 TFLOP/s989.5 TFLOP/s1979 TFLOP/s
B20075 TFLOP/s2250 TFLOP/s4500 TFLOP/s

Why is MFU not closer to 1? To answer that you have to look at how computation is actually done on a GPU: data has to move from memory to the compute units and back. That is the next section.

Arithmetic intensity and the roofline

How long does a computation take? The lecture's procedure for any operation on an accelerator has three steps:

  1. Send inputs from memory to the accelerator.
  2. Perform the computation.
  3. Send outputs from the accelerator back to memory.

The time depends on two hardware speeds: the accelerator speed in FLOP/s, and the memory bandwidth in bytes/s. The lecture uses the H100 numbers from its facts.py:

h100_flop_per_sec = 1979e12 / 2      # half of the 1979 TFLOP/s "with sparsity" number, i.e. dense
h100_bytes_per_sec = 3.35e12         # memory bandwidth (bytes/s)
assert h100_flop_per_sec == 1979e12 / 2
assert h100_bytes_per_sec == 3.35e12

The rule

Assume communication and computation overlap perfectly. Then the time is the larger of the two:

\[ T = \max\!\Bigl(\underbrace{\frac{\text{bytes}}{\text{bytes/s}}}_{\text{communication}},\;\underbrace{\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{FLOP/s}}}_{\text{computation}}\Bigr). \]

  • Memory-bound: communication time > computation time.
  • Compute-bound: computation time > communication time.

Compare the two ratios directly. The accelerator intensity is the work the hardware can do per byte moved, and the arithmetic intensity is the work the computation does per byte moved:

\[ I_{\text{accel}}=\frac{\text{FLOP/s}}{\text{bytes/s}}=\frac{989.5\times10^{12}}{3.35\times10^{12}}\approx 295\ \text{FLOP/byte}, \qquad I_{\text{arith}}=\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes}}. \]

Memory-bound when \(I_{\text{arith}}\lt I_{\text{accel}}\); compute-bound otherwise. (Since both compare times, the two tests are equivalent.)

Worked examples from the lecture

Each of these is a function in the source with an assert that fixes the bound. Here is the code, condensed, with the accounting:

# ReLU on n = 2^20 bf16 values: read x, write y (bf16 = 2 bytes)
n = 1024 * 1024
bytes = (2 * n) + (2 * n)        # 4n bytes  (= 4,194,304)
flops = n                        # n comparisons
arithmetic_intensity = flops / bytes      # 1/4 FLOP/byte
assert arithmetic_intensity < h100_accelerator_intensity    # memory-bound

# GeLU: GELU(x) = 0.5 x (1 + tanh(sqrt(2/pi) (x + 0.044715 x^3)))
flops = 20 * n                   # an estimate: tanh can be approximated in various ways
arithmetic_intensity = flops / bytes      # 5 FLOP/byte; still memory-bound

# Dot product of two length-n bf16 vectors
bytes = (2 * n) + (2 * n) + 2    # read x, read w, write one scalar
flops = 2 * n - 1                # n multiplications, n-1 additions
arithmetic_intensity = flops / bytes      # ~1/2 FLOP/byte; memory-bound

# Matrix-vector product, n = 1024
bytes = (2 * n) + (2 * n * n) + (2 * n)   # x, w (n*n entries), y
flops = n * (2 * n - 1)                    # n dot products
arithmetic_intensity = flops / bytes       # ~1 FLOP/byte; memory-bound

# Matmul, n = 1024
bytes = (2 * n * n) + (2 * n * n) + (2 * n * n)   # read x, read w, write y: 6n^2 bytes
flops = n * n * (2 * n - 1)                        # n^2 dot products: ~2n^3 FLOPs
arithmetic_intensity = flops / bytes               # ~n/3 = 341 FLOP/byte; compute-bound
assert arithmetic_intensity > h100_accelerator_intensity

The matmul example reads its inputs once and writes once, so its intensity grows with \(n\) (about \(n/3\)). The vector operations do \(O(1)\) FLOPs per element and so stay memory-bound no matter how large they get.

The lecture ties this to MFU: for a given computation, the best achievable utilization is \(\text{MFU}=\min\bigl(1,\;I_{\text{arith}}/I_{\text{accel}}\bigr)\). A memory-bound operation therefore caps MFU at its intensity divided by about 295.

Why this matters for training vs. inference

Training multiplies large activation and gradient matrices, so its matmuls are compute-bound. Inference during decoding multiplies a matrix by a single vector (batch 1), so it is memory-bound: most of the time is spent reading weights. That is why inference is memory-bound, and why batching and quantization help.

The lecture's summary: matrix multiplications are compute-bound, elementwise operations are memory-bound, and in general we will find ourselves memory-bound. The question to ask is whether we can increase arithmetic intensity (for example by fusing operations so that data stays on-chip). Fusion is the subject of later lectures.

Gradients: forward and backward FLOPs

So far we have built tensors and pushed them through operations (the forward pass). Now we compute gradients (the backward pass). Start with a toy linear model with loss \(y = \tfrac12 (x\,w - 5)^2\):

x = torch.tensor([1., 2, 3])
w = torch.tensor([1., 1, 1], requires_grad=True)   # we want the gradient w.r.t. w
pred_y = x @ w                                     # forward: 1+2+3 = 6
loss = 0.5 * (pred_y - 5).pow(2)                   # 0.5 * 1 = 0.5

loss.backward()                                    # backward
assert torch.equal(w.grad, torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]))   # d loss/d w = (pred - 5) * x = 1 * x

PyTorch's autograd builds that gradient automatically. The rest of this section is about how many FLOPs that costs.

One layer, counted by hand

The lecture's model is a 2-layer linear network with \(B=1024\) points and dimension \(D=256\) (no nonlinearity; \(h_1 = xw_1\), \(h_2 = h_1 w_2\), loss = (mean of \(h_2\))²):

x  = torch.ones(B, D)
w1 = torch.randn(D, D, requires_grad=True)
w2 = torch.randn(D, D, requires_grad=True)

h1 = einsum(x, w1, "batch in, in out -> batch out")    # x @ w1
h2 = einsum(h1, w2, "batch in, in out -> batch out")   # h1 @ w2
loss = (h2.mean() - 0)**2                              # regress everything to 0 (arbitrary)
loss.backward()

Focus on the second layer, \(h_2 = h_1 w_2\). Forward: one matmul of shape \((B\times D)(D\times D)\), so

\[ \text{forward FLOPs} = 2\,B\,D\,D = 2\cdot1024\cdot256\cdot256 = 134\,217\,728 \approx 1.34\times10^{8}. \]

Backward needs two gradients: \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial h_1\) (to pass upstream) and \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2\) (the parameter gradient). The source checks both against autograd:

h1_grad = einsum(h2.grad, w2, "batch out, in out -> batch in")     # dL/dh1 = dL/dh2 @ w2^T
assert torch.allclose(h1.grad, h1_grad)

w2_grad = einsum(h2.grad, h1, "batch out, batch in -> in out")      # dL/dw2 = h1^T @ dL/dh2
assert torch.allclose(w2.grad, w2_grad)

num_backward_flops = (2 * B * D * D) + (2 * B * D * D)              # 2 matmuls of 2BDD each = 4BDD

So the backward pass costs \(4BDD\), twice the forward. Each matmul in backward has the same cost as the forward matmul.

All layers: the 2-4-6 rule

The same count applies to every parameter in an MLP. For \(N\) parameters and \(D_{\text{data}}\) data points (tokens in a Transformer):

  • Forward pass: \(2\,(\#\text{data points})(\#\text{parameters})\) FLOPs.
  • Backward pass: \(4\,(\#\text{data points})(\#\text{parameters})\) FLOPs.
  • Total: \(6\,(\#\text{data})(\#\text{parameters})\) FLOPs per training step.

The lecture says this is derived for MLPs, but it is also a good approximation for Transformers at short context lengths. (Context-length effects are the attention term, which this formula leaves out.)

At the lecture's defaults (\(B=1024\), \(D=256\), \(L=2\)): forward \(2\cdot1024\cdot256\cdot256\cdot2 = 2^{28}\), backward \(2^{29}\), total \(6BN = 6\cdot1024\cdot131072 = 805{,}306{,}368\). Those are the FLOPs of one step, not of one matmul.

A deep network to account for

The toy model used for the training accounting is a deep stack of linear layers with ReLU. Consider \(L\) layers of \(D\)-dimensional inputs, activations and outputs:

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(dim, dim) / math.sqrt(dim))
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x @ self.weight      # linear
        x = F.relu(x)            # activation
        return x

class DeepNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, num_layers):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block(dim) for i in range(num_layers)])
    def forward(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return x

D, L = 8, 3
model = DeepNetwork(dim=D, num_layers=L)
num_parameters = get_num_parameters(model)
assert num_parameters == (D * D) * L          # 192 for D=8, L=3: no biases

A Block has a single \(D\times D\) weight and no bias, so the parameter count is exactly \(LD^2\). The forward pass on a batch of \(B\) inputs is \(L\) matmuls of shape \((B\times D)(D\times D)\).

Optimizers and their memory

The lecture first walks up a ladder of optimizers, each one adding an idea to the previous:

  • SGD: step = \(-\eta\,g\).
  • Momentum = SGD plus exponential averaging of the gradient.
  • AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan, Singer, 2011) = SGD with each coordinate divided by the root of the accumulated squared gradients.
  • RMSProp = AdaGrad with exponential (rather than cumulative) averaging of \(g^2\).
  • Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) = RMSProp plus momentum.

The lecture implements AdaGrad by hand, to show exactly which state an optimizer keeps. The update is \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, g / \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{i\le t} g_i^2 + 10^{-5}}\):

class AdaGrad(torch.optim.Optimizer):
    def __init__(self, params, lr=0.01):
        super(AdaGrad, self).__init__(params, dict(lr=lr))

    def step(self):
        for group in self.param_groups:
            lr = group["lr"]
            for p in group["params"]:
                state = self.state[p]                    # optimizer state for this parameter
                grad = p.grad.data
                # Get squared gradients g2 = sum_{i<t} g_i^2
                g2 = state.get("g2", torch.zeros_like(grad))
                # Update optimizer state
                g2 += torch.square(grad)
                state["g2"] = g2
                # Update parameters
                p.data -= lr * grad / torch.sqrt(g2 + 1e-5)

The optimizer state is the extra memory. AdaGrad keeps one accumulator per parameter, the running sum of squared gradients (g2), so it needs one extra buffer of the same shape as the parameters. The paper: Duchi, Hazan and Singer, 2011.

The memory budget of a training step

The lecture's accounting of memory for the toy network (\(D=4\), \(L=3\), batch \(B=2\), bf16 parameters, gradients and activations, fp32 optimizer state):

num_parameters = D * D * L                       # 48
parameter_memory = 2 * num_parameters           # 96 bytes   (2 bytes for bf16)
gradient_memory = 2 * num_parameters            # 96 bytes   (2 bytes for bf16)
optimizer_state_memory = 4 * num_parameters     # 192 bytes  (4 bytes for fp32; AdaGrad's second moments)
activation_memory = 2 * (B * D * L)            # 48 bytes   (2 bytes for bf16)
total_memory = parameter_memory + activation_memory + gradient_memory + optimizer_state_memory   # 432 bytes

num_parameters = D * D * L
flops = 6 * B * num_parameters                  # 6 * 2 * 48 = 576 FLOPs for one step

The lecture's rule for the optimizer state: AdaGrad uses 4 bytes per parameter for its second moments; Adam uses 8 bytes per parameter for the first and second moments. It is customary to keep the state in fp32 for stability, because it accumulates averages over many steps. The values are summed as \(2+2+4 = 8\) bytes per parameter for AdaGrad (params, grads, state) before activations, and \(2+2+8=12\) bytes per parameter for Adam or AdamW, which is the number used in the Q2 calculator at the top.

Defaults reproduce the lecture's toy example: 48 parameters, 96 + 96 + 192 + 48 = 432 bytes. Scale the same formula up: for a 7B-parameter model with bf16 parameters and gradients and AdamW state, the static part is \(12\times 7\times10^{9}\approx 84\) GB before activations.

Activations are the part you cannot predict from parameters alone

Activations scale with batch size and sequence length, not with the parameter count. That is why the Q2 "largest model" estimate is only an upper bound, and why the next two sections (gradient accumulation and checkpointing) exist.

The training loop

Put the pieces together. The lecture's training loop fits a true linear function \(y = x\cdot w^{\star}\) with \(w^{\star}=(0,1,\dots,15)\) using random batches, a 2-layer DeepNetwork and the hand-written AdaGrad:

D = 16                                          # dimensionality
true_w = torch.arange(D, dtype=torch.float32)   # true weights (0, 1, ..., 15)

B = 4                                           # batch size
def get_batch():                                # data loader: (x, y) pairs
    x = torch.randn(B, D)
    true_y = x @ true_w
    return (x, true_y)

L = 2
model = DeepNetwork(dim=D, num_layers=L)
optimizer = AdaGrad(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)

num_train_steps = 3
for t in range(num_train_steps):
    x, y = get_batch()                          # 1. get data
    pred_y = model(x).mean()                    # 2. forward (compute prediction)
    loss = F.mse_loss(pred_y, y)                # 3. loss
    loss.backward()                             # 4. backward (compute gradients)
    optimizer.step()                            # 5. update parameters
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)       # 6. free the gradients

Caveat from reading the code: model(x).mean() is a scalar, which mse_loss broadcasts against the batch targets. This is a toy loop for seeing the mechanics (data, forward, backward, step, zero-grad), not a meaningful regression, and the model is nowhere near converged after three steps.

Gradient accumulation

Large batch sizes improve training stability, but activation memory grows with batch size, so a large batch may not fit. Gradient accumulation gets the gradient of a large batch without holding the whole batch in memory:

  • Compute the gradient on each micro-batch.
  • Accumulate the gradients (do not zero them out between micro-batches).
  • Every batch_size / micro_batch_size micro-steps, update the parameters and zero the gradients.

The lecture's example: \(B=64\), \(D=1024\), \(L=16\), so the full-batch activation memory is \(2BDL = 2\,097\,152\) bytes (2 MiB) in bf16. Using micro-batches of \(B/4 = 16\) gives \(2\cdot16\cdot1024\cdot16 = 524\,288\) bytes, one quarter of that, at the cost of four forward/backward passes per update.

B, D, L = 64, 1024, 16
activation_memory = 2 * B * D * L                     # 2,097,152 bytes (bf16)
micro_batch_size = B / 4                              # 16
activation_memory = 2 * micro_batch_size * D * L      # 524,288 bytes: 1/4 the memory
# Gradients are the same size as the parameters, so accumulation does not change their memory.

The trade-off: the number of forward/backward passes per update goes up, but each pass is still a full-size matmul, so the FLOPs per token do not change. Gradient accumulation trades a little throughput (more launches, smaller matmuls) for memory. Accumulation is exact: the gradient of the sum of micro-batch losses equals the gradient of the full batch, provided the loss is averaged in the right way.

Activation checkpointing

For training you must store the activations of every layer, because the backward pass needs them. For inference you do not compute gradients, so you only need the current layer's activation. Can training memory be reduced? Yes, with activation checkpointing (also called gradient checkpointing or rematerialization). The philosophy is to trade memory for compute:

  • Forward: keep only the activations at a subset of layers (the checkpoints).
  • Backward: recompute the missing activations starting from the last checkpoint.
# Store all activations:    x g1 h1 g2 h2 g3 h3 g4 h4
# Activation checkpointing: x    h1    h2    h3    h4

class DeepNetworkCheckpointed(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, num_layers):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block(dim) for i in range(num_layers)])
    def forward(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers:
            # KEY: only store activations at checkpoints, recompute the rest
            x = torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(layer, x)
        return x

x = torch.randn(B, D, requires_grad=True)     # B=64, D=1024, L=16 in the lecture
activation_memory = 2 * B * D * L             # 2 MiB (2,097,152 bytes) if everything is stored
memory = get_max_memory_usage(lambda: model(x).sum().backward())          # measured at run time
model = DeepNetworkCheckpointed(dim=D, num_layers=L)
checkpointed_memory = get_max_memory_usage(lambda: model(x).sum().backward())   # measured at run time

The lecture measures the peak memory of both versions with get_max_memory_usage. Those runtime numbers depend on the GPU and the allocator, so they are not reproduced here. What the code shows is that the checkpointed model stores one tensor per layer (the block input) and recomputes everything inside each block during backward.

How often to checkpoint?

The lecture frames it as a choice of spacing. The diagram below uses \(L=9\) layers, as the source does in its comments.

Read the table in the lecture carefully: with \(L\) layers, storing everything costs \(O(L)\) memory and no recomputation; storing nothing costs \(O(1)\) memory but \(O(L^2)\) compute, because layer \(i\) is recomputed from the start each time; storing every \(\sqrt{L}\) layers costs \(O(\sqrt{L})\) memory with \(O(L)\) recomputation. The calculator uses the simplest model consistent with those statements, so the numbers are indicative. The exact cost depends on the implementation.

Trade-off in one line

Checkpointing spends roughly one extra forward pass (about 33% more FLOPs in the usual accounting) to cut activation memory from \(O(L)\) to \(O(\sqrt{L})\). It is the standard way to fit longer sequences or larger batches.

Transformers, and where to take this next

The lecture's last accounting exercise is the Transformer. The lecture says the accounting for a Transformer is more complicated but follows the same idea, and that Assignment 1 asks you to do it. Two external write-ups are linked for reference: a blog post on memory usage in Transformer training (erees.dev) and one on Transformer FLOPs (adamcasson.com).

For orientation, the rules you have already learned already give the answer for the dense parts. Training FLOPs \(\approx 6\,N\,D\) for \(N\) parameters and \(D\) tokens. Parameter, gradient and optimizer memory scale with \(N\) and the dtypes. Activation memory scales with batch size, sequence length, width and depth, which is why it is the hard part.

Appendix: the hardware lookup and the benchmark

These helper functions appear in the lecture source. They are not the lesson, but they show where the numbers in this guide come from:

get_promised_flop_per_sec, benchmark, get_memory_usage (source) 
def get_memory_usage(x: torch.Tensor):
    return x.numel() * x.element_size()

def get_promised_flop_per_sec(dtype: torch.dtype) -> float:
    """Return the peak FLOP/s for `device` operating on `dtype`."""
    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        return 1                                    # no CUDA: can't get FLOP/s
    properties = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(cuda_if_available())
    if "A100" in properties.name:
        if dtype == torch.float32:              return 19.5e12
        if dtype in (torch.bfloat16, torch.float16): return 312e12
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown dtype: {dtype}")
    if "H100" in properties.name:
        if dtype == torch.float32:              return 67.5e12
        if dtype in (torch.bfloat16, torch.float16): return 1979e12 / 2   # 1979 is sparse; dense is half
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown dtype: {dtype}")
    if "B200" in properties.name:
        if dtype == torch.float32:              return 75e12
        if dtype in (torch.bfloat16, torch.float16): return 4.5e15 / 2   # 4.5e15 is sparse
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown dtype: {dtype}")
    return None                                     # unknown GPU: caller handles it

def benchmark(func, num_trials: int = 5) -> float:
    """Return the number of seconds required to perform `func`."""
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.synchronize()                    # wait for previous CUDA work
    def run():
        func()
        if torch.cuda.is_available():
            torch.cuda.synchronize()                # wait for this run's CUDA work
    total_time = timeit.timeit(run, number=num_trials)
    return total_time / num_trials

def get_num_parameters(model: nn.Module) -> int:
    return sum(param.numel() for param in model.parameters())

Three details are worth remembering. The FLOP/s table is keyed by GPU name and dtype, and it raises on unknown dtypes. benchmark averages five timed runs and calls synchronize on both sides, because CUDA launches are asynchronous. get_num_parameters counts every parameter element, which is how the assertions \(\text{params} = D^2 L\) are checked.

Key takeaways

  • Everything is operations on tensors: parameters, gradients, activations, optimizer states and data. Memory is always numel × bytes per element.
  • einops names the dimensions, so you do not have to remember what -2 or -1 means.
  • Training costs \(6\cdot(\#\text{data})\cdot(\#\text{parameters})\) FLOPs per step (2 forward, 4 backward), and it is a good Transformer approximation at short context.
  • Arithmetic intensity versus accelerator intensity decides whether an operation is compute-bound or memory-bound. Matmuls on large matrices are compute-bound; elementwise ops and matrix-vector products are memory-bound. Inference is largely memory-bound.
  • Precision: bf16 keeps fp32's range with fp16's size. Mixed precision keeps optimizer state in fp32. fp8 and fp4 need scaling to cover the range.
  • Memory of training is parameters + gradients + optimizer state (AdamW: 12 bytes per parameter in the lecture's accounting) + activations. Gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing reduce the last term, the first one by splitting the batch and the second by recomputation.
