Self-check quiz

1. A tensor has shape (4, 8) and is stored in fp32. How many bytes is it, and what changes in bf16?
32 values × 4 bytes = 128 bytes. In bf16 each value is 2 bytes, so 64 bytes. The number of values is unchanged; only the bytes per value changes.
2. Why does torch.tensor([1e-8], dtype=torch.float16) become 0 while the same value in bf16 does not?
fp16 has a 5-bit exponent, so its smallest positive subnormal is 2-24 ≈ 6.0 × 10-8. 10-8 is below that, so it rounds to 0 (underflow). bf16 has an 8-bit exponent, the same as fp32, so its smallest subnormal is about 9.2 × 10-41 and 10-8 is representable (with only 7 mantissa bits of precision).
3. Compute the FLOPs of \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D}\) times \(w\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times K}\). For \(B=16384, D=32768, K=8192\), what is the ideal time on one H100 dense bf16?
\(2BDK = 2\cdot16384\cdot32768\cdot8192 = 2^{43} \approx 8.80\times10^{12}\) FLOPs. At 989.5 TFLOP/s peak, that is \(8.80\times10^{12}/989.5\times10^{12} \approx 8.9\) ms. At MFU 0.5 it would take about 17.8 ms.
4. Why is a matrix-vector product memory-bound but a large matmul compute-bound?
For an n×n matrix times a vector, FLOPs ≈ 2n² and bytes ≈ 2n² (the matrix must be read), so the intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte, far below the H100's ≈ 295. For an n×n matmul, FLOPs ≈ 2n³ and bytes ≈ 6n² (read two matrices, write one), so intensity ≈ n/3. At n = 1024 that is about 341, above 295, so it is compute-bound. The intensity grows with the size of the matrices.
5. Using the lecture's numbers, how long would 70B parameters on 15T tokens take on 1024 H100s at MFU 0.5?
\(6ND = 6\cdot70\times10^{9}\cdot15\times10^{12} = 6.3\times10^{24}\) FLOPs. Per day the cluster delivers \(989.5\times10^{12}\cdot0.5\cdot1024\cdot86400 \approx 4.377\times10^{22}\) FLOPs. Ratio: about 144 days.
6. Why does AdamW need 12 bytes per parameter in the lecture's accounting, and what does the calculation leave out?
bf16 parameters (2) + bf16 gradients (2) + two fp32 Adam moments (4 + 4) = 12 bytes. It leaves out activations (which depend on batch size and sequence length) and, in the usual mixed-precision recipe, the optimizer's fp32 master copy of the weights (another 4 bytes). So 8 × 80 GB / 12 bytes ≈ 53B parameters is an upper bound.
7. Gradient accumulation halves the micro-batch. What happens to activation memory, gradient memory and the number of updates per optimizer step?
Activation memory halves (it scales with the micro-batch). Gradient memory stays the same, since gradients have the size of the parameters and are accumulated in place. The number of forward/backward passes per optimizer update doubles (it is B / micro-batch), so the model takes twice as many micro-steps to make one update.
8. With activation checkpointing and L = 16 layers, roughly how many layer outputs are stored with the √L spacing, and how many layers are recomputed?
Keeping every √L = 4th layer stores about 4 checkpoints plus one segment of 4 layers at peak, so about \(L/k + k = 8\) activations at peak instead of 16. The recomputation is roughly \(L - L/k = 12\) layer forwards per backward. (Exact counts depend on the implementation; this is the simple model in the calculator above.)

Summary of the lecture's own wording: "Everything is operations on tensors (parameters, gradients, activations, optimizer states, data)... 6 (# data points) (# parameters) FLOPs per training step... Matrix multiplications are compute-bound, elementwise operations are memory-bound... Gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing: reduce memory to use bigger batch sizes."

LLM Architecture & Hyperparameters

lecture_03.pdf pre-norm RMSNorm SwiGLU RoPE d_ff ratio aspect ratio z-loss QK-norm GQA / MQA sliding-window attention
TL;DR. Lecture 3 is a tour of what ~20 recent dense LMs have in common and where they differ. The consensus "LLaMA-like" recipe is: pre-norm (norm outside the residual stream), RMSNorm, no bias terms, a gated FFN (SwiGLU / GeGLU) with \(d_{ff}\approx\tfrac{8}{3}d_{model}\), serial blocks, and RoPE applied to queries and keys in every attention layer. Hyperparameters are boringly consistent: \(d_{ff}/d_{model}\approx 4\) (or 2.5-3.5 for GLUs), \(h\cdot d_{head}\approx d_{model}\), \(d_{model}/n_{layer}\) between 100 and 200, vocabularies of 32-50k (monolingual) or 100-260k (multilingual), weight decay 0.1 and (mostly) no dropout. Newer additions are stability tricks (z-loss, QK-norm, logit soft-capping) and attention variants (MQA/GQA for cheap inference, interleaved sliding-window + full attention for long context). The lecture's theme: the best way to learn is hands-on experience; the second best is to learn from others' experience - so we read the "data" of many published models.

1. Recap: the original vs. the modern transformer

The lecture starts from the original transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) and the simple modern variant you implement in assignment 1. Four things differ:

ChoiceOriginal transformer (2017)Modern (what you implement)
Position informationsinusoidal embeddings added to the input: \(PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})\), \(PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos(\cdot)\)Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) applied to q and k in every attention layer
FFN non-linearityReLU: \(\mathrm{FFN}(x)=\max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2\)SwiGLU (gated), no biases
Normalizationpost-norm, LayerNorm (inside the residual path)pre-norm (norm in front of each sub-block, off the residual path), RMSNorm
Bias termsyes in linear layers and LayerNormnone in linear layers or norms

The big question for the rest of the lecture: why did we pick these, and what should you pick? The slides answer it empirically: in 2024-2026 more than 19 new dense models were released, many with tiny architecture tweaks. The instructors keep a spreadsheet of these models (embedded below as slide 9) and the pattern is a clear dominance of "LLaMA-like" architectures, with trends over the years toward QK-norm and hybrid (local + global) attention.

2. Where to put the norm: pre-norm vs. post-norm

This is "the one thing everyone agrees on" (in 2024): put the LayerNorm so that it does not sit on the main residual signal path (figure from Xiong et al. 2020). Almost all modern LMs are pre-norm; BERT was post-norm, and the lecture notes one funny outlier: OPT-350M is post-norm (no known reason).

\(x_{l+1}=\mathrm{LN}\big(x_l+\mathrm{Sublayer}(x_l)\big)\): every layer's output passes through a LayerNorm, including the identity path. The gradient has to travel through a normalization at every layer.

\(x_{l+1}=x_l+\mathrm{Sublayer}(\mathrm{LN}(x_l))\), plus a final LN before the output head. The residual stream is untouched, so gradients flow straight from the loss to early layers.

If norms inside the residual stream are bad, why not post-norm outside the stream? The slide's "double norm" figure (norm before and after the sub-layer, both off the stream) is used by recent models such as Grok and Gemma 2; OLMo 2 only does the non-residual post-norm (norm applied to the sub-layer output, before adding).

Why pre-norm works: the evidence

Original vs. today's justification

Original stated advantage of pre-LN: no learning-rate warmup needed. Today the reasons are stability and the ability to use larger learning rates for large networks (fewer gradient spikes, nicer gradient propagation). The slides' data (BLEU/validation-loss curves for English-Vietnamese, IWSLT, BERT pre-training) show pre-norm converging at least as well as post-norm, and robustly without warmup.

3. LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm

LayerNorm (original transformer; GPT-1/2/3, OPT, GPT-J, BLOOM) normalizes mean and variance over the feature dimension:

\[ y=\frac{x-\mathbb{E}[x]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[x]+\epsilon}}\odot\gamma+\beta \]

RMSNorm (LLaMA family, PaLM, Chinchilla, T5) does not subtract the mean and has no bias:

\[ y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{\lVert x\rVert_2^2/d+\epsilon}}\odot\gamma \]

Modern explanation: RMSNorm is faster and just as good (fewer operations: no mean; fewer parameters: no \(\beta\)). Does that make sense? Matrix multiplies are \(99.8\%\) of FLOPs, so a cost argument based on FLOPs looks weak - and this is the lecture's "important lesson": FLOPs are not runtime.

So RMSNorm still matters because of data movement: a LayerNorm op is memory-bound (FLOP/byte ratio 3.5 in the figure), and RMSNorm removes one reduction (the mean) and one parameter vector to read. Runtime - and, surprisingly, quality - gains were reported in Narang et al. 2021 (the slides date it 2020) (223M-parameter T5-like models, 11.1T ops each):

Model (223M params, 11.1T ops)Step/sEarly lossFinal lossSGLUEXSumWebQWMT EnDe
Vanilla Transformer3.502.182 ± 0.0051.83871.6617.7823.0226.62
RMS Norm3.682.167 ± 0.0081.82175.4517.9424.0727.14
Rezero3.512.262 ± 0.0031.93961.6915.6420.9026.37
Rezero + LayerNorm3.262.223 ± 0.0061.85870.4217.5823.0226.29
Rezero + RMS Norm3.342.221 ± 0.0091.87570.3317.3223.0226.19
Fixup2.952.382 ± 0.0122.06758.5614.4223.0226.31

Play with it: what does the mean subtraction actually do?

Code: RMSNorm

import torch, torch.nn as nn

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.gamma = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))          # only a scale, no beta

    def forward(self, x):                                  # x: (..., d)
        in_dtype = x.dtype
        x = x.float()                                      # do the reduction in fp32
        rms = torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return (x * rms).to(in_dtype) * self.gamma

Compare with LayerNorm, which additionally computes x.mean(-1), subtracts it, uses the variance (a second pass/reduction), and adds a learned bias \(\beta\).

4. Dropping bias terms

Most modern transformers have no bias terms anywhere. Original FFN: \(\max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2\). Most implementations today (if not gated): \(\mathrm{FFN}(x)=\sigma(xW_1)W_2\). Reasons given: memory (like RMSNorm: fewer parameters to move around, and the compute/param trade-off is poor) and optimization stability.

LayerNorm recap (slide)

(1) Basically everyone does a non-residual norm (often pre-norm): keep the good parts of residual connections; nicer gradient propagation, fewer spikes; some add a second norm outside the stream. (2) Most people use RMSNorm: works as well as LayerNorm, but fewer parameters to move around saves wall-clock time. (3) People drop bias terms since the compute/param trade-offs are not great.

5. Activations and gated linear units

There is a whole zoo: ReLU, GeLU, Swish, ELU, GLU, GeGLU, ReGLU, SeLU, SwiGLU, LiGLU. What are they, what do people use, and does it matter?

ActivationFFNNotable models
ReLU\(\mathrm{FF}(x)=\max(0,xW_1)W_2\)original transformer, T5, Gopher, Chinchilla, OPT
GeLU\(\mathrm{FF}(x)=\mathrm{GELU}(xW_1)W_2,\ \ \mathrm{GELU}(x)=x\,\Phi(x)\)GPT-1/2/3, GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, BLOOM
SwiGLU / GeGLU (gated, below)see belowLLaMA 1/2/3, PaLM, Mistral, OLMo, T5 v1.1, Gemma 2/3/4, most models after 2023

Gated activations (*GLU)

GLUs change the "first part" of the FF layer. Instead of a single linear map followed by a non-linearity, multiply by an entrywise linear term from a second matrix:

\[ \max(0,xW_1)\ \longrightarrow\ \max(0,xW_1)\otimes(xV),\qquad \mathrm{FF}_{\mathrm{ReGLU}}(x)=\big(\max(0,xW_1)\otimes xV\big)W_2 \]

Note the extra parameter matrix \(V\). The other gated variants simply swap the non-linearity:

\[ \mathrm{FF}_{\mathrm{GeGLU}}=(\mathrm{GELU}(xW)\otimes xV)W_2,\qquad \mathrm{FF}_{\mathrm{SwiGLU}}=(\mathrm{Swish}_1(xW)\otimes xV)W_2,\quad \mathrm{Swish}_1(z)=z\cdot\sigma(z) \]
GeGLU: T5 v1.1, mT5, LaMDA, Phi-3, Gemma 2, Gemma 3, Gemma 4
SwiGLU: LLaMA 1/2/3, PaLM, Mistral, OLMo, most models post-2023
The 2/3 rule

Gated models have three weight matrices (\(W,V,W_2\)) instead of two, so they shrink \(d_{ff}\) by 2/3 to keep the parameter count equal: \(2\cdot d\cdot 4d = 3\cdot d\cdot \tfrac83 d = 8d^2\).

Code: SwiGLU

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    """FFN(x) = (Swish(x W) * (x V)) W2,   Swish(z) = z * sigmoid(z) = F.silu(z)."""
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None):
        super().__init__()
        d_ff = d_ff or int(8 * d_model / 3)                 # 2/3 of the usual 4 * d_model
        d_ff = 64 * ((d_ff + 63) // 64)                     # round up to a hardware-friendly multiple (illustrative)
        self.w  = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)      # gate branch (activated)
        self.v  = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)      # linear branch
        self.w2 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.w2(F.silu(self.w(x)) * self.v(x))

Do GLUs work? Yes, fairly consistently

Shazeer (2020) compared FFN variants on GLUE-style tasks (table below; the gated variants lead the average; ReGLU is best). Narang et al. (2020) corroborated this at 223M parameters with pre-training loss and downstream scores.

Gating and activations: summary

Many variations (ReLU, GeLU, *GLU) exist across models. *GLU is not necessary for a working model (GPT-3 does fine with GeLU), but it is now rare to see anything else; the outlier cited is Nemotron-4 340B (squared ReLU). Evidence points to somewhat consistent gains from SwiGLU/GeGLU.

6. Serial vs. parallel layers

A normal transformer block is serial: attention first, then the MLP on its output. Could we parallelize the block? GPT-J (originally), PaLM and GPT-NeoX use parallel layers. The GPT-J formulation quoted on the slide:

\[ \text{serial: } y=x+\mathrm{MLP}\big(\mathrm{LN}(x+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(x)))\big)\qquad \text{parallel: } y=x+\mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(x))+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(x)) \]

The parallel formulation gave roughly 15% faster training at large scale because the MLP and attention input matrix multiplies can be fused and a single LayerNorm shared. The ablation saw a small quality degradation at 8B scale and none at 62B, so the authors extrapolated the effect to be quality-neutral at 540B. Recent models with parallel layers: Cohere Command A, Falcon 2 11B, Command R+. Most models today still use serial blocks.

Summary of the architecture part (slide): pre-vs-post norm: everyone does non-residual norm (except OPT-350M), likely with good reason. LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm: RMSNorm has clear compute wins and sometimes even better performance. Gating: GLUs are consensus now. Serial vs. parallel: most models use serial layers.

7. Position embeddings

Attention on its own is permutation-equivariant, so the model needs some position signal. The slides group the schemes by family:

TypeDefinitionNotable models
Sineadd fixed sines and cosines: \(\mathrm{Embed}(x,i)=v_x+PE_{pos}\), with \(PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})\), \(PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos(\cdot)\)original transformer
Absoluteadd a learned position vector to the embedding: \(\mathrm{Embed}(x,i)=v_x+u_i\)GPT-1/2/3, OPT
Relativeadd a term into the attention computation: \(e_{ij}=\dfrac{x_iW^Q\,(x_jW^K+a^K_{ij})^\top}{\sqrt{d_z}}\)T5, Gopher, Chinchilla
RoPE (next section)rotate q and k by a position-dependent angleGPT-J, PaLM, LLaMA, most 2024+ models

(The slides' model spreadsheet also lists ALiBi (BLOOM, Baichuan 2) and newer hybrid schemes such as SWA + full RoPE or RoPE + NoPE; see section 12.)

8. RoPE: rotary position embeddings

The design goal

We want a position-dependent map \(f(x,i)\) such that the attention score depends only on the relative offset:

\[ \langle f(x,i),\,f(y,j)\rangle = g(x,y,i-j) \]

How do the existing schemes fail? Sine: the inner product of two (embedding + PE) vectors expands into cross terms, \(\langle v_x,v_y\rangle+\langle v_x,PE_j\rangle+\langle PE_i,v_y\rangle+\langle PE_i,PE_j\rangle\), and these are not functions of \(i-j\) alone. Absolute: obviously not relative. Relative embeddings: \(e_{ij}\) is not an inner product of position-transformed vectors.

The idea: rotate

Inner products are invariant to arbitrary rotation of both vectors. Take "we know" in "we know that" (rotate "we" by 0 positions and "know" by 1) and in "of course we know" (rotate "we" by 2 and "know" by 3): the relative angle between the two vectors is the same in both, so their inner product is the same. The position enters as a rotation, not as an addition, so there are no cross terms.

Which rotation? Pair coordinates and rotate in 2D

There are many rotations of a d-dimensional space. RoPE (Su et al. 2021) pairs up coordinates and rotates each pair in its own 2D plane (motivation: multiplying by \(e^{im\theta}\) in complex numbers), with a different frequency per pair, \(\theta_i=10000^{-2i/d}\):

\[ f_{\{q,k\}}(x_m,m)=R^d_{\Theta,m}\,W_{\{q,k\}}\,x_m,\qquad R^d_{\Theta,m}=\mathrm{blockdiag}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}\cos m\theta_i&-\sin m\theta_i\\ \sin m\theta_i&\cos m\theta_i\end{pmatrix}\right)_{i=1..d/2} \]

Because rotations compose, \((R_m q)^\top(R_n k)=q^\top R_{n-m}\,k\): the score depends only on \(n-m\). The slide also shows a Gemma 4 alternative: rotate only the first pairs ("just first 2" on the slide) and leave the rest position-free to carry purely semantic information.

Interactive: RoPE rotation and relative-position invariance

Code: RoPE

The slide shows the usual implementation: build the cos/sin tables for the positions once, then apply them to queries and keys inside every attention layer (values are not rotated), "to enforce position invariance".

import torch

def rope_cache(seq_len, head_dim, base=10000.0, device=None):
    inv_freq = base ** (-torch.arange(0, head_dim, 2, device=device).float() / head_dim)  # (d/2,) = theta_i
    pos = torch.arange(seq_len, device=device).float()                                    # (n,)
    freqs = torch.outer(pos, inv_freq)                                                    # (n, d/2) = m * theta_i
    emb = torch.cat([freqs, freqs], dim=-1)                                               # (n, d)
    return emb.cos(), emb.sin()

def rotate_half(x):                       # (x1, x2) -> (-x2, x1): a 90-degree turn inside each pair
    h = x.shape[-1] // 2
    return torch.cat([-x[..., h:], x[..., :h]], dim=-1)

def apply_rope(q, k, cos, sin):           # q, k: (batch, heads, n, head_dim)
    q = q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin    # = R_m q
    k = k * cos + rotate_half(k) * sin    # = R_n k
    return q, k

# inside each attention layer:
#   q, k, v = proj(x)
#   q, k = apply_rope(q, k, cos[:n], sin[:n])
#   out = softmax(q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_head) + causal_mask) @ v

This implementation pairs coordinate \(i\) with \(i+d/2\) (the "half" layout used by many HF/LLaMA codebases) while the paper pairs adjacent coordinates \((2i,2i+1)\) as in the widget above. The two are the same family of rotations up to a fixed permutation of the head dimension. RoPE is applied per head, so \(d=d_{head}\).

9. Hyperparameters: what matters and what doesn't

The slide opens with the questions you may have had in 224n: how much bigger should the feedforward size be than the hidden size? Must num_heads divide the hidden size? What should the vocabulary size be? Then the model-setting questions: do people even regularize these huge LMs, and do they scale depth or width? The answer the lecture keeps returning to is that most models are boringly conservative, and that consensus is itself informative.

9.1 Feedforward ratio: d_ff / d_model

Two dimensions matter here: the FFN hidden size \(d_{ff}\) and the model width \(d_{model}\). The "almost always true" rule is

\[ d_{ff}=4\,d_{model}. \]

Exception 1: GLU variants. A gated FFN has three weight matrices instead of two, so to keep parameters equal the hidden size shrinks by 2/3: \(d_{ff}=\tfrac{8}{3}d_{model}\approx 2.67\,d_{model}\). The slide's table:

Model\(d_{ff}/d_{model}\)

Qwen 14B2.67
DeepSeek 67B2.68
Yi 34B2.85

Exception 2: T5. T5 is the bold outlier. For the 11B model the authors set \(d_{ff}=65{,}536\) with \(d_{model}=1024\): a 64x multiplier, chosen (per the T5 paper's quoted reasoning on the slide) because modern accelerators are efficient on large dense matmuls. The follow-up T5 v1.1 uses GeGLU with the standard 2.5. Other recent exceptions: Gemma 2 (8x), and SmolLM / Gemma 3 / Gemma 4 (4x with GLU).

Why this range? Kaplan et al. (2020) find a basin between about 1 and 10 where this ratio is near-optimal. The defaults \(4\) and \(2.66\) have worked for nearly all modern LLMs; T5 shows that even 64 can train, but the slide suggests it is suboptimal, since the T5 v1.1 follow-up moved to 2.5.

9.2 Heads, head dimension, and model dimension

The second consensus: \(h\cdot d_{head}=d_{model}\), so the per-head projections add back up to the model width. It is not required: you may use \(d_{head}>d_{model}/h\), and some models do. The slide's examples (note PaLM's row, discussed below):

9.5 Dropout and weight decay

Do people regularize these huge LMs? The arguments against are reasonable: pre-training data is trillions of tokens, more than the parameter count, and SGD makes only a single pass over the corpus, so memorization is hard. In practice the picture is mixed (the slide's table, with footnote):

ModelDropout*Weight decay
Original transformer0.10
GPT-20.10.1

T5 v1.100
PaLM0(variable)
OPT0.10.1

* Most papers simply do not discuss dropout. On open models, the table closely matches not using dropout; this may not hold for closed models.

Many older models used dropout during pretraining. Newer models (except Qwen) rely only on weight decay.

Why weight decay for LLMs?

Andriushchenko et al. (2023) observe that weight decay in LLM pretraining is not mainly about controlling overfitting (training and validation loss track each other closely). Its effect interacts with the learning-rate schedule: with a cosine schedule, weight decay changes the training dynamics noticeably, while with a constant LR the benefit is different. The slide's figure is below.

Summary: hyperparameters

Feedforward: the factor-of-4 rule (8/3 for GLUs) is standard, with some evidence behind it. Head dim: \(h\cdot d_{head}=d_{model}\) is standard, though with little validation. Aspect ratio: a wide range of "good" values (roughly 100-200); systems concerns dictate the value. Regularization: you still regularize LMs, but mostly through effects on optimization dynamics.

10. Stability tricks

Recently there has been a lot of attention on stable training. The bad case is the blue curve below: loss and gradient-norm spikes that can derail a run. Where do they come from? Mostly from softmaxes, which are ill-behaved because of exponentials (overflow) and division by a near-zero normalizer (in low precision).

Output softmax stability: the z-loss

Recall the softmax calculation. With unnormalized logits \(U_x\),

\[ \log P(x)=\log\frac{e^{U_x}}{Z}=U_x-\log Z,\qquad Z=\sum_{x'}e^{U_{x'}}. \]

Nothing forces the normalizer to stay at a reasonable value, so \(\log Z\) can drift. PaLM adds an auxiliary term that pushes \(\log Z\) toward 0, so that the softmax is approximately normalized and its logits stay in a safe range:

\[ \mathcal{L}_z=\alpha\,(\log Z)^2,\qquad \alpha=10^{-4}\ \text{(PaLM)}. \]

The slide also shows the earlier self-normalization form (Devlin et al. 2014), \(\sum_i\big[\log P(x_i)-\alpha(\log Z(x_i))^2\big]\), which penalizes the same quantity. Other models with z-loss: Baichuan 2 (2023), DCLM (2024), OLMo 2 (2025), OLMo 3 (2025).

Attention softmax stability: QK-norm

The query and key vectors are normalized (LayerNorm or RMSNorm) before the dot product in attention. This bounds the attention logits, since \(|q\cdot k|\le\|q\|\,\|k\|\), and the norms are fixed by the normalization, so the logits cannot blow up. QK-norm appears in DCLM, OLMo 2, Gemma 2, Qwen 3, OLMo 3 and Gemma 4 (per the slide). It originated in vision and multimodal transformers (Dehghani et al. 2023; Idefics; Chameleon).

Logit soft-capping

Soft-capping squashes logits into \((-c,c)\) with a scaled tanh, applied in each attention layer and at the final layer:

\[ \text{logits}\ \leftarrow\ c\cdot\tanh\!\left(\frac{\text{logits}}{c}\right) \]

The slide's quoted paragraph sets the cap to 50.0 for the self-attention layers and 30.0 for the final layer. It prevents logits from blowing up, but can have performance costs, since large logits lose gradient (the derivative is \(1-\tanh^2(z/c)\)).

11. Attention variants: MQA, GQA, sliding windows

Most models do not touch the attention heads much, with a few exceptions. The main themes: GQA / MQA reduce the number of key/value heads to save inference cost; sparse or sliding-window attention (GPT-3's sparse layers, GPT-4 and Mistral, Gemma 4) restricts the attention pattern to save compute; and "exotic" SSM hybrids (Jamba, Falcon 3, Qwen 3.5) are for the next lecture.

11.1 What does attention cost?

Notation from the slides: \(d\) hidden dim, \(b\) batch, \(n\) sequence length (assumed \(n\lt d\)), \(h\) heads, \(k=d/h\) head dim.

Prefill (all tokens at once)

Total arithmetic is \(O(bnd^2)\) and total memory accesses are \(bnd+bhn^2+d^2\) (the terms are \(X\), the softmax matrix, and the projections). The arithmetic intensity, compute divided by memory, is \(O\big((1/k+1/(bn))^{-1}\big)\): high, so the GPU stays busy.

Exact counts behind the big-O (for the calculator below)

Intensity \(I=\dfrac{bnd^2}{bnd+bhn^2+d^2}\). Inverting, \(1/I=\dfrac1d+\dfrac{hn}{d^2}+\dfrac1{bn}\). With \(h=d/k\), \(hn/d^2=n/(kd)\). So for \(n\lt d\) the \(1/k\) term dominates, which is the slide's \(O\)-form. Longer contexts make the \(bhn^2\) softmax traffic grow quadratically, so intensity falls as \(n\) grows.

11.2 Incremental decoding and the KV cache

Generation is different: we cannot parallelize across the sequence, because each new token needs the keys and values of all earlier tokens. So we store them in a KV cache and only compute the new token's projections.

Intensity in incremental decoding is the crux. The per-token arithmetic is still \(O(bnd^2)\), but the memory accesses are \(bn^2d+nd^2\) (reading K and V, plus the projection). The intensity is therefore \(O\big((n/d+1/b)^{-1}\big)\): bad. Good intensity needs large batches and short sequences (\(n\)) or large model dimensions (\(d\)). The \(n/d\) term is hard to reduce, so the fix is to shrink the number of K and V items that must be read: that is MQA and GQA.

11.3 MQA and GQA: fewer key/value heads

Multi-query attention (MQA; Shazeer 2019): keep many query heads, but only one key head and one value head shared by all of them. The KV cache, and the memory read per decoding step, shrink by a factor of \(h\). Total memory access becomes \(bnd+bn^2k+nd^2\) and intensity \(O\big((1/d+n/(dh)+1/b)^{-1}\big)\): the attention-read term is \(h\) times smaller than in MHA.

Grouped-query attention (GQA; Ainslie et al. 2023) interpolates: \(g\) KV heads with \(1\lt g\lt h\). It is a simple knob for expressiveness (key-query ratio) versus inference efficiency. MLA (multi-head latent attention, DeepSeek-V2) is a more recent variant of the same idea.

Worked check for the defaults: \(2\cdot 80\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 2\,\text{B}=327{,}680\) bytes (320 KiB) per token; at \(n=4096\), \(b=1\), that is about 1.34 GB. With 64 MHA KV heads it would be 8x larger.

11.4 Does MQA hurt? Sometimes.

MQA pays a small perplexity hit (Shazeer 2019, Billion-Word LM benchmark; table below, with the MQA row's \(d_{ff}\) increased to keep the parameter count matched). GQA gets low or no quality loss at a fixed compute budget (Ainslie et al. 2023).

11.5 Sparse and sliding-window attention

Attending to the entire context is quadratic in \(n\). Sparse or structured attention trades expressiveness for runtime. Child et al. (2019, Sparse Transformer) show the patterns: a strided pattern and a fixed pattern, each a subset of the full causal mask.

Sliding-window attention (SWA): each token attends only to the last \(w\) tokens. Mistral 7B uses it together with GQA, and GPT-OSS and Gemma 4 use sparse or local layers as well.

11.6 The standard trick: interleave full and local attention

The current default is to interleave a few full attention layers with many local (sliding-window) ones. Cohere Command A uses a full-attention layer every 4th layer: long-range information goes through the full layers with NoPE (no position encoding), while short-range information goes through RoPE + SWA layers. Other models: LLaMA 4, Gemma 3 and Gemma 4, and OLMo 3 (SWA + full with RoPE). Recent examples of interleaved attention on the slides: Gemma 4, OLMo 3, Qwen 3.5 and Qwen 3-Next.

13. Key takeaways

  • Pre-norm is the consensus. Keep normalization off the residual path: better gradient flow, fewer spikes, and no warmup required (the original stated advantage).
  • RMSNorm and no biases. RMSNorm matches LayerNorm quality with fewer operations and parameters. FLOPs are not runtime: data movement matters, so drop unnecessary memory traffic.
  • Gated FFNs (SwiGLU / GeGLU) are the default. Use \(d_{ff}\approx\tfrac83 d\) to keep parameters matched with the classic \(4d\).
  • Serial blocks dominate. Parallel layers (GPT-J, PaLM, Command A) give speed gains from fused matmuls but are not the default.
  • RoPE is the default position encoding. It rotates q and k so scores depend only on relative offset, with no cross terms and no added position vectors.
  • Hyperparameters are conservative. \(d_{ff}\approx4d\) (or 2.67d gated), \(h\,d_{head}\approx d_{model}\), \(d_{model}/n_{layer}\approx100\) to 200, vocabulary 32-50k (monolingual) or 100-260k (multilingual), weight decay 0.1 with little or no dropout.
  • Stability tricks are cheap insurance. z-loss (PaLM \(10^{-4}\)), QK-norm (the largest perplexity gain on the slide's table), and logit soft-capping (more about stability than quality).
  • Inference shapes attention. Decoding is memory-bound through the KV cache. MQA and GQA shrink it by a factor of \(h/g\); sliding-window and interleaved full attention cut its context-dependent cost further. SSM hybrids come next lecture.

15. Self-check quiz

Why does pre-norm train more stably than post-norm, and what did the original paper claim as its advantage?
In post-norm, a LayerNorm sits on the residual path, so every block's output is renormalized and the gradient must pass through many normalizations to reach early layers (Xiong et al. 2020 show gradient attenuation for post-LN and gradient spikes in training). In pre-norm the residual stream is untouched, so gradients flow directly from the loss to early layers. The original stated advantage was removing learning-rate warmup; today the reasons given are stability and the ability to use larger learning rates.
A gated FFN (SwiGLU) with d = 4096 uses d_ff = 8/3 d. How many FFN weights per layer compared with the plain 4d FFN?
Plain: 2 * d * 4d = 8 d^2 = 134,217,728 weights. Gated: 3 * d * (8/3) d = 8 d^2 = 134,217,728 (up to rounding of d_ff to an integer: 8/3 * 4096 = 10922.67, so 3 * 4096 * 10923 is about 134.2M). The two are iso-parameter by construction, so the gated FFN buys its extra expressiveness at no parameter cost.
RMSNorm skips the mean. Why does it still matter for runtime when matrix multiplies are 99.8% of FLOPs?
FLOPs are not runtime. Matrix multiplies are compute-bound, but normalization and element-wise ops are memory-bound: they move data without doing many FLOPs per byte. Ivanov et al. show normalization is 0.17% of FLOPs but 25.5% of runtime, element-wise 0.03% of FLOPs but 13.5% of runtime. RMSNorm removes one reduction and one parameter vector, so it saves data movement.
Why does RoPE make attention scores depend only on the relative position m - n?
RoPE rotates the query at position m by R_m and the key at position n by R_n, with R_m a block-diagonal rotation. Rotations compose and are orthogonal: (R_m q)^T (R_n k) = q^T R_m^T R_n k = q^T R_{n-m} k. Only the offset n - m remains. The widget above verifies this numerically: shifting both positions by the same amount leaves the score unchanged.
For a LLaMA-2-70B-like config (L = 80, g = 8 KV heads, k = 128, bf16), how big is the KV cache per token, and how much larger would MHA with 64 KV heads be?
Per token: 2 (K and V) * 80 * 8 * 128 * 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes (320 KiB). With 64 KV heads it is 8 times larger: 2,621,440 bytes (2.5 MiB). At n = 4096 and b = 1 the GQA cache is about 1.34 GB per sequence.
You have a 7B-parameter budget and want aspect ratio d/L = 128. What width and depth?
Using N approximately 12 L d^2 and d = 128 L: N = 12 d^3 / 128, so d = (N * 128 / 12)^(1/3) = (7e9 * 128 / 12)^(1/3), approximately 4.2k. Then L = d / 128, about 33 layers. This is close to the LLaMA-7B shape (d = 4096, L = 32, ratio 128).
Explain why a sliding window of w = n/2 does not halve the attention cost, and compute the fraction for n = 8192.
Causal full attention has n(n+1)/2 query-key pairs, about n^2/2. With a window w, the pairs are n w - w(w-1)/2: the first w queries have a growing triangle, and the remaining n - w queries each attend to exactly w keys. For w = n/2 this is n^2/2 - n^2/8 = 3n^2/8, i.e. 75% of the causal pairs. For n = 8192, w = 4096: 33,558,528 full pairs vs 25,167,872 windowed pairs, a ratio of about 0.75. The saving is smaller than 2x because the early queries, which have short causal prefixes, are unaffected.
What does z-loss penalize, and what does the logit soft-cap do to a logit of 100 with cap 30?
z-loss adds alpha (log Z)^2 with alpha = 1e-4 (PaLM), where Z = sum_x e^{U_x}. It keeps the softmax normalizer close to 1 (log Z near 0), preventing drift in the logit scale. Soft-capping maps x to c tanh(x/c): for x = 100 and c = 30, 30 tanh(3.33) is about 29.9. The logit is squashed close to the cap, and the gradient factor 1 - tanh^2 is about 0.005.

Attention alternatives and mixtures of experts

lecture_04.pdf long-context attention linear attention / SSM hybrids DeepSeek sparse attention MoE routing load balancing MLA
TL;DR. Two ways to make the Transformer cheaper without making it dumber. (1) Attention alternatives. Dense attention costs \(O(n^2)\) in context length \(n\). The "basic toolkit" is local (sliding window) + global/strided patterns plus good kernels (FlashAttention). The radical option is linear attention: reorder \((QK^\top)V = Q(K^\top V)\) so that attention becomes an RNN with a fixed-size matrix state \(S_t=S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top\). Adding data-dependent gates gives Mamba-2, adding an erase-along-the-key "delta rule" gives Gated DeltaNet. Production models mix a few full-attention layers with many linear ones (MiniMax M1 7:1, Nemotron 3 / Qwen 3.5 about 3:1), or keep dense attention but attend sparsely with a cheap learned indexer (DeepSeek Sparse Attention, DSA). (2) Mixture of experts. Replace the one big FFN by \(N\) FFN "experts" and a router that sends each token to its top-\(k\); total parameters grow with \(N\) while FLOPs grow only with \(k\). Almost everyone uses token-choice top-\(k\) routing; DeepSeek-style fine-grained + shared experts are common; training uses heuristic load-balancing losses (Switch loss, or DeepSeek-V3's bias-based "aux-loss-free" balancing), a float32 router and a router z-loss for stability. We finish by walking through DeepSeek MoE v1, v2, v3, and the two extras that make V3 work: MLA (latent KV cache) and MTP (multi-token prediction).

The slides are text-light and figure-heavy, and there is no executable lecture_04.py. Everything below is reconstructed from the slides; code blocks are short illustrative implementations written for this guide (and run to check the numbers quoted in them), not code shown in class. Where I add a number that is not on a slide (for example the MLA dimensions of DeepSeek-V3) I say so.

Cost of attention at long context, and the basic toolkit

The lecture opens with an observation: advertised context windows keep growing (the slide plots context window against release date, 2018-2025, for many labs), yet attention is the one operation whose cost grows quadratically with that window. The second plot on the slide shows per-layer compute against sequence length (0 to 15000 tokens): the feed-forward cost is a straight line, the attention cost is a parabola that overtakes it. The question for the first half of the lecture: how do we control those costs?

Per token and per layer, with model width \(d\), a context of \(n\) keys, MHA projections (\(4d^2\) weights, so \(8d^2\) FLOPs) and a non-gated 4x FFN (\(8d^2\) weights, \(16d^2\) FLOPs):

\[ F_{\text{proj+FFN}} = 8d^2 + 16d^2 = 24d^2, \qquad F_{\text{score}} = \underbrace{2nd}_{QK^\top} + \underbrace{2nd}_{\text{weights}\times V} = 4nd . \]

The two are equal at \(n^\star = 6d\). For \(d=4096\) that is about 25K tokens: beyond it, attention dominates a layer. (Causal prefill averages over positions, so the score term is about half this per token; decode pays the full \(4nd\) plus a read of the whole KV cache from memory.) Play with it:

The "basic" toolkit: local + global attention and systems engineering

Before anything radical, the lecture lists what already works: (a) combine local and global attention, and (b) systems engineering (kernels that never materialise the \(n\times n\) matrix). Both leave the model a standard softmax-attention Transformer.

Sparse masks: what each query may see

  • Sliding window / local (Longformer): query \(i\) sees keys \(i-w+1,\dots,i\). Cost per query \(O(w)\), total \(O(nw)\). Information still propagates: after \(L\) layers the receptive field is \(Lw\).
  • Dilated window: same count of keys but spaced out, larger receptive field.
  • Strided (Sparse Transformer, OpenAI 2019): the last \(l\) positions plus every \(l\)-th position back. With \(l\approx\sqrt n\) the cost is \(O(n\sqrt n)\).
  • Fixed (Sparse Transformer): attend inside your own block of length \(l\) plus the last \(c\) "summary" columns of every block.
  • Global tokens (Longformer): a few positions (e.g. [CLS], question tokens) attend to everything and are attended by everything. Sliding + global = \(O(n(w+g))\).

GPT-3 alternated dense and locally banded sparse layers; the slide's bottom-left diagram shows several local layers followed by a global layer (and "last layer is always global"). The same local-plus-occasional-global recipe survives in modern models.

Systems engineering: FlashAttention

The right panel of slide 3 is the other half of the toolkit: FlashAttention keeps the exact \(O(n^2)\) arithmetic but tiles the computation so the score matrix never leaves on-chip memory (see the GPU lecture). On an A100 the lecture's bar chart (attention forward+backward, TFLOPs/s) reads:

The slide's punchline: "But what if we want more radical and potentially large gains?" That motivates changing the operator itself.

Linear attention, Mamba-2 and gated delta nets

The reordering trick

For \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_k}\), \(K\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_k}\), \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_v}\), attention is \(\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\rho(QK^\top)V\) with \(\rho\) the (row-)softmax. Forming \(QK^\top\) costs \(n^2d_k\) and multiplying by \(V\) costs \(n^2d_v\). If \(\rho\) is the identity (or a feature map applied to \(Q,K\) separately, as in Katharopoulos et al. 2020, after Shen et al. 2018), associativity of matrix multiplication lets us group differently:

\[ (QK^\top)V \;=\; Q\,(K^\top V),\qquad \underbrace{n^2d_k+n^2d_v}_{\text{quadratic}}\;\longrightarrow\;\underbrace{2\,n\,d_k d_v}_{\text{linear in }n}. \]

The lecture's comment: "this is very silly, but surprisingly important". Silly because dropping the softmax removes the nonlinearity that gives attention its sharp retrieval; important because of what comes next. (For causal models the parallel form needs a lower-triangular mask on \(QK^\top\) before multiplying by \(V\), and the reordering is then replaced by the recurrence below.)

The recurrent form: attention is an RNN with a matrix state

Process tokens left to right and keep the running sum \(S_t=\sum_{s\le t}k_sv_s^\top\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_v}\):

\[ S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top,\qquad y_t = q_t^\top S_t . \]

Inference is now \(O(d_kd_v)\) per token with a constant-size state, no KV cache growing with \(n\). The "duality": train with the parallel (quadratic, matmul-friendly) form, decode with the serial (linear) form. If you additionally weight the old state by a scalar \(\gamma\), \(S_t=\gamma S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top\), you get RetNet.

Check it yourself

The two forms give the same output for a causal model. Run this (checked here, max difference about \(4\times10^{-7}\)):

import torch
torch.manual_seed(0)
n, dk, dv = 6, 4, 3
Q, K, V = torch.randn(n, dk), torch.randn(n, dk), torch.randn(n, dv)

# parallel (training) form: causal-masked (Q K^T) V, quadratic in n
mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(n, n))
y_par = ((Q @ K.T) * mask) @ V

# recurrent (inference) form: constant-size state S in R^{dk x dv}
S = torch.zeros(dk, dv); ys = []
for t in range(n):
    S = S + torch.outer(K[t], V[t])      # S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T
    ys.append(Q[t] @ S)                  # y_t = q_t^T S_t
y_rec = torch.stack(ys)
assert torch.allclose(y_par, y_rec, atol=1e-5)          # same function
# without a mask the reordering is plain associativity:
assert torch.allclose((Q @ K.T) @ V, Q @ (K.T @ V), atol=1e-5)

From linear attention to Mamba-2: add a gate

Plain linear attention accumulates forever and cannot forget. Slide 7 generalises with a per-position scalar gate \(\gamma_t\) and a skip term:

\[ \text{Linear attn: } S_t=S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top,\ y_t=q_t^\top S_t \qquad\qquad \text{Mamba-2: } S_t=\gamma_t S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top,\ \ y_t=q_t^\top S_t+v_t^\top D,\ \ \gamma_t=f(x_t). \]

The decay is input-dependent: the model decides how much of the past to keep at every token ("gating is good!"). The duality survives: \(\gamma\) can be computed for all positions in parallel and folded into a masked, decayed parallel form, so training stays matmul-friendly (the lecture defers the proof to the Mamba-2 paper, "structured state space duality"). The slide also shows the Mamba block diagrams (sequential and parallel Mamba blocks).

Gated DeltaNet: gate the input and erase along the key

Slide 9 pushes one more step:

\[ S_t=\gamma_t\,(I-\beta_t k_tk_t^\top)\,S_{t-1}+\beta_t k_tv_t^\top,\qquad y_t=q_t^\top S_t,\qquad \gamma_t=f(x_t),\ \beta_t=f(x_t). \]
  • \(\beta_t\) is a "no input operation" gate: with \(\beta_t=0\) the token writes nothing and the state only decays.
  • \((I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)\) erases whatever was stored in the direction of the current key before writing the new value. For \(\|k_t\|=1,\beta_t=1\) the update is \(S_t=S_{t-1}+k_t(v_t-k_t^\top S_{t-1})^\top\): it writes only the prediction error, the delta rule from fast-weight programmers / test-time training (the state \(S\) is a tiny linear model trained online to map keys to values).
modelstate updatewhat the gate does
Linear attention\(S_t=S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top\)nothing: pure accumulation
RetNet\(S_t=\gamma S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top\)fixed scalar decay
Mamba-2\(S_t=\gamma_tS_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top\), \(+v_t^\top D\) in the outputdata-dependent decay
Gated DeltaNet\(S_t=\gamma_t(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)S_{t-1}+\beta_tk_tv_t^\top\)data-dependent decay, selective write strength, erase along \(k_t\)

A toy associative-memory experiment shows why the delta rule helps. Store \(N\) random unit-norm key/value pairs in a \(d\times d\) state, then try to retrieve each value with its own key, \(\hat v_i=k_i^\top S\). The relative error is \(\|\hat v_i-v_i\|/\|v_i\|\) (averaged over stored pairs). This is a miniature simulation written for this guide (seeded random data, not from the slides): with fixed capacity \(d^2\), both rules degrade when \(N\) approaches \(d\), but the delta rule degrades more gracefully, and when a key is re-written with a new value, the plain sum returns old+new while the delta rule returns the new value.

Hybrid models: a little full attention, a lot of linear

Linear/state-space layers are cheap and have constant-size state, but recall of exact tokens from far back is their weakness. The practical answer is a hybrid: mostly linear (or SSM) layers, with a full softmax-attention layer every few blocks. The lecture shows four data points.

Is a hybrid actually good? The evidence is thin

The lecture is candid: "not many controlled ablations, but some evidence of low losses at small hybrid ratios." The slide shows the ByteDance Seed / UC Santa Cruz paper A Systematic Analysis of Hybrid Linear Attention (Wang et al.): a table of update rules (vector-state RNNs such as HGRN / Hawk; outer-product matrix-state models RetNet, GLA, Mamba-2, RWKV-6, HGRN-2; and the delta-rule family DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet), then RULER sub-task accuracy and average recall as a function of the linear:full ratio (3:1, 6:1, 12:1, 24:1, pure linear). The pattern the slide points to: recall is best at small linear:full ratios and deteriorates toward pure linear. Read it as: a modest number of full-attention layers recovers most of what linear layers lose.

Sparse adaptation: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)

An alternative to replacing softmax attention is to keep it but let each query attend to only \(k\) well-chosen keys. Slide 12 shows the prototype used in DeepSeek-V3.2 (and GLM-5): a lightning indexer computes a cheap relevance score between the query token \(h_t\) and every preceding token \(h_s\),

\[ I_{t,s}=\sum_{j=1}^{H^I} w^I_{t,j}\;\mathrm{ReLU}\!\big(q^I_{t,j}\cdot k^I_s\big), \]

where \(H^I\) is a small number of indexer heads and \(q^I_{t,j},w^I_{t,j}\) are derived from the query token, \(k^I_s\) from the preceding token. ReLU instead of softmax keeps the indexer light. A fine-grained token selection keeps the entries with the top-\(k\) index scores, and the main attention runs only over those: \(u_t=\mathrm{Attn}\big(h_t,\{c_s\mid I_{t,s}\in\mathrm{Top\text{-}k}(I_{t,:})\}\big)\). The slide's two takeaways: "the indexer can be very lightweight, giving significant gains" and it can be adapted post hoc to a model pretrained densely on short context (first a warm-up that trains only the indexer, then continued training of everything).

The slide's RULER table for GLM-4.7-Flash with DSA. "Warm-up" trains only the indexer with the base model frozen; "DSA" trains both jointly for 150B tokens:

The next calculator shows why the decode-cost curve flattens. The cost model is an assumption of mine (the shape matches the slide's plot): per attended key the main attention costs 1 unit, per scanned key the indexer costs a fraction \(r\) of that.

Cheaper KV caches: MQA, GQA and MLA

MLA appears at the end of the lecture as "what else you need to make DeepSeek-V3", but it belongs here: it attacks the same long-context cost from the memory side. During decoding the dominant cost is reading the KV cache, which holds \(2\,L\,h_{kv}\,d_h\) numbers per token (keys and values, \(L\) layers, \(h_{kv}\) KV heads of dimension \(d_h\)).

  • MHA: \(h_{kv}=h\), one KV pair per query head.
  • MQA: \(h_{kv}=1\), all query heads share one K and V. Cache shrinks by \(h\), quality drops a little.
  • GQA: \(h_{kv}=g\) with \(1\lt g\lt h\), groups of query heads share a KV head. In the GQA paper's T5-XXL numbers (below), GQA-8 is nearly as fast as MQA at near-MHA quality.
  • MLA (DeepSeek-V2): cache a low-rank latent \(c_t^{KV}\) (plus a small RoPE key) and reconstruct per-head K and V from it.

MLA: express K and V through a low-dimensional latent

Slides 57 and 58. Compress the hidden state into a latent, then expand it per head:

\[ c_t^{KV}=W^{DKV}h_t,\qquad k_t^{C}=W^{UK}c_t^{KV},\qquad v_t^{C}=W^{UV}c_t^{KV}. \]

Benefit: when KV-caching we only store \(c_t^{KV}\) (dimension \(d_c\), 512 in DeepSeek-V2/V3), "which can be much smaller". Moreover \(W^{UK}\) can be merged into the query projection, so per-head keys are never materialised. (The slide notes that queries are compressed too, \(c_t^Q=W^{DQ}h_t\), \(q_t^C=W^{UQ}c_t^Q\), for memory savings during training.)

Complexity: RoPE conflicts with latent caching. Without RoPE the score is \(\langle hW^Q,\,W^{UK}c^{KV}\rangle=\langle h\,W^QW^{UK\top},\,c^{KV}\rangle\): the two matrices fuse (marked red on the slide). With RoPE a position-dependent rotation sits between them, \(\langle hW^QR_q,\;R_kW^{UK}c^{KV}\rangle\), and cannot be absorbed because it changes with position. Solution: keep a few extra non-latent key dimensions (\(d_r=64\) in V2/V3) that carry RoPE and are cached separately. Per layer and token the cache is \(d_c+d_r\) numbers.

Interactive: KV-cache size for MHA, GQA, MQA and MLA

Defaults are DeepSeek-V3 style: 61 layers, 128 heads of dimension 128, \(d_c=512\), \(d_r=64\) (these dimensions come from the DeepSeek papers, not the slides). GQA uses 8 KV heads. The MHA, GQA and MQA rows are counterfactuals (V3 uses MLA). MLA gives \(61\times576=35{,}136\) elements per token, versus \(61\times 2\times128\times128\approx 2.0\)M for MHA.

The ablation from the DeepSeek-V2 paper (MoE models with MHA vs MLA at two sizes) shows MLA is not just smaller but at least as good, while for dense 7B models MHA beats GQA-8, which beats MQA:

Mixture of experts: what and why

Slide 15 (Fedus et al. 2022): replace the big feed-forward network by many big feed-forward networks plus a selector (router) layer. Only a few experts run for each token, so you can increase the number of experts without affecting FLOPs. For a token \(x\) with \(N\) experts and top-\(k\) routing:

\[ y=\sum_{i\in \mathrm{Top}\text{-}k(s(x))} g_i(x)\,E_i(x),\qquad s(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_r x). \]

Total parameters scale with \(N\); compute per token scales with \(k\). The usual placement is: replace the MLP by an MoE layer; less common is MoE for attention heads (ModuleFormer, JetMoE). The slide's opening image also lists GPT-4 (rumoured MoE, hence the question mark), Grok, DeepSeek-MoE / V3, Llama 4 and OLMoE.

A minimal MoE layer

Short PyTorch module written for this guide (shapes and parameter count checked: \(d=16\), 8 experts, hidden 32, \(k=2\) gives \(8\times1072+128=8704\) parameters). It shows the whole mechanism: float32 router, top-\(k\), renormalised gates, per-expert dispatch.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, d, dff, E, k):
        super().__init__(); s.k = k
        s.router  = nn.Linear(d, E, bias=False)                       # W_r
        s.experts = nn.ModuleList([nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, dff), nn.GELU(),
                                                 nn.Linear(dff, d)) for _ in range(E)])
    def forward(s, x):                          # x: (tokens, d)
        logits = s.router(x.float())            # router in float32 (stability)
        p = logits.softmax(-1)                  # s_{i,t}
        w, idx = p.topk(s.k, -1)                # top-k experts per token
        w = w / w.sum(-1, keepdim=True)         # renormalise the k gates
        y = torch.zeros_like(x)
        for e, ex in enumerate(s.experts):      # dispatch: only tokens routed to e
            tok, slot = (idx == e).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
            if len(tok): y[tok] += w[tok, slot, None] * ex(x[tok])
        return x + y, p, idx                    # residual + routed experts

m = MoE(d=16, dff=32, E=8, k=2)
out, p, idx = m(torch.randn(10, 16))
sum(q.numel() for q in m.parameters())          # 8704 = 8 experts x 1072 + router 128

Interactive: routing step-through

Why MoEs are getting popular

  1. Same FLOPs, more parameters, better loss (slide 16, Fedus et al. 2022): with compute per token fixed, test loss falls smoothly as the number of experts goes 1, 2, 4, ..., 256.
  2. Faster to train (slide 17): Switch-Base reaches T5-Base's final perplexity about 7x faster. OLMoE (1.3B active, 6.9B total, 128 H100s) against a 1.3B dense model needs roughly 3x fewer FLOPs or tokens for the same HellaSwag, and is about 2x faster in wall-clock.
  3. Highly competitive with dense models (slide 18): MMLU vs activated parameters; DeepSeek-V2 sits at the top left, ahead of Mixtral, DBRX, Qwen1.5, Llama 2/3 and Command R at equal active size.
  4. Parallelizable to many devices (slide 19): each expert FFN fits on a device and experts are placed on different accelerators (expert parallelism, see the systems section).

Evidence from the "results" slides

  • From the West (slide 20): Llama 4 Maverick against Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek v3.1 and GPT-4o. Maverick: cost $0.19-0.49 per 1M tokens (3:1 blended) versus $4.38 for GPT-4o; MMMU 73.4, MathVista 73.7, ChartQA 90.0, DocVQA 94.4, LiveCodeBench 43.4, MMLU Pro 80.5, GPQA Diamond 69.8. Also the OpenAI gpt-oss models (Humanity's Last Exam) and Grok. Takeaway: MoEs are most of the highest-performing open models, and they are quick.
  • Qwen (slide 21): Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B is on par with 7B dense models at 2.7B active parameters (table below).
  • DeepSeek ablations (slide 22): dense vs hash-routed vs Switch at identical FLOPs (chart below).
  • DeepSeek-V3 (slide 23): the 671B MoE against DeepSeek-V2.5, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3.1-405B, GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet on MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500, AIME 2024, Codeforces and SWE-bench Verified; V3 leads the open models on most.

Why not everyone yet?

  • Infrastructure is complex. Sparsity pays off when you have many accelerators: data parallelism puts different slices of data on different machines, and experts add a model-parallel dimension. At small scale the advantage mostly disappears, and serving needs many machines just to hold all the experts (Fedus et al.).
  • Training objectives are heuristic and sometimes unstable (Zoph et al. 2022): the slide shows a training-loss curve with a large spike. Both are treated below.

Routing functions

Slide 26 ("MoE: what varies?"): (1) the routing function, (2) expert sizes, (3) training objectives. Slide 27 (Fedus et al.): many routing algorithms boil down to "choose top-\(k\)", along different axes of the token-by-expert score matrix.

  • Token chooses expert (token-choice top-\(k\)): every token picks its \(k\) best experts. Loads can be uneven.
  • Expert chooses token (expert-choice): every expert picks its top-\(c\) tokens: perfectly balanced loads, but some tokens may get no expert and others many.
  • Global routing via optimisation: solve a matching / linear assignment problem over the whole batch (BASE layers, used in papers like Clark et al. 2022).

Slide 28 shows a recent ablation: "almost all the MoEs do standard token-choice top-\(k\)". Token-choice (TC) beats expert-choice (EC) in training loss, C4 validation loss and HellaSwag; MMLU-var is similar.

Interactive: three routing rules on the same scores

In the DeepSeekMoE table above, even a hash layer (no learned router) beats a dense model at the same FLOPs: part of the MoE gain is simply "more parameters, selected somehow". Learned routing (Switch) adds a further, consistent gain. Older routing ideas such as RL-learned routes (Bengio et al. 2013) and linear-assignment routing are not common now.

Top-k routing in detail

Slide 31 (Dai et al. 2024) writes the DeepSeek v1/v2 layer for token \(t\) at layer \(l\), with hidden state \(u_t^l\):

\[ h_t^l=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big(g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t^l)\big)+u_t^l,\quad g_{i,t}=\begin{cases}s_{i,t},& s_{i,t}\in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}\mid 1\le j\le N\},K)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\quad s_{i,t}=\mathrm{Softmax}_i\big(u_t^{l\top}e_i^l\big). \]

The gate is a logistic-regression-like linear classifier over experts (the \(e_i\) are learned expert centroids). This "softmax, then top-\(k\), no renormalisation" ordering is the DeepSeek v1/2 router (Grok and Qwen do it too). Mixtral, DBRX and DeepSeek-V3 instead apply the normalising non-linearity after the top-\(k\) (V3 uses sigmoid affinities and divides by the sum of the selected ones).

Expert sizes: fine-grained and shared experts

Slide 32, from DeepSeekMoE (the idea comes from DeepSpeed-MoE and is used by DeepSeek and Qwen): use smaller but more numerous experts (split each FFN into \(m\) pieces of width \(1/m\) and route to \(m\) times as many) plus a few shared experts that are always on. The three panels: (a) conventional top-2 over \(N\) experts; (b) fine-grained segmentation, \(2N\) experts with \(K=4\); (c) shared-expert isolation, one shared expert plus \(K=3\) routed (DeepSeekMoE).

Why it helps: top-2 of 8 experts gives 28 combinations; top-8 of 64 experts gives \(\binom{64}{8}\approx4.4\times10^9\). Shared experts hold common knowledge so routed experts can specialise. Ablations: in the DeepSeekMoE paper (slide 33) "more experts, shared experts all seem to generally help" (four configurations compared on HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC, TriviaQA, NaturalQuestions: GShard-like, plus shared-expert isolation, plus fine-grained segmentation, and both). OLMoE (slide 34) disagrees on shared experts: gains from fine-grained experts (8, 32, 64 experts at matched active parameters), none from shared experts (32 routed vs 31 routed + 1 shared are indistinguishable).

Interactive: active vs total parameters

An MoE FFN has \(3\,d\,d_e\) parameters per expert (gated FFN) and a router of \(d\,N_r\) per layer. Active parameters count the \(k\) routed plus shared experts; attention, embeddings and dense layers are always active. The presets use the public configs (my arithmetic reproduces the published totals: Mixtral 46.7B / 12.9B, OLMoE 6.9B / 1.3B, DeepSeekMoE-16B 16.4B / 2.8B, DeepSeek-V3 671B / 37.6B; attention dimensions are from the model papers, not the slides). Pick "custom" to use the sliders.

Training MoEs: non-differentiable routing and load balancing

Slide 36: the major challenge is that we need sparsity for training-time efficiency, but sparse gating decisions are not differentiable. Three families of solutions: (1) reinforcement learning to optimise the gating policy, (2) stochastic perturbations, (3) heuristic "balancing" losses. The lecture asks "guess which one people use in practice?" The answer is (3).

1. Reinforcement learning

Slide 37: REINFORCE-style RL for the router does work (Bengio et al. 2013; Clark et al. 2020 compare S-BASE, RL-R with a REINFORCE baseline, Hash, and others across expert counts 1 to 512 on validation loss), "but not so much better that it is a clear win". RL is the "right solution", but gradient variance and complexity mean it is not widely used.

2. Stochastic approximations

  • Shazeer et al. 2017 (slide 38): add Gaussian noise before the top-\(k\): \[ G(x)=\mathrm{Softmax}(\mathrm{KeepTopK}(H(x),k)),\quad H(x)_i=(xW_g)_i+\mathrm{StandardNormal}()\cdot\mathrm{Softplus}((xW_{noise})_i), \] with \(\mathrm{KeepTopK}(v,k)_i=v_i\) if \(v_i\) is among the top \(k\), else \(-\infty\). Effects: experts become a bit more robust, and the softmax lets the model learn to rank the \(K\) experts.
  • Fedus et al. 2022 (slide 39): multiplicative uniform jitter on the router logits, router_logits *= uniform(1-eps, 1+eps), done with the router in float32. Same goal of less brittle experts. It was later removed by Zoph et al. 2022: in the slide's stability table, baseline is stable in 4 of 6 runs (quality -1.755 plus-minus 0.02), input jitter 10-2 in 3 of 3 (-1.777 plus-minus 0.03), dropout 0.1 in 3 of 3 (-1.822 plus-minus 0.11): jitter helps stability but costs quality.

3. Heuristic balancing losses

Systems efficiency requires that experts are used evenly (an overloaded expert is a straggler, an idle expert is wasted capacity). The Switch Transformer auxiliary loss for \(N\) experts and a batch \(\mathcal B\) of \(T\) tokens (slide 40):

\[ \text{loss}=\alpha\,N\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i\,P_i,\qquad f_i=\frac1T\sum_{x\in\mathcal B}\mathbb 1\{\arg\max p(x)=i\},\qquad P_i=\frac1T\sum_{x\in\mathcal B}p_i(x). \]

\(f_i\) is the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert \(i\) (non-differentiable), \(P_i\) the fraction of router probability mass given to it (differentiable). With perfectly uniform \(f_i=P_i=1/N\) the sum is \(1/N\) and the loss equals \(\alpha\), its minimum. The derivative with respect to \(p_i(x)\) is \(\frac{\alpha N}{T^2}\sum\mathbb 1\{\arg\max p(x)=i\}\propto f_i\): the more frequently an expert is used, the stronger it is downweighted.

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
def switch_aux_loss(p, idx, alpha=1e-2):         # p: (T, E) router probs, idx: (T, k) chosen experts
    T, E = p.shape; k = idx.shape[1]
    f = F.one_hot(idx, E).sum(1).float().mean(0) / k   # fraction of dispatches per expert
    P = p.mean(0)                                      # mean router probability per expert
    return alpha * E * (f * P).sum()
# uniform routing gives exactly alpha (0.0100); a skewed router gives more:
# skewed logits (E=8, T=4096, k=2): 0.0141

DeepSeek v1/v2: per-expert and per-device balancing (slide 41)

With \(N'\) routed experts, \(K'\) selected, \(T\) tokens and affinities \(s_{i,t}\):

\[ \mathcal L_{\text{ExpBal}}=\alpha_1\sum_{i=1}^{N'} f_iP_i,\quad f_i=\frac{N'}{K'T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb 1(\text{token }t\text{ selects expert }i),\quad P_i=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T s_{i,t}. \]

This is the Switch loss (the factor \(N'/K'\) in \(f_i\) plays the role of Switch's \(N\)). Per-device balancing is the same objective aggregated by device: with experts split in \(D\) groups \(\mathcal E_1,\dots,\mathcal E_D\), \(\mathcal L_{\text{DevBal}}=\alpha_2\sum_{i=1}^D f_i'P_i'\), \(f_i'=\frac1{|\mathcal E_i|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal E_i}f_j\), \(P_i'=\sum_{j\in\mathcal E_i}P_j\) (the devices are what systems efficiency actually cares about).

DeepSeek-V3: per-expert biases, "auxiliary-loss-free" balancing (slide 42)

V3 adds a per-expert bias \(b_i\) used only for selection, not for the gate value:

\[ g'_{i,t}=\begin{cases}s_{i,t},& s_{i,t}+b_i\in\mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}+b_j\mid 1\le j\le N_r\},K_r)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \]

The bias is adjusted by online learning: after each step, \(b_i\mathrel{-}=\gamma\) for overloaded experts and \(b_i\mathrel{+}=\gamma\) for underloaded ones (make a loaded expert less likely to get tokens, a starved one more likely). No gradient flows through \(b\), so the loss is not polluted. "But the approach is not fully aux-loss free": V3 still adds a tiny complementary sequence-wise auxiliary loss \(\mathcal L_{\text{Bal}}=\alpha\sum_i f_iP_i'\) (with \(P'_i\) from normalised scores) to prevent extreme imbalance inside a single sequence.

def update_bias(bias, sel, E, gamma=1e-2):       # sel: (T, k) selected expert ids this step
    load = F.one_hot(sel, E).sum((0, 1)).float()
    return bias + gamma * torch.sign(load.mean() - load)   # overloaded -> bias down, starved -> up
# selection: topk(sigmoid(logits) + bias); gate value uses sigmoid(logits) only (then normalised)

(The bias is added at 4x the scale of the scores in the simulation just to make it converge in a few dozen steps; the point is the shape: unbalanced routing stays at a high straggler load forever, a very small \(\gamma\) is slow, a moderate \(\gamma\) pulls it to about 1.2 within tens of steps, and a large \(\gamma\) gets there in a few steps but then jitters.)

What happens when load balancing is removed? (slide 43, OLMoE)

OLMoE Figures 9-10: without the load-balancing loss (LBL) the training and validation losses are worse, and expert assignment in the first MoE layer collapses: within the first billion tokens, one or two experts receive almost all the tokens (up to about 100% for a single expert early on, later two experts at 40-70%), the other experts get nothing and receive no gradient, so they never recover. With the LBL, all 8 experts hover near 12.5%.

Training MoEs: the systems side

MoEs parallelize nicely: each expert FFN can fit on one device, which enables expert parallelism on top of data / model parallelism. Slide 44 shows the GShard-style layout (all-to-all dispatch of tokens to the device that holds their expert, expert FFNs run locally, all-to-all combine) and the standard picture of how weights and data are split over cores for data parallel, model parallel, model+data, expert+data, expert+model+data.

But routing creates complexity: the number of tokens per expert is data-dependent. Slide 45 (MegaBlocks) shows three ways to compute the expert matmuls:

  1. Batched matmul: pad every expert to the same capacity (tokens beyond it are dropped): simple, but wastes compute on padding and drops tokens.
  2. Block-diagonal matmul: the same thing written as one matmul with a block-diagonal matrix, equal-sized blocks.
  3. Block-sparse matmul: variable-sized blocks along the diagonal, so load-imbalanced routing and different-sized experts are computed exactly with no dropping and no padding.

"Modern libraries like MegaBlocks (used in many open MoEs) use smarter sparse matrix multiplication."

Capacity factor and token dropping

With a fixed buffer of \(C=c_f\cdot Tk/E\) slots per expert, overflow tokens are dropped. The calculator estimates how many assignments are lost for a given load imbalance, treating expert popularity as a smooth skew.

MoE parallelism and architecture changes (slide 46)

New ideas from Nemotron 3: "LatentMoE": down-project the activations into a smaller latent dimension before the all-to-all dispatch, run the experts in the latent space, and up-project after the combine. All-to-all communication volume (the MoE bottleneck) shrinks in proportion, so the savings can be spent on more or bigger experts for the same bandwidth.

A fun side issue: stochasticity of MoE models

Slide 47: MoEs have extra non-determinism. Token dropping from capacity overflow happens at the batch level, so tokens of different users compete for the same expert slots: other people's queries can drop your token, and the output of your prompt can depend on what else was in the batch (the slide's permutation figure: (1) route, (2) permute and drop tokens that exceed expert capacity, (3) compute, (4) un-permute and scale).

Stability: float32 router and the z-loss

Slide 48 (Zoph et al. 2022): MoE training has loss spikes. The router's softmax is the culprit: exponentials amplify small perturbations. The paper's footnote: with 10 logits of value 128 and one logit 128.5, a bfloat16 roundoff of 0.5 changes the softmax output by 36% (the probability of that dominant logit goes from \(\approx 0.142\) to \(\approx 0.091\)), because bfloat16 cannot represent 128.5 and rounds the value. Our own check in bf16 rounding: 128.5 rounds to 128, 129.5 to 130, so resolution at this magnitude is 1.0.

Solution: use float32 just for the expert router, and sometimes add an auxiliary z-loss that penalises large router logits:

\[ L_z(x)=\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\Big(\log\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{x^{(i)}_j}\Big)^2 . \]

The log-sum-exp is the log-normaliser of the softmax; squaring it keeps it close to 0 (logits near 0), so the exponentials stay in a safe numerical range. Slide 49 (OLMoE, loss weight 0.001): without the z-loss, training loss and the C4 validation loss show large spikes, HellaSwag drops, MMLU-var is noisier. With it, curves are smooth.

def router_z_loss(logits, weight=1e-3):          # logits: (tokens, E), float32
    return weight * torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1).pow(2).mean()
# bf16 failure mode: the max logit is subtracted for stability, then the rounding of
# 128.5 -> 128 changes softmax weights by ~36% (Zoph et al. footnote)

Fine-tuning (slide 50)

Sparse MoEs can overfit on smaller fine-tuning data (SuperGLUE curves in the slide: sparse models reach higher training accuracy but lower validation). Zoph et al.'s solution: fine-tune only the non-MoE parameters; the slide's bar chart compares updating all parameters, non-MoE, MoE-only, attention-only and FFN-only, and updating only non-MoE parameters is about as good as all while MoE-only is much worse. The DeepSeek solution: use lots of data, 1.4M SFT examples (code, math, writing, QA, reasoning, summarisation, in English and Chinese).

Upcycling: initialising an MoE from a dense model

Slide 51: can a pretrained dense LM initialise a MoE? Yes: upcycling copies the dense FFN weights into every expert (attention, embeddings and norms are copied once), adds a freshly initialised router, and continues training. The slide's left figure shows the original dense block and the upcycled block; the right plot (C4 validation token accuracy against extra pretraining time in TPU-core-days, for Base, Large and XL models) shows upcycled models improving faster than simply continuing to train the dense model.

MiniCPM-MoE (slide 52): initialised from MiniCPM-2.4B, top-\(k\)=2 of 8 experts, about 4B active parameters, 13.6B total, about 520B tokens of training. Gains over the base model:

balancingexpert-level + device-level aux loss+ communication balancing lossaux-loss-free bias + small sequence-wise aux loss
attentionstandard MHAMLAMLA (+ MTP)

V2 new things (slide 55): Top-M device routing: for each token first select the \(M\) devices with the highest affinity scores, then do the top-\(K\) among experts on those \(M\) devices; with \(M\ge3\) quality is roughly aligned with unrestricted top-\(K\). This bounds the fan-out of the all-to-all. The communication balancing loss \(\mathcal L_{\text{CommBal}}=\alpha_3\sum_{i=1}^D f_i''P_i''\) (with \(f_i''=\frac{D}{MT}\sum_t\mathbb 1(\text{token }t\text{ is sent to device }i)\)) balances communication both in and out: each device should receive about \(MT\) hidden states. V3 new things (slide 56): sigmoid affinities \(s_{i,t}=\mathrm{Sigmoid}(u_t^\top e_i)\), \(g'_{i,t}\) kept for the top-\(K_r\), then \(g_{i,t}=g'_{i,t}/\sum_{j}g'_{j,t}\); the output is \(h_t'=u_t+\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\mathrm{FFN}^{(s)}_i(u_t)+\sum_{i=1}^{N_r}g_{i,t}\mathrm{FFN}^{(r)}_i(u_t)\); aux-loss-free balancing; sequence-wise aux loss.

Bonus: what else you need to make DeepSeek V3 (slides 57 to 59)

  • MLA (above): cache a 512-dim latent plus a 64-dim RoPE key instead of per-head K, V.
  • MTP, multi-token prediction (slide 59): small, lightweight extra modules predict several steps ahead. Module \(k\) combines the previous depth's hidden state \(h_i^{k-1}\) with the embedding of the token \(t_{i+k}\): \(h_i'^k=M_k[\mathrm{RMSNorm}(h_i^{k-1});\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{Emb}(t_{i+k}))]\), passes through one Transformer block \(h^k_{1:T-k}=\mathrm{TRM}_k(h'^k_{1:T-k})\) and the shared output head \(P^k_{i+k+1}=\mathrm{OutHead}(h^k_i)\). Each module adds a cross-entropy loss on its target. V3 only uses MTP one token ahead (depth 1). The same idea is what speculative decoding drafters such as EAGLE use at inference (figure on the slide). See the paper for ablations.

MoE summary

  • MoEs take advantage of sparsity: not all inputs need the full model.
  • Discrete routing is hard, but top-\(k\) heuristics seem to work.
  • There is now lots of empirical evidence that MoEs work and are cost-effective.

Self-check quiz

Why does the reordering \((QK^\top)V=Q(K^\top V)\) not work for ordinary softmax attention, and what does the recurrent form of linear attention buy at inference?
Softmax is applied element-wise to the \(n\times n\) score matrix \(QK^\top\) before multiplying by \(V\); it is not linear, so you cannot move \(Q\) outside. Linear attention drops (or factorises) \(\rho\), so associativity applies: cost goes from \(n^2d_k+n^2d_v\) to \(2nd_kd_v\). Causally it is the recurrence \(S_t=S_{t-1}+k_tv_t^\top,\ y_t=q_t^\top S_t\): decoding needs only a fixed \(d_k\times d_v\) state per head (no growing KV cache) and \(O(d_kd_v)\) work per token, while training can still use the parallel masked-matmul form (the "duality").
What do Mamba-2's \(\gamma_t\) and Gated DeltaNet's \(\beta_t\) and \((I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)\) do to the state?
\(\gamma_t=f(x_t)\) is an input-dependent scalar decay: the model decides how much of the past state to keep. In Gated DeltaNet, \(\beta_t\) is the write strength (\(\beta_t=0\) is a "no input" step that writes nothing) and \((I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)\) erases whatever the state currently stores along the direction of the current key before the new \(k_tv_t^\top\) is added. With \(\|k\|=1,\beta=1\) this writes only the prediction error \(v_t-S_{t-1}^\top k_t\) (the delta rule, as in fast weights / test-time training), so re-writing a key replaces the old value instead of summing with it.
A 48-layer model has \(2h_{kv}d_h=2048\) KV numbers per layer. Compare the bf16 KV cache at 128K tokens for all-full attention and a 3:1 linear:full hybrid whose linear layers keep 0.5M state elements each.
All full: \(48\times131072\times2048\times2\) bytes \(\approx 25.8\) GB. Hybrid 3:1: 12 full layers give \(12\times131072\times2048\times2\approx6.4\) GB, and 36 linear layers give \(36\times524288\times2\approx37.7\) MB: total about 6.5 GB, roughly 4x smaller, and the linear part does not grow with \(n\). (Use the hybrid-cache calculator.)
Compute the KV cache per token of MLA for \(L=61,d_c=512,d_r=64\) and compare with MHA at 128 heads of dimension 128.
MLA: \(61\times(512+64)=35{,}136\) elements per token. MHA: \(2\times61\times128\times128=1{,}998{,}848\) elements per token, about 57x more. MQA would be \(2\times61\times128=15{,}616\) and GQA with 8 KV heads \(124{,}928\). MLA caches a latent plus a shared RoPE key; \(W^{UK}\) is absorbed into the query projection, and the RoPE part is kept separate because the position-dependent rotation prevents absorbing it.
Explain the Switch load-balancing loss \(\alpha N\sum_i f_iP_i\). Why use both \(f_i\) and \(P_i\), and what is its minimum?
\(f_i\) is the (non-differentiable) fraction of tokens dispatched to expert \(i\), \(P_i\) the (differentiable) mean router probability for it. The gradient flows through \(P_i\) and is weighted by \(f_i\): popular experts get pushed down more. With uniform \(f_i=P_i=1/N\) the sum is \(1/N\), so the loss is \(\alpha\), the minimum; any imbalance increases \(\sum f_iP_i\). Balance matters because the most loaded expert or device sets the step time and idle experts are wasted parameters; OLMoE shows that without it routing collapses onto 1 to 2 experts.
How does DeepSeek-V3 balance experts "without an auxiliary loss", and what is still not loss-free about it?
Each routed expert has a bias \(b_i\) added to its affinity only for top-\(k\) selection; the gate value still uses the unbiased score. After every step \(b_i\) is decreased by \(\gamma\) for overloaded experts and increased by \(\gamma\) for underloaded ones (online control, no gradient). That removes the interference of a balancing gradient with the language-modelling gradient. V3 still includes a very small sequence-wise auxiliary loss to avoid extreme imbalance within a single sequence, so it is "not fully aux-loss free".
Why does the router run in float32 and why add a z-loss?
The softmax over experts is an exponential: a small rounding error in a large logit changes probabilities a lot (Zoph et al.: in bfloat16, a 0.5 roundoff on a logit near 128 changes the softmax output by 36%). Float32 for the router reduces roundoff; the z-loss \(\frac1B\sum_i(\log\sum_je^{x_j^{(i)}})^2\) keeps the router logits small so the softmax stays in a numerically benign range. In OLMoE, removing the z-loss (weight 0.001) gives repeated loss spikes.

Key takeaways

  • Attention cost is \(O(n^2)\) in compute and \(O(n)\) in decode memory traffic (the KV cache). At layer level, attention scores overtake projections plus FFN at about \(n=6d\).
  • Basic toolkit: sliding-window and strided/global patterns (Longformer, Sparse Transformer) plus exact fast kernels (FlashAttention-2 about 176 TFLOP/s on an A100 on the slide).
  • Linear attention is an RNN with a matrix state: train in the parallel form, decode in the recurrent form. Gates make it expressive (Mamba-2 decay; Gated DeltaNet decay plus erase-and-write).
  • Hybrids are the production answer: MiniMax M1 7:1, Nemotron 3 and Qwen 3.5 about 3:1; controlled ablations are thin but favour small linear:full ratios.
  • DSA keeps dense attention but selects the top-\(k\) keys with a cheap ReLU indexer; it can be retrofitted by indexer warm-up then joint training.
  • MQA/GQA/MLA shrink the KV cache; MLA caches a 512-d latent plus a 64-d RoPE key (35K elements per token for V3 versus about 2M for MHA) with no quality loss in DeepSeek's ablation.
  • MoE gives more parameters at the same FLOPs: 7x faster than dense to equal perplexity (Switch), about 3x tokens / 2x wall-clock (OLMoE). Total memory is large, active parameters small.
  • Almost everyone uses token-choice top-\(k\); expert-choice and RL routing lose in practice. Trend: many small routed experts (up to 256) plus 0 to 4 shared experts. OLMoE: fine-grained helps, shared experts do not.
  • Training: sparse routing is not differentiable, so use heuristic balancing (Switch loss, per-device loss, V3 bias updates), a float32 router and a z-loss for stability; MoEs overfit small SFT sets; upcycling (MiniCPM-MoE, Qwen-MoE) works.
  • Systems: expert parallelism with all-to-all, block-sparse kernels (MegaBlocks), top-M device routing, LatentMoE down-projection to cut communication; batch-level token dropping makes outputs depend on co-batched requests.

GPUs

lecture_05.pdf GPU architecture memory hierarchy roofline matmul shapes FlashAttention

TL;DR. LLM progress now rides on parallel hardware: GPU parallel throughput grew more than 1000x in ten years while single-thread gains from Dennard scaling stopped. A GPU is many simple streaming multiprocessors (SMs) that run threads in lockstep groups of 32 (warps), with a memory hierarchy in which closer means faster and smaller. Most kernels are limited by bytes moved, not FLOPs, and the roofline model makes that precise. Every trick in this lecture (low precision, operator fusion, recomputation, coalescing, tiling) reduces bytes per FLOP. Shape matters too: tile-aligned, wave-friendly matrix dimensions keep the matmul units busy. FlashAttention combines tiling with an online softmax so the N x N attention matrix never has to be written to HBM.

This guide follows the lecture's three parts: (1) how GPUs work and what their parts are, (2) how to reason about GPU performance (roofline, the six tricks, and the "matrix mystery" of shape-dependent speed), and (3) putting it together to understand FlashAttention. Every number below comes from the slides or is derived from them; where I add a derivation or a model assumption I say so.

Why compute drives progress

The lecture starts from a simple observation: for language models, more compute predictably buys lower loss. The scaling-law curves of Kaplan et al. (2020) show validation loss falling as a power law in compute (PF-days), so faster hardware, better utilization and better parallelization translate directly into better models, at least for now.

The traditional source of hardware speed-up, Dennard scaling (roughly 1980 to the 2000s), has tapped out. Progress now comes from parallel scaling. The slide, adapted from Bill Dally's HotChips keynote, shows that parallel scaling with GPUs has grown by more than 1000x in about ten years. The lecture's conclusion: there is no LLM scaling without GPU scaling.

1000x+

over 20 years, 3.0x every 2 years
