13. Self-check quiz

A thread block has 128 threads and each thread uses 160 registers on an SM with 65,536 registers. How many blocks fit, and what is the occupancy?
Registers per block = 128 x 160 = 20,480. 65,536 / 20,480 = 3.2, so 3 blocks fit. That is 3 x 128 / 32 = 12 warps out of 64, so occupancy = 12 / 64 = 18.75% (0.1875).
Why does a bank conflict serialize accesses even when only some threads conflict, and when does it not happen?
Each bank serves one address per cycle. If several threads in a warp hit different addresses in the same bank, those accesses run one after another. Threads reading the exact same address are served together by broadcast, so they do not conflict. With a stride of s words, thread i uses bank (i x s) mod 32, and the conflict degree is gcd(s, 32). Stride 1 gives no conflicts; stride 32 gives a 32-way conflict; stride 33 gives none.
The lecture launches 160 thread blocks on a B200 (148 SMs). How many waves run, and what fraction of the SM-time is used?
Two waves: 148 blocks in the first, 12 in the second. Total SM-slots used across two waves = 2 x 148 = 296, and 160 are busy, so the efficiency is 160 / 296 = 54%. Choosing a block count that is a multiple of 148 (for example 148 or 296) avoids the partial wave.
Why does the naive GeLU need about 11x more HBM traffic than the fused kernel?
The eager version runs 9 ops. Counting reads and writes of an N-element float32 tensor gives 13 reads and 9 writes (22N passes), because every intermediate is written to HBM and read back. The fused kernel reads x once and writes y once (2N passes). 22 / 2 = 11. The lecture's trace shows 3.384 ms for the naive kernels and 0.305 ms for the fused one, a ratio of 11.1x.
Why does the benchmark call torch.cuda.synchronize() before starting the timer, and why use CUDA events?
CUDA kernel launches are asynchronous, so without synchronization the CPU timer measures the launch, not the GPU work. Warmup runs also need to finish before timing starts. CUDA events are recorded in the GPU stream, so they measure GPU time and not CPU overhead around the call. Synchronizing again before reading the elapsed time makes sure the end event has been reached.
In the softmax kernel, why is the row max subtracted before exponentiating, and why does the result not change?
exp(x) overflows in float32 for large x (for example exp(100) is about 2.7e43, which is above the float32 maximum of about 3.4e38 for inputs above about 88.7). Subtracting the max makes every exponent at most 0, so exp is at most 1. Softmax is invariant to adding a constant c to all inputs of a row: exp(x - c) / sum exp(x_j - c) = exp(x) / sum exp(x_j), since the factor exp(-c) cancels. In the example, exp(-100) is stored as a subnormal (about 3.78e-44), which is why the output row is [3.78e-44, 3.78e-44, 1.0].
In the tiled matmul with BLOCK_M = BLOCK_N = 64, how many times is each loaded element of A reused, and what is the arithmetic intensity?
Each element A[m, k] is used by every output column tile, i.e. by all BLOCK_N = 64 columns of its output tile, so it is reused 64 times per HBM load. In the formula, HBM reads per output tile scale as n^3 (1/BM + 1/BN) = n^3 / 32 elements, against 2n^3 for the naive kernel. Arithmetic intensity is 2n^3 FLOPs over 4 x n^3/32 bytes = 16 FLOP/byte (BM/4 in general), against 0.25 FLOP/byte naively.

Parallelism: collectives, hardware, and distributed training

lecture_07.py collective ops NCCL NVLink / InfiniBand data / tensor / pipeline parallelism torch.distributed
TL;DR. Lecture 6 made one GPU fast by avoiding trips to slow memory (fusion, tiling). Lecture 7 does the same one level up: with many GPUs the "slow memory" is another GPU, and the goal is to orchestrate computation so that as little data as possible crosses the slow links (NVLink within a node, InfiniBand/Ethernet across nodes). The vocabulary is a small set of collective operations (broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce, all-to-all); the three basic ways to cut a network are along the batch (data parallelism: all-reduce gradients), the width (tensor parallelism: all-gather activations in every layer, needs NVLink) and the depth (pipeline parallelism: point-to-point sends of activations, tolerates slow links but suffers pipeline bubbles).

1. Big picture: same theme, one level up

Last week was parallelism inside a single GPU; this week it is parallelism across GPUs. In both cases compute (the arithmetic units) is far from the data it needs, and the unifying theme is: orchestrate computation to avoid data-transfer bottlenecks.

The generalized memory hierarchy

LevelWhat it isSpeedTrick used to avoid it
1Single node, single GPU: L1 cache / shared memoryfastestfusion, tiling (lecture 6)
2Single node, single GPU: HBM~8 TB/s (B200)fusion, tiling
3Single node, multi-GPU: NVLink / NVSwitch1.8 TB/s per GPU (NVLink 5.0)replication / sharding (this lecture)
4Multi-node, multi-GPU: InfiniBand / Ethernet~0.05 TB/s; slowest
Why go multi-GPU at all?

(1) Your parameters + optimizer state + gradients + activations do not fit on one GPU. (2) You want more FLOPs to train faster. These two motives drive everything below: sharding fixes (1), data/pipeline splitting fixes (2), and the art is to get both without drowning in communication.

The trade you can make

For any piece of data you can re-compute it, keep it in local memory, or keep it in another GPU's memory and communicate it. All of the parallelism strategies are different points on this triangle (the lecture's summary says exactly this).

2. Collective operations: the programming model

Collective operations are the conceptual primitives of distributed programming; they date from the parallel-computing literature of the 1980s. Collective means you specify a general communication pattern over many devices and let the library implement it, which is both easier and usually faster than hand-managing point-to-point messages.

Three groups: foundations broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce; workhorses all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce; and all-to-all (needed for mixture-of-experts). Mnemonic from the lecture: reduce = apply an associative/commutative operation (sum, min, max); scatter is the inverse of gather; all = the destination is every device.

Interactive explorer: step through every collective on N ranks

Pick an operation and a world size. Each row is a rank, each box is one slot of its buffer (colour = slot/chunk, or source rank for all-to-all). Outlined boxes are the ones written in this step; curved arrows on the right are the messages. All-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce use the ring algorithm (next section); broadcast/scatter/gather/reduce are drawn as direct root-to-all transfers (real libraries use trees/pipelines for these).

The operations, with the lecture's tensors (4 ranks)

OperationInput (per rank)Output (per rank)Use case
Broadcastrank0 = [0,1,2,3]every rank = [0,1,2,3]rank 0 loads a checkpoint, sends to all
Scatterrank0 = [0,1,2,3]rank r = [r]stepping stone to reduce-scatter
Gatherrank r = [r]rank0 = [0,1,2,3]stepping stone to all-gather
Reducerank r = [r]rank0 = [6] (0+1+2+3)stepping stone to all-reduce
All-gatherrank r = [r]every rank = [0,1,2,3]each rank holds a parameter shard; gather the full parameters for the forward pass
Reduce-scatterrank r = [r, r+1, r+2, r+3] (rank0=[0,1,2,3], rank1=[1,2,3,4], ...)rank0=[6], rank1=[10], rank2=[14], rank3=[18]after backward, sum gradients over data shards but keep storage distributed
All-reducesame as reduce-scatterevery rank = [6,10,14,18]after backward, sum gradients over data shards and replicate (DDP)
All-to-allrank r = [4r, 4r+1, 4r+2, 4r+3]rank0=[0,4,8,12], rank1=[1,5,9,13], rank2=[2,6,10,14], rank3=[3,7,11,15]MoE: each rank has a split of the data and a subset of experts; route tokens to experts
All-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather

Reduce-scatter leaves rank \(j\) with the fully summed chunk \(j\); all-gather then replicates all chunks. Splitting the operation in two gives flexibility: ZeRO/FSDP (next lecture) do the reduce-scatter on gradients but delay the all-gather (or do it on parameters only when needed), so that no rank ever stores everything.

All-to-all

For balanced splits it is just a transpose of the (rank x slot) matrix. It also supports unbalanced splits (as MoE routing produces), but you want the splits as balanced as possible because the slowest sender/receiver bounds the time.

3. Ring algorithms and the bandwidth cost of all-reduce

Let the tensor have \(S\) bytes, there be \(N\) ranks, and each GPU have a link of bandwidth \(B\) (bytes/s per direction). In the ring algorithm the ranks are arranged in a cycle and the tensor is cut into \(N\) chunks of \(S/N\) bytes.

  • Reduce-scatter: in each of \(N-1\) steps every rank sends one chunk to its right neighbour (which adds it into its copy). Per-rank traffic: \((N-1)\,S/N\).
  • All-gather: \(N-1\) steps, again \(S/N\) per step: per-rank traffic \((N-1)\,S/N\).
  • All-reduce = both: \(2\,\frac{N-1}{N}\,S\) bytes per rank, so (ignoring latency) \(t_{\text{ring}} = \dfrac{2(N-1)}{N}\dfrac{S}{B}\;\to\;\dfrac{2S}{B}\) for large \(N\).

The crucial property: the time is essentially independent of the number of GPUs, because every link is busy at every step. Compare the naive scheme "everyone sends to rank 0, which sums and broadcasts": rank 0's single link must carry \((N-1)S\) in and \((N-1)S\) out, so \(t_{\text{naive}} = 2(N-1)S/B\), which grows linearly in \(N\). Add a latency term \(\alpha\) per hop (\(2(N-1)\) hops for the ring) and rings stop being ideal for small messages at large \(N\) (NCCL then switches to trees).

Reduce-scatter and all-gather ring schedule

The indexing used in the explorer above: in reduce-scatter step \(s=0,\dots,N-2\), rank \(r\) sends chunk \((r-s-1)\bmod N\) to rank \(r+1\); after \(N-1\) steps rank \(r\) holds the complete chunk \(r\). In the all-gather phase, step \(s\), rank \(r\) sends chunk \((r-s)\bmod N\). (Real NCCL also splits chunks into smaller slices and uses multiple rings/trees concurrently; the principle is the same.)

4. Hardware: how GPUs are connected

Classic (in the home)

GPUs in the same machine communicate through the PCI(e) bus (the lecture quotes PCIe v7.0 x16 as 242 GB/s); GPUs in different machines communicate over Ethernet (the lecture quotes ~200 MB/s for this classic setup). (The source shows a Springer figure of such a machine; not embedded.)

Modern (in the data center)

  • Node: 8 GPUs connected by NVLink to an NVSwitch (B200 NVLink 5.0: 1.8 TB/s; compare HBM at 8 TB/s).
  • Pod: ~256 nodes connected by InfiniBand (path: PCIe → HCA/InfiniBand NIC → InfiniBand cable; ~0.05 TB/s).
  • Cluster / datacenter: N pods connected by Ethernet (via PCIe → CPU).

Bypassing the CPU

  • Plain Ethernet goes through the CPU: copy data into a kernel socket buffer, build TCP packets, copy into the NIC ring buffer.
  • RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) lets one GPU read/write another GPU's memory without involving the CPU. InfiniBand supports RDMA; standard Ethernet does not.
  • RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) gives Ethernet the CPU bypass: similar to InfiniBand but cheaper and somewhat weaker; used by Meta.
  • GB200/GB300 NVL72: 72 GPUs in a single NVLink domain (the lecture says 8 GPUs per tray x 9 trays per rack; vendor documentation counts compute trays of 4 GPUs, but the 72-GPU rack-scale NVLink domain is the point).
Why this matters for the strategies below

Anything that talks every layer (tensor parallelism) must stay inside one NVLink domain; things that communicate once per step (data-parallel gradients) can cross InfiniBand if overlapped; pipeline parallelism sends only boundary activations and survives the slowest links.

5. NCCL and torch.distributed

NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communication Library, pronounced "nickel") translates collective operations into low-level packets sent between GPUs: it (1) detects the hardware topology (nodes, switches, NVLink vs PCIe), (2) optimises the path (rings/trees) between GPUs, (3) launches GPU kernels to send/receive data. PyTorch's torch.distributed gives a clean interface (all_gather_into_tensor, reduce_scatter_tensor, all_reduce, send/recv, ...) over several backends: gloo for CPU, nccl for GPU. It also contains higher-level algorithms such as FullyShardedDataParallel (not used in this course).

Process setup (shared by every example)

One OS process per rank. mp.spawn starts world_size processes, each calling the function with its own rank as the first argument. MASTER_ADDR/PORT only designate where rank 0 lives for coordination (the rendezvous); the tensors themselves flow over NCCL.

def setup(rank: int, world_size: int):
    """Initializes the distributed environment (called at start of process)."""
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"   # where rank 0 lives (coordination only)
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "15623"
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        dist.init_process_group("nccl", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
    else:
        dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)

def cleanup():
    torch.distributed.destroy_process_group()

def spawn(func, world_size, *args, **kwargs):
    args = (world_size,) + args + tuple(kwargs.values())
    mp.spawn(func, args=args, nprocs=world_size, join=True)   # func(rank, world_size, *args)

def get_init_params(num_inputs, num_outputs, rank):
    torch.random.manual_seed(0)   # same seed => identical init on every rank
    return nn.Parameter(torch.randn(num_inputs, num_outputs, device=cuda_if_available(rank)) / math.sqrt(num_outputs))

(When the lecture is run under the tracing tool edtrace multiprocessing is disabled; spawn then runs rank 0 inline with all dist.* functions replaced by no-ops. That is infrastructure, not part of the algorithms.)

All-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather for real

def collective_operations_main(rank: int, world_size: int):
    """Runs asynchronously in every process (rank = 0..world_size-1)."""
    setup(rank, world_size)

    ### All-reduce
    dist.barrier()   # wait for all processes to get here (keeps the prints tidy)
    data = tensor([0., 1, 2, 3], device=cuda_if_available(rank)) + rank   # both input and output
    print(f"Rank {rank} [before all-reduce]: {data}", flush=True)
    dist.all_reduce(tensor=data, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)    # modifies tensor in place
    print(f"Rank {rank} [after all-reduce]: {data}", flush=True)

    ### Reduce-scatter
    dist.barrier()
    input  = torch.arange(world_size, dtype=torch.float32, device=cuda_if_available(rank)) + rank
    output = torch.empty(1, device=cuda_if_available(rank))               # allocate output
    dist.reduce_scatter_tensor(output=output, input=input, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)

    ### All-gather
    dist.barrier()
    input  = output                                                        # input = output of reduce-scatter
    output = torch.empty(world_size, device=cuda_if_available(rank))
    dist.all_gather_into_tensor(output_tensor=output, input_tensor=input, async_op=False)

    # Indeed, all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather!
    cleanup()

With 4 ranks and data = [0,1,2,3] + rank the all-reduce gives [6,10,14,18] on every rank; the reduce-scatter leaves rank \(r\) with [6+4r]; the all-gather of those four numbers reproduces [6,10,14,18] on every rank, i.e. exactly the all-reduce result.

API shape to remember

All of these operate in place or into a pre-allocated output. reduce_scatter_tensor takes an input of size \(N\cdot k\) and writes size \(k\); all_gather_into_tensor takes size \(k\) and writes \(N\cdot k\). async_op=False blocks until the collective is enqueued/done; async_op=True returns a handle so you can overlap communication with compute (which the lecture does not do).

6. Benchmarking collective bandwidth

How fast does communication actually happen? The lecture times an all-reduce and a reduce-scatter of 100 * 1024**2 fp32 elements (400 MiB) on 4 GPUs. The measurement hygiene matters:

  • Warm-up run first (NCCL builds communicators and allocates buffers lazily; the first call is not representative).
  • torch.cuda.synchronize(): CUDA kernels are asynchronous, so without this the timer stops before the communication kernel finishes.
  • dist.barrier(): ensures every rank has finished before reading the clock (otherwise a fast rank measures only part of the operation).
Full benchmark code (all-reduce and reduce-scatter) 
def all_reduce(rank: int, world_size: int, num_elements: int):
    setup(rank, world_size)
    data = torch.randn(num_elements, device=cuda_if_available(rank))

    # Warmup
    dist.all_reduce(tensor=data, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()   # wait for CUDA kernels to finish
    dist.barrier()             # wait for all the processes to get here

    # Perform all-reduce
    start_time = time.time()
    dist.all_reduce(tensor=data, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    dist.barrier()
    end_time = time.time()
    duration = end_time - start_time

    # Measure the effective bandwidth
    dist.barrier()
    size_bytes = data.element_size() * data.numel()
    sent_bytes = size_bytes * 2 * (world_size - 1)   # 2x because send + receive; world_size-1 steps in all-reduce
    total_duration = world_size * duration
    bandwidth = sent_bytes / total_duration
    print(f"... measured bandwidth = {round(bandwidth / 1024**3)} GB/s")
    # Notes: effective bandwidth ~ 2 * size_bytes / total_duration
    #        independent of world_size, and of topology (ring or tree)
    cleanup()


def reduce_scatter(rank: int, world_size: int, num_elements: int):
    setup(rank, world_size)
    input  = torch.randn(world_size, num_elements, device=cuda_if_available(rank))  # each rank has a matrix
    output = torch.empty(num_elements, device=cuda_if_available(rank))

    # Warmup, then timed run: same pattern as above
    dist.reduce_scatter_tensor(output=output, input=input, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); dist.barrier()
    start_time = time.time()
    dist.reduce_scatter_tensor(output=output, input=input, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); dist.barrier()
    duration = time.time() - start_time

    dist.barrier()
    data_bytes = input.element_size() * input.numel()   # how much data in the input
    sent_bytes = data_bytes * (world_size - 1)          # how much needs to be sent (no 2x here)
    total_duration = world_size * duration
    bandwidth = sent_bytes / total_duration
    # Notes: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather, so all-reduce moves 2x the data
    #        in 2x the time compared to reduce-scatter => similar bandwidth.
    cleanup()

The effective-bandwidth formula, derived: an all-reduce makes every rank send \(2\frac{N-1}{N}S\) bytes; the code instead computes total bytes \(2S(N-1)\) and divides by \(N\cdot t\), which is the same number:

\[ \text{bw}_{\text{all-reduce}}=\frac{2S(N-1)}{N\,t},\qquad \text{bw}_{\text{reduce-scatter}}=\frac{D\,(N-1)}{N\,t},\; D=\text{input bytes}=N\cdot(\text{elements}\cdot 4). \]

This is NCCL-tests' "bus bandwidth": it is deliberately normalised so that it is about the hardware link speed regardless of \(N\) or ring-vs-tree.

7. Three ways to cut a network

Part 2 of the lecture implements each strategy from scratch on a deep MLP (num_layers matrices of shape num_dim x num_dim, GeLU after every layer, loss = mean squared magnitude of the output). MLPs are the compute bottleneck of a Transformer, so this is representative. Sample data: batch_size=128, num_dim=1024. A neural network has two axes you can slice: the data axis (batch) and the model axis (width or depth).

StrategyCut alongEach rank storesCommunicationNeeds
Databatchall parameters, a slice of the dataall-reduce of gradients (DDP); all-gather + reduce-scatter (FSDP/ZeRO, next lecture)moderate links; communication can be overlapped with backward
Tensor (and expert)width1/N of each layer, all dataall-gather/all-reduce of activations in every layer; all-to-all for MoEvery fast interconnect (NVLink)
Pipelinedeptha block of layerspoint-to-point send/recv of activationsworks on slow links; must fight pipeline bubbles
Sequencesequence lengtha chunk of every sequence(mentioned in the summary only)combined with the others in practice

8. Data parallelism (DDP)

Sharding strategy: each rank gets a slice of the data (rank \(r\) takes rows \([r\cdot b,(r+1)b)\) with \(b=B/N\); in practice each rank loads only its own slice). Every rank holds all parameters and its own AdamW optimizer state. The only difference from single-GPU training is one line: all-reduce (average) the gradients before optimizer.step().

def data_parallelism_main(rank, world_size, data, num_layers, num_steps):
    setup(rank, world_size)

    # Get the slice of data for this rank:  --- B0 --- B1 --- B2 --- B3 ---
    batch_size = data.size(0)                                   # 128
    num_dim = data.size(1)                                      # 1024
    local_batch_size = int_divide(batch_size, world_size)       # 32 (asserts no remainder)
    start_index = rank * local_batch_size
    end_index = start_index + local_batch_size
    data = data[start_index:end_index].to(cuda_if_available(rank))

    # Each rank has ALL the parameters (identical init: same seed) and its own optimizer state
    params = [get_init_params(num_dim, num_dim, rank) for layer in range(num_layers)]
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=1e-3)

    for step in range(num_steps):
        # Forward pass
        x = data
        for param in params:
            x = x @ param
            x = F.gelu(x)
        loss = x.square().mean()          # average squared magnitude (local!)

        # Backward pass
        loss.backward()

        # Sync gradients across workers (ONLY difference between standard training and DDP)
        for param in params:
            dist.all_reduce(tensor=param.grad, op=dist.ReduceOp.AVG, async_op=False)

        # Update parameters
        optimizer.step()

Why averaging gradients is exact

With equal shards, the mean loss over the global batch is the mean of the shard means, and gradients are linear: \(\nabla\frac1B\sum_i \ell_i = \frac1N\sum_r \nabla\Big(\frac1b\sum_{i\in r}\ell_i\Big)\). Try it on a toy model \(\ell_i=(wx_i-y_i)^2\) with 128 samples:

Observations from the lecture

Losses are different across ranks (computed on local data); gradients are all-reduced to be the same; therefore parameters remain the same across ranks. Note the all-reduce is on the critical path as written (async_op=False, after the whole backward): real implementations overlap it with the remaining backward computation.

Where DDP hurts

Every rank stores all parameters, gradients and optimizer state (AdamW keeps two extra copies). FSDP/ZeRO fixes this by sharding them and using all-gather + reduce-scatter, the topic of the next lecture. The cost of the all-reduce is \(\approx 2P\) bytes per rank for \(P\) gradient bytes, independent of the batch size.

9. Tensor parallelism

Sharding strategy: every rank gets part of every layer (here \(1/N\) of the columns of each weight matrix) and sees all the data. Activations must be exchanged.

def tensor_parallelism_main(rank, world_size, data, num_layers):
    setup(rank, world_size)

    data = data.to(cuda_if_available(rank))        # ALL ranks get the data (batch_size x num_dim)
    batch_size = data.size(0)                       # 128
    num_dim = data.size(1)                          # 1024
    local_num_dim = int_divide(num_dim, world_size) # shard num_dim: 256

    # Model: each rank gets 1/world_size of the parameters of every layer
    #  |  |  |  |
    # W0 W1 W2 W3        (each W_r is num_dim x local_num_dim)
    params = [get_init_params(num_dim, local_num_dim, rank) for layer in range(num_layers)]

    # Forward pass
    x = data
    for layer in range(num_layers):
        # Compute activations (batch_size x local_num_dim) -- only on a slice of the parameters
        x = x @ params[layer]
        x = F.gelu(x)

        # Allocate memory for activations (world_size x batch_size x local_num_dim)
        activations = [torch.empty(batch_size, local_num_dim, device=cuda_if_available(rank)) for _ in range(world_size)]

        # Send activations via all gather
        dist.all_gather(tensor_list=activations, tensor=x, async_op=False)

        # Concatenate them to get batch_size x num_dim
        x = torch.cat(activations, dim=1)

    # Backward pass: homework exercise

Why does this compute the right thing? Splitting \(W=[W_0\,|\,W_1\,|\cdots|\,W_{N-1}]\) by columns gives \(xW=[xW_0\,|\cdots|\,xW_{N-1}]\), and GeLU is elementwise, so it can be applied to each slice independently; concatenating the slices along the width recovers the full activation, which the next layer needs in full. Step through a miniature version (batch 2, width 4, 2 ranks):

Cost

An all-gather runs in every layer on the critical path (the next layer cannot start until it has the whole activation), and each rank receives \((N-1)/N\) of a \(B\times d\) activation per layer. That is a lot of traffic per unit of compute, which is why tensor parallelism requires very fast interconnects (NVLink) and is normally kept within one node (typically \(\le 8\) GPUs). (The lecture leaves the backward pass as a homework exercise.)

10. Pipeline parallelism and the bubble

Sharding strategy: each rank gets a subset of consecutive layers and activations are transferred between ranks. Done naively, rank 1 idles while rank 0 works on the whole batch and vice versa. The cure is to cut the batch into micro-batches so that rank 1 can start on micro-batch 0 while rank 0 processes micro-batch 1.

def pipeline_parallelism_main(rank, world_size, data, num_layers, num_micro_batches):
    setup(rank, world_size)

    data = data.to(cuda_if_available(rank))                 # use all the data
    batch_size = data.size(0)                                # 128
    num_dim = data.size(1)                                   # 1024

    # Split up layers
    local_num_layers = int_divide(num_layers, world_size)    # 4 layers / 2 ranks = 2

    # Each rank gets a subset of layers
    local_params = [get_init_params(num_dim, num_dim, rank) for layer in range(local_num_layers)]

    # Forward pass: break up into micro batches to minimize the bubble
    micro_batch_size = int_divide(batch_size, num_micro_batches)   # 128 / 4 = 32
    if rank == 0:
        micro_batches = data.chunk(chunks=num_micro_batches, dim=0)          # the data
    else:
        # Allocate memory for incoming activations
        micro_batches = [torch.empty(micro_batch_size, num_dim, device=cuda_if_available(rank)) for _ in range(num_micro_batches)]

    for x in micro_batches:
        # Get activations from previous rank
        if rank - 1 >= 0:
            dist.recv(tensor=x, src=rank - 1)

        # Compute layers assigned to this rank
        for param in local_params:
            x = x @ param
            x = F.gelu(x)

        # Send to the next rank
        if rank + 1 < world_size:
            dist.send(tensor=x, dst=rank + 1)

    # Not handled: overlapping communication/computation to eliminate pipeline bubbles
    # Backward pass: homework exercise

Note the communication primitives: unlike data/tensor parallelism these are point-to-point dist.send/dist.recv (blocking), not collectives; only \(\text{micro\_batch\_size}\times\text{num\_dim}\) floats cross each stage boundary per micro-batch.

Pipeline schedule simulator: GPipe vs 1F1B

With \(p\) stages, \(m\) micro-batches and forward/backward costs \(t_f,t_b\) per micro-batch per stage, the pipeline needs \(m+p-1\) slots, so the idle ("bubble") fraction is \[ \text{bubble}=\frac{(p-1)(t_f+t_b)}{(m+p-1)(t_f+t_b)}=\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}. \] GPipe runs all forwards, then all backwards; it stores activations of all \(m\) micro-batches. 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward, as in PipeDream-Flush / Megatron) starts backwards as early as possible, which has the same bubble but keeps at most \(p\) micro-batches' activations alive. Choose the schedule below; light boxes are forwards, solid boxes are backwards, the number is the micro-batch. The simulation respects the dependencies (F\(_i\) on stage \(s\) needs F\(_i\) from stage \(s-1\); B\(_i\) on stage \(s\) needs B\(_i\) from stage \(s+1\)) and measures the bubble from the resulting timeline.

Reading the picture

The bubble shrinks as \(m\) grows, but a larger \(m\) means smaller micro-batches (less efficient matmuls) and, for GPipe, more stored activations. 1F1B removes the memory growth without changing the bubble, which is why it is the default in practice. The lecture only implements the forward pass with micro-batches and states explicitly that overlapping communication and computation to eliminate bubbles is not handled.

11. Communication-volume calculator for DP, TP and PP

The three strategies move very different things. For the lecture's MLP with \(L\) layers of width \(d\) (\(P=Ld^2\) parameters), batch \(B\), bytes per element \(b\):

\[ \underbrace{V_{\text{DP}}=\frac{2(N-1)}{N}\,P\,b}_{\text{ring all-reduce of grads, per rank}},\qquad \underbrace{V_{\text{TP}}=L\cdot\frac{N-1}{N}\,B\,d\,b}_{\text{all-gather of activations, per rank, fwd}},\qquad \underbrace{V_{\text{PP}}=B\,d\,b}_{\text{per stage boundary, fwd}}. \]

DP scales with the model size (and is independent of batch); TP and PP scale with the activation size \(B\cdot d\). TP pays it in every layer, PP only at the \(p-1\) cut points. (Backward roughly doubles the TP/PP numbers; the lecture leaves the backward pass as homework, so the forward-pass volumes are shown.)

12. What is missing, and where this goes next

  • Communication/computation overlap: use async_op=True, CUDA streams, and bucketing so that gradient all-reduces run while backward is still computing, and so that pipeline stages are never blocked on a blocking recv.
  • More general models: attention etc. (the implementations here are on pure MLPs).
  • Other forms of parallelism: sequence parallelism (cut along sequence length), expert parallelism (MoE; uses all-to-all), and combinations (3D parallelism). Production systems compose all of them: e.g. Megatron-LM scaling (tensor + pipeline + data) reached 52% MFU on a 1T-parameter model over 3072 GPUs, and MegaScale combined data/tensor/pipeline/sequence parallelism for 55.2% MFU on a 175B model over 12,288 GPUs (figures from the course's reference list).
  • JAX/TPUs: you only define the model and the sharding strategy and the JAX compiler (XLA/GSPMD) inserts the collectives (see the Levanter release post). The point of using PyTorch here is to see how everything is built from the primitives.
  • Next lecture: FSDP/ZeRO: use all-gather and reduce-scatter so that parameters, gradients and optimizer state are all sharded.
Beyond the lecture: a common 3D layout

In practice: tensor parallelism inside a node (NVLink), pipeline parallelism across nodes in a pod (InfiniBand tolerates point-to-point activations), and data parallelism (usually FSDP/ZeRO) across the remaining dimension. This is the hierarchy-matching principle of section 1 applied literally.

13. Summary

  • Many ways to parallelize: data (batch), tensor/expert (width), pipeline (depth), sequence (length).
  • Data parallelism: DDP uses all-reduce; FSDP/ZeRO uses all-gather + reduce-scatter.
  • Tensor parallelism requires very fast interconnects (e.g. NVLink).
  • Pipeline parallelism can work with slow interconnects, but you must work to reduce pipeline bubbles.
  • You can re-compute, store in memory, or store in another GPU's memory and communicate.
  • Hardware is getting faster, but we will always want bigger models, so the hierarchical structure remains.

14. Self-check

Rank 0..3 hold [r, r+1, r+2, r+3]. What is the result of reduce-scatter (sum), and of all-reduce?
Reduce-scatter: rank 0 gets [6], rank 1 [10], rank 2 [14], rank 3 [18] (sum over ranks of element \(j\) = \(6+4j\)). All-reduce: every rank gets [6,10,14,18], which equals all-gather applied to the reduce-scatter output.
Why does the ring all-reduce move \(2\frac{N-1}{N}S\) bytes per GPU, and why is that nearly independent of \(N\)?
The tensor is cut into \(N\) chunks. Reduce-scatter takes \(N-1\) steps, each sending one chunk (\(S/N\)) per link, and all-gather takes another \(N-1\). Total \(2(N-1)S/N\to 2S\). All links work simultaneously, so more GPUs do not make the per-link load grow, unlike the naive "send everything to rank 0" scheme where rank 0's link carries \((N-1)S\).
In the benchmark, why warm up, call torch.cuda.synchronize() and dist.barrier()?
The first NCCL call pays one-time setup (communicator, buffers). CUDA calls are asynchronous, so without synchronize the clock stops before the kernel completes. Without the barrier a rank could stop timing before slower ranks finish, so the duration would not reflect the whole collective.
In data parallelism, losses differ across ranks, yet parameters stay identical. Why?
Each rank starts from identical parameters (same seed), computes a local gradient on its own shard, and the all-reduce(AVG) makes the gradient identical everywhere (equal to the global-batch gradient for equal shards). Each rank applies the same deterministic optimizer update (with identical optimizer state) so parameters never diverge; only the gradients are communicated.
For L=4, d=1024, B=128, N=4 fp32, how many bytes does each rank receive per forward layer in the lecture's tensor-parallel implementation, and how many does DP send in total per step?
TP: all-gather of a \(128\times1024\) fp32 activation (524,288 B) of which \(3/4\) is received: 393 KB per layer, 1.57 MB over 4 layers. DP: \(P=4\cdot1024^2=4.19\)M parameters = 16.8 MB of gradients; ring all-reduce sends \(2\cdot\frac34\cdot16.8=25.2\) MB per rank.
Why is tensor parallelism confined to NVLink domains while pipeline parallelism can cross InfiniBand?
TP needs a collective on the critical path of every layer (volume \(\propto L\,B\,d\)), so bandwidth/latency directly slow every layer. PP transfers an activation only at the \(p-1\) stage boundaries, as point-to-point messages, and can overlap them with other micro-batches, so a 20-36x slower link is tolerable.
With p = 4 stages and m = 8 micro-batches, what is the bubble fraction, and what changes between GPipe and 1F1B?
\((p-1)/(m+p-1)=3/11\approx 27\%\) for both (with any ratio of backward to forward cost). GPipe must keep the activations of all \(m=8\) micro-batches on stage 0; 1F1B keeps at most \(p=4\). Raising \(m\) shrinks the bubble (m=32: 8.6%) at the cost of smaller micro-batches.
Why is all-to-all the collective that MoE models need?
Each rank holds a slice of the tokens and a subset of experts; each token must be routed to whichever rank hosts its chosen expert, and results routed back. That is every rank sending a (possibly unequal) piece to every other rank: all-to-all, which for balanced splits is a transpose.

Key takeaways

  1. The multi-GPU problem is the single-GPU problem with a deeper hierarchy: HBM (8 TB/s) → NVLink (1.8 TB/s) → InfiniBand (~0.05 TB/s) → Ethernet. Minimise traffic on the slow levels.
  2. Learn the eight collectives by their input/output; reduce-scatter + all-gather = all-reduce, and that split is what FSDP/ZeRO exploits.
  3. Ring all-reduce costs \(\approx 2S/B\) regardless of \(N\); measured "bus bandwidth" is \(2S(N-1)/(N t)\).
  4. DDP = local backward + all-reduce(AVG) of gradients; one line differs from single-GPU training.
  5. TP = column-sharded weights + all-gather of activations every layer; needs NVLink.
  6. PP = layers split across ranks + micro-batches + send/recv; bubble \((p-1)/(m+p-1)\); 1F1B reduces memory not bubble.
  7. Always: benchmark with warm-up, synchronize, and barrier.

Parallelism basics at scale

lecture_08.pdf multi-GPU collectives ZeRO / FSDP pipeline tensor sequence / context expert (MoE) 3D / 4D critical batch size
TL;DR. One GPU cannot hold or compute a frontier model, so training is split across GPUs and machines. There are three ways to cut the work. Data parallelism splits the batch; plain DP replicates the whole model (about 16 bytes per parameter with Adam), and ZeRO / FSDP shard that replicated state at a communication cost of at most 1.5x. Model parallelism splits the network: pipeline parallelism cuts it by depth (bubble ratio (p−1)/m, so it needs many micro-batches), tensor parallelism cuts each matrix by width (an all-reduce per layer, so it needs NVLink-speed links and stays inside a node), expert parallelism spreads MoE experts out, and sequence / context parallelism splits activations along the sequence. Real runs combine these as 3D / 4D parallelism, nested so that the most communication-heavy dimension sits on the fastest link.

1. Why multiple GPUs

The lecture starts from two limits of a single accelerator. On compute, the performance of the fastest machines has grown to exaFLOPs, far beyond what one GPU delivers. On memory, model sizes have grown faster than GPU memory, so a single GPU cannot fit most large models (the slide plots parameter count against the memory of one GPU, and the gap widens over time). The answer is multi-GPU, multi-machine parallelism: split the memory and the compute requirements across GPUs and machines.

The bandwidth hierarchy

The network has layers, and each layer is much slower than the one inside it. A typical ordering, from the slide's node diagram:

  1. Inside a GPU: HBM to SMs (terabytes per second).
  2. Inside a node: GPU to GPU over NVLink through NVSwitch (the slide quotes 400 GT/s per lane for NVLink 3.0).
  3. Across nodes: InfiniBand HDR (50 GT/s per lane), reached through HCAs and switches.
  4. Through the host: PCIe 4.0 and xGMI (16 GT/s per lane), which is the slowest path for GPU-to-GPU traffic.

The rule the whole lecture follows: put the traffic that is most frequent and largest on the fastest link.

What we want from multi-machine scaling

Two properties: linear memory scaling (the largest model that fits grows in proportion to the number of GPUs) and linear compute scaling (model FLOPs per second grow in proportion to the number of GPUs). Everything below is a trade-off between these two goals and communication. Doing it with only a few simple collective primitives is what makes it practical.

2. Collective communication, and the hardware under it

The parallel strategies are built from a handful of collectives, operations in which a group of GPUs exchanges data together. The slides use five:

  • Broadcast: one GPU sends its data to all others.
  • Reduce: all GPUs send data that is combined (summed) onto one GPU.
  • All-gather: each GPU holds a shard; afterwards every GPU holds all the shards concatenated.
  • Reduce-scatter: each GPU contributes a full vector; the sum is split so that each GPU ends with one reduced shard.
  • All-reduce: every GPU ends with the full sum on all GPUs.
The identity that drives ZeRO

An all-reduce can be implemented as reduce-scatter followed by all-gather. In the bandwidth-limited regime, this two-step version is the best you can do. The slide's "important detail" is exactly this equivalence, and ZeRO exploits it: the reduce-scatter leaves each GPU with only the gradient slice it needs, and the all-gather is needed only when the parameters are used.

With a ring implementation (a standard result that is not on the slides), each GPU sends and receives about \( \frac{N-1}{N}S \) bytes in each of the two phases for a vector of size \(S\) on \(N\) GPUs. The total per-GPU traffic of an all-reduce is therefore about \( 2\frac{N-1}{N}S \), which approaches \(2S\) for large \(N\). This is why the slides count DP communication as "2 × #params".

TPUs versus GPUs: the network shape differs

TPU networking (slide 9) is a toroidal mesh: each chip talks to its neighbours, and the edges wrap around. A mesh is cheap to build and can be very fast for nearest-neighbour traffic, so it suits tensor parallelism.

GPU networking is all-to-all inside a SuperPOD of up to 256 GPUs: any GPU can reach any other, through NVSwitch and then through InfiniBand spine and leaf switches on the A100 system. A tree or all-to-all fabric is better for less structured traffic, such as routing tokens to experts (expert parallelism).

Newer TPU generations move toward switched, tree-like topologies (the slide mentions TPU8i and a switched scale-out network called "Virgo" for TPU8t), presumably for MoE traffic.

SuperPOD (slide 9)Dense PFLOP/sBisection GB/sReduce GB/s
A100, 1 DGX / 8 GPUs2.52,400150
A100, 32 DGX / 256 GPUs806,400100
H100, 1 DGX / 8 GPUs163,600450
H100, 32 DGX / 256 GPUs51257,600450

The slide's speedup column: bisection 1.5x (one DGX) and 9x (256 GPUs); reduce 3x and 4.5x (H100 over A100).

Why not connect everything? The slide gives no formula; the usual limits are cost, power and switch port count, which bound how many GPUs can share an all-to-all fabric. The slides point to a 384-GPU system (Huawei CloudMatrix 384, from a SemiAnalysis write-up) as an example of pushing the all-to-all domain further. The practical picture is a fast scale-up domain (one node, or an NVLink-connected rack) inside a slower scale-out network.

Part 1 recap

The unit of compute is now the datacenter. For multi-machine scaling we want linear memory and compute scaling, built from simple collectives. The topology (mesh vs tree vs all-to-all, and the bandwidth at each level) decides which parallelism is affordable where.

3. Data parallelism, and why naive DP does not scale in memory

Start from ordinary SGD. Each step updates the parameters \( \theta \) with the gradient of the loss summed over the mini-batch of size \(B\):

\[ \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \sum_{i=1}^{B} \nabla \ell(x_i) \]

Naive data parallelism splits the \(B\) examples across \(M\) machines. Each machine computes gradients on its \(B/M\) examples, the gradients are all-reduced, and every machine applies the same update.

AspectWhat the slide says
Compute scalingEach GPU processes \(B/M\) examples, so per-step compute drops linearly.
CommunicationAbout \(2\times\)#params transmitted per batch (the all-reduce). Fine when the batch is big enough to amortise it.
Memory scalingNone. Every GPU holds a full copy of the parameters and optimizer state.

The memory problem: about 16 bytes per parameter

The slides count the state that must live on every GPU in naive DP. With mixed precision and Adam, per parameter:

  • 2 bytes: BF16 (or FP16) model parameters.
  • 2 bytes: BF16 gradients.
  • 4 bytes: FP32 master weights (the copy you accumulate the update into).
  • 4 (or 2) bytes: Adam first moment (FP32, or BF16).
  • 4 (or 2) bytes: Adam second moment (FP32, or BF16).

The first moment, second moment and master weights together form the optimizer state. With FP32 moments the total is \(2+2+4+4+4 = 16\) bytes per parameter, which the slide describes as "5 copies of weights". With BF16 moments it is 12 bytes. Writing \(K\) for the bytes of optimizer state per parameter (\(K=12\) for the all-FP32 case, \(K=8\) with BF16 moments), the memory per GPU in naive DP is \( (2+2+K)\Psi \), where \( \Psi \) is the parameter count. For a 7.5B model with \(K=12\), that is \(16 \times 7.5 = 120\) GB on every GPU, before any activations.

Consequence

Data parallelism buys compute scaling but no memory scaling. Adding GPUs makes training faster, not able to fit a larger model. ZeRO is the fix for the replicated state.

4. ZeRO and FSDP: shard the replicated state

Core idea: split up the expensive parts (the state) and use the reduce-scatter / all-gather equivalence. Data parallelism stays the same from the outside; each GPU just stores a slice of the state. ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2019) defines three stages, and FSDP in PyTorch is essentially ZeRO-3.

StageWhat is sharded across the \(N\) data-parallel GPUsMemory per GPU (bytes per parameter)Communication per step
Baseline DPnothing\(2+2+K\)one all-reduce, \(\approx 2\Psi\)
ZeRO-1 (\(P_{os}\))optimizer state\(2+2+K/N\)reduce-scatter gradients + all-gather parameters, \(\approx 2\Psi\). Same cost as all-reduce.
ZeRO-2 (\(P_{os+g}\))optimizer state + gradients\(2+(2+K)/N\)\(\approx 2\Psi\) (almost free)
ZeRO-3 / FSDP (\(P_{os+g+p}\))optimizer state + gradients + parameters\((2+2+K)/N\)2 all-gathers + 1 reduce-scatter, \(3\Psi\), i.e. 1.5x the DP traffic

Stage 1: optimizer state sharding

Everyone keeps the parameters and gradients, but each worker owns a slice of the optimizer state and updates only its slice of the parameters. The steps:

  1. Each GPU computes a full gradient on its share of the batch.
  2. Reduce-scatter the gradients: each GPU ends up with the summed gradient for its slice. Cost: \(\Psi\) communication.
  3. Each GPU updates its parameter slice using its gradient slice and its optimizer state.
  4. All-gather the updated parameters so everyone has the full model again. Cost: \(\Psi\).

Total: \(2\Psi\), exactly the cost of the all-reduce it replaces. Memory per GPU falls from \((4+K)\Psi\) to \((4+K/N)\Psi\). The slide's conclusion: ZeRO stage 1 is free in the bandwidth-limited regime, so there is little reason not to use it.

Stage 2: gradient sharding

Gradients are also sharded. Each worker still has to compute a full gradient for its own micro-batch during the backward pass, but it can reduce each layer's gradient to the worker that owns it and then free the local copy. Concretely: after a layer's gradients are computed, reduce them immediately to the right worker; once gradients are no longer needed in the backward graph, free them; then update the owned parameters and all-gather. Communication stays at \(2\Psi\) (ignoring overhead).

Stage 3 (FSDP): shard everything

Parameters are sharded too, so no GPU holds the full model. Parameters are requested on demand: all-gather the parameters of a layer just before it is used in the forward pass, free them right after, and do the same in the backward pass; then reduce-scatter the gradients. A "baby" version costs 2 all-gathers and 1 reduce-scatter, each of \(\Psi\), so \(3\Psi\) in total, i.e. 1.5x plain DP.

The ZeRO memory calculator

Set the parameter count, the number of data-parallel GPUs, the optimizer-state size \(K\) and the stage. The per-GPU memory uses the formulas in the table above, and the default values reproduce slide 18.

How far does ZeRO go on 8 A100s?

The slide's "will it fit?" example uses pure BF16 training with Kahan summation, so the optimizer state is smaller, and BF16 for everything except the master weights: 12 bytes per parameter in total (2 parameter + 2 gradient + 8 optimizer state, i.e. \(K=8\)). With 8 GPUs of 80 GB, the largest model is:

BaselineMax size (params)Formula for bytes / param
Baseline DP6.66 B12
ZeRO stage 116 B\(2+2+8/8 = 5\)
ZeRO stage 224.62 B\(2 + (2+8)/8 = 3.25\)
ZeRO stage 353.33 B\((2+2+8)/8 = 12/8 = 1.5\)
Where ZeRO stops helping

Stages 1 and 2 keep the full parameters on every GPU, so they do not scale model memory. Stage 3 scales the state, but it still does not reduce activation memory, which depends on the batch and sequence length on each GPU. The slide's conclusion: "Better ways to split up the model are needed."

Practice: who uses which stage

Section 12 lists the real runs from the slides. In short: the 7B model trained on Dolma used FSDP (probably fitting within one node), Gemma 2 used ZeRO-3-like sharding with model parallelism (TP + SP) and DP, and DeepSeek and Yi used ZeRO-1 with tensor and pipeline parallelism.

5. The limits of data parallelism: critical batch size

Two problems remain with DP even when memory is sharded. First, compute scaling: with data parallelism you need the number of machines to be smaller than the batch size, and as you approach that limit the communication overhead grows. Second, there are diminishing returns to bigger batches. The slide's plot of predicted training speed captures both.

The curve has the form given in the critical-batch-size literature (McCandlish et al. 2018, "An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training", the paper that introduced the critical batch size): the number of steps needed falls as \( 1 + B_{\text{noise}}/B \). Rescaled, the speed relative to the best possible is \( \frac{B}{B+B_{\text{noise}}} = \frac{x}{1+x} \), which reproduces the plotted points: about 1% at \(B = 0.01\,B_{\text{noise}}\), 50% at \(B = B_{\text{noise}}\), and about 99% at \(B = 100\,B_{\text{noise}}\). The slide does not state this formula itself; it is the standard interpretation of its plot.

What this means for scale

Once you have enough GPUs that the per-GPU batch would fall below about the noise scale, adding GPUs with pure DP stops helping. That is why the rest of the lecture adds model parallelism (pipeline, tensor, expert, context), which scales memory and compute without requiring a larger batch.

Comparing the strategies as the batch shrinks

The TPU book's analysis (slide 56, "Model vs Tensor parallel") plots the ratio of FLOP time to communication time against the batch per chip, \(B/N\), on a 4x4x4 mesh. FSDP only, MP only and mixed FSDP+MP cross the compute-bound line at different batch sizes. The slide's annotations: no scheme works when the batch per chip is below about 400; only mixed FSDP+MP works up to about 850; above 850 both mixed and pure FSDP work. (The axis is the global batch divided by the number of chips.)

6. Model parallelism: cutting the network itself

Data parallelism and ZeRO keep the batch split and the model whole (or whole after gathering). Model parallelism splits the parameters across GPUs, as ZeRO-3 does, but it communicates activations instead of parameters. Three ways of cutting the model:

StrategyWhat is cutWhat crosses the wireScales
Data / ZeRObatchgradients (all-reduce) or parameters (all-gather)compute (not memory, unless ZeRO)
Pipeline (PP)layers (depth)activations between consecutive stages, point to pointmemory and compute, with bubbles
Tensor (TP)matrices (width)activation-sized all-reduces inside every layermemory and compute, needs fast links
Expert (EP)MoE expertstokens routed to experts (all-to-all)expert parameters and compute
Sequence / context (SP, CP)sequence positionsactivations around the sequence splitactivation memory

Naive layer-wise parallelism wastes the cluster

Layer-wise parallelism assigns a subset of the layers to each GPU, and activations and partial gradients are passed back and forth. The problem is utilisation: with \(n\) GPUs and one batch, each GPU is active only \(1/n\) of the time. Forward flows through GPU 0, then 1, then 2, and so on; the backward pass then has to propagate back through the same chain. Each GPU idles waiting for the other stages.

7. Pipeline parallelism: micro-batches and bubbles

The fix is to split the batch into micro-batches (the slide uses 4) and pipeline them through the stages. Send micro-batch 1 forward, and while it moves on, start micro-batch 2 on the first stage, and so on. The idle triangles at the start and the end are the pipeline bubble.

The bubble ratio

With \(p\) stages and \(m\) micro-batches, the ratio of bubble time to useful compute is \( \frac{p-1}{m} \) (the slide's formula). As a share of wall-clock time, the idle fraction is \( \frac{p-1}{m+p-1} \). For \(p=4\) and \(m=4\) that is \(3/7 \approx 43\%\) idle. For \(p=4\) and \(m=32\) it is \(3/35 \approx 9\%\). So you need many micro-batches (a big batch) to hide the bubble, which is exactly what the slide says.

Schedule explorer

The explorer simulates a discrete-event schedule. The unit of time is one forward pass; a backward pass costs 2 units (the usual rule of thumb). The three schedules:

  • GPipe: all forwards for all micro-batches, then all backwards. Simple, but every stage holds the activations of all \(m\) micro-batches at the peak.
  • 1F1B: each stage does a warm-up of forwards, then alternates one forward and one backward, then drains the backwards. The bubble is the same as GPipe's, but peak activation memory is bounded by the pipeline depth instead of \(m\).
  • Zero-bubble style: split each backward into B (gradients with respect to the activations, which the previous stage needs) and W (gradients with respect to the weights, which nothing downstream needs). W can be run whenever a device is otherwise idle. This simplified greedy version does not reproduce the handcrafted ZB-H1 / ZB-H2 schedules of the paper (the slide's Figure 3); it only shows the principle.

Try p = 4, m = 8, 1F1B: the simulated bubble is 27.3%, matching \( 3/11 \). Switch to zero-bubble style at the same settings and the idle share falls to about 20%. Increase \(m\) to 32 and every schedule's bubble shrinks, which is the batch-size dependence the slide emphasises.

How the bubble depends on micro-batches

The "under 10%" rule follows from solving \( \frac{p-1}{m+p-1} \le 0.1 \), which gives \( m \ge 9(p-1) \). Interleaving (dashed) cuts the bubble for a given \(m\) by splitting each device's layers into \(v\) chunks, at the price of \(v\) times more point-to-point messages.

Why pipeline parallelism anyway?

Pipelines look terrible, so why use them? The slide gives two reasons:

  1. Memory: each stage holds only \(1/p\) of the parameters, unlike DDP.
  2. Communication: pipelines send only the activations at the boundary (size \(b \times s \times h\)), point to point, once per micro-batch. FSDP instead moves parameters and gradients on every layer.

Therefore pipelines are used on the slower inter-node links to scale memory. The catch is that performance depends heavily on the batch size: the slide's plot shows throughput per GPU dropping steeply with pipeline size at batch 8, while batch 128 stays near its peak.

Trading bandwidth for utilisation

Some more elaborate patterns (the slide's "assign multiple stages to each device" figure, i.e. interleaving) reduce the bubble, but they send more activations and need more bandwidth. Utilisation and bandwidth are traded against each other.

Zero-bubble pipelining

Split the backward pass into two parts, as in the schedule explorer above: B (backpropagate activations, \( \nabla_x L \)) and W (compute weight gradients, \( \nabla_W L \)). B is on the critical path, because the previous stage waits for it. W can be scheduled whenever the device would otherwise be idle, which can fill the bubble. The slide's Figure 3 shows two handcrafted schedules, ZB-H1 and ZB-H2, against the 1F1B schedule of Figure 2.

8. Tensor parallelism: splitting the matrices

Pipeline parallelism cuts the model along depth. Tensor parallelism cuts it along width, using a simple property of matrix multiplication: a product can be decomposed into submatrices whose partial results are summed.

The MLP split

In the MLP \( Y = \mathrm{GeLU}(XA) \), \( Z = \mathrm{Dropout}(YB) \), split \(A\) by columns into \(A_1, A_2\) and \(B\) by rows into \(B_1, B_2\), and put one half on each GPU. Each GPU computes \( Y_i = \mathrm{GeLU}(XA_i) \) with no communication, then \( Z_i = Y_i B_i \). The result is the sum \( Z = Z_1 + Z_2 \), which needs one all-reduce. The slide names the two operators used by Megatron:

  • f: identity in the forward pass, all-reduce in the backward pass.
  • g: all-reduce in the forward pass, identity in the backward pass.

Row and column splits across a transformer block

ComponentHow it is splitWhy
QKV projections, up-projection of the MLPcolumn-wiseoutput is partitioned; no communication needed here
Attention output projection, down-projection of the MLProw-wisepartial sums, combined by the all-reduce
LayerNorm, dropout, routersreplicatedcheap; need the full activation

Attention splits naturally by heads: each GPU computes a subset of heads (column-wise QKV), then the output projection is row-wise. So each transformer block needs an all-reduce after attention and one after the MLP.

Pros and cons versus pipeline parallelism

Pros of TP

No bubble: if the network is fast enough, no device waits for another. Low complexity: a model can be wrapped without major infrastructure changes. It does not need a large batch to work well.

Cons of TP

Much larger communication than pipelining. Pipeline sends \(bsh\) point to point per micro-batch. Tensor parallelism sends \(8bsh\frac{n_{\text{devices}}-1}{n_{\text{devices}}}\) per layer, as all-reduces.

Use tensor parallelism whenever the interconnect is low-latency and high-bandwidth, which in practice means within one node (up to 8 GPUs). Beyond that, the all-reduce per layer crosses the slow link.

When TP appears in practice

9. Activation memory: the third memory term

So far only parameter memory has been discussed. Activations (the intermediate results kept for the backward pass) can be large too, and tensor and pipeline parallelism reduce the parameter memory linearly, but not all of the activation memory. The slide's reference is Korthikanti et al. 2022, "Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models".

The per-layer formula

Store everything, no parallelism. With \(s\) the sequence length, \(b\) the micro-batch, \(h\) the hidden size, \(a\) the number of heads and \(t\) the tensor-parallel size, the activation memory per layer (in bytes, with 16-bit activations) is

\[ \text{mem}_{\text{layer}} = sbh\left(34 + 5\frac{as}{h}\right) \]

  • The \(5\frac{as}{h}\) term comes from the quadratic attention terms (the attention scores and their dropout masks). As with FlashAttention, this term can be dropped by recomputation.
  • Tensor parallelism splits the matrix multiplies in attention and MLP, so the large terms are divided by \(t\), but a \(10sbh\) term remains. It is the LayerNorm (\(4sbh\)), dropout (\(2sbh\)) and inputs to attention and MLP (\(4sbh\)): pointwise operations that every GPU duplicates.
ConfigurationActivation memory per transformer layer
no parallelism\(sbh\left(34 + 5\frac{as}{h}\right)\)
tensor parallel (baseline)\(sbh\left(10 + \frac{24}{t} + 5\frac{as}{ht}\right)\)
tensor + sequence parallel\(sbh\left(\frac{34}{t} + 5\frac{as}{ht}\right)\)
tensor parallel + selective activation recomputation\(sbh\left(10 + \frac{24}{t}\right)\)
tensor + sequence parallel + selective recomputation\(sbh\left(\frac{34}{t}\right)\)

Sequence parallelism: make the pointwise terms scale too

Observation: all the \(10sbh\) terms are pointwise operations over the sequence. So split LayerNorm and dropout along the sequence axis. The communication pattern changes to match: in the forward pass the operator \(\bar{g}\) becomes an all-gather and \(g\) a reduce-scatter; in the backward pass the two are reversed. The total communication volume is the same as the all-reduce, but the activation memory of these layers is divided by \(t\). The slide's table shows that tensor + sequence + selective recomputation gives \( sbh\cdot 34/t \), which scales fully with more machines.

Worked example (GPT-3 175B-like defaults)

\(sbh = 2048 \times 12288 \times 1 \approx 25.2\) million elements, so the byte count is 25.2 MB times the coefficient, with 16-bit activations. Without parallelism the coefficient is \(34 + 5 \cdot 96 \cdot 2048 / 12288 = 34 + 80 = 114\), so one layer needs about 2.87 GB per micro-batch sample. With \(t = 8\) and sequence parallelism the coefficient is \(34/8 + 10 = 14.25\), about 358 MB per layer. With selective recomputation as well, \(34/8 = 4.25\), about 107 MB.

10. Expert parallelism and the other axes

Expert parallelism (EP) applies to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Instead of splitting each matrix multiply, split the experts across GPUs and route each token's activations to the GPU that holds its expert. The slide notes that, for MLPs, EP behaves roughly like TP: high bandwidth, and it reduces the activation traffic (a Megatron guideline quoted there). But splitting matrix multiplies can reduce efficiency compared with routing whole activations, since each expert's matrices stay large.

Megatron guideline 4: prefer EP over TP for expert layersWhy
Better GEMM efficiencylarger local matrix sizes improve GPU utilisation
Lower communicationEP has less communication overhead than TP for MoE layers
Simpler computation grapheasier to overlap communication with computation
Token permutationwhen EP = number of experts, local token permutation is eliminated

The slide's example: for Mixtral 8x7B, EP8 x TP1 outperforms EP4 x TP2.

Composing EP with the others, and the attention / MoE mismatch

EP can be composed with every other strategy, but there are two notes. First, DP usually shares replicas with the EP split, so EP is less than DP in size. Second, DP and TP can interact badly and lower utilisation. A deeper issue: MoEs apply to the MLPs, not to attention (with some exotic exceptions). The attention and MLP parts of a model therefore want different parallel layouts:

  • High TP is useful for attention, since attention cannot use EP.
  • Low TP is useful for the MLP, since EP is preferred there.

Megatron Core's answer is MoE parallel folding, which decouples the two sets of groups: attention uses TP x CP x DP x PP, while MoE layers use ETP x EP x EDP x PP (expert-TP, expert, expert-DP, pipeline). The slide's point is that a single set of groups is no longer enough.

Context parallelism and ring attention

Context parallelism (CP) splits the activations of a long sequence across GPUs. Ring attention (Liu et al. 2023) passes key/value blocks around a ring of GPUs while each GPU computes attention for its own query block, overlapping communication with computation. Long-context training phases use large CP: the Nemotron 3 Super and Llama 3 examples later in this lecture both do.

11. 3D (4D) parallelism: putting it together

The slides give simple rules of thumb from the literature:

  1. Until the model fits in memory: use tensor (and expert) parallelism up to the number of GPUs in a node, and pipeline parallelism across machines. (Or use ZeRO-3, depending on bandwidth.)
  2. Then: scale the rest of the way with data parallelism.

If the batch is small, gradient accumulation trades a larger effective batch for better communication efficiency: the collectives run once per accumulated batch instead of once per micro-batch.

Parallelism order in practice

The Llama 3 paper orders the dimensions as [TP, CP, PP, DP], from innermost (fastest link, most communication) to outermost (slowest link, most latency tolerance). FSDP is the outermost dimension because it can prefetch and overlap its sharded weight and gradient traffic.

What Megatron recommends, and what the scaling study found

The slides show Megatron's current recommendations split into "basics" and "extras". The basics: (1) minimise model parallelism and maximise data parallelism (use the distributed optimizer to shard optimizer state across DP ranks); (2) keep EP and TP communication inside the NVLink domain (EP x TP fits in one node, typically 8 GPUs); (3) use pipeline parallelism to distribute layers across nodes while keeping EP x TP inside NVLink. The extras: prefer EP over TP for expert layers (guideline 4), and enable context parallelism for sequences of 8K tokens and longer (guideline 5). Note from the same page: for very large MoEs such as DeepSeek-V3, EP communication may exceed NVLink bandwidth, and then 1F1B all-to-all overlap is used.

Narayanan et al. 2021 (Megatron-LM with PTD-P, pipeline + tensor + data) scaled from 1.7B to 1T parameters on up to 3072 GPUs. The slide's table (below) shows that the recipe has the same shape throughout: tensor parallel grows to 8 and stays there, pipeline parallel grows to fit the model, and data parallel shrinks as the model grows.

The scaling picture: "careful 3D parallelism gives linear gains". Narayanan's PTD-P curves keep per-GPU throughput flat as GPUs are added, where ZeRO-3 alone falls off.

Recomputation can pay for itself

Recomputing activations in the backward pass costs roughly one extra forward pass. But it cuts activation memory enough to fit a larger batch, which in turn hides the pipeline bubble and amortises communication. The net throughput is higher at large batch sizes, as the slide shows.

Feasibility calculator for a 3D configuration

Choose the GPU count and the TP, CP, PP sizes. The world size is \( \text{GPUs} = TP \times CP \times PP \times DP \), so DP is what is left over. The calculator checks that DP is an integer, whether TP fits in a node, whether the model state fits in 80 GB per GPU under the chosen ZeRO stage, and what the pipeline bubble is for the chosen number of micro-batches. Activation memory is not included.

Check the calculator's defaults against the Llama 3 405B row of the table in section 12: 8192 GPUs, TP 8, CP 1, PP 16 give DP = 64, and \(m = 32\) with DP 64 and sequence 8192 gives \(32 \times 64 \times 8192 \approx 16.8\)M tokens per step, the "16M" of the paper. The pipeline ratio here is the naive \((p-1)/m\) estimate, not the exact schedule of that run.

The slides close with real configurations. They are the best way to see how the pieces combine. Keep in mind that the sources do not always agree, and the notes flag where.

From the slide's Llama 3 table. The paper's stated order of dimensions is [TP, CP, PP, DP] (innermost to outermost); DP here is FSDP, the outermost dimension, since it tolerates latency best.

Why this order. The innermost parallelism needs the highest bandwidth and lowest latency, so it is kept within a server: TP 8 is the NVLink domain. The outermost parallelism may cross a multi-hop network and must tolerate latency: FSDP, which prefetches sharded weights and reduces gradients asynchronously. The paper's memory estimator and performance-projection tool were used to find configurations that avoid GPU memory overflow with minimal communication overhead.

Failures at this scale. Over a 54-day pre-training period, Llama 3 saw many unexpected interruptions. About 78% were attributed to hardware (confirmed or suspected). The largest category was faulty GPUs.

DeepSeek and DeepSeek-V3

The DeepSeek infrastructure section quoted on the slide describes a framework (HAI-LLM) that combines data, tensor, sequence and 1F1B pipeline parallelism, in the Megatron style, with FlashAttention and ZeRO-1 for the optimizer states. Overlap is engineered where possible: the backward pass of the last micro-batch overlaps the reduce-scatter of ZeRO-1, and GEMMs overlap the all-gather / reduce-scatter of sequence parallelism. Training is in BF16 with FP32 gradient accumulation, and the cross-entropy is computed on the fly to save memory.

For DeepSeek-V3 the slide gives: PP 16, EP 64-way across 8 nodes, ZeRO-1, with the EP all-to-all overlapped with 1F1B. The Megatron-based table on the slide lists DeepSeek-V3 as 671B parameters on 1024 GPUs with TP 2, PP 16, EP 64, and an overview table lists TP 1. The two rows disagree: 2 x 16 x 64 = 2048, not 1024, while TP 1 gives exactly 1024. The slides therefore leave the TP value of DeepSeek-V3 ambiguous.

Three patterns follow. Tensor parallelism is generally at most 8, the node size. Expert parallelism can be large (64 for DeepSeek-V3 and Nemotron 3), but it is hard to use. Long-context phases use large CP, because activation memory grows with the sequence and CP splits it.

Megatron-style check

Narayanan's table satisfies GPUs = TP x PP x DP in every row. Llama 3 adds CP: 8 x 1 x 16 x 64 = 8,192 and 8 x 16 x 16 x 8 = 16,384. If a proposed configuration does not multiply out to the GPU count, it cannot run as written. The feasibility calculator checks DP = GPUs / (TP x CP x PP) for this reason.

Key takeaways

  • Scaling beyond one GPU is necessary for both compute and memory. Linear memory and linear compute scaling are the two goals.
  • All of the strategies are built from a few collectives. All-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather, and ZeRO uses that identity to shard the 16-byte-per-parameter state.
  • ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 are almost free in communication, ZeRO-3 costs 1.5x. None of them shrinks activation memory.
  • Pipeline parallelism needs many micro-batches: the bubble ratio is \((p-1)/m\). Zero-bubble and interleaving reduce it at a bandwidth or complexity price.
  • Tensor parallelism has no bubble but needs an all-reduce per layer, so it lives inside a node on NVLink.
  • Sequence / context parallelism removes the remaining pointwise activation memory; expert parallelism spreads MoE experts out.
  • There is no single solution. Real runs combine all of them, nested by bandwidth, and the rules of thumb make the combination interpretable: TP and EP inside the node, PP across nodes until the model fits, DP for the rest, with gradient accumulation when the batch is small.
