Self-check

Why is naive data parallelism 16 bytes per parameter, and what are the 16?
2 bytes BF16 parameters, 2 bytes BF16 gradients, 4 bytes FP32 master weights, 4 bytes FP32 Adam first moment and 4 bytes FP32 Adam second moment: \(2+2+4+4+4 = 16\). With BF16 moments the total is 12 (K = 8). With K = 12 for the all-FP32 optimizer state, the baseline is \((2+2+K)\Psi = 16\Psi\), so a 7.5B model needs 120 GB per GPU.
For a 7.5B model on 64 GPUs, what does ZeRO-1 need per GPU, and what does ZeRO-3 need?
ZeRO-1: \((4 + 12/64)\times 7.5 \approx 31.4\) GB. ZeRO-3: \((16/64)\times 7.5 = 1.875 \approx 1.9\) GB. These are the slide 18 numbers. ZeRO-2 gives \((2 + 14/64)\times 7.5 \approx 16.6\) GB.
Why is ZeRO-1 "free" but ZeRO-3 costs 1.5x?
ZeRO-1 replaces the all-reduce (which is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, \(2\Psi\)) with exactly the same two collectives, just applied to the sharded state. ZeRO-3 must also all-gather the parameters for the forward pass and again for the backward pass, and reduce-scatter the gradients: \(2\Psi + \Psi\), i.e. \(3\Psi\), which is 1.5 times the all-reduce.
A pipeline has \(p = 4\) stages and \(m = 4\) micro-batches. What is the bubble ratio, and what share of the wall-clock time is idle?
The ratio of bubble time to useful compute is \((p-1)/m = 3/4 = 0.75\). The idle share of wall-clock time is \((p-1)/(m+p-1) = 3/7 \approx 42.9\%\), which the schedule explorer reproduces for GPipe and 1F1B (makespan 21 units; each GPU does 12 units of work, so 9 of the 21 are idle).
Why should tensor parallelism stay inside a node?
It needs an all-reduce per layer (\(8bsh(n-1)/n\) elements per layer, versus \(bsh\) point to point per micro-batch for a pipeline boundary). That traffic is only affordable on the fast intra-node interconnect (NVLink, up to 8 GPUs on the slides). Across nodes it would dominate the step time, which is why pipeline parallelism is used across machines.
In the critical-batch-size picture, what happens at \(B = B_{\text{noise}}\)?
With efficiency \(x/(1+x)\), \(x = B/B_{\text{noise}}\), you get \(1/2\): half of the best possible speed per step. Below that batch size, doubling the batch nearly doubles progress per step ("perfect scaling"); well above it, extra batch helps little ("ineffective scaling").
Why does sequence parallelism apply to LayerNorm and dropout but not to the matmuls in tensor parallelism?
Tensor parallelism already splits the matmuls across GPUs, so their activations are divided by \(t\). The remaining \(10sbh\) terms are pointwise operations over the sequence (LayerNorm, dropout, and the inputs to attention and MLP), which TP duplicates on each GPU. Sequence parallelism splits exactly these operations along the sequence axis, with an all-gather / reduce-scatter pair in place of the all-reduce.
Why are the Llama 3 dimensions ordered [TP, CP, PP, DP], and why is FSDP the outermost?
The order follows network needs: innermost is the most bandwidth-hungry and latency-sensitive (TP, kept inside the NVLink node), outermost is the most latency-tolerant. FSDP tolerates a slow multi-hop network because it prefetches sharded weights and reduces gradients asynchronously, so it takes the outer position.

Scaling laws: the basics

lecture_09.pdf (57 slides) scaling laws power laws Kaplan 2020 Chinchilla 2022 compute-optimal data repetition critical batch muP
TL;DR. Scaling laws are simple power-law (straight lines on log-log axes) relations between loss and data size D, parameter count N and training compute C. They let you predict a big run from small ones, choose hyperparameters before paying for them, and decide how to split a fixed compute budget between model size and tokens. Kaplan et al. (2020) argue that most extra compute should go to model size (Nopt ∝ C0.73). Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) re-fit the same question with three methods and got roughly equal scaling of model and data (Nopt, Dopt ∝ C0.5, about 20 tokens per parameter for approaches 1 and 2). The disagreement is still partly unresolved, and the lecture's warning is that the choice matters and that extrapolation is easy to get wrong.

1. Why scaling laws? "Taking scaling seriously"

The lecture opens with a thought experiment: a friend gives you ten thousand B200 GPUs for a month and asks you to build a good open-source LM. You need (A2) an infrastructure team and a distributed training framework, (A4) a strong pretraining dataset, and then (the part the lecture cares about) a model to run. "Run a big model, but which one?" Scaling is hard because there are many knobs: wide or deep? how many heads? which nonlinearity? Cargo-culting the choices of existing LMs does not explain how those choices were optimized in the first place.

The lecture's answer is "simple, predictive laws for the behaviour of LMs". Two strategies are contrasted:

Old and unpleasant

Tune hyperparameters on the big model itself. Expensive, and you only learn after you have paid for the run.

New (over?) optimism

Tune on small models, fit a scaling law, extrapolate to the large model. This is cheap, but only as good as the extrapolation.

The slide deck organises the material in two parts. Part 1 covers the history and theory of data scaling (sample complexity, rates). Part 2 covers LLM scaling behaviour along three questions:

QuestionConcrete formWhere the lecture answers it
1. Data vs performanceAre there simple rules for how data size affects loss?Sections 2 to 4
2. Data vs model sizeDo we train on more data or on bigger models at a fixed budget?Sections 8 to 11
3. Hyperparameters vs performanceHow should we set hyperparameters on the big model?Sections 5 to 7
Definition

A scaling law is a simple formula, usually a power law, that predicts an error metric (usually loss) from a resource (data, parameters, compute). The slide deck's claim is that such laws hold across many phenomena, including non-standard settings (Kaplan et al. 2020 show fits for downstream tasks such as word unscrambling and Persian QA, where accuracy against compute is sigmoidal).

Slide 13 prints three fits (the constants are read from the plot legends). They match the paper's summary equations 1.1–1.3, except for the compute constant noted below:

QuantityFit printed on slide 13Kaplan et al. 2020 constants
Loss vs non-embedding paramsL = (N / 8.8·1013)−0.076αN ≈ 0.076, Nc ≈ 8.8·1013
Loss vs dataset sizeL = (D / 5.4·1013)−0.095αD ≈ 0.095, Dc ≈ 5.4·1013
Loss vs compute (optimal)L = (Cmin / 2.3·108)−0.050αCmin ≈ 0.050, Ccmin ≈ 3.1·108 PF-days (paper text, Eq. 1.3)
Discrepancy in the sources

The compute constant differs between the slide plot legend (2.3·108) and the paper's printed value in Eq. 1.3 (3.1·108 PF-days). The source does not say which constant the plotted curve uses. The exponents (0.050, 0.076, 0.095) are the values that agree across the sources.

The key scaling-law facts from the lecture

  • Test loss vs data size is a straight line on log-log axes (a "scale-free" or power-law relation).
  • Error vs training data size is monotone and logistic-like across regimes (Hestness et al. 2017, slide 14).
  • Scaling laws are lower bounds on what is achievable with given resources. Two cautions from the slides: (1) scaling laws can "break" if applied blindly; (2) you can usually do better than the law predicts, so treat it as a floor.

2. Early history: data scaling

The lecture traces the idea back to theorists' sample-complexity bounds, which are upper bounds on error (not realised loss values):

  • Finite hypothesis class (slide 6): ε(ĥ) ≤ minh ε(h) + 2√((1/m)·log(2k/δ)), for k hypotheses and m samples.
  • Smooth densities: a rate bound for generative modelling of smooth densities, cited to Hall 1989 on slide 6.

Empirical work followed:

1993 Cortes et al., "Learning Curves: Asymptotic Values and Rate of Convergence". Earliest data scaling-law paper in the lecture: learning curves for classifiers, with test error approaching an asymptote at a power-law rate in training-set size.
2001 Banko and Brill: log-linear improvement with data on confusion-set disambiguation. Their conclusion (slide 9 quote): reconsider the trade-off between spending on algorithm development and spending on corpus development, because no learner tested is near asymptote at corpus sizes then used.
2012 Kolachina et al.: power-law relation between data and downstream performance, with a table of candidate curve families (Exp3, Exp4, ExpP3, Pow3, Pow4, ILog2) fitted to BLEU vs training size.
2017 Hestness et al. "Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically". Predictable power-law scaling on machine translation, language modelling and speech, with the three-region shape below.
2020 Kaplan et al. "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (OpenAI). Power laws for parameters, data and compute, with joint and compute-optimal forms.

Hestness et al. (2017) is the first large-scale neural scaling paper in the lecture. Its claim is that the power-law region is where you can extrapolate, and the three regions summarise its shape:

RegionBehaviourWhat to do
Small-data regionModel is in the "best guess" regime; error barely depends on dataDo not fit a law here
Power-law regionLog-log linear: error ∝ data−βFit and extrapolate
Irreducible-error regionError plateaus at the Bayes/entropy floorMore data will not help

Slide 11 pairs three further passages from Hestness et al. (2017) with labels:

  • "Emergence": the quoted passage says a large enough training set is needed before the power-law trend appears, and small tests can mislead. This foreshadows section 12.
  • "Scaling by compute": computational limits. Training large models on large data may be bounded by how fast you can compute, not by data.
  • "Speed = accuracy": the performance–accuracy trade-off, where a speedup that loses accuracy may still be recoverable.
Why is the 2017 paper "very ahead of its time"?

It reports power-law fits for MT, LM and speech before transformers existed, and it sketches a three-region shape for the learning curve.

3. Why do power laws show up? Mean estimation and nonparametric learning

The lecture's first foundational question: why should error be a power law (linear in log-log)? We know error should decrease monotonically with data. The slides answer: "estimation error naturally decays polynomially". This is worked through with two toy examples.

3.1 Toy example: mean estimation

Take n samples x1 … xn ∼ N(μ, σ²) and estimate the mean by μ̂ = (1/n) Σ xi. Standard arguments give

\[ \mathbb{E}\big[(\hat\mu - \mu)^2\big] = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}. \]

Taking logs gives log(Error) = −log n + 2 log σ: a straight line of slope −1 on a log-log plot. More generally, any polynomial rate 1/nα is a scaling law with exponent α. The chart below shows this for two noise levels; the slope is the same and only the offset (2 log σ) changes.

3.2 Nonparametric learning: boxes in d dimensions

The second example is a nonparametric estimator. Inputs x1 … xn are uniform in the unit box in 2D, the response is yi = f(xi) + N(0,1), and we estimate f by cutting the box into cells of side n−1/4. There are about √n cells, each containing about √n samples, so the error is approximately 1/√n plus smoothness terms. In d dimensions the same argument gives

\[ \text{Error} \approx n^{-1/d} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \log(\text{Error}) = -\tfrac{1}{d}\log n + C. \]

The takeaway from the slide: flexible nonparametric learning has a dimension-dependent scaling law, and the slope is −1/d. Higher-dimensional inputs need more data for the same error, which is the curse of dimensionality written as a scaling exponent. The calculator below shows this directly.

3.3 Intrinsic dimensionality and the "mystery" of the exponent

The slide "Scaling law exponents: an intriguing mystery" makes the point that most classical models (regression and similar) have a 1/n rate, so they predict the same slope. Real neural scaling curves show different slopes for machine translation, speech and language modelling. So the classical argument explains that a power law exists, but not why the exponent is what it is.

Bahri et al. (2021), as summarised on slide 20, argue that:

  1. Scaling laws arise from polynomial learning rates 1/nα.
  2. The slope α is closely connected to the intrinsic dimensionality of the data.

The lecture is explicit that this is not airtight: intrinsic-dimension estimators are sketchy. The slide plots estimated intrinsic dimension (x) against a fitted slope (y) for several datasets (teacher-student, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, MNIST, FashionMNIST), with reference lines for the slopes printed on the slide and wide scatter.

Caveat

The "1/d" intuition is a useful mental model but not a law for real data. Use it to reason about order of magnitude, not to predict an exponent from a dimension estimate.

4. Other data-scaling questions: mixtures, composition, repetition

The lecture then asks what else changes the data-scaling curve.

QuestionFinding or method (from slides)
Composition / mixtureData composition affects the offset of the curve, not its slope (Hashimoto 2021, distribution-shift scaling laws; slides 21–22).
Mixture selectionFit mixture-dependent laws on small-scale models to predict large-run loss (Data Mixing Laws; DataDecide). Slide 23 says this is hard in practice, and the empirical baseline is to take the best small mixture.
RepetitionWith finite unique data, repeated tokens are worth less than fresh ones. The data-constrained law (Muennighoff et al. 2023) is below.
SelectionData selection should adapt to scale (slide 26). Slide 26 labels the best filtering strength by compute regime: highly aggressive filtering at small compute, mildly aggressive at medium compute, and lightly aggressive at large compute.

4.1 Scaling under data repetition

In practice the data is finite. Muennighoff et al. (2023) model repeated data as partially valuable. With UD unique tokens and RD repetitions (epochs minus one), the effective data is

\[ D' = U_D + U_D\, R_D^{*}\left(1 - e^{-R_D / R_D^{*}}\right), \]

with a learned constant RD*. The authors' fit gives RD* ≈ 15.4 (their Appendix A; the slide's legend defines D′, UD, RD* and RD). For small RD the formula reduces to D′ ≈ D (repeats are nearly as good as fresh data), and D′ saturates at UD(1 + RD*) no matter how many epochs you run.

Reading the slide's numbers

With UD = 12B the slide's epoch markers are 12B (1 epoch), 48B (4), 120B (10), 480B (40), 1.2T (100). Up to about 4 epochs (RD = 3) the formula gives about 93% of raw value; at 40 epochs about 38%; at 100 epochs about 16% (the cap 16.4·UD ≈ 197B). The "no benefit beyond ~4 epochs" folk rule is a reading of this curve, not an exact threshold.

5. Model-side scaling: architecture, optimiser, depth and width

The lecture's central reframing: scaling laws are also a design tool. "How can we efficiently design huge LMs?" Choices like LSTM vs Transformer, Adam vs SGD, depth vs width, and how many tokens to train on are usually settled by brute force. A scaling-law design procedure answers them cheaply.

Resource-allocation questions
  • Train models longer, or train bigger models?
  • Collect more data, or get more GPUs?
Hyperparameter list (Kaplan et al. case study)
  • Architecture
  • Optimiser
  • Aspect ratio / depth
  • Batch size

5.1 Architecture: Transformers vs LSTMs

The brute-force test of "are Transformers better than LSTMs?" is to train a GPT-3-sized LSTM at a cost of tens of millions of dollars. The scaling-law test is to fit both families over a range of sizes and compare the curves (slide 30, cited to Kaplan et al.). The LSTM curves lie above the Transformer curves across the plotted range.

Tay et al. (2022, cross-architecture scaling, slide 31) extends the comparison to many architectures (ALBERT, DConv, Evolved, Funnel, Transformer-GLU, LConv, MLP-Mixer, MoE Transformer, Performer, Switch Transformer, Universal Transformer): each family is plotted on its own curve against FLOPs.

5.2 Optimiser: Adam vs SGD

Hestness et al. (2017) compared SGD and Adam on depth-10 recurrent highway networks. The lecture notes this is pre-transformer work (RHN = recurrent highway networks). Both fit power laws against training-set size. Adam's trend is lower, and its slope is nearly identical (−0.095 vs −0.094).

5.3 Depth and width

  • Going from 1 to 2 layers makes a huge difference in loss. More layers give diminishing returns below about 107 parameters (slide 33, Kaplan et al.).
  • The aspect ratio (depth vs width) and other Transformer hyperparameters are not scale-invariant in an obvious way. Slide 34 (Kaplan et al.'s Figure 5) shows that loss changes only a few percent over a wide range of feed-forward ratio, aspect ratio and attention-head dimension at fixed parameter count. Its annotations say a (6, 4288) model is within 3% of the (48, 1600) model used in the GPT-2 reference [RWC+19], and that about 21% extra compute compensates for a 1% loss increase in the attention-head panel.

5.4 Not all parameters are equal

The lecture pushes the abstraction one step further: "we've been thinking about parameters, but not all parameters are equal". Embedding-layer parameters do not behave like the others. Kaplan et al. use non-embedding parameters N in their law. Pearce and Song (section 11, Explanation 2) argue that the choice between total and non-embedding counts is one source of the Kaplan–Chinchilla gap. Mixture-of-experts scaling makes it clearer still: the total parameter count and the active parameter count give different optima.

6. Batch size: the critical batch

Batch size is known to have strong diminishing returns past a certain point. The lecture defines the critical batch size Bcrit precisely (McCandlish et al. 2018, "An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training").

Procedure from slide 38: pick a target loss, then sweep batch sizes and count the steps S and the examples E needed to reach it. The two quantities trade off:

\[ \frac{S}{S_{\min}} - 1 = \left(\frac{E}{E_{\min}} - 1\right)^{-1}, \qquad B_{\text{crit}} = \frac{E_{\min}}{S_{\min}}. \]

Equivalently, with x = B / Bcrit: the step ratio is 1 + 1/x and the example ratio is 1 + x. Below Bcrit you get near-linear speedup in wall-clock steps for little extra data; above it, extra batch buys little. The slide says this balance gives roughly 2× the optimal steps / passes, and that Bcrit is claimed to be close to the ratio of the trace of the gradient covariance to the squared gradient norm.

The minimum compute to reach the target is

\[ C_{\min}(C) \equiv \frac{C}{1 + B / B_{\text{crit}}(L)}, \qquad\text{(at } B \ll B_{\text{crit}}\text{)}. \]

The slide's scatter (WebText2 train loss vs critical batch size, two model sizes, and a fit Bcrit = 2.1·108 tokens · L−4.8) makes the key point: the smaller the loss target, the bigger the critical batch.

7. Hyperparameter transfer: muP and scale-aware learning rates

Hyperparameters are where scaling laws become a practical tool. The lecture's teaser covers two papers:

  • Yang et al. 2022 (muP, "Tensor Programs V"): if you parameterise initialisation and learning rate in a width-aware way (the "maximal update" parameterisation), the optimal learning rate stays stable as width grows. Under standard practice the optimum shifts left (smaller LR) as width increases, as the left panel of slide 40 shows.
  • Yao et al. 2024 (cited on slide 40 next to the "our work" panel): scale-aware initialisation and learning-rate scaling. The learning rate should be set as a function of scale, not tuned once on a single size.
Caution (slide 41, Tay et al. 2023)

Scaling is predictable for pretraining loss, but downstream metrics (SuperGLUE accuracy vs parameters for several architectures) are much less predictable. Scaling behaviour in loss does not automatically transfer to task accuracy.

The lecture's summary of what can be predicted before training:

Predictable from small models
  • Optimiser choice (Adam vs SGD ranking persists).
  • Model depth and aspect ratio.
  • Architecture choice (the offset ranking persists).
  1. Train a few smaller models.
  2. Establish a scaling law (for example Adam vs SGD).
  3. Select the optimal hyperparameter by extrapolating the law to the target size.
  • Downstream accuracy can be much less predictable than loss (slide 41).
  • Optimal learning rate changes with scale unless the parameterisation is scale-aware (slide 40).
  • Extrapolating a single exponent across regimes can mislead (section 13).

8. Data vs model size: the joint law and Kaplan's allocation

The lecture's "one important use of scaling laws": do we need more data or bigger models? "Clearly lots of data is wasted on small models." Joint data–model scaling laws describe how the two relate.

Rosenfeld et al. (2020) fit a joint law of the form Error = n−α + m−β + C (slide 43), where n is data and m is model size. Kaplan et al. (2020) fit

\[ L(N, D) = \left[\left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N/\alpha_D} + \frac{D_c}{D}\right]^{\alpha_D} \qquad\text{(Kaplan Eq. 1.5)} \]

with the same constants as in section 1 (Nc ≈ 8.8·1013, αN ≈ 0.076, Dc ≈ 5.4·1013, αD ≈ 0.095). The paper reports that it fits the data well and that it governs the degree of overfitting. The step-based form (Eq. 1.6) uses Smin instead.

Kaplan et al. then ask: for a fixed compute budget C = 6ND, how should you split it? Their Eqs. 1.7–1.8 (and the summary on slide 45) give

\[ N_{\text{opt}} \propto C^{0.73}, \qquad D_{\text{opt}} \propto C^{0.27}, \]

with the batch-size and step components B ∝ C0.24 and S ∝ C0.03, which multiply to D = B·S ∝ C0.27. The implication is that most extra compute should go into bigger models and data grows slowly: tokens-per-parameter falls as compute rises.

Model–data joint scaling is accurate (slide 44, Rosenfeld et al. 2020). Fit the exponents on small data and small models, then predict the rest. The lecture says this works for the ImageNet and WikiText-103 test cases shown on the slide.

Source discrepancy you should know about

The slide 45 summary "Kaplan claims Nopt = C0.73, Dopt = C0.27" is the paper's conclusion. The lecture's own figure of the same comparison (slide 45) shows the Chinchilla approaches on top of Kaplan's line. The gap between 0.73/0.27 and roughly 0.5/0.5 is the central content of section 9.

9. Chinchilla: three ways to fit a scaling law

Hoffmann et al. (2022) argue that the Kaplan fits are "quite off". They propose three approaches; the lecture says "they mostly (minus method 3) suggest similar constants".

9.1 Approach 3 in detail

Chinchilla's Approach 3 fits (Eq. 10 in the paper, the parametric decomposition in their Appendix D.2):

\[ \hat L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}, \qquad E = 1.69,\; A = 406.4,\; B = 410.7,\; \alpha = 0.34,\; \beta = 0.28. \]

The three terms are, respectively: the entropy of natural text (irreducible loss), the approximation error of a model with N parameters, and the stochastic-approximation error of training on D tokens in one epoch. The formulas give exponents a = β/(α + β) ≈ 0.45 for Nopt ∝ Ca and b = α/(α + β) ≈ 0.55 for Dopt ∝ Cb; the paper's table reports 0.46 and 0.54. Derivation (minimise L̂ subject to C = 6ND):

Derivation of the optimal allocation

Minimising E + A N−α + B D−β with D = C/(6N) gives

\[ N_{\text{opt}} = G\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}, \quad D_{\text{opt}} = \frac{C}{6 N_{\text{opt}}}, \quad G = \left(\frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\right)^{1/(\alpha+\beta)}. \]

So Nopt ∝ Cβ/(α+β) and Dopt ∝ Cα/(α+β). With the printed constants, G ≈ 1.345, and the exponents evaluate to 0.452 and 0.548. The table's intervals are 0.454–0.455 and 0.542–0.543. The gap from 0.452 and 0.548 probably comes from the two-decimal rounding of the printed α and β; I did not verify the unrounded fit.

9.2 The three methods' exponents

Approaches 1 and 2 agree within their intervals. Approach 3 is the outlier among Chinchilla's three, and the lecture flags its details as the source of later disputes (section 11). All three are far from Kaplan's 0.73.

9.3 Tokens per parameter

The practical consequence is the tokens-per-parameter ratio D/N. The slide lists what real models do:

ModelTokens per parameter
GPT-3≈ 2
Chinchilla≈ 20
LLaMA-65B≈ 22
Llama 2 70B≈ 29

The "≈ 20" rule of thumb comes from approaches 1 and 2. Table A3 of the paper (Appendix D.3) gives approach-2 rows of 20 B tokens for 1 B parameters and 1.7 T tokens for 67 B (ratios 20 and 25). The paper's approach-3 rows give larger ratios: 27 at 1 B, 41 at 10 B and 61 at 67 B. The ratio rises with compute under Approach 3, so "20" is a useful but approximate number.

9.4 IsoFLOP and the "everywhere" view

IsoFLOP is easy to run and usually clean. The lecture shows it applied in other settings as well: diffusion models (Gulrajani et al. 2023) and mixture-of-experts (Abnar et al. 2025). For a fixed budget, the loss against model size is a parabola-like curve with an optimum; the minima trace the frontier.

Note the mismatch between this IsoFLOP figure (63 B at Gopher's budget, Approach 2) and the Eq. 10 frontier computed in section 10 (about 32 B at the same budget, Approach 3 with the printed constants). That gap is a central part of the Kaplan–Chinchilla debate.

10. Calculators: compute-optimal allocation, IsoFLOP and overtraining

The three interactive tools below use the Chinchilla constants (Eq. 10) and the Pearce & Song constants (slide 52). The compute-optimal frontier closed form is from the derivation in section 9.1.

10.1 Chinchilla optimal-allocation calculator

Choose a compute budget C and a set of constants. The calculator returns the compute-optimal parameter count, token count and predicted loss, and plots the frontier across budgets. The default budget is Gopher's 5.76·1023 FLOPs (slide 47). Switch to the Pearce & Song constants to compare.

10.2 IsoFLOP calculator (Approach 3 surface)

For one budget C, the calculator sweeps the model size N and sets D = C/(6N). It evaluates the Eq. 10 loss and marks the minimum. The minimum is the IsoFLOP optimum for that budget under the fitted surface.

Reading an IsoFLOP curve

Left of the minimum, the model is too small for the tokens you can afford at that budget, so the A/Nα term dominates. Right of the minimum, the model is large and under-trained, so B/Dβ dominates. The minimum is where the two terms balance. A "valley" in this plot is a sign that a compute-optimal model exists for that budget.

10.3 Overtraining: why train past the optimum?

Chinchilla answers "what is the best model for a fixed training compute". The lecture's key caveat: most of the compute in a real deployment is inference, so you should over-train. Every token served costs roughly 2N FLOPs, so a smaller model trained on more tokens can be cheaper overall. The calculator below fixes the parameter count and varies tokens per parameter.

The lecture's list (slide 54): GPT-3 about 2, Chinchilla about 20, LLaMA-65B about 22, Llama 2 70B about 29, Mistral 7B about 110, Llama 3 70B about 215. The more usage a model gets, the more it pays to front-load compute in a smaller model.

Note on the overtraining view

Sardana and Frankle (2024, "Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal") make this point formally: the training-optimal model is not the deployment-optimal one, and their analysis extrapolates over 300× training compute to a 1.4 B model on 900 B tokens, looking at task performance rather than validation loss.

11. Why do Kaplan and Chinchilla disagree?

The lecture spends a slide on "why do we have this big difference?" when both sets of authors fit joint scaling laws. It lists explanations from the literature.

Explanation 1 (Porian et al. 2024)

Explanation 2 (Pearce and Song) is the difference between non-embedding and total parameter counts, plus small nonlinearities. The slide reports a local exponent of 0.78 for non-embedding parameters (close to Kaplan's 0.73) and 0.51 for total parameters (close to Chinchilla's 0.50), so the exponent depends on which count you use. The lecture's summary: "non-embedding vs total param choice + small nonlinearities."

Fun addendum: errors in Chinchilla Method 3. Besiroglu et al. (2024) recovered the raw data from the original paper, refitted Approach 3, and got results more consistent with Methods 1 and 2. The residuals on slide 53 centre near −0.05 for the original Hoffmann et al. fit and near 0 for the reanalysis. The lecture calls this "likely flawed in the original paper", which should be read as a published reanalysis, not a settled fact.

What is still open

The source disagreement is about the exponent (0.73 vs about 0.5), the parameter count used, and the fitting procedure. The lecture does not claim a single correct answer. The practical advice is to fit your own law on your own setup, and to check the exponent against the procedure you intend to use.

12. The emergence debate

The lecture's emergence material is brief. Hestness et al. (2017) list "Emergence" as a theme (section 2): small-data tests may not reach the power-law region and can mislead. The modern version of the debate is about abilities that appear abruptly in benchmark accuracy as scale increases.

  • Emergence view: some abilities are absent below a threshold and then appear, so a power law in loss does not predict the behaviour on these tasks (Wei et al. 2022).
  • Mirage view: the abrupt jump can be an artefact of discrete metrics (exact match, multiple choice) applied to a smoothly improving underlying quantity. Schaeffer et al. (2023), "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?", argue this. This is outside the lecture slides; cited here from memory.
  • Link to scaling laws: loss scales smoothly (slide 41, Tay et al. 2023), but downstream accuracy can be unpredictable, which is the reason the lecture gives for caution about downstream extrapolation.

13. Extrapolation pitfalls and a power-law fitter

Scaling laws are only as reliable as the extrapolation. The lecture's warnings, collected from the slides and the paper discussions:

  1. Floors. Real loss has an irreducible term E (the entropy of text). A pure power-law fit to a curve with a floor bends over and over-predicts the improvement. The calculator below demonstrates this.
  2. Regime changes. The small-data region (Hestness) is not power-law. Fitting there gives the wrong exponent.
  3. Exponent sensitivity. The Kaplan–Chinchilla disagreement is about 0.25 in the model-size exponent (0.73 vs 0.46 to 0.50). Over four decades of extrapolation, a 0.25 exponent gap changes the predicted size ratio by roughly an order of magnitude.
  4. Composition and mixture. Scaling laws from one data mixture do not transfer to another without re-fitting the offset (slide 21–22).
  5. Downstream vs loss. Loss is smooth, task accuracy often is not (slide 41, Tay et al. 2023). Predicting task accuracy is harder than predicting loss.
  6. Lower bounds. A scaling law is a lower bound on the achievable loss for the family of models studied. Better architectures and data can beat it (slide 25, "you can always potentially do better").

13.1 Power-law fitter and extrapolator

Choose a dataset with a known curve, fit a straight line in log-log space to the points in a window, and extrapolate. The chart shows the true curve (solid) and the fitted power law (dashed). "Pure power law" is Kaplan's L(N) or L(D), which really is a power law, so the fit is exact. "Floor + power law" is the Chinchilla E + A/N0.34 in the infinite-data limit, where the fit is not exact.

13.2 Kaplan's joint law, interactively

The joint law (Eq. 1.5) gives loss for any (N, D). Set a model size and a data size and see the predicted loss and the compute C = 6ND. The horizontal line is the loss with infinite data (the L(N) limit).

13.3 The published Kaplan fits as curves

The two marginal fits from section 1 as log-log curves, with the constants printed on slide 13.

14. Key takeaways

0.73 vs 0.5
Kaplan vs Chinchilla model-size exponent
Kaplan: Nopt ∝ C0.73. Chinchilla approaches 1–3: about 0.46–0.50.
≈ 20
tokens per parameter
Chinchilla rule of thumb (approaches 1 and 2). Deployed models use 2 to 215.
≈ 15.4
R*D for repeated data
Beyond about 4 epochs, repeats add little, and effective data saturates at UD(1 + R*).
−1/d
nonparametric error exponent
Error ≈ n−1/d; higher dimension means a shallower slope.
  • Data scaling: test loss is linear in log-log against data size. Estimation error decays polynomially, so power laws are natural. The exponent is not explained by classical theory (intrinsic dimension is a sketchy explanation).
  • Composition changes the offset of the data-scaling curve. Repetition has diminishing returns, roughly saturating after a few epochs.
  • Model-side design: architecture, optimiser, depth and batch size can be compared with scaling curves on small models.
  • Critical batch: steps and examples trade off; the smaller the loss target, the larger the critical batch (Bcrit ∝ L−4.8 on the slide's fit).
  • Allocation: fix C = 6ND, then choose N and D. Kaplan says most compute goes into size; Chinchilla says model and data scale together. Deployment favours over-training.
  • Caution: scaling laws are lower bounds that can break when applied blindly. Floors, regime changes, mixture shifts and downstream metrics all make extrapolation harder than it looks.

15. Self-check quiz

Why is a power law the natural shape for error vs data?
Estimation error from finite samples decays polynomially. For the mean, E[(μ̂ − μ)²] = σ²/n gives a log-log slope of −1. For nonparametric regression in d dimensions the error is about n−1/d. Any polynomial rate is a power law on log-log axes.
What is the slope of error vs samples for a nonparametric estimator on 3-dimensional inputs?
−1/3. The error scales as n−1/d with d = 3, so the log-log slope is −1/3. Reaching error ε needs n = ε−3 samples.
Kaplan says Nopt ∝ C0.73. Chinchilla says about C0.5. Which way should a fixed budget be spent?
Kaplan: most extra compute goes into parameters, and data grows slowly (D ∝ C0.27). Chinchilla: scale parameters and tokens together (roughly equal exponents), so tokens per parameter stay near a constant (about 20). With a fixed compute budget, Chinchilla would train a smaller model on more tokens than Kaplan's allocation.
Write the Chinchilla Approach 3 loss and its printed constants.
L̂(N, D) = E + A/Nα + B/Dβ with E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34, β = 0.28. E is the irreducible entropy term, A/Nα is the model-size term and B/Dβ is the data term.
At the Gopher budget (5.76·1023 FLOPs), the Eq. 10 frontier gives about 32 B parameters. Chinchilla used 70 B. Is that a contradiction?
Not a contradiction, but a sensitivity warning. Under the printed constants the loss curve is flat near its minimum: 70 B and 32 B differ by only about 0.007 in predicted loss. The IsoFLOP figure (Approach 2) gives about 63 B at this budget, which is closer to Chinchilla's model. The lecture flags Approach 3 as the method whose details are disputed.
Repeated data: with R* = 15.4, roughly how much is 4 repetitions worth, and what is the ceiling?
With RD = 4: D′/UD = 1 + 15.4(1 − e−4/15.4) ≈ 4.52, against 5 raw passes, so repeats are worth about 90% of fresh tokens. The ceiling is UD(1 + R*) ≈ 16.4·UD, no matter how many epochs.
Why does a pure power-law fit over-predict the improvement when there is an irreducible floor?
The true curve E + A/Nα flattens toward E. A straight log-log fit on a window where the curve is still steep has a larger slope in magnitude than the local slope near the floor, so it keeps falling when the true curve has levelled off, and it predicts too low a loss at large scale. The fitter in section 13.1 shows this when the target is far from the window.

Inference

lecture_10.py inference memory-bound roofline KV cache GQA / MLA / CLA quantization speculative sampling continuous batching PagedAttention

TL;DR. Training is compute-bound and fully parallel over the sequence; generation is sequential and, at small batch sizes, memory-bound: every new token reads all weights and the whole KV cache. On an H100 (989 TFLOP/s, 3.35 TB/s) a matmul needs arithmetic intensity above about 295 FLOP/byte to be compute-bound, and single-token decoding has intensity about 1, so the only lever is to move fewer bytes. The lecture walks through three lossy levers (shrink the KV cache with GQA/MLA/CLA/local attention; quantize; prune and distil), one lossless lever (speculative sampling, which is exact), and the systems ideas that make dynamic traffic efficient (continuous batching and PagedAttention).

Why inference matters

Inference shows up in actual use (chatbots, code completion, agents, batch data processing), in model evaluation (for example scoring instruction following), and in reinforcement learning, where you sample many generations and then score them. Training is a one-time cost; inference is paid again on every request, so efficiency compounds. The lecture quotes OpenAI at about 8.6T tokens per day and DeepSeek V4 trained on 32T tokens, as scale references.

Two properties make inference different from training:

  • Chatbots: most tokens are read by humans, so the human is the bottleneck, not the GPU.
  • Agents: query, then internal trace, then output for a human. The number of generated tokens can grow without bound, and tokens generated equal compute spent.

Who does inference

  • Providers of closed models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.).
  • Providers of open-weight models (Together, Fireworks, Baseten, DeepInfra, Groq, Cerebras, etc.).

Open-source serving stacks

  • vLLM: from Berkeley, pioneered PagedAttention, popular and a good default. GitHub
  • SGLang: from Berkeley, pioneered RadixAttention, good for agentic workloads. project
  • TensorRT-LLM: from NVIDIA, highly optimized for GPUs. docs
  • llama.cpp: C++ only, supports CPU inference, runs locally. GitHub

What does "fast" mean?

MetricDefinitionMatters for
TTFT (time-to-first-token)How long the user waits before any output appears.Interactive applications
Latency (seconds per token)How fast tokens appear for one query.Interactive applications
Throughput (tokens per second)How fast tokens appear summed over many queries.Batch processing, cost per token
Why inference is harder than training

In supervised training you see every token at once, so the whole sequence is a big parallel matmul (the Transformer is built for that). In inference you must generate one token, feed it back, and repeat. You cannot parallelize over generation, so it is hard to keep the compute units busy.

The inference workload: arithmetic intensity

The lecture reviews the accounting from the scaling book. Notation is einops-like: symbols denote dimensions. B batch, T query length (tokens we generate logits for), S sequence length (tokens we condition on), D model dimension, H head dimension, N number of query heads, K number of key/value heads, G query heads per KV head, F MLP up-projection dimension, L number of layers, V vocabulary size.

Conventions used throughout: \(F = 4D\) (the MLP up-projects 4x), \(D = NH\) (model dimension is split over heads), \(N = KG\) (for GQA, query heads are split into K groups), and \(S = T\) during training (condition on S tokens to predict T tokens).

Take the matrix multiply \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times D}\) times \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times F}\), in bf16 (2 bytes per element). The lecture counts FLOPs and HBM traffic:

StepBytes movedFLOPs
Read X (B x D)\(2BD\)–
Read W (D x F)\(2DF\)–
Compute Y = X W–\(2BDF\)
Write Y (B x F)\(2BF\)–
Total\(2BD + 2DF + 2BF\)\(2BDF\)

Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte transferred, and we want it high. Simplifying with \(D, F \gg B\) (take \(D = cB\), \(F = cB\), and let \(c \to \infty\)) gives intensity \(= B\).

Source code: matmul accounting and the limit (sympy) 
B, S, T, D, F, N, K, H, L, V = symbols("B S T D F N K H L V", positive=True)
c = symbols("c", positive=True)  # Just a constant that helps with taking limits

flops = 0
bytes_transferred = 0
bytes_transferred += 2*B*D   # Read X (B x D), 2 bytes for bf16
bytes_transferred += 2*D*F   # Read W (D x F)
flops += 2*B*D*F            # Compute Y = X @ W
bytes_transferred += 2*B*F   # Write Y (B x F)

assert flops == 2*B*D*F
assert bytes_transferred == 2*B*D + 2*D*F + 2*B*F

intensity = (flops / bytes_transferred).simplify()  # @inspect intensity
# Assuming B is much less than D and F, then we can simplify:
intensity = intensity.subs(D, c*B).subs(F, c*B).limit(c, oo).simplify()
assert intensity == B

# Accelerator intensity of H100:
flops_per_second = 989e12
memory_bandwidth = 3.35e12
accelerator_intensity = flops_per_second / memory_bandwidth
assert round(accelerator_intensity) == 295
# compute-bound iff B > 295

The lecture's sympy calls are simplify and a limit in c. The same result can be read off the closed form: \(I = 2BDF / (2BD + 2DF + 2BF) \approx B\) when \(D, F \gg B\).

The H100 accelerator intensity is the ratio of peak compute to peak bandwidth: \(989\,\text{TFLOP/s} / 3.35\,\text{TB/s} \approx 295\) FLOP/byte. The rule:

  • If the operation's intensity is greater than 295, it is compute-bound (good).
  • If it is less than 295, it is memory-bound (bad).

So this matmul is compute-bound iff \(B > 295\). The extreme case \(B = 1\) is a matrix-vector product: intensity 1, reading a whole \(D \times F\) matrix to do only \(2DF\) FLOPs. The lecture says this is basically what inference looks like.

Interactive: roofline for one matmul

Set the batch and the matrix shape. The calculator uses the exact counts (\(2BDF\) FLOPs, \(2(BD+DF+BF)\) bytes) and the H100 peaks from the source.

Check it

Default: \(B=1\), \(D=5120\), \(F=13824\). Intensity is about 1, far below 295, so the matmul is memory-bound. Raising \(B\) to 512 pushes the intensity to roughly 450 and the regime flips to compute-bound. That is the whole story of this lecture in one slider.

Prefill and generation: intensity of MLP and attention

Inference has two stages:

  1. Prefill: given the prompt, encode all its tokens into vectors. This is parallel, like training.
  2. Generation (decode): produce response tokens one at a time. This is sequential.

The lecture then counts FLOPs and bytes for the MLP and attention layers, with \(T\) = number of tokens generated (logits computed) and \(S\) = number of previous tokens conditioned on. Prefill is \(T = S\); generation is \(T = 1\).

MLP layers (matrix multiplies only)

The gated MLP has three matrices: \(W_{up}\) and \(W_{gate}\) of shape \(D \times F\), and \(W_{down}\) of shape \(F \times D\). Per step the lecture counts:

  • Read X (B x T x D): \(2BTD\) bytes. Read the three weights: \(3 \cdot 2DF\) bytes.
  • Compute \(U = X W_{up}\) and \(G = X W_{gate}\): \(2BTDF\) FLOPs each. Write U and G: \(2BTF\) bytes each.
  • Compute \(Y = \text{GeLU}(G) \odot U\) times \(W_{down}\): \(2BTDF\) FLOPs. Write Y: \(2BTD\) bytes.

Totals: \(\text{FLOPs} = 6BTDF\), \(\text{bytes} = 4BTD + 4BTF + 6DF\). Assuming \(BT \ll D, F\) the intensity tends to \(BT\).

Source code: MLP intensity 
flops = 0
bytes_transferred = 0
bytes_transferred += 2*B*T*D          # 1. Read X (B x T x D)
bytes_transferred += 3 * 2*D*F        # 2. Read Wup, Wgate, Wdown
flops += 2*B*T*D*F                    # 3. U = X @ Wup
bytes_transferred += 2*B*T*F          # 4. Write U
flops += 2*B*T*D*F                    # 5. G = X @ Wgate
bytes_transferred += 2*B*T*F          # 6. Write G
flops += 2*B*T*D*F                    # 7. Y = GeLU(G)*U @ Wdown
bytes_transferred += 2*B*T*D          # 8. Write Y

assert flops == 6*B*T*D*F
assert bytes_transferred == 4*B*T*D + 4*B*T*F + 6*D*F

intensity = (flops / bytes_transferred).simplify()
# Assume that B*T is much smaller than D and F:
intensity = intensity.subs(D, c*B*T).subs(F, c*B*T).limit(c, oo).simplify()
assert intensity == B*T

Attention layers (matmuls, with FlashAttention-style IO)

Here \(S\) previous tokens are in the KV cache and \(T\) new tokens are being scored. Reads: Q (B x T x D), K and V (B x S x D). FLOPs: \(QK^\top\) is \(2BSTD\) and the softmax-weighted \(AV\) is another \(2BSTD\), so \(4BSTD\) in total. Bytes: \(2BTD + 4BSD\) for reads, plus \(2BTD\) for the write, i.e. \(4BSD + 4BTD\) in total.

The intensity is therefore

\[ I_{\text{attn}} = \frac{4BSTD}{4BSD + 4BTD} = \frac{ST}{S+T} \]

It has no dependence on \(B\) or \(D\). Plugging in the two stages:

  • Prefill (\(T = S\)): \(I = S/2\). Large for long prompts, so compute-bound.
  • Generation (\(T = 1\)): \(I = S/(S+1) \lt 1\). Always memory-bound, and batching cannot help.
Source code: attention intensity 
flops = 0
bytes_transferred = 0
# 1. Read Q (B x T x D), K (B x S x D), V (B x S x D) from HBM
bytes_transferred += 2*B*T*D + 2*B*S*D + 2*B*S*D
# 2. Compute A = Q @ K
flops += 2*B*S*T*D
# 3. Compute Y = softmax(A) @ V
flops += 2*B*S*T*D
# 4. Write Y (B x T x D) to HBM
bytes_transferred += 2*B*T*D

assert flops == 4*B*S*T*D
assert bytes_transferred == 4*B*S*D + 4*B*T*D

intensity = (flops / bytes_transferred).simplify()
assert intensity == S*T / (S + T)

prefill_intensity = intensity.subs(T, S).simplify()
assert prefill_intensity == S/2       # Good!
generate_intensity = intensity.subs(T, 1).simplify()
assert generate_intensity < 1          # Bad!
Why batching helps the MLP but not attention

In the MLP, every sequence in the batch multiplies by the same weights (\(W_{up}, W_{gate}, W_{down}\) do not depend on \(B\)), so the weight read is shared and intensity grows with \(B\). In attention, every sequence has its own KV cache (Q, K, V all depend on \(B\)), so nothing is shared and intensity stays at about 1 no matter how large the batch is.

LayerPrefill (T = S)Generation (T = 1)Batching helps?
MLP\(BS\) (compute-bound for large \(BS\))\(B\) (needs concurrent requests)Yes
Attention\(S/2\)\(S/(S+1) < 1\)No

The lecture's summary: prefill is compute-bound, generation is memory-bound. Generation attention intensity below 1 is, in the lecture's words, impossible to improve by tuning alone.

Interactive: intensity calculator for the two stages

Vary \(B\), \(T\) and \(S\) with the Llama 2 13B MLP shape (\(D = 5120\), \(F = 13824\)). The MLP line uses the exact byte and FLOP counts above; the attention line uses \(ST/(S+T)\). The dashed line is the H100 ridge at 295.

One generation step with a KV cache

Naively, to produce token \(t\) you feed the whole history through the Transformer again: generating \(T\) tokens costs \(O(T^3)\) FLOPs overall, since one forward pass over \(t\) tokens is \(O(t^2)\). Much of that work is shared across prefixes, so the lecture stores the KV cache in HBM: for every sequence (B), token (S), layer (L) and KV head (K), it stores an H-dimensional key and value vector. A decode step then computes Q, K, V for only the one new token, appends K and V to the cache, and attends over the whole cache.

Step through one decode step

Click next or play to follow one generation step through the layers. The dimmed boxes are not active in the current step.

Latency, throughput and the batch-size tradeoff

The lecture models a Transformer's per-step cost with just two terms: parameters and KV cache. Each decode step must read all parameters and the whole KV cache of every sequence in the batch. Ignoring overhead and assuming perfect overlap of compute and memory:

\[ \text{latency} = \frac{\text{memory}}{\text{memory bandwidth}}, \qquad \text{throughput} = \frac{B}{\text{latency}} \]

Here \(\text{memory} = B \cdot (\text{KV bytes per sequence}) + \text{parameter bytes}\), with parameters in bf16 (2 bytes) and KV per sequence \(= S \cdot K H \cdot L \cdot 2 \cdot 2\) bytes (2 for key plus value, 2 for bf16).

Source code: performance model (sympy, then substituted) 
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TransformerPerformanceStats:
    """
    Performance stats of a Transformer:
    - num_params: number of parameters (in bytes)
    - memory: total memory usage (parameters + KV cache) in bytes
    - latency: time to generate one token (seconds/token)
    - throughput: tokens generated per second
    """
    num_params: int
    memory: int
    latency: float
    throughput: float

def compute_transformer_performance_stats(config) -> TransformerPerformanceStats:
    # Number of parameters in the Transformer
    num_params = 2*V*D + D*F*3*L + (2*D*N*H + 2*D*K*H)*L

    # How much memory the parameters take
    parameter_size = 2*num_params  # 2 for bf16 (training requires a larger multiple)

    # How much the KV cache takes per sequence (S tokens, K heads, H head dim, L layers)
    kv_cache_size_per_seq = S * (K*H) * L * 2 * 2  # 2 for key + value, 2 for bf16

    # Total memory usage
    memory = B * kv_cache_size_per_seq + parameter_size

    # *Latency* is determined by memory IO (read all parameters and KV cache for each step)
    latency = memory / memory_bandwidth

    # *Throughput* is the inverse of latency, but we're generating B tokens in parallel
    throughput = B / latency
    ...

def llama2_13b_config(args={}):
    return {
        S: 1024,   # Sequence length
        D: 5120,   # Model dim
        F: 13824,  # Feed-forward dim
        N: 40,     # Number of query heads
        K: 40,     # Number of key/value heads
        H: 128,    # Head dimension
        L: 40,     # Number of layers
        V: 32000,  # Vocabulary size
        memory_bandwidth: 3.35e12,  # Memory bandwidth (bytes/second)
        **args
    }

Note that the source's parameter count \(2VD + 3DFL + (2DNH + 2DKH)L\) includes the embedding and output matrices (\(2VD\)); the printed Llama 2 13B count is 13.02B parameters, i.e. 26.03 GB in bf16.

The source's comment for the GQA run says "worse latency, but better throughput". That is true relative to the B = 1 MHA baseline (9.97 ms vs 8.02 ms). What increasing batch size does:

  • It worsens latency, because the KV cache (size \(O(B)\)) must be read on every step.
  • It improves throughput, because the cost of reading the parameters is amortized over \(B\) tokens.

The tradeoff is therefore: small batches for latency, large batches for throughput. The lecture also gives three parallelism points: launching \(M\) copies of the model keeps latency the same and multiplies throughput by \(M\) ("easy parallelism"); sharding the model and KV cache is harder; and time-to-first-token is essentially prefill time, so use small batches during prefill and large batches during generation.

Shrinking the KV cache: the lossy shortcuts

The lecture's key message: since inference is memory-bound and most of the memory is the KV cache at large batch, shrink the KV cache without hurting accuracy. Four families follow.

Grouped-query attention (GQA)

Use N query heads but only K key and value heads; each KV head serves \(N/K\) query heads. MHA is \(K = N\), MQA is \(K = 1\), and GQA sits in between. This reduces the KV cache by a factor of \(N/K\). The source's speed plot (GQA paper) shows time per sample against GQA group count: MHA is flat and slow, MQA is flat and fast, and GQA approaches MQA as groups decrease.

Accuracy: the GQA paper's summarization table (T5-based, from the lecture) shows MHA-XXL at 47.2 average and GQA-8-XXL at 47.1 with about 0.28 s inference time versus 1.51 s for MHA-XXL, while MQA-XXL is 46.6 at 0.24 s.

Multi-head latent attention (MLA)

Normal attention caches \(K = W_K h\) and \(V = W_V h\), which is \(N \cdot H\) numbers per token per layer. MLA caches only a compressed latent \(c = W_c h\) with \(C\) dimensions and projects it back up to \(K = W_K c\), \(V = W_V c\) when needed. DeepSeek V2 reduces \(N \cdot H = 16384\) to \(C = 512\).

Wrinkle: MLA is not compatible with RoPE in its compressed form, so the design adds 64 extra dimensions for the positional part. The cache is \(512 + 64 = 576\) numbers per token per layer. The latency and throughput gains follow from the smaller cache, as before.

Accuracy, per the lecture (DeepSeek V2 paper):

  • MHA beats GQA (though it is more expensive) on the hard benchmarks: for the dense 7B, MHA scores 37.0 BBH, 45.2 MMLU, 42.9 C-Eval, 43.5 CMMLU, against 35.6, 41.2, 37.7, 38.4 for GQA with 8 groups and 33.2, 37.9, 30.0, 34.6 for MQA.
  • MLA is slightly better than MHA and much cheaper. In the MoE comparison the lecture shows, the small model goes from 110.6K to 15.6K KV elements per token, and the large model from 860.2K to 34.6K, with equal or better scores on BBH, MMLU, C-Eval and CMMLU for MLA.

Cross-layer attention (CLA)

GQA shares KV across heads; CLA shares KV across layers. Adjacent layers reuse one KV cache, so the cache shrinks by the number of layers per group. The source reports that CLA improves the accuracy vs. KV-size Pareto frontier, for 1B models: the red CLA2 points reach a lower perplexity than the non-CLA points at the same KV bytes per token.

Local (sliding-window) attention

Attend only to a local window, which is most relevant for modeling much of the time. Effective context then grows linearly with depth (each layer extends the receptive field by a window). The KV cache is independent of sequence length, because only the last \(W\) tokens are kept. The problem is that this can hurt accuracy, so the fix is to interleave local and global (full) attention layers. The lecture cites Longformer, the Sparse Transformer and Mistral 7B for this family.

DeepSeek V4 attention

DeepSeek V4 supports a 1M-token context. Its attention combines several mechanisms: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses every \(m\) tokens into one; DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) selects the top-\(k\) compressed entries with a lightning indexer; and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses even more aggressively. The figure shows sliding-window entries and selected compressed entries concatenated into one shared-KV multi-query attention.

KV-cache size calculator

Per token, per layer, the cache holds keys and values (factor 2) for each KV head or latent, in 2-byte bf16. The calculator below uses the Llama 2 13B shape (\(H = 128\), \(L = 40\), \(N = 40\)) and chooses the attention variant. MLA uses the \(C = 512\) + 64 RoPE dimensions from the source, and CLA divides by the number of layers that share one cache.

\[ \text{bytes/token} = \begin{cases} 4\,K H L & \text{MHA / GQA / MQA} \\ 2\,(C + 64)\,L & \text{MLA} \\ 4\,K H L / \ell & \text{CLA, } \ell \text{ layers share a cache} \end{cases} \]

Quantization

Key idea: reduce the precision of numbers. Less memory means higher latency and throughput for memory-bound inference, but accuracy must be watched.

FormatBytesRange or note
fp324Needed for parameters and optimizer states during training.
bf162Default for inference.
fp8 (e4m3)1Range [-240, 240] on H100. The lecture: "can train if you dare" (arXiv 2310.18313).
int81Range [-128, 127]. Less accurate than fp8, but cheaper; inference only (arXiv 2303.17951).
int40.5Range [-8, 7]. Cheaper and even less accurate (arXiv 2303.17951).

Mechanics: scale and zero point

The lecture's example: \(x = 5.2342\), scale \(0.1\), zero point 4. Quantize by dividing by the scale, rounding, and adding the zero point; dequantize by reversing it.

Source code: quantize and dequantize a number 
x = 5.2342  # @inspect x
scale = 0.1
zero_point = 4
x_quant = round(x / scale) + zero_point  # Quantize  @inspect x_quant
x_approx = (x_quant - zero_point) * scale  # Dequantize @inspect x_approx

Result: x_quant = 56 and x_approx = 5.2, so the rounding error is \(5.2342 - 5.2 = 0.0342\).

Caveat: the lecture's example does not clamp the result to the int4 range. The value 56 would overflow [-8, 7]; in a real int4 scheme the scale would be chosen so the largest weights map into the range.

Interactive: quantize a number and see the staircase

Change the value, scale and zero point. The plot is the dequantized value as a function of the original input, which shows the staircase of the rounding grid and the error at the current point.

Post-training quantization vs. quantization-aware training

  • Quantization-aware training (QAT): during training, quantize and dequantize in the forward pass to simulate the error. Pro: weights learn to work with quantization. Con: needs expensive large-scale training.
  • Post-training quantization (PTQ): done after training, so much cheaper. Run sample data to pick a scale and zero point per layer or tensor.
  • GPTQ (PTQ): uses Hessian information to update the not-yet-quantized weights so they compensate for the error already introduced (arXiv 2210.17323).

Activation-aware quantization (AWQ)

Observation: some activation channels are large, and the weights that multiply them matter more. So select the most salient weights (0.1 to 1 percent) by looking at activations, and give them more precision. The figure contrasts three options on a toy example: plain round-to-nearest INT3 (PPL 43.2), keeping 1 percent salient channels in FP16 (PPL 13.0, but mixed precision is bad for hardware), and scaling the salient channels up before quantizing (PPL 13.0, uniform INT3).

The lecture quotes AWQ's result: fp16 to int3 gives 4x lower memory and a 3.2x speedup.

Bits per parameter vs. latency

Weights are the dominant term at batch 1, so the speed gain is roughly the byte ratio. The calculator uses the Llama 2 13B parameter count and the same memory-bound latency model. The KV cache stays in bf16 here.

Interactive: precision vs. latency

Choose the weight format and batch. The bar chart compares the latency of every precision at the current batch.

Note on AWQ's "4×"

Pure bit-width arithmetic gives \(16/3 \approx 5.3\times\) for int3 weights against bf16, not 4x. The lecture quotes the paper's 4x without explaining the gap; per-group scales and zero points add storage. The calculator above shows the raw ratio.

Pruning and distillation

Key idea: rip out parts of an expensive model to make it cheaper, then fix it up. The lecture cites an NVIDIA paper (arXiv 2407.14679, the Minitron work).

The algorithm, as the lecture lists it:

  1. Identify the important {layer, head, hidden dimension} on a small calibration dataset (1024 samples).
  2. Remove the unimportant layers (and other structure) to get a smaller model.
  3. Distil the original model into the pruned model.

Two recipes from the lecture's summary:

From scratch

  1. Define a faster model architecture.
  2. Train the faster model.

Distillation

  1. Define a faster model architecture.
  2. Initialize its weights from the original model (which has a different architecture).
  3. Repair the faster model by distillation.

The lecture's code has a TODO after this section, so the numbers come only from the figure.

Lossless shortcut: speculative sampling

Recall the two stages again. Prefill is parallel and compute-bound, and it also gives you probabilities for every position. Generation is one token at a time and memory-bound. In other words, checking a guess is faster than generating it.

Speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., arXiv 2211.17192; Chen et al., arXiv 2302.01318) exploits that asymmetry:

  • Use a cheap draft model \(p\) to guess a few tokens, for example \(K = 4\).
  • Evaluate all of them with the target model \(q\) in one parallel pass, and accept each one if it looks good.

This is modified rejection sampling with proposal \(p\) and target \(q\). Two modifications: always generate at least one candidate (otherwise rejection sampling could loop forever), and the bonus token when every draft is accepted.

Key property: the output is an exact sample from the target

The method is lossless, not approximate. Accept each draft token \(x\) with probability \(\min(1, q(x)/p(x))\). When rejected, resample from the residual \((q - p)_+\), normalized. The marginal distribution of the output token is exactly \(q\).

Proof by example: two tokens {A, B}

Let the target be \([q(A), q(B)]\) and the draft \([p(A), p(B)]\). Suppose the draft oversamples A, so \(p(A) > q(A)\), which forces \(p(B) \lt q(B)\). The residual \(\max(q - p, 0)\) is then \([0, 1]\) (after normalization by the rejected mass). The probability of emitting each token:

  • \(P[\text{emit } A] = p(A) \cdot \dfrac{q(A)}{p(A)} + p(B) \cdot 1 \cdot 0 = q(A)\). A is kept with probability \(q(A)/p(A)\) when drafted; it is never resampled.
  • \(P[\text{emit } B] = p(B) \cdot 1 + p(A)\left(1 - \dfrac{q(A)}{p(A)}\right) \cdot 1 = q(B)\). B is accepted when drafted, plus the rejected A mass that resamples to B.

Check with \(q = [0.3, 0.7]\), \(p = [0.6, 0.4]\): \(P[A] = 0.6 \cdot 0.5 = 0.3\) and \(P[B] = 0.4 + 0.6 \cdot 0.5 = 0.7\). Both match \(q\).

ArS (greedy)XSum ROUGE-20.15714.1 ms/token1×
SpS (greedy)XSum ROUGE-20.1567.00 ms/token2.01×

The quality is unchanged within noise (the method is exact), and speed improves by about 2x. Caveat: 14.1 / 7.52 = 1.88, not the 1.92 printed in the table; the difference presumably comes from how the paper averages timings. The reported figures are the source's values.

How many draft tokens?

The tradeoff: more draft tokens per round amortize the target pass, but each extra draft costs time and is accepted with a probability that decays with its position. The expected-speedup calculator below makes that concrete.

Expected speedup: the acceptance formula

Let \(\alpha\) be the acceptance rate: the probability that a token drawn from the draft is accepted. Because a draft token \(x\) is accepted with probability \(\min(1, q(x)/p(x))\), the overall rate is

\[ \alpha = \sum_x p(x) \min\!\left(1, \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\right) = \sum_x \min\big(p(x), q(x)\big) = 1 - \mathrm{TV}(p, q). \]

With a constant \(\alpha\) per position, one round produces the accepted prefix plus one token from the target (the resample or the bonus). The expected number of tokens emitted per target call is (the standard result from Leviathan et al.):

\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{tokens per round}] = \sum_{i=0}^{K} \alpha^i = \frac{1 - \alpha^{K+1}}{1 - \alpha}. \]

If the draft step costs a fraction \(c\) of a target step, one round costs \(Kc + 1\) target-equivalent steps. The idealized speedup over plain autoregressive decoding is

\[ \text{speedup} = \frac{1 - \alpha^{K+1}}{(1 - \alpha)(Kc + 1)}. \]

The source does not state \(c\); the formula is an idealization that ignores batching overheads and assumes the target's parallel verify costs about one target step. As a sanity check: the figure's HumanEval acceptance at \(K = 4\) is about 0.80, which gives \(\mathbb{E} = 3.36\) tokens per round. With \(c = 0.1\) the formula predicts about 2.4x, close to the measured 2.46x.

Algorithm as a flow

Extensions: better draft models

Since the method is lossless, all the gains come from making the draft agree with the target more often (higher \(\alpha\)) and cheaper:

  • Try to make the draft model as close to the target as possible (distillation). In practice the lecture cites a 70B target with an 8B draft, and an 8B target with a 1B draft.
  • Medusa: the draft model generates multiple tokens in parallel using several heads on the target (arXiv 2401.10774).
  • EAGLE: the draft model takes high-level features from the target model and predicts the next feature (arXiv 2401.15077).

Summary from the lecture: exact sampling from the target (thanks to the math); it exploits the asymmetry between checking and generation; and there is lots of room for innovation on the draft model, which involves training.

Dynamic workloads: continuous batching

Batching across sequences in live traffic is tricky for three reasons:

  1. Requests arrive at different times. Waiting to fill a batch is bad for the early requests.
  2. Sequences share prefixes (system prompts, or many samples from the same prompt).
  3. Sequences have different lengths, and padding to the longest is inefficient.

Training gets a dense block of tokens (batch times sequence length). Inference gets a ragged array, because requests arrive and finish at different times. The lecture's static-batching diagram (scaling book) shows the waste: slots that finished early sit idle until the whole batch ends.

The solution is iteration-level scheduling (Orca, OSDI 2022): decode step by step, and add new requests to the running batch as they arrive, instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish. The lecture links the Orca paper and a talk.

Attention then has its own problem: batching requires equal shapes, but each request has a different length. The lecture's answer is selective batching:

  • Attention: process each sequence separately (each has its own length and KV cache).
  • Non-attention layers (MLP, projections): concatenate all sequences into one tall matrix, for example lengths 3, 9 and 5 become a single \([3+9+5, H]\) tensor.
Interactive: static vs. continuous batching

Five requests arrive with different lengths (3, 9, 5, 4, 2 iterations) into a batch of three slots. The toy schedule is computed from those numbers. Left: static batching fills a batch, runs it to completion, then starts the next. Right: continuous batching admits a waiting request as soon as a slot frees up.

PagedAttention and vLLM

The vLLM paper (arXiv 2309.06180) introduced PagedAttention. The previous status quo was to allocate, for each request, a contiguous section of KV cache for the prompt plus the response up to a maximum length. That wastes memory in two ways:

  • Internal fragmentation: the response may be much shorter than the maximum, so the reserved slots are never used.
  • External fragmentation: unused gaps between the contiguous sections cannot be used by new requests.

The solution comes from operating systems: divide the KV cache of a sequence into non-contiguous blocks, and map logical block numbers to physical blocks with a block table, the way virtual memory does with pages.

Sharing across sequences

Multiple sequences can share KV blocks:

  • A shared system prompt across users.
  • Parallel sampling: many responses to one prompt (for example in program synthesis).

The solution is to share prefixes and use copy-on-write at the block level: blocks are reference-counted; a block is shared until one sequence needs to write to it, at which point it is copied and the reference count drops.

Step through a block table

The stepper follows two requests through a pool of 9 physical blocks of 4 tokens each. The physical IDs follow the figures above; a real allocator picks any free block, so the IDs are illustrative. Block 7, for example, holds "Four score and seven" for request A.

Other vLLM optimizations (from the lecture)
  • A kernel that fuses the block read with attention, reducing kernel-launch overhead.
  • The latest attention kernels (FlashAttention, FlashDecoding).
  • CUDA graphs to avoid kernel-launch overhead.

Summary: use ideas from operating systems (paging) to make memory useful for dynamic workloads.

Summary: the lecture's big picture

  • Inference is important: real use, evaluation and reinforcement learning all sample from the model.
  • It has different characteristics from training: it is memory-bound during generation and dynamic (requests arrive and finish unpredictably).
  • Techniques: new architectures (GQA, MLA, CLA, local attention, linear attention or state-space models such as Mamba 2 and GatedDeltaNet, and diffusion models), quantization, pruning and distillation, and speculative sampling.
  • Ideas borrowed from systems: speculative execution and paging.
  • New architectures have huge potential for improvement.

The lecture's section on taking shortcuts is explicitly a recipe for the lossy half: reduce inference complexity without hurting accuracy. The recipes are "from scratch" (define a faster architecture, train it) or "distillation" (define a faster architecture, initialize its weights from the original, repair by distillation). The lossless half, speculative sampling, is the one that needs no accuracy check at all, because the output distribution is provably the target's.

Self-check quiz

Why is single-token generation memory-bound, and what does batching buy?
Generation's MLP matmul has \(T = 1\), so its intensity is about \(B\). The H100 ridge is 295 FLOP/B, so with \(B \lt 295\) the step waits on memory: it must read all \(\approx 26\) GB of bf16 weights for one step. Batching amortizes that read over \(B\) tokens, so throughput rises with \(B\) while latency per step rises too, because the KV cache grows as \(O(B)\).
Why does batching not help attention, even though it helps the MLP?
Attention's intensity is \(ST/(S+T)\) and has no \(B\). Each sequence reads its own KV cache; nothing is shared across the batch, so the bytes scale with \(B\) just like the FLOPs. At \(T = 1\) it is \(S/(S+1) \lt 1\), and no batch size fixes it.
Compute the MHA decode latency for Llama 2 13B at B = 1 and explain its 8.02 ms.
Parameters: \(2VD + 3DFL + (2DNH + 2DKH)L \approx 13.02\)B, so \(2 \times 13.02\text{B} = 26.03\) GB of bf16 weights. The KV cache for one sequence of 1024 tokens with K = 40 is \(1024 \cdot 40 \cdot 128 \cdot 40 \cdot 4 \approx 0.84\) GB. Memory \(\approx 26.87\) GB, and \(26.87\text{ GB} / 3.35\text{ TB/s} \approx 8.02\) ms per token.
Why does speculative sampling leave the output distribution unchanged?
A drafted token \(x\) is kept with probability \(\min(1, q(x)/p(x))\), so it is emitted with mass \(p(x)\min(1, q/p) = \min(p, q)\). When rejected, the output is resampled from \((q-p)_+\) normalized. The rejected mass \(\sum_x (p(x) - q(x))_+\) exactly equals the residual's total mass, so \(P[\text{emit } x] = \min(p,q)(x) + (q-p)_+(x) = q(x)\). The lecture's \(\{A, B\}\) example shows this directly: \(P[A] = q(A)\) and \(P[B] = q(B)\).
With acceptance rate α = 0.8 and K = 4 draft tokens, how many tokens does one target call yield on average, and what is the ideal speedup if drafting costs c = 0.1 of a target step?
\(\mathbb{E} = (1 - 0.8^5)/(1 - 0.8) = (1 - 0.32768)/0.2 = 3.3616\) tokens per round. Cost per round is \(Kc + 1 = 1.4\) target-equivalents, so the speedup is \(3.3616 / 1.4 \approx 2.40\)x.
How much smaller is GQA's KV cache than MHA's, and how big is MLA's cache per token relative to MHA?
GQA reduces the cache by \(N/K\): with 40 query heads and K = 8 it is 5x smaller. For DeepSeek V2, MHA would cache \(N \cdot H = 16384\) numbers per token per layer for keys and the same for values; MLA caches \(C + 64 = 576\) numbers, about \(16384 \cdot 2 / 576 \approx 57\)x fewer. (The 57x compares the key-plus-value MHA cache with the MLA latent; check the paper's exact comparison.)
What are the two kinds of KV-cache fragmentation in the pre-PagedAttention status quo, and how do blocks fix them?
Internal fragmentation: each request reserves the maximum length, but generates fewer tokens, so the reserved slots are never used. External fragmentation: the gaps between contiguous reservations are too small for new requests. Paging stores each sequence in fixed-size blocks mapped by a block table, so the blocks can be anywhere and a block is only allocated when tokens need it. Waste is then limited to the last, partly filled block per sequence.

Key takeaways

  • Decode is memory-bound: intensity about \(B\) for the MLP and about 1 for attention; the H100 ridge is 295 FLOP/B.
  • Prefill is compute-bound: MLP intensity \(BS\), attention \(S/2\).
  • Metrics: TTFT (prefill time) and latency for interactive use; throughput for batch use. Small batches favor latency, large batches favor throughput.
  • Shrink the KV cache (lossy): GQA (\(N/K\) smaller), MLA (576 numbers per token in DeepSeek V2), CLA (share across layers), local attention (cache bounded by the window).
  • Quantize (lossy): bf16 to int8 or int4 halves or quarters the weight bytes; PTQ (GPTQ, AWQ) is cheap; AWQ protects the salient 0.1 to 1 percent of channels.
  • Prune and distill (lossy): remove layers and dimensions chosen on 1024 calibration samples, then distil the original into the smaller model.
  • Speculative sampling (lossless): draft K tokens, verify in one pass, accept with \(\min(1, q/p)\), resample from \((q-p)_+\). Expected tokens per round \((1-\alpha^{K+1})/(1-\alpha)\).
  • Dynamic serving: continuous (iteration-level) batching and selective batching; PagedAttention with block tables and copy-on-write sharing (vLLM).

Scaling: case studies and details

lecture_11.pdf (58 slides) Chinchilla in practice muP / hyperparameter transfer WSD schedules critical batch size compute- vs inference-optimal Muon
TL;DR. Lecture 10 gave the Chinchilla recipe. This lecture asks whether it works in practice and what it costs. Public recipes from MiniCPM, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, Hunyuan, Llama 3, MiniMax and StepFun answer three questions: (1) which hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, width-dependent init) stay fixed as you scale, (2) how to make the scaling fit cheap (WSD-style schedules that let one run serve many token budgets), and (3) which architecture and optimizer choices scale predictably. The main findings: the Chinchilla-style fit does predict held-out final losses for several recipes, but the fitted data-to-parameter ratio varies a lot between papers (roughly 20 to 96 tokens per parameter), learning-rate fits are fragile, and muP fixes the width dependence only partly (weight decay and RMSNorm gains break it).
What this source is

The lecture is PDF-only: there is no lecture_11.py in the folder, so there is no executable code to quote. Where the slides show an algorithm or a configuration (Muon, the muP rules, the MiniCPM settings) it is reproduced below, and every number in the widgets was recomputed from the formulas printed on the slides. Figures that exist only as pictures are embedded from rendered slides instead of being redrawn.

1. The three questions

The lecture opens with three questions that organise everything after it:

  • Does Chinchilla's approach to scaling actually work once people use it on real models?
  • Can we save compute when training and fitting these scaling laws?
  • Should we pick particular architectures or parametrizations so that models scale nicely?

The motivating question is practical: what are the best practices for scaling and hyperparameter tuning of language models? The slides treat initialization, optimizers and hyperparameters (learning rate and batch size) as scale-sensitive: a setting that is best at 100M parameters is often not best at 1B. Every recipe below is an answer to that sensitivity.

2022 Chinchilla (DeepMind): fit \( L(N,D) \) from runs, pick the model size and token count for a compute budget. The newest scaling-detail paper the earlier lectures used.
2024 MiniCPM (Tsinghua), DeepSeek LLM, Hunyuan-Large, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5. Public recipes with explicit scaling analyses and learning-rate or batch rules.
2025 MiniMax-01: architecture scaling laws plus Chinchilla method 1. Muon in NanoGPT and at scale.

3. MiniCPM: muP to stabilize, WSD to save compute, fitted ratios

MiniCPM (2024, Tsinghua) is a small high-performance family: 1 to 2.5B parameters that beat most open 2B models and match many 7B models (slide 7; MiniCPM-1.2B and 2.4B). The lecture notes it is not state of the art even in 2024, but its scaling work is the most detailed public account. It uses two techniques: muP to stabilize and simplify scaling, and a WSD learning-rate schedule to make the fit cheap.

3.1 The MiniCPM configuration

The slide's tensor-program table (table 7) lists exactly which parts of the network are rescaled. Here \(d_m\) is the model width, \(d_{base}\) the base width where hyperparameters were tuned, and \(L\) the number of layers:

NameSpecific operation
Embedding output scalingmultiply the output of the embedding by scale_emb (= 12)
Residual connection scalingscale the increment at each residual connection by scale_depth / √L (scale_depth = 1.4)
Initialization of tensorsinit std of each 2-D tensor = init_std / √(d_m / d_base) (init_std = 0.1); other parameters initialized to 0.1
Learning-rate scaling of tensorsLR of each 2-D tensor = 1 / (d_m / d_base) times the LR of other parts (lr = 0.01)
LM head scalingoutput logits multiplied by 1 / (d_m / d_base)

The scaling recipe is short: use muP for initialization, fix the aspect ratio of the network, and scale the overall size. The aspect-ratio table on slide 9 keeps \(d_{ff} = 2.5\,d_m\) and head dimension 64:

NameN (B)d_md_ffd_hn_hL
9M0.0093208006458
