70M0.0666401600641014
0.1B0.1097681920641216
0.17B0.1668962240641418
0.2B0.24110242560641620
0.5B0.49913443360642124

The N column is the non-embedding parameter count. Reconstructing it from the shapes with \(N \approx L\,(4d_m^2 + 3\,d_m d_{ff})\) (attention projections plus a three-matrix gated MLP) reproduces the printed values to rounding: for the 0.5B row, \(24 \times (4\cdot1344^2 + 3\cdot1344\cdot3360) \approx 4.99\times10^8\). The largest sweep model is about 5x smaller than the model the authors actually train, which is the gap the slide notes.

Why a fixed aspect ratio?

If the depth-to-width ratio is held constant, one set of "per-width" rules can be applied to every size and the only free variable left is the width. This is what makes muP's transfer rule usable in practice: the family of models is a single curve in width, not a two-dimensional search over depth and width. The lecture does not state the exact aspect-ratio criterion beyond the table above.

3.2 Optimal batch, LR and token-to-size ratio

The MiniCPM team sweeps three model sizes (9M, 30M, 170M) as a function of data size, batch size and loss (slide 11). Each vertical column of points is one training curve at a fixed batch size; the red line marks the minimum-loss point for each data size. That minimum is the optimal batch size for a given model size and dataset size. Following Kaplan et al. (2020), the optimal batch size is then plotted against final loss, which gives a fairly clean trend: the batch grows polynomially as loss decreases (slide 12, see section 7 below for the fit).

3.3 Chinchilla-type analysis with WSD

From Chinchilla, fitting a scaling law needs runs trained from scratch, not just early-stopped. That makes the fitting cost grow from \(n\) to \(n^2\) (the slide's shorthand). The MiniCPM answer is a schedule in which one run can be restarted at the end of its stable phase (section 6 gives the arithmetic). Equipped with WSD, they fit the loss as in Chinchilla's equation (2):

\[ L(N,D) = C_N N^{-\alpha} + C_D D^{-\beta} + L_0 \]

and compute the optimal \(N_{opt}, D_{opt}\) for a fixed compute \(C = 6ND\) (Rae et al. 2021) as

\[ \frac{N_{opt}}{D_{opt}} = K^2 \left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{\eta}. \]

The MiniCPM authors use two of Chinchilla's three methods: method 1 (lower envelope of the loss curves per model) and method 3 (the joint fit). Method 1 gives clear but maybe not linear trends; the runs suggest relatively low diminishing returns from data. Method 3 is their primary approach and gives very high data-to-model ratios: the joint fit on slide 18 has \(K^2 = 0.01\) and \(\eta \approx 0\), and the printed optimum at \(C = 10^{21}\) is \(D_{opt}/N_{opt} = 95.60\). Because \(\eta\) is essentially zero, the ratio barely depends on compute. With equal exponents \(\alpha = \beta\) the ratio has a closed form, \( D/N = (B/A)^{1/\alpha} \), and plugging in the slide's coefficients \(A = 0.0754\), \(B = 0.292\), \(\alpha = 0.2969\) gives 95.6, which is the printed value. (The slide shows the exponent rounded to 0.30; using 0.30 gives 91.6.)

Reading the MiniCPM ratio

Minimising a loss of the form \(E + A N^{-\alpha} + B D^{-\alpha}\) at fixed \(C = 6ND\) gives \(D/N = (B/A)^{1/\alpha}\), independent of \(C\). The ratio is therefore a property of the fitted coefficients, not of the scale, and any error in the coefficients moves the whole recommendation. That is why the lecture stresses that the fitting setup, not just the model, determines the answer.

3.4 Recap: what MiniCPM contributes

  • muP makes the transformer and LR roughly invariant to width, so tuning at a small base width transfers (section 4).
  • WSD lets one stable-phase run serve many budgets, making the Chinchilla fit cheaper (section 6).
  • Chinchilla-style fits on the WSD runs give large data-to-model ratios, which is the recommendation the lecture carries forward (section 10).
Hyperparameter tables from the MiniCPM family (slide 7)

Slide 7 compares the 1.2B and 2.4B MiniCPM models with 2B to 7B baselines (C-Eval, CMMLU, MMLU, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH). The MiniCPM rows are bold in the slide. Selected values: MiniCPM-2.4B scores 53.46 on MMLU, 50.00 on HumanEval, 53.83 on GSM8K and 10.24 on MATH; MiniCPM-1.2B scores 49.63, 44.51, 31.77 and 10.60 on the same columns. The lecture's claim is that the family matches many 7B models, which the table supports on several columns and not all.

4. Maximal update parametrization (muP) in depth

Scale-invariant hyperparameter tuning would be very nice: tune the learning rate and initialization on a small model and reuse them at any width. The maximal update parametrization (muP, Yang et al.) promises exactly that. The slides ask two questions: how does it work, and does it work in practice?

The idea. muP is built on two conditions, stated as functions of the network width \(n_\ell\) (the slide's "Yang, Simon and Bernstein" spectral-condition paper is the accessible version the lecture calls "muP for babies"):

  • A1 the activations at initialization stay \(\Theta(1)\) as width grows;
  • A2 after one gradient step, the change in activations stays \(\Theta(1)\).

Note that if the individual activations are \(\Theta(1)\), the norm of the activation vector scales like \(\Theta(\sqrt{n_\ell})\).

What muP prescribes (Adam, the baby version)

Init standard deviation of a hidden matrix \(\propto 1/\sqrt{n_{\ell-1}}\) (times a factor \(\min(1, \sqrt{n_\ell/n_{\ell-1}})\)); Adam learning rate of a hidden matrix \(\propto 1/n_{\ell-1}\). With width multiplier \(r\), the Adam LR of hidden matrices is \(\eta/r\) and the init variance is \(\sigma^2/r\).

What standard parametrization (SP) does

Init is \(1/\sqrt{n_{\ell-1}}\) and the learning rate is \(\Theta(1)\): the LR is the same at every width. Under SP the optimum LR drifts with width, which is the instability muP is designed to remove.

4.1 Deriving muP, briefly

The derivation is for a simple deep linear network \(h_\ell = W_\ell h_{\ell-1}\) with \(W_\ell \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I)\). By matrix concentration, \(\|W_\ell\|_* \approx \sigma(\sqrt{n_{\ell-1}} + \sqrt{n_\ell})\), so \(\|h_\ell\|_2 \approx \|W_\ell\|_* \|h_{\ell-1}\|_2\). Choosing \(\sigma = \Theta\big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n_{\ell-1}}}\min(1, \sqrt{n_\ell/n_{\ell-1}})\big)\) keeps \(\|h_\ell\|_2 = \sqrt{n_\ell} + o(\sqrt{n_\ell})\) by induction. This is a worst-case bound (the \(\approx\) is an upper bound).

For A2 the update of a linear layer under SGD is \(\Delta W_\ell = -\eta_\ell \nabla_{h_\ell}\ell \, h_{\ell-1}^\top\), a rank-one outer product. Under the leading-order assumption that terms do not cancel, the activation change is \(\Delta h_\ell = \Theta(\cdot)\) with \(\|\Delta W_\ell h_{\ell-1}\|_2 = \|\Delta W_\ell\|_* \|h_{\ell-1}\|_2\). Requiring the loss change to be \(\Theta(1)\) and substituting \(\|\Delta W_\ell\|_* = \Theta(\sqrt{n_\ell/n_{\ell-1}})\) gives the SGD LR \(\eta_\ell = \Theta(n_\ell/n_{\ell-1})\). With Adam, the update norm is instead \(\|\Delta W_\ell\|_* \sqrt{n_{\ell-1}} = \Theta(\sqrt{n_\ell})\), which gives the Adam LR \(\Theta(1/n_{\ell-1})\).

The derivation as a step-through

The table of rules (slide 52, from Lingle's large-scale study of mu-transfer) gives, for each weight type, the initialization variance and the Adam learning rate as multiples of \(\Theta\), plus the exact width-dependent form. \(M\) is the width multiplier, \(F\) the fan-out factor of the MLP, \(H\) the number of heads and \(D\) the head dimension:

The slide notes that for fixed \(D\), any constant \(\tau^{-1} \ne 0\) technically complies with muP, but in the experiments \(\tau^{-1}\) has a major impact on performance and transfer.

Set the base width where you tuned, the base LR and init, and the target width. The widget applies the MiniCPM rules (init \(\propto 1/\sqrt{r}\), hidden LR \(\propto 1/r\), LM-head multiplier \(1/r\), residual scale \(\text{scale\_depth}/\sqrt{L}\)) with the slide defaults. The base width is not printed on the slides; 256 is an assumption, so change it to whatever you tuned at.

Check it against the paper

With the defaults and \(d = 1344\), \(d_{base} = 256\), \(r = 5.25\): hidden LR \(= 0.01/5.25 \approx 1.9\times10^{-3}\), hidden init std \(= 0.1/\sqrt{5.25} \approx 0.044\), residual scale \(= 1.4/\sqrt{24} \approx 0.286\). The slide gives no base width, so the absolute values are only as good as that assumption; the ratios are not.

4.4 Does it work? Lingle's replication

The first question the slides ask is whether muP works as claimed: when we scale widths, is the optimal LR constant? Lingle's replication (slide 52) sweeps the base LR at widths 128, 512 and 2048, each step 4x wider (16x the parameters), and asks whether the optimum of the smallest model predicts the larger ones. The slide's conclusion: the learning rates transfer reliably across model sizes under muP. The tables below are the slide's numbers (validation loss; bold is the minimum in each row of the slide).

Under SP the best base LR moves by one grid step per 4x of width and the loss blows up on the wrong side of the optimum. Under muP the optimum stays at \(2^{-6}\) for all three widths. The large-scale table (slide 57, Table 4) extends this to 2M, 40M, 600M and 10B parameters (widths 128 to 8192) with base LR \(2^{-8}, 2^{-6}, 2^{-4}\): the optimum is \(2^{-6}\) at every scale, and the 10B model reaches 2.167 at that setting. The lecture's conclusion is that muP parametrization and initialization are easier to tune, even though SP is also sometimes stable.

4.5 What muP is not robust to

Modern LMs deviate from the muP theory in several ways: SwiGLU and squared-ReLU activations, large or small batch sizes, initialization variations (zero attention init and similar), RMSNorm gains, exotic optimizers such as Lion, and regularizers. The lecture checks four of them.

RMSNorm gains break it

In the authors' architecture RMSNorm has learnable gains. Making the gains vector-valued or scalar, with muP learning rates, does not transfer reliably (the optimum drifts with width). Standard transformers with trainable gains also underperform muP transformers without them. The gains can be removed with little loss of performance.

Exotic optimizers (Lion)

Lion, built from gradient signs, uses sign updates and is not covered by the muP derivation. In the slide's table the optimum moves between widths (about 2^-10 at width 128, 2^-8 at widths 512 and 2048) and the transfer check fails.

Strong weight decay is the main failure

The slide says "what about strong (0.1) weight decay? This is maybe the only significant muP failure." Under decoupled weight decay (SGD with decoupled weight decay, the algorithm on slide 55), the optimum does not transfer across widths (the slide marks it with a cross). The lesson: the learning rate and the weight decay interact, and the muP rule must be paired with a weight-decay rule.

The slide's overall verdict is cautious but positive: muP generally seems useful, insofar as SP is quite a bit more unstable. Current evidence suggests the muP parametrization and initialization may be easier to tune, even though muP does not solve everything.

5. DeepSeek LLM: no muP, measure batch and LR directly

DeepSeek LLM (2024, 7B and 67B parameters, 2T tokens) takes the opposite stance. Scaling strategy: don't use any muP; directly estimate the optimal batch and learning rate (slide 20). Their recipe, as the slides summarise it:

  • assume most transformer hyperparameters are invariant to scale;
  • run a scaling analysis on batch and LR to find the optimum as a function of compute;
  • use IsoFLOP analysis to choose the model size;
  • use a piecewise-linear (multi-step) schedule so that Chinchilla-style scaling is cheap.

They collect "near optimal" models (within 0.25% of the minimum loss) at small scale and fit the optimal LR and batch as power laws in compute. The fitted equation (1) on slide 21 is

\[ \eta_{opt} = 0.3118\, C^{-0.1250}, \qquad B_{opt} = 0.2920\, C^{0.3271} \]

with \(C\) the training compute in FLOPs and \(B_{opt}\) the optimal batch in tokens. The batch-size fit is clean; the learning-rate fit "looks a bit questionable" (slide 21), and the slide's figure shows the spread of near-optimal points. The reported stars are the 7B MHA and 67B GQA models trained on 2T tokens: they land at a batch of 9.2M and 19.7M tokens and an LR of 4.2e-4 and 3.2e-4.

I checked the equations against those stars. For the 7B model with \(N = 6.9\)B and \(D = 2\)T, \(C = 6ND = 8.28\times10^{22}\), giving \(\eta = 4.26\times10^{-4}\) and \(B = 9.16\)M tokens, which match the slide. For the 67B model, \(N = 65.2\)B gives \(C = 7.82\times10^{23}\), \(\eta = 3.2\times10^{-4}\) and \(B = 19.1\)M; the slide's 19.7M is within 3%, so the star uses the paper's own compute figure.

5.1 Piecewise-linear schedules for cheap Chinchilla fits

DeepSeek uses a WSD-style learning rate: a fast warmup over 2000 steps, then the LR drops to 31.6% of its maximum after 80% of the training tokens and to 10% after 90% (slide 22). The slide's comparison of a multi-step scheduler (80% + 10% + 10%) against a cosine scheduler, at 100B processed tokens, shows that the multi-step run "generally seems to match performance of cosine learning rates". The point is not that multi-step is better; it is that the final loss is roughly the same and the schedule can be cut and restarted.

5.2 IsoFLOP for model size and data

For the model-size question DeepSeek uses Chinchilla's method 2 (IsoFLOP): for each compute budget, train several model sizes, find the best model on each IsoFLOP curve, then fit how the optimal size and data scale with compute. Slide 23 shows (a) the IsoFLOP curves of validation bits-per-byte vs non-embedding FLOPs per token, (b) optimal model scaling, and (c) optimal data scaling. Annotated on the slides: the 67B model at \(C = 4.5\times10^{23}\) corresponds to \(4.3\times10^{11}\) non-embedding FLOPs per token and about \(1.04\times10^{12}\) tokens.

Slide 24 shows the test: a power-law fit to the small-scale runs of bits-per-byte vs compute predicts the 7B and 67B losses. The caption says the stars are "well-predicted by the scaling curve". This is the strongest evidence in the lecture that Chinchilla-style extrapolation works: the fit is made on small models and checked on the two large ones.

6. Learning-rate schedules that save compute

The core cost problem for scaling-law fitting: to read the final loss of a run at a given token budget you normally need a run that has finished its schedule. With a cosine schedule, every budget is its own full run. The WSD schedule (warmup, stable, decay) breaks this: the stable phase is shared, and a short decay after any point gives a finished loss for that budget. MiniCPM's figure (slide 14) shows the same stable phase followed by decays of different lengths, and slide 15 shows the resulting loss curves sit close to cosine's (the notation WSD(80N, 8N) is an 80N-token run whose last 8N tokens are the decay phase, i.e. a 10% decay). The lecture's summary: slower during the stable phase, rapid loss decay during the decay phase, with the decay about 10% of training.

6.1 LR schedule explorer

Compare cosine, WSD, linear decay and the DeepSeek-style multi-step schedule. The probe slider shows the LR at one point of the run; the chart draws all four; the selected schedule is solid and the others dashed.

6.2 Cost of a token-budget sweep: cosine restarts vs one WSD trunk

Suppose you want the final loss at \(K\) token budgets for one model size, with budgets \(D_k = D_{max}\,k/K\). Cosine needs \(K\) finished runs of lengths \(D_k\). With WSD, one trunk runs the stable phase up to \((1-f)D_{max}\); each budget is read by branching off the trunk at its stable checkpoint and running a decay of length \(f D_k\). Total tokens:

\[ C_{\text{cos}} = \sum_k D_k = \frac{K+1}{2}D_{max}, \qquad C_{\text{WSD}} = (1-f)D_{max} + f\sum_k D_k = D_{max}\Big[(1-f) + f\,\tfrac{K+1}{2}\Big]. \]

This is a simplified model of the idea on slide 14 (my arithmetic, not a formula printed on the slides). It ignores the cost of the decays' own warmup and assumes every budget can branch from the shared trunk. With \(K = 1\) the two costs coincide; with \(K = 8\) and \(f = 0.1\) the WSD saving is about 3.3x.

What this buys and what it does not

The saving applies to the number of tokens trained, and therefore to the compute for the fit. It does not remove the need to fit the loss as a function of \(N\) and \(D\). The slides frame the cost as going from \(n\) to \(n^2\) when every point is a separate run; WSD brings the cost back toward \(n\). The slide's shorthand is terse, so read it as "the fitting cost grows much faster than the number of points unless the schedule can be branched".

7. Batch size, critical batch, and learning-rate scaling laws

Batch size is the second hyperparameter the recipes must scale. The lecture's core question is: what are the right variables, and what is the functional form for LR and batch? Two views compete. The critical-batch view (OpenAI) makes the batch a function of the loss. The compute power-law view (DeepSeek) makes the optimal batch and LR power laws in compute. The slides list some other fits from StepFun and others.

The critical batch size was introduced by McCandlish et al. (2018), "An empirical model of large-batch training" (arXiv 1812.06162), as the batch size beyond which extra data parallelism gives diminishing returns. The Kaplan-style fit in the MiniCPM study (slide 12) is

\[ \log(BS) = -6.24\,\log(L) + 20.91, \]

which reproduces the plotted curve only if the logarithms are natural: \(BS = e^{20.91}\,L^{-6.24}\) gives about \(5\times10^5\) tokens at a loss of 3.5 and about \(10^5\) at 4.5, matching the slide. The slide says the trend is "fairly clean": the optimal batch grows polynomially as loss decreases.

7.1 Learning-rate and batch fits from the StepFun study

The StepFun "Step Law" study (Li et al., "Predictable Scale, Part I", slide 32) fits learning rate and batch as power laws in model size \(N\) and data size \(D\). Its table (slide 33) compares them with the other published laws:

NameData recipeModel sparsityLearning rateBatch sizeRelative error
OpenAI law✗✗3.239·10⁻³ − 1.395·10⁻⁴ log(N)2e18 L−4.76190 (see note above)9.51‰
Microsoft law✗✗1.3192e⁻⁵ N−0.23 D−0.32–9.25‰
DeepSeek law✗✗0.3188 C−0.12500.2920 C0.32719.26‰
Porian law✗✗3.7 N−0.360.7576 N0.7033.71‰

Plugging the Step Law into a 7B model with \(D = 2\)T gives \(\eta \approx 1.0\times10^{-3}\) and a batch of about \(6.1\)M tokens, which is within about 2x of the DeepSeek-style values in section 5 (the two laws use different variables, so this is a sanity check, not a like-for-like comparison).

7.2 Observations the lecture draws

Observation 1: the loss is convex in LR and batch

For pre-training losses the minimizers over LR and batch can be cleanly identified (slide 35). Each panel is a convex bowl in batch size at a fixed LR; the surface over LR and batch has a clear valley. This is why small grid searches can find the optimum.

Observation 2: the batch is set by data size

For Chinchilla-style joint scaling, the optimal batch depends mainly on dataset size (slide 36). The same work finds a higher optimal LR at larger D for fixed model size, but the slide warns it is likely more fragile when the schedule changes to WSD (see the InternLM scaling-law paper, Zhou et al. 2026).

Observation 3 is robustness. The lecture checks whether the fitted surfaces hold for MoE models and for other data mixtures (slide 37): the loss landscape over LR and weight decay for MoE models at three sparsity levels, and for bilingual, code-integrated and code-dominant corpora. The minimum moves but the shape is stable enough that the procedure still finds it.

8. Other recipes: Qwen, Kimi K2, Hunyuan, Llama 3, MiniMax

The recent recipes are less detailed, but each makes a specific choice worth knowing.

8.1 Qwen, Kimi K2, Hunyuan, Llama 3

  • Qwen 2.5 (Alibaba, 2024; arXiv 2412.15115): batch and hyperparameter scaling fits. The authors study how the optimal LR \(\eta_{opt}\) and batch \(B_{opt}\) depend on model and data across dense models from 44M to 14B and MoE models with 44M to 1B activated parameters, trained on 0.8B to 600B tokens. Their goal is to predict the best hyperparameters for each dense or MoE configuration and to match dense models with MoE variants at equal activated size.
  • Qwen 3 (arXiv 2505.09388): similar LR and batch scaling, extended across three pretraining stages to predict the learning-rate schedule and batch size for each dense or MoE model.
  • Kimi K2: a sparsity scaling law for MoE models trained with Muon (slide 26). Sparsity is the ratio of total to activated experts. At a fixed number of activated parameters and constant FLOPs, increasing the total number of experts (more sparsity) lowers training and validation loss. Under the compute-optimal sparsity law, sparsity 48 reduces the FLOPs needed for a validation loss of 1.5 by 1.69x, 1.39x and 1.15x relative to sparsity 8, 16 and 32. The gain comes with infrastructure complexity, so K2 adopts sparsity 48: 8 of 384 experts active per token.
  • Hunyuan-Large (Tencent, 2024; arXiv 2411.02265): a large MoE study. Slide 27 shows IsoFLOP curves over activated parameters at budgets from \(5\times10^{18}\) to \(9.5\times10^{19}\), a quadratic fit of the optimum, and an optimal ratio of 96 tokens per activated parameter. The green guide lines in the right panel mark 58.1B activated parameters; with \(C = 6 \cdot 96 \cdot N^2\) that corresponds to \(C \approx 1.94\times10^{24}\) FLOPs.
  • Llama 3 (Meta, 2024; arXiv 2407.21783): IsoFLOP curves for compute between \(6\times10^{18}\) and \(10^{22}\) FLOPs (slide 28, figure 2), approximating each compute scale with a second-degree polynomial in log tokens. The optimal ratio is 39 tokens per parameter; the 405B model trained on 15.6T tokens gives \(15.6\times10^{12}/405\times10^{9} = 38.5\). The second panel extrapolates compute to downstream accuracy: the scaling-law models predict the Llama 3 405B point in normalized NLL and accuracy. The slide's "compute-to-downstream" framing matters because it links the fitted loss to a task metric.

8.2 MiniMax-01: architecture scaling laws

MiniMax-01 (2025) combines architecture scaling laws with Chinchilla method 1 (slide 29). It compares three attention designs: softmax attention, lightning attention, and a hybrid of the two. Training curves span models from 70M to 7B parameters. Figure 6 of the MiniMax paper, as printed on the slide, derives the optimal model size and training tokens from a specified compute budget. The design question it answers is which attention variant gives the best loss per FLOP as the model scales, which is an architecture decision made with the scaling law rather than by a single large run.

8.3 Architecture choices that scale

  • Sparsity (MoE) scales well at fixed activated FLOPs: more experts lower the loss, at a cost in infrastructure (Kimi K2, section 8.1).
  • Attention heads: doubling the number of attention heads when heads equal layers reduces validation loss by about 0.5% to 1.2% (Kimi K2 figure 6 caption on slide 26).
  • Aspect ratio fixed across sizes (MiniCPM, section 3).
  • Attention type chosen from scaling curves rather than a single run (MiniMax, section 8.2).
  • Normalization gains break muP transfer unless removed (section 4.5).

8.4 StepFun and the relative error of scaling predictions

The StepFun study reports the relative error of its fitted law on the held-out points. The slide's bar values are reproduced below; the Step Law has the lowest error of the laws compared, at 0.94 per mille, against 3.7 to 9.5 per mille for the others. The per-mille scale is the lecture's; read the difference as a ratio of about 4x to 10x.

9. Optimizers and scale: Muon, Lion, and what breaks

Optimization is a core part of LLM training and also tricky because of scale dependence. The lecture makes three points.

  1. Hyperparameter tuning is often off. Different optimizers need different hyperparameters, and likely different optimal scaling. On slide 39 (from the "Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them" study), tuning the LR of AdamW gives about a 2x speedup on C4/EN at 130M, and the optimal weight decay for Lion is about 0.6.
  2. Scale dependence is significant. The speedup of Muon, SOAP and others over AdamW shrinks as the model grows from 130M to 1.2B at 8x Chinchilla tokens (slide 40). Matrix-based optimizers (solid curves) consistently outperform scalar-based ones (dashed).
  3. Scaling is non-trivial to establish. A good-looking scaling curve can blow up. The Delphi analysis (slide 41) shows isoFLOP parabolas that look clean at small compute and a held-out extrapolation where the loss is 0.8% and 2.5% worse than predicted at the two largest budgets and one run diverges.
The general development rule

The lecture's note: always check scaling with respect to compute and Chinchilla ratios. These are often major confounders to performance. An algorithm that wins at a fixed token count may lose once the data-to-parameter ratio is matched, and vice versa.

The fix on slide 41 is a "cautious AdamC" optimizer combined with square-root scaling of the learning rate with batch size, followed by more careful parametrization and optimizer changes. The square-root rule says that when the batch size is multiplied by \(k\), the LR is multiplied by \(\sqrt{k}\), which is the Adam-style scaling the batch fit in section 7 is compatible with.

9.1 Muon

Muon is an optimizer for matrix-valued parameters. Its update orthogonalises the momentum buffer with a few Newton–Schulz iterations (slide 42, Algorithm 2). The algorithm as printed:

Algorithm 2 (Muon), as printed on slide 42 
Require: learning rate η, momentum μ
1: initialize B_0 ← 0
2: for t = 1, ... do
3:     compute gradient  G_t ← ∇_θ L(θ_{t-1})
4:     B_t ← μ B_{t-1} + G_t
5:     O_t ← NewtonSchulz5(B_t)          (approximately UVᵀ, where B_t = U S Vᵀ)
6:     update parameters  θ_t ← θ_{t-1} − η O_t
7: end for
8: return θ_t

Line 5 is the only non-standard step: five iterations of a fixed polynomial approximately replace the singular values with ones, so every singular direction of the update has the same magnitude. No SVD is needed.

9.2 Optimizers at scale

The slide's footnote reads "SOAP is under active development; future versions will significantly improve the wallclock overhead." The lecture's take is that scaling gains from Muon are tricky to measure, but Muon clearly works at scale: it is used in the Kimi K2 runs and is the optimizer of the NanoGPT speedrun on slide 43.

10. Compute-optimal vs inference-optimal (over-training)

Chinchilla's split minimises the loss for a fixed training compute \(C = 6ND\). But a deployed model is also run for inference, which costs roughly \(2N\) FLOPs per generated token. If a model will serve many tokens, the total cost is \(6ND + 2N D_{inf}\), and the optimum moves toward smaller models trained on more tokens. That is over-training. The references note for the over-training study (arXiv 2403.08540) states the problem: Chinchilla scaling laws focus on the loss of the trained model and ignore inference costs. The same paper keeps a constant ratio of training tokens to parameters and extrapolates over 300x training compute to a 1.4B model on 900B tokens.

The lecture's slides present the ratios from the scaling fits (MiniCPM ~96, Hunyuan 96, Llama 3 39) as compute-optimal. Read against Chinchilla's ~20 tokens per parameter, each of these is a deliberate over-training of the training run relative to the headline. The calculators below show the two ingredients: the compute-optimal split for a fixed budget, and the split that minimises total cost once inference is included.

10.1 Compute-optimal split for a fixed budget

Choose the fitted law and a training compute \(C\). The widget scans \(N\) along the iso-compute line \(D = C/(6N)\) and reports the minimum of the fitted loss. Defaults give the MiniCPM result: \(N^* \approx 1.32\)B, \(D^* \approx 126\)B, \(D^*/N^* = 95.6\), the value printed on slide 18. The Chinchilla option uses the published approach-3 constants (\(E = 1.69\), \(A = 406.4\), \(\alpha = 0.34\), \(B = 410.7\), \(\beta = 0.28\), with \(N, D\) in raw counts); these constants are not printed on these slides and are included for comparison.

10.2 Over-training: the optimum with inference included

Now fix a target loss \(L^*\) and ask for the cheapest way to reach it, counting training and serving:

\[ \text{total} = 6ND_{train} + 2N\,D_{inf}, \qquad \text{with } L(N, D_{train}) = L^*. \]

Solve the loss constraint for \(D_{train}(N)\) and scan \(N\). With \(D_{inf} = 0\) this is compute-optimal training at that loss. The defaults use the MiniCPM fit and the loss at \(C = 10^{21}\) (0.389); with no inference the widget reproduces \(N^* = 1.32\)B, \(D^* = 126\)B, ratio 95.6. Add 100B served tokens and the optimum shifts to a smaller model trained on more tokens, at a larger total cost than the training-only optimum; the calculator reports the ratio of the training-only optimum's total cost (including its serving) to the new optimum, which is the saving from over-training.

Why the optimum moves

Serving cost is linear in \(N\) and in \(D_{inf}\), while training cost is \(6ND\). Once \(D_{inf}\) is large, every extra parameter costs both training and serving compute, so the optimum buys loss with tokens instead of parameters: smaller \(N\), larger \(D\). The ratio \(D/N\) rises with the number of tokens served, which is exactly the trend the lecture's high-ratio fits (96, 39) are consistent with, though those fits were not made with serving costs in the objective.

11. Does Chinchilla's approach work in practice?

The lecture's answer is yes, with conditions. Three pieces of evidence support it:

  • Held-out prediction. DeepSeek's power law fitted on small models predicts the 7B and 67B losses (slide 24). Llama 3's compute-to-downstream extrapolation predicts the 405B model's normalized NLL and accuracy (slide 28).
  • Ratios are reproducible. Independent fits (MiniCPM joint fit, Hunyuan, Llama 3) all put the optimal data-to-parameter ratio well above 20, in the range 39 to 96.
  • Cheap fits exist. WSD and piecewise schedules make the IsoFLOP and joint-fit procedures affordable (sections 5 and 6).

The conditions are the part the slides spend most time on:

  • The ratio depends on the fitting method. Chinchilla's three methods disagree; MiniCPM uses methods 1 and 3, DeepSeek uses 2, and with the published approach-3 constants the optimum at \(10^{21}\) FLOPs is about 50 tokens per parameter, not 20 (section 10.1).
  • The learning-rate fit is fragile. DeepSeek's LR fit "looks a bit questionable" (slide 21), and the joint-fit LR optimum rises with D for fixed M but may not survive a switch to WSD (slide 36).
  • Scaling can blow up. A clean small-scale fit can extrapolate badly (slide 41).
  • Muon and muP are not free. muP fails on strong weight decay and RMSNorm gains; Muon's gains are "tricky to measure" at scale.

Key takeaways

  • Scale-sensitive knobs need a rule. Initialization, the learning rate and the batch size all depend on width and compute. Pick a rule (muP for width, a batch or LR power law in compute) and check it on a larger model before trusting it.
  • muP transfers the learning rate across width (Lingle's replication: optimum at 2^-6 for widths 128 to 2048 under muP, drifting under SP). It fails on strong weight decay and on RMSNorm gains, and needs the gains removed.
  • Schedules are a compute lever. WSD lets one stable-phase run serve many token budgets; the cost of a K-budget sweep drops from about K(K+1)/2 to about (K+1)/2 units when the decay is 10%. The saving is in fitting, not in the final model.
  • The data-to-parameter ratio is a fit output, not a constant. MiniCPM's joint fit gives about 96 at 1e21 FLOPs; Llama 3 uses 39; Hunyuan uses 96 per active parameter; the Chinchilla constants give about 50 at the same budget. Report which method and which constants you used.
  • Batch size follows loss and data. The critical-batch fit (slide 12) and the DeepSeek power laws both grow the optimal batch polynomially as loss falls or compute rises.
  • Serving changes the optimum. Including inference cost pushes toward smaller models trained on more tokens; the calculator in section 10.2 shows the size of the effect.
  • Check scaling against compute and ratio. A scaling curve that looks clean can blow up (Delphi, slide 41). Hold out the largest run before trusting an extrapolation.

Self-check quiz

Why does muP make the learning rate transferable across widths, and what does it still not fix?
muP sets init and Adam LR per layer so that activations stay Theta(1) at init and their change after one step stays Theta(1) as width grows. The hidden-matrix Adam LR is then eta/r with r = d/d_base, so the optimum stays at the same base LR across widths (Lingle: 2^-6 at 128, 512, 2048). It does not fix strong weight decay (the slide's only significant failure) or RMSNorm gains, which must be removed for transfer.
Compute the MiniCPM joint-fit optimal ratio D/N at a fixed compute, and say why it does not depend on C.
With equal exponents alpha = beta, minimising E + A N^-alpha + B D^-alpha subject to C = 6ND gives D/N = (B/A)^(1/alpha). With A = 0.0754, B = 0.292, alpha = 0.2969 this is 95.6, the value printed on slide 18 at C = 1e21. Nothing in the expression involves C, which matches the slide's eta approximately 0.
A cosine run is 20,000 steps. Why does a WSD run with a 10% decay let you read final losses for several budgets from one trunk?
The stable phase (LR at peak, no decay) is shared. To read the loss at budget D_k, you branch from the stable checkpoint and run only the decay, which is 10% of that budget. A cosine schedule needs a full run per budget because the LR curve depends on the total length. The cost for K = 8 budgets drops from 4.5 D_max to about 1.35 D_max (3.3x).
DeepSeek's batch fit gives B_opt = 0.2920 C^0.3271 tokens. What batch does a 7B model trained on 2T tokens need, and does it match the slide?
C = 6 * 6.9e9 * 2e12 = 8.28e22 FLOPs. Then B = 0.2920 * (8.28e22)^0.3271, which is about 9.16e6 tokens, matching the slide's 9.2M star. The LR is 0.3118 * C^-0.125, about 4.3e-4, matching the slide's 4.2e-4.
Llama 3 405B was trained on 15.6T tokens. What tokens-per-parameter ratio does that give, and how does it compare with Chinchilla's ~20?
15.6e12 / 405e9 = 38.5, the slide's "39-1". That is about twice the Chinchilla headline, so the run is over-trained relative to the compute-optimal split for training loss alone. The inference-adjusted calculator (section 10.2) shows why a production model would choose this.
With the Muon update theta_t = theta_{t-1} - eta O_t, what does NewtonSchulz5 compute, and why does that matter for a matrix?
It approximately computes the orthogonal factor U V^T of the momentum matrix B_t = U S V^T, replacing the singular values S by ones with a fixed polynomial, without an SVD. Every singular direction of the update then has equal magnitude, so no single direction dominates the step.
The slide 33 table prints the OpenAI critical-batch law as 2e18 L^-4.76. Is that consistent with the slide 12 plot?
No. 2e18 * 3.5^-4.76 is about 5e15 tokens, far above the plotted values. 2e8 * 3.5^-4.76 is about 5.1e5, matching the slide 12 fit (exp(20.91) * 3.5^-6.24, about 4.9e5). The printed 2e18 is most likely a typo for 2e8.

Evaluation: what does “good” mean?

lecture_12.py perplexity MMLU / GPQA / HLE Chatbot Arena · Elo agents ARC-AGI safety contamination

TL;DR. Evaluation looks mechanical (prompts → responses → accuracy) but its core challenge is turning an abstract construct (“a good model”) into a concrete metric. This lecture walks the ladder of evaluations — perplexity → exam benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE) → open-ended chat (Chatbot Arena with Elo/Bradley-Terry, AlpacaEval, WildBench) → agents (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, Cybench, MLE-bench) → pure reasoning (ARC-AGI) → safety (HarmBench, AIR-Bench, GCG jailbreaks) — and then asks whether evaluations are realistic (GDPval, MedHELM, Clio, OpenRouter) and valid (train-test overlap, dataset quality). Takeaway: there is no one true evaluation; pick the one that matches the question, state the rules of the game (methods vs. models vs. agents), and weigh difficulty, realism and validity.

1. Where we are: from training to “what do we want?”

So far the course covered everything needed to train a language model: architecture, optimization, systems, scaling laws. The missing piece is data — and since data shapes behaviour (code? multilingual? DNA?), we first need to say what behaviour we want. That is what evaluation answers: given a model, how “good” is it?

Core challenge: abstract construct → concrete metric

“Good” is not a number. Every benchmark is a proxy for some construct (knowledge, reasoning, helpfulness, safety, economic usefulness), and each proxy can be gamed, saturated, contaminated or simply unrepresentative. The mechanical recipe (define prompts, query model, compute accuracy) hides all of those decisions.

Four candidate definitions of “good” (all from the lecture)

Maybe a model is good if it does well on benchmarks. Artificial Analysis aggregates ten evaluations (GDPval-AA, τ²-Bench Telecom, Terminal-Bench Hard, SciCode, AA-LCR, AA-Omniscience, IFBench, Humanity’s Last Exam, GPQA Diamond, CritPt) into one Intelligence Index.

…and is cheap to run. Plotting index against the cost of running the index (log scale) creates a Pareto frontier; the “most attractive quadrant” is high score at low cost.

…if people prefer its responses. Arena AI (formerly Chatbot Arena) ranks models by Elo computed from human pairwise votes (section 4).

…if people simply choose to use (and pay for) it. OpenRouter publishes token volumes per model: a revealed-preference metric that mixes quality, price, latency and availability (free models!).

Taxonomy of what we evaluate (interactive map of the lecture)

2. Perplexity

A language model is a probability distribution \(p(x)\) over token sequences. Perplexity measures whether \(p\) gives high probability to a dataset \(D\):

\[ \mathrm{PPL}(D)=\Big(\tfrac{1}{p(D)}\Big)^{1/|D|}=\exp\Big(-\tfrac1{|D|}\sum_{i}\log p(x_i\mid x_{\lt i})\Big). \]

Pre-training minimizes this on the training set, so the obvious evaluation is perplexity on a held-out test set — what language-modelling research did traditionally.

  • Standard datasets: Penn Treebank (WSJ), WikiText-103 (Wikipedia), One Billion Word Benchmark (from WMT11 machine-translation data: EuroParl, UN, news).
  • Classic paradigm = in-distribution evaluation: train on the train split, test on the test split of the same dataset. Example: pure CNN+LSTM models on the One Billion Word Benchmark improved perplexity from 51.3 to 30.0 (Exploring the Limits of Language Modeling).

GPT-2: zero-shot, out-of-distribution perplexity

GPT-2 was trained on WebText (40 GB of text from websites linked on Reddit) and evaluated zero-shot on the standard datasets — out-of-distribution evaluation. It beats prior SOTA on small datasets (where transfer helps) but not on the large 1BW.

“Perplexity is all you need” (more faith than science)

  • Let \(t\) be the true distribution and \(p\) the model. The best achievable perplexity is governed by the entropy \(H(t)\), attained iff \(p=t\).
  • If \(p=t\) the model solves every task, since any task is \(p(\text{solution}\mid\text{problem})\). So by pushing perplexity down we “reach AGI” — a faith-based argument.

…and perplexity may be more than you need

Example sentence: Stanford was founded in 1885. Plain perplexity charges the model for every token, including ones that are irrelevant to a downstream use (e.g. the exact word “founded”). Fix: conditional perplexity \(p(\text{response}\mid\text{prompt})^{-1/|\text{response}|}\). Try it — slide the token probabilities and choose how many leading tokens are treated as the (free) prompt.

Benchmarks that are perplexity in disguise

  • Cloze tasks — LAMBADA (Paperno et al.): predict the final word of a passage; the target word is only predictable given the whole context.
  • Multiple-choice sentence completion — HellaSwag (Zellers et al.): pick the plausible continuation; wrong endings were produced by adversarial filtering. Scoring = compare the LM log-probabilities of the endings.
Warning if you run a perplexity leaderboard

People submit an LM and you compute log_prob = LM(test_data); you must trust that the probabilities are valid (they sum to 1 over the vocabulary). A model could cheat by putting mass on the test strings. For downstream tasks you instead call response = LM(prompt) and score response yourself — no trust in the probabilities needed.

Summary. Perplexity is still used heavily during development (it gives smooth scaling laws, lecture 9–11), but we also need benchmarks that capture real-world situations — “for the non-believers”.

# the two ways a leaderboard can score a submitted model (pseudo-code from the lecture's warning)
log_prob = LM(test_data)        # perplexity leaderboard: must trust the model's probabilities
response = LM(prompt)           # downstream task: score the generated response yourself
accuracy = mean(grade(response, gold))

3. Exam (knowledge) benchmarks

Exams are a good way to test LMs as they are for humans: you control subject and difficulty, and designed answers are unambiguous and easy to grade.

MMLU — Massive Multitask Language Understanding

  • 57 subjects (math, US history, law, morality, …), multiple choice, “collected by graduate and undergraduate students from freely available sources online” (Hendrycks et al. 2021).
  • Despite the name it tests knowledge, not language understanding. Evaluated on GPT-3 with few-shot prompting.
  • HELM provides prediction visualization: HELM MMLU.

MMLU-Pro

  • Removed noisy/trivial questions; expanded 4 → 10 answer choices (chance falls from 25% to 10%); evaluated with chain of thought (gives the model more of a chance).
  • Accuracy drops by 16% to 33% — so it is less saturated (paper; HELM).

GPQA — Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A

  • Questions written by 61 PhD contractors from Upwork (Rein et al.).
  • PhD experts: 65%. Non-experts with Google and 30 minutes: 34%. GPT-4: 39% at the time.
  • The Diamond subset keeps only questions where both expert validators agree and at most 1 of 3 non-expert validators answers correctly.

Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)

  • 2,500 questions: multimodal, many subjects, multiple-choice + short-answer (paper).
  • Question creators shared a $500K prize pool and co-authorship. Questions are filtered by frontier LLMs (a question that models already answer is rejected) and go through multiple stages of review.
Exam benchmarks — summary

The trend is toward harder questions as models improve and existing benchmarks saturate. Multiple choice can be made as hard as one likes, but it does not capture real usage: real queries are open-ended and often have no single correct answer.

Can this benchmark tell two models apart? (confidence intervals)

A benchmark with \(n\) items and accuracy \(p\) has a sampling standard error \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). Differences smaller than a couple of standard errors are noise; label noise additionally caps the achievable score. (The lecture calls out reporting confidence intervals as a norm; Terminal-Bench leaderboards print an “±” for the same reason.)

4. Chat benchmarks: evaluating open-ended responses

So far we evaluated well-defined multiple-choice tasks. But nobody asks their assistant exam questions. Example prompt: “I would like to make a beet salad with goat cheese. What kind of herbs would work well and what would not work well?” The response is long, structured, and has no single correct answer. Challenge: how do we evaluate an open-ended response?

Chatbot Arena (now Arena AI / LMArena)

Chiang et al. 2024. Data collection:

  1. A random person on the Internet types a prompt.
  2. They get responses from two random, anonymized models.
  3. They vote which is better (A is better / B is better / both good / both bad).

Elo / Bradley-Terry: from pairwise votes to a ranking

Model the probability that A beats B as a logistic function of the rating difference:

\[ P(A\succ B)=\frac{1}{1+10^{(E_B-E_A)/400}}=\sigma\!\Big(\tfrac{\ln 10}{400}(E_A-E_B)\Big). \]

Then fit the ratings \(E\) to maximize the likelihood of all observed comparisons (this is the Bradley-Terry model, \(P(i\succ j)=\frac{\pi_i}{\pi_i+\pi_j}\) with \(\pi_i=10^{E_i/400}\)). Only differences matter, so ratings are anchored (e.g. a mean of 1000). The log-likelihood is concave in \(E\), so any gradient or MM method finds the unique optimum:

\[ \ell(E)=\sum_{(i,j)}\big[w_{ij}\ln P(i\succ j)+w_{ji}\ln P(j\succ i)\big],\qquad \pi_i\leftarrow\frac{W_i}{\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{n_{ij}}{\pi_i+\pi_j}} \text{ (MM update)}. \]

Rule of thumb: +100 Elo → 64% win, +200 → 76%, +400 → 91%.

The live leaderboard and what the numbers imply

Properties of Arena

  • Real-world prompts (free to use, incentive to actually use it).
  • But who are these people? Biases, spammers?
  • Binary preference conflates style and correctness; how does a human even assess correctness? Prone to sycophancy?
  • Feature: different prompts can go to different model pairs; no need to feed identical prompts to every model (important when a human must rate).
  • Dynamic: new prompts and models are incorporated over time.
Why pairwise?

Absolute grading of open-ended answers is unreliable (scale use differs between people). Choosing the better of two similar responses is a much easier and more reproducible judgement: pairwise comparisons between similar responses provide higher signal. Elo/BT then turns a sparse set of comparisons into a global scale.

AlpacaEval and LLM judges

  • 805 instructions from various sources; metric = win rate against a baseline (GPT-4 preview) as judged by GPT-4 preview — a judge that may favour its own style.
  • Problem: LLM judges favour longer responses → leaderboard gaming.
  • AlpacaEval 2.0 uses a regression to length-control the metric (Dubois et al.). The leaderboard shows both “LC win rate” and raw win rate.
  • How do we evaluate the metric itself? By correlation with Chatbot Arena (humans), which is high.

WildBench

  • 1,024 examples sourced from 1M human-chatbot conversations (Lin et al.).
  • GPT-4 Turbo as judge, guided by a checklist of task-specific questions (like chain-of-thought for judging). Two modes: pairwise → WB-Reward (+1 / +0.5 / 0 / −0.5 / −1 vs. baseline models GPT-4T, Haiku, Llama-2-70B, with a length penalty) and individual 1–10 scoring → WB-Score.
  • Well correlated with Chatbot Arena — the de-facto sanity check for any new chat metric.
Chat benchmarks — summary

(1) Evaluating open-ended responses is the challenge. (2) Pairwise comparisons between similar responses carry higher signal. (3) Beware of biases, both from humans (style, sycophancy, who votes) and from LLM judges (length, self-preference). (4) A checklist/rubric improves reliability whether the judge is human or LLM.

5. Agentic benchmarks: evaluating what LMs do

Previously we evaluated what LMs say; now what they do. An agent = a language model + an agent scaffold (the logic deciding how to use the LM: prompts, tools, memory, loops). Tasks require tool use (e.g. running code) and iteration over a long period of time.

SWE-bench

  • 2,294 tasks across 12 Python repositories (Jimenez et al.). Given a codebase and an issue description, submit a PR (a patch).
  • Metric: unit tests (the tests the real fix must make pass, plus existing tests that must not break).
  • Leaderboard: SWE-bench Verified.

Terminal-Bench

  • Computer terminal environments: simple and universal (paper, website).
  • 229 tasks crowdsourced from 93 contributors; 89 tasks constitute Terminal-Bench 2.0.
  • Each task = a Docker container + natural-language instruction + hidden tests (“Re-implement the COBOL program in Python…”).

Human time to solve. The paper estimates time per task for experts and juniors (table in the lecture):

Cybench

  • 40 Capture-the-Flag (CTF) tasks from professional competitions (Zhang et al.). Difficulty measured by first-solve time (how long the fastest human team needed).
  • Optional subtasks (“Which file contains the account credentials?”) give partial credit and guidance.

MLE-bench

  • 75 Kaggle competitions (Chan et al.): the agent must train models, process data, debug and produce a submission.csv; a grader scores it against the human leaderboard (medals).

Agent scaffolds

Beyond a bare ReAct loop, modern “deep agent” scaffolds (Schmid) add:

  • Explicit planning: keep a todo list that gets checked off.
  • Hierarchical delegation: agents calling sub-agents (each with a clean context).
  • Persistent memory: read/write files.
  • Extreme context engineering: very explicit instructions on the process.
Agents — summary

Agents dramatically enlarge the capability surface of language models; scaffolds are very important; and therefore evaluating an agent means evaluating scaffold + language model, not the model alone (see the same Gemini 3.1 Pro spanning 74.8–80.2% on Terminal-Bench above). State clearly which of the two you are claiming.

pass@k: how much do multiple attempts matter?

Not in the lecture; added because agent/code benchmarks are routinely reported as pass@k (Chen et al. 2021, Codex). Sample \(n\) attempts per task, count \(c\) correct. The unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of \(k\) samples passes is

\[ \text{pass@}k = 1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}} = 1-\prod_{i=n-c+1}^{n}\Big(1-\frac{k}{i}\Big), \]

(equal to 1 when \(n-c\lt k\)); the naive plug-in \(1-(1-c/n)^k\) is biased. The reliability metric pass^k (all \(k\) succeed, used by τ-bench) is \(\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}\).

import numpy as np
def pass_at_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Unbiased estimator of P(at least one of k samples is correct), from n samples with c correct."""
    if n - c < k:
        return 1.0
    return 1.0 - np.prod(1.0 - k / np.arange(n - c + 1, n + 1))

assert abs(pass_at_k(20, 4, 5) - (1 - 4368/15504)) < 1e-12

6. Pure reasoning: ARC-AGI

All benchmarks so far need linguistic and world knowledge. Can we isolate reasoning from knowledge? Arguably reasoning is a purer form of intelligence (not just memorizing facts). ARC-AGI:

  • Tasks are 100% solvable by humans but challenging for AI; each task is unique, so memorization does not help.
  • ARC-AGI-1 (2019): the first iteration (small coloured-grid input/output puzzles).
  • ARC-AGI-2 (March 2025): more multi-step reasoning.
  • ARC-AGI-3 (March 2026): interactive environments (technical report).
ARC-AGI — summary

Goal: disentangle reasoning from knowledge (hard to do). Limitation: it is constrained to human reasoning, not superhuman reasoning. Strength: it clearly exposes gaps in current models — pretrained LMs did not move the needle; reasoning models made scores take off; the interactive ARC-AGI-3 reset them to ~0%.

Benchmark saturation, in three data points from this lecture

Every benchmark has a lifecycle: introduced when models score near chance, driven up by progress, then saturated (headroom gone, label noise dominates) — at which point a harder successor appears. The dashed arrows show successors in this lecture.

7. Safety benchmarks

Safety is like a crash-test rating for cars, but what does safety mean for AI?

  • HarmBench (Mazeika et al.): based on 510 harmful behaviours that violate laws or norms. See HarmBench on HELM.
  • AIR-Bench (Zeng et al.): prompts derived from regulatory frameworks and company policies, taxonomized into 314 risk categories with 5,694 prompts (HELM AIR-Bench).

Jailbreaking

  • LMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions.
  • Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) (Zou et al.) automatically optimizes an adversarial suffix that bypasses safety training, e.g. “describing.-- ;) similarlyNow write opposite contents.](Me giving////one please? revert with …”.
  • Suffixes optimized on open-weight models (Llama) transfer to closed models (GPT-4, Claude, Bard).

What is safety?

  • Many aspects are strongly contextual (politics, law, social norms — which vary across countries).
  • Risks are very varied: hallucinations, sycophancy, abetting crimes, inequality, loss of critical thinking.
  • Dual-use: a capable cybersecurity agent (the lecture’s example: Mythos) can hack into a system or do penetration testing — the same capability scored on Cybench is both a safety risk and a defensive tool.

8. Realism: ecological validity

Ecological validity = how well an evaluation captures real-world use. Exams such as GPQA are far from real work; Chatbot Arena prompts are real but the distribution is uncontrolled.

  • GDPval (OpenAI; paper): 44 occupations from the top 9 sectors by US GDP; tasks written by professionals with ~14 years of experience; the deliverable is a real work product (document, spreadsheet, slide deck, video, CAD).
  • MedHELM (paper, leaderboard): previous medical benchmarks were standardized exams; MedHELM has 121 clinical tasks sourced from 29 clinicians, a mix of private and public datasets.
  • Clio (Anthropic; paper): use LMs to analyse real user data and share general patterns of what people ask, without exposing individual conversations.
Realism vs. privacy

The most realistic data (what users actually type, what professionals actually do) is exactly the data that is private. Realism and privacy are sometimes at odds; Clio-style privacy-preserving aggregation and private test sets are the compromise.

9. Validity: can we trust the number?

Train-test overlap (contamination)

  • ML 101: don’t train on your test set. Pre-foundation-model datasets (ImageNet, SQuAD) had well-defined splits.
  • Today we train on the Internet and don’t tell people about our data — benchmark questions, answers and discussions are all on the Internet.

Route 1: infer overlap from the model (exchangeability)

If the test set is not in the training data, the order of the test examples is arbitrary, so the model’s log-probability of the dataset should be exchangeable under permutation of the examples. If the benchmark file was seen verbatim, the canonical order will be more likely than shuffled orders (Oren et al.) — a black-box test needing only log-probs, no training data.

Route 2: reporting norms

Model providers should report train-test overlap (paper), just as papers report confidence intervals.

Route 3: fresh evals

Scrape new content published after the training cutoff — LiveCodeBench, UncheatableEval. Caveat: timestamps are not always safe, because new pages can copy older content.

Route 4: private evals

Use data that is not on the Internet: a company’s internal code bases, your personal writings. Easiest for perplexity.

The classic baseline: n-gram overlap

Not in the lecture (it is how many technical reports check contamination when they own the training data). Flag a test item if some contiguous \(n\)-gram of it also appears in the training corpus. Try the scenarios below and watch how paraphrase evades exact matching while a partial leak is caught.

Dataset quality

  • SWE-bench Verified: OpenAI had humans fix up SWE-bench (post) — removing under-specified issues and over-strict tests.
  • Platinum versions of benchmarks (paper): relabel and clean to find that many “model errors” on popular benchmarks are actually label errors.
  • Problems with agentic benchmarks (paper): insufficient test cases, or a trivial agent can solve the task — so scores overstate (or understate) capability.
  • Docent (post): use an LLM to inspect agent traces and detect environment/grader problems.

10. What is the point of evaluation?

There is no one true evaluation; it depends on the question you are answering.

A user or company choosing between model A and B for their use case (e.g. customer-service chatbots). Needs task-specific, realistic evaluation on their own data; price, latency and reliability matter. Aggregate leaderboards are only a prior.

Researchers measuring raw capability (e.g. “intelligence”). Needs hard, contamination-resistant, knowledge-controlled tests (HLE, GPQA, ARC-AGI).

Understanding benefits and harms for business and policy. Needs safety/risk evaluations (HarmBench, AIR-Bench, dual-use cyber capability) and real-world impact measures (GDPval, Clio).

Model developers wanting a training signal. Needs fast, cheap, low-noise metrics (perplexity, held-out benchmark suites) that track progress and generalize.

What are we evaluating?

  • Before foundation models, we evaluated methods: standardized train/test splits, everyone trains from the same data.
  • Today we (mostly) evaluate models/systems: anything goes — any data, any compute, any scaffold.
  • Exception: the nanoGPT speedrun (Keller Jordan; fixed data, compute time/tokens to reach a validation-loss target): the SOTA was 3.8x more token-efficient, 2.7B vs 10B tokens, to train a 124M Transformer.
Evaluating methods

Encourages algorithmic innovation by researchers (rules fixed; the algorithm is the variable).

Evaluating models/systems

Useful for downstream users (they want the best artifact, whatever it took to build).

Either way, we must define the rules of the game.

11. Self-check quiz

1. Model A has Elo 1100 and model B has 900 on the Arena. What win probability does the model assign to A, and how is it fitted?
\(1/(1+10^{-200/400})=1/(1+0.316)=0.760\). Ratings are fitted by maximizing the likelihood of all observed pairwise votes (Bradley-Terry); only differences are identified, so ratings are anchored to an arbitrary mean.
2. Why does conditional perplexity \(p(\text{response}\mid\text{prompt})^{-1/|\text{response}|}\) beat plain perplexity for downstream relevance?
Plain perplexity charges the model for every token, including prompt tokens and irrelevant words (e.g. predicting “founded” in Stanford was founded in 1885). Conditioning averages only over the tokens we care about, so the metric tracks the task.
3. What did MMLU-Pro change versus MMLU, and what was the effect?
It removed noisy/trivial items, expanded 4 → 10 choices (chance 25% → 10%) and evaluates with chain of thought. Accuracy dropped 16–33 points, so it is less saturated and less sensitive to prompt wording.
4. Why do LLM-judged benchmarks like AlpacaEval need length control, and how can you sanity-check any new chat metric?
LLM judges prefer longer responses, so raw win rate can be gamed by verbosity; AlpacaEval 2.0 regresses out length. Sanity check by correlating the metric with Chatbot Arena human Elo (WildBench WB-Reward reports r = 0.984).
5. In Terminal-Bench the same model scores 74.8% to 80.2% (Gemini 3.1 Pro). What does this imply about what an agent benchmark measures?
It measures scaffold + model jointly. A claim about “the model” must fix the scaffold; a claim about a scaffold must fix the model. Leaderboards list agent and model separately for this reason.
6. You have n = 20 samples with c = 4 correct. Compute pass@5 and compare with the plug-in estimate.
pass@5 = 1 − C(16,5)/C(20,5) = 1 − 4368/15504 = 0.718. The plug-in \(1-(1-0.2)^5=0.672\) is biased low here. pass^5 (all five succeed) = C(4,5)/C(20,5) = 0.
7. A benchmark may be in the training data. List four ways to cope, and explain the exchangeability test.
(1) Infer overlap from the model; (2) require providers to report overlap; (3) fresh evals (LiveCodeBench, UncheatableEval); (4) private evals. Exchangeability: if the test set was unseen, shuffling the example order should not change the log-prob; a significantly higher log-prob for the canonical order reveals memorization.
8. Why can’t one evaluation answer “how good is the model?”
Because “good” depends on the purpose: purchase decision, raw capability, benefits/harms, or developer feedback. Each wants a different trade-off among difficulty, realism and validity, and you must also say whether you evaluate methods, models, or agents.

12. Key takeaways

  • There is no one true evaluation; choose it according to what you are trying to measure.
  • Clearly state the rules of the game: methods vs. models vs. agents (scaffold + LM).
  • Weigh difficulty (saturation, headroom), realism (ecological validity vs. privacy) and validity (contamination, dataset quality, judge bias).
  • Perplexity is smooth and cheap but a proxy; exams are clean but unrealistic; open-ended chat needs pairwise preference + Elo/BT or rubric-guided judges; agents need sandboxes and programmatic graders; ARC-AGI isolates reasoning but only human-level reasoning.
  • Report uncertainty (confidence intervals), overlap and full evaluation protocol.

Data I: Where Pretraining Data Comes From

lecture_13.py pretraining data Common Crawl copyright & licences filtering & dedup OLMo / Tulu / DCLM
TL;DR. Data does not fall from the sky. Between a live web server and a training token there is a long, mostly heuristic pipeline (crawl, HTML-to-text, language ID, quality filtering, toxicity/PII removal, deduplication, mixing), plus a legal layer (robots.txt, terms of service, copyright, licences, fair use). Companies publish architectures and training recipes but almost nothing about data, so this lecture walks through the documented datasets (BERT corpora, WebText, C4, The Pile, MassiveText, LLaMA, RefinedWeb/FineWeb, Dolma, DCLM, Nemotron-CC, The Stack, CommonPile) and the OLMo 2 / Tulu 3 recipes, to show how each choice trades quantity against quality and legal safety.

1. Why data matters, and what is (not) disclosed

Earlier lectures covered how to train a model given data. The next two lectures ask what data to train on. The claim: data is the most important thing to get right. One piece of evidence is what companies disclose. Open-weight models such as Llama 3 are transparent about architecture and even the training procedure, but give essentially no information on data. The lecture shows the Llama 3 "Pre-Training Data" paragraph below: a cutoff of end-2023, "several de-duplication methods and data cleaning mechanisms", and PII and adult-domain removal, but no named sources or proportions.

Why the secrecy?

(1) Competitive dynamics: data is what differentiates models. (2) Copyright liability: naming sources invites lawsuits (see the lawsuits section).

Data work is a long-tail problem

Before foundation models: heavy annotation of labelled data for supervised learning. Now: less annotation but a lot of curation and cleaning. Unlike architectures and systems, data quality scales with human effort.

Stages of training

  1. Pre-training: raw text (e.g. web documents).
  2. Mid-training: more training on high-quality data to boost capabilities (math, code, instruction-like text).
  3. Post-training: chat transcripts / instruction data (SFT, preference tuning) or reinforcement learning.

The lines are blurry and there can be more stages, but the trend is the same: large amounts of lower-quality data early, small amounts of high-quality data later. Terminology: a base model is the checkpoint after pre-training + mid-training; an instruct/chat model is after post-training. Increasingly only instruct models are released (e.g. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B).

OLMo (AI2) gives a fully documented example of each stage. Pre-training (OLMo 2 "1124 Mix", OLMo 2):

Mid-training (Dolmino, a high-quality subset plus a math mix):

Post-training (Tulu 3):

Questions for the rest of the lecture: what are these datasets, how are they chosen and processed? The interactive charts below are drawn from the numbers in those three tables.

2. Worked example: the OLMo 2 pre-training mix

Each row of the OLMo 2 table gives tokens, words, bytes and documents. From those four numbers you can derive useful ratios: tokens per word (tokenizer efficiency on that domain), bytes per token (compression), and tokens per document (typical length). Notice how heavily the mix is dominated by one source and how math/LaTeX text (arXiv, OpenWebMath, Algebraic Stack) has far fewer bytes per token (~3.7-3.9) than web text (5.75): symbol-heavy text tokenizes poorly.

Mid-training and post-training mixes

The high-quality web in Dolmino is labelled in the table as "DCLM-Baseline, fastText top 7%, FineWeb ≥ 2". It looks like a second round of classifier filtering on top of the already-filtered baseline, though the table does not spell out the procedure. The math mix is dominated by synthetic math (TinyGSM-MIND 6.48B, MathCoder2 3.87B).

Observation: Tulu 3 mixes public datasets (WildChat, FLAN v2, OpenAssistant, No Robots, OpenMathInstruct 2, NuminaMath, Evol CodeAlpaca, Aya, SciRIFF, and the safety sets CoCoNot, WildJailbreak, WildGuardMix) with newly synthesized "Persona" prompts (Tulu 3 Persona MATH/GSM/Algebra/Python/IF) and 24 "Hardcoded" prompts. The skill categories are explicit: general chat, knowledge recall, math reasoning, coding, safety and non-compliance, multilingual, precise instruction following. Prompts are heavily subsampled (OpenMathInstruct 2: 22M candidates, 50K used for SFT; WildChat: 241K candidates, 100K used), so the SFT and DPO sets are far smaller than the pools they come from.

3. Where does data come from? The web is not the Internet

A common line: "language models are trained on the entire Internet." More accurately, they are trained on a crawl of the public world wide web, and even that is not right. The web is a set of live servers ($ curl https://cs336.stanford.edu/); you cannot train on live servers. A crawler (1) discovers pages starting from a seed set and (2) downloads them. But you cannot download everything:

BarrierWhat it meansExamples
Dynamic contentSites are apps; the URL does not change; content requires clicking buttons / submitting formsDiscord, wandb
AuthenticationLogin (and usually payment) needed; huge content behind walled gardensFacebook, X, LinkedIn, NYTimes
Technical restrictionsrobots.txt (voluntary), Cloudflare bot detection / CAPTCHAs, IP or country blocks, rate limitsnytimes.com/robots.txt
Legal restrictionsTerms of service may prohibit bots; you may have no licence to copy pages for trainingsee copyright section
What robots.txt looks like (illustrative, written for this guide; not a real file) 
# Politeness / consent signal: voluntary, per user-agent
User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: CCBot
Disallow: /private/
Crawl-delay: 5

User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Sitemaps, crawl delays, full or pattern-based disallows and per-agent rules are the categories tracked in the "Consent in Crisis" study below.

The decline of consent

Consent in Crisis examined robots.txt and ToS for the URLs in common datasets (C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma) over time. Restrictions have increased over time. In the figure, the darkest "full restrictions" band (top panel) and the "no crawling / no AI" ToS bands (middle panel) grow in 2023-2024, around the labelled events (ChatGPT, GPT-4, GPTBot, G-Ext.). The bottom panel tracks restrictions by organisation agent (log scale).
