When crawlers misbehave

Factors at play: ToS, robots.txt, and server load (degrades service, costs the website money). Then there is copyright.

Shadow libraries

Library Genesis (LibGen), Z-Library, Anna's Archive and Sci-Hub are technically part of the web. They disregard copyright and bypass paywalls (e.g. Elsevier), have received takedown orders and lawsuits and are blocked in various countries, but controls are circumvented with servers in many countries. Some argue they make freely available what should be free; from a legal perspective it is piracy and copyright infringement. Scale: LibGen ~4M books (2019); Sci-Hub ~88M papers (2022).

Summary

The Internet is huge, but there are many technical and legal restrictions on what you can access. Everything else in the lecture is about what you do with the part you can lawfully and technically get.

4. What data can we legally use? Copyright, licences, fair use, ToS

Intellectual property and copyright

IP law's goal is to incentivize the creation of intellectual goods. Types: copyright, patents, trademarks, trade secrets. Copyright goes back to 1709 England (Statute of Anne); in the US the most recent major act is the Copyright Act of 1976. It protects "original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device."

  • Collections (e.g. telephone directories) are not original works and are not copyrightable unless the selection/arrangement is creative.
  • Copyright covers expression, not ideas (e.g. quicksort).
  • Scope expanded from "published" (1909) to "fixed" (1976). Registration is not required for protection (unlike patents); the threshold is extremely low — your website is copyrighted.
  • Registration is required before the creator can sue for infringement; it costs $65.
  • Protection lasts 75 years (per the lecture), after which the work enters the public domain (Shakespeare, Beethoven, most of Project Gutenberg).
Summary

Basically everything on the Internet is copyrighted. Two ways to use a copyrighted work: (1) get a licence; (2) appeal to the fair use clause.

Licences

A licence (from contract law) is granted by a licensor to a licensee: effectively a promise not to sue. The Creative Commons licence, created by Lessig and Eldred in 2001 to bridge the public domain and existing copyright, enables free distribution of copyrighted work: Wikipedia, Open Courseware, Khan Academy, Free Music Archive, 307M images from Flickr, 39M images from MusicBrainz, 10M videos from YouTube, ...

Many developers also license data directly: Google and Reddit, OpenAI and Shutterstock, OpenAI and StackExchange.

Fair use (section 107)

Four factors decide whether fair use applies:

#FactorFavours fair useDisfavours
1Purpose and character of useeducational, transformativecommercial, reproductive
2Nature of the workfactual, non-creativefictional, creative
3Amount and substantiality useda snippetthe whole work
4Effect on the (potential) marketno market harmsubstitutes for the original

Examples of fair use: watching a movie and writing a summary; reimplementing an algorithm (idea) rather than copying the code (expression); Google Books indexing and showing snippets (Authors Guild v. Google, 2002-2013). Copyright is not about verbatim memorization: plots and characters (Harry Potter) can be copyrightable, parody is likely fair use — copyright is about semantics (and economics).

Considerations for language models
  • Copying the data (the very first step of training) is already a potential violation even if you do nothing with it.
  • Training should be transformative (far from copy/paste): the model should capture the general idea (wizards), not the concrete expression (Harry Potter).
  • LMs can definitely affect the market (writers, artists), regardless of copyright.

Terms of service impose additional restrictions even when you have a licence or a fair-use argument. Example: YouTube's ToS prohibits downloading videos even if they carry a Creative Commons licence.

Interactive: copyright / licence decision flow

Interactive: fair-use scorecard

Lawsuits so far

2023 The New York Times v. OpenAI: allegation of training on and reproducing NYT articles.
2024 Authors (Bartz, Graeber, ...) v. Anthropic: pirating millions of books and training on plaintiffs' books. 2025 summary judgement: training on the plaintiffs' works is fair use, but pirating copies is not (even without training). Anthropic also bought and scanned books (fair use, but "too late"). Outcome: Anthropic paid $1.5B to authors to settle.
2025 Authors (Kadrey, Silverman, ...) v. Meta: allegation of training on plaintiffs' books (revealed in the Llama paper). Summary judgement: training on books (in this instance) is fair use (TechCrunch); the torrenting allegation is still pending.
Summary

So far training has been deemed fair use for specific instances (unclear in general); pirating books is clearly illegal; the area is very active and evolving.

5. The curation pipeline: live web to training tokens

Key lesson: live service → raw data → processed data (transformation, filtering, deduplication). Most of this is heuristic, which means many opportunities to improve. Every dataset in this lecture is a different instantiation of the same flow. Step through it:

6. Common Crawl and HTML-to-text

Common Crawl is a non-profit founded in 2007. Roughly every month it runs a crawl adding 3-5 billion pages; crawls overlap a little but try to diversify; ~300 billion pages so far. How many URLs exist is hard to estimate (O(billions)); the Google index is at least 100 PB. The April 2026 crawl has 2.19B pages (372.2 TB).

2007
Common Crawl founded
3-5B
pages per monthly crawl
300B
pages so far
~170 KB
per page (372.2 TB / 2.19B)

Crawling uses Apache Nutch: start with seed URLs (hundreds of millions at least), pop a URL, download, add its hyperlinks to the queue. Policies: selection (which pages), politeness (obey robots.txt, do not overload servers), re-visit (how often pages change). Challenge: URLs are dynamic and many URLs lead to essentially the same content.

Two formats: WARC (raw HTTP response, e.g. HTML) and WET (converted to text — a lossy process). Converting HTML yourself with trafilatura or resiliparse matters for downstream accuracy (DCLM):

Other pipelines make different choices: The Pile (Pile-CC) uses WARC + jusText ("better than WET"); RefinedWeb uses trafilatura on WARC; Nemotron-CC uses jusText because it yields more tokens. There is no single "right" extractor: quality and quantity trade off.

Interactive: how many tokens survive?

A back-of-envelope calculator for the DCLM funnel. Document-level survival rates come from the DCLM figure (percentages are of the original number of documents); tokens-per-doc, words-per-token and bytes-per-token are taken from the OLMo 2 table's DCLM-Baseline row (3.71T tokens, 3.32T words, 21.32T bytes, 2.95B docs).

Common Crawl size sanity check

7. Specialised sources: Wikipedia, GitHub, arXiv, books, StackExchange

Wikipedia: free online encyclopedia, founded 2001; as of May 2026, 67M articles in 361 language editions (English, Spanish, German, French most common). Scope: no original thought (no opinions, promotions, personal pages), articles by notability (significant coverage from reliable sources). Authors: anyone can edit, vandalism is reverted; a small number of Wikipedians contribute the majority (e.g. Steven Pruitt, 5M edits). Access: periodic dumps every few weeks — no crawling needed.

Aside: data-poisoning attacks

Poisoning web-scale training datasets is practical: since dumps are periodic, an attacker can inject malicious edits right before a dump and they are captured before being rolled back. Concealed data poisoning showed how to inject examples making a model ascribe negative sentiment to a trigger phrase (e.g. "iPhone"). Takeaway: even high-quality sources can contain bad content.

Code helps programming tasks, and (folklore) reasoning more broadly. GitHub: founded 2008, acquired by Microsoft 2018; as of May 2026 420M+ repositories (28M public). Each repo has directory structure, commit history, issues, PRs, comments; lots of duplicates (copies, forks). You may train on public repos with a permissive licence (MIT, Apache).

  • Repositories: download through the git protocol rather than scraping the website.
  • Metadata: GitHub API gives issues/PRs/comments; hourly snapshots of the event stream are on GitHub Archive.
  • Software Heritage: non-profit (2016) preserving software from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, PyPI, ...; focuses on repositories not metadata; 28.8M source files as of May 2026.

arXiv: free paper sharing since 1991 (physics, math, CS, statistics, ...), ~3M submissions. Each submission: metadata, PDF, optional LaTeX source. Light approval (not peer review). Authors choose all-rights-reserved or Creative Commons (e.g. CC-BY); title/abstract metadata is CC0. Bulk download from Amazon S3, no crawling. LLaMA used the LaTeX, removing comments, inline-expanding macros and dropping the bibliography.

Smashwords (founded 2008): anyone can self-publish an e-book; 2024: 150K authors, 500K books. BooksCorpus (Zhu et al.): self-published books priced at $0 scraped from Smashwords, 7K books, 985M words; taken down for violating Smashwords ToS. Project Gutenberg (1971, Michael Hart): ~75K books (2025), mostly English, only copyright-cleared (mostly public domain); PG-19 = Gutenberg books before 2019. Books3 (Presser 2020): 196K books from the shadow library Bibliotik including works by Stephen King, Min Jin Lee, Zadie Smith; taken down for copyright infringement.

Collection of Q&A sites started with StackOverflow (2008), grown to maths, literature, etc.; reputation points and badges incentivise participation. The Q&A format is close to instruction tuning / real applications, and rich metadata (users, votes, comments, badges, tags) enables filtering (e.g. LLaMA sorted answers by score, using 28 largest sites). Data dumps in XML (anonymised, with metadata) at archive.org.

8. A tour of datasets, 2018-2025

2018-19 BERT Wikipedia + BooksCorpus; sequences are documents, not shuffled sentences (contrast: 1B Word Benchmark of machine-translation sentences).
2019 GPT-2 WebText outbound links of Reddit posts with ≥3 karma (karma = quality proxy): 8M pages, 40 GB. OpenWebText = open replication (Reddit URL dump, fastText to drop non-English, near-dup removal).
2019 CCNet dedup paragraphs + language ID (fastText) + KenLM 5-gram perplexity vs Wikipedia; BERT on CCNet beats BERT on Wikipedia.
2019 C4 (T5) rule-filtered April-2019 Common Crawl: 1.4T tokens down to 806 GB / 156B tokens.
2020 GPT-3 Common Crawl (quality-classified) + WebText2 + Books1/Books2 + Wikipedia: 570 GB, 400B tokens.
2021 The Pile 22 curated domains, 825 GB (~275B tokens), grassroots on Discord.
2021 MassiveText / Gopher 10.5 TB, but only 300B tokens (12%) trained on.
2023 LLaMA CCNet-CC + C4 + GitHub + Wikipedia + Gutenberg/Books3 + arXiv + StackExchange: 1.2T tokens.
2023 RefinedWeb / FineWeb (2024) web only, trafilatura + MinHash; FineWeb 15T tokens.
2024 Dolma, DCLM, Nemotron-CC 3T / 3.8T (from 240T pool) / 6.3T tokens.
2022-25 The Stack, CommonPile permissively licensed code (3.1 TB) and a fully openly-licensed 8 TB dataset.

Pre-2020: BERT, WebText, CCNet, C4

BERT (Devlin et al.): Wikipedia + BooksCorpus. Important: training sequences are documents, not isolated sentences as in the 1 Billion Word benchmark [Chelba et al. 2013] (sentences from machine translation).

WebText / OpenWebText (GPT-2, Radford et al. 2019): pages that are outgoing links from Reddit posts with ≥3 karma, a surrogate for quality; 8M pages, 40 GB. OpenWebText extracted all URLs from the Reddit submissions dataset, used fastText to remove non-English, removed near-duplicates.

CCNet (Wenzek et al.): an automatic way to build large high-quality pre-training sets, especially for low-resource languages (e.g. Urdu). Components: deduplication (paragraphs, after light normalisation), language ID (fastText, keep target language), quality filtering (keep documents that look like Wikipedia under a KenLM 5-gram model). BERT trained on CCNet(CommonCrawl) outperforms Wikipedia. "CCNet" names both the tool and the released dataset.

C4 (Raffel et al. 2019, T5): the paper is famous for casting all NLP tasks as text-to-text, but a major contribution is the cleaned corpus. Observation: Common Crawl is mostly not useful natural language. Starting from one snapshot (April 2019, 1.4T tokens), apply manual heuristics:

  • Keep only lines that end in punctuation and have ≥5 words; remove pages with fewer than 3 sentences.
  • Remove any page that contains a "bad word" (LDNOOBW list), a { (no code), "lorem ipsum", "terms of use", etc.
  • Keep English only via langdetect with probability ≥0.99.

Result: 806 GB, 156B tokens (from 1.4T: 11%). C4 was analysed in Documenting Large Webtext Corpora. Bonus: a "WebText-like" subset kept only pages from OpenWebText links, 12 dumps giving 17 GB (vs 40 GB WebText, suggesting Common Crawl is incomplete) — and improved GLUE, SQuAD, etc.

Interactive: C4-style rule filter

The rules below are the C4 heuristics from the lecture (the bad-word list is a harmless toy in this demo). Pick a page and see which lines survive and whether the page is kept.

Illustrative Python for the C4 rules (not from the lecture's code) 
import re
def c4_filter(page, bad_words, min_words=5, min_sentences=3):
    kept = [l for l in page.split("\n")
            if re.search(r'[.!?"]$', l.strip()) and len(l.split()) >= min_words]
    text = page.lower()
    if len(kept) < min_sentences: return None
    if "{" in text or "lorem ipsum" in text or "terms of use" in text: return None
    if any(re.search(r"\b" + re.escape(b) + r"\b", text) for b in bad_words): return None
    return "\n".join(kept)

2020-2021: GPT-3, The Pile, MassiveText

GPT-3 (Brown et al., Sec. 2.2): Common Crawl (processed), WebText2 (WebText with more links), the "mysterious" Internet-based books corpora Books1/Books2, and Wikipedia: 570 GB, 400B tokens. Common Crawl was processed by training a quality classifier to distinguish {WebText, Wikipedia, Books1, Books2} from the rest, and fuzzy-deduplicating documents (including against WebText and the benchmarks).

The Pile (Gao et al.): a reaction to GPT-3, part of the push for open-source LMs; a grassroots volunteer effort coordinated on Discord. 22 curated high-quality domains, 825 GB (~275B tokens). Highlights: Pile-CC (Common Crawl via WARC + jusText, "better than WET"); PubMed Central (5M papers; NIH-funded work must be public); arXiv (LaTeX); Enron emails (500K emails from 150 senior-management users, released in the 2002 investigation); Project Gutenberg; Books3; StackExchange. It trained GPT-J, GPT-NeoX and others.

MassiveText / Gopher (Rae et al.): components MassiveWeb, C4, Books, News, GitHub, Wikipedia (the last four with few details). MassiveWeb filtering: keep English, dedup, train-test overlap removal, manual-rule quality filtering rather than a classifier (e.g. 80% of words must contain at least one alphabetic character), and Google SafeSearch for toxicity rather than word lists. Result: 10.5 TB of text but Gopher trained on only 300B tokens (12%). Gopher was subsumed by Chinchilla and never released, but the description of data is good.

2022-2023: LLaMA, RefinedWeb, FineWeb

LLaMA (Touvron et al.): CommonCrawl processed with CCNet but the classifier labels pages as referenced by Wikipedia or not; C4 (more diverse; rule-based); GitHub (permissive licences, manual-rule filtering); Wikipedia (June-August 2022, 20 languages); Project Gutenberg and Books3 (from The Pile); arXiv (removed comments, inline-expanded macros, bibliography); StackExchange (28 largest sites, sorted answers by score). 1.2T tokens. Reproduced by Together's RedPajama v1; Cerebras's SlimPajama is a 627B-token MinHashLSH-deduplicated subset.

RefinedWeb (Penedo et al.): "web data is all you need". trafilatura on WARC; Gopher rules; no ML-based filtering (avoid bias); fuzzy dedup with MinHash over 5-grams. Released 600B of 5T tokens (used for Falcon). FineWeb (HF) started as a replication and improved it: 95 Common Crawl dumps, URL filtering, language ID (keep if p(en)>0.65), Gopher + C4 + more manual rules, MinHash dedup, anonymising emails and public IPs (PII). Result: 15T tokens.

Interactive: MinHash-style fuzzy deduplication

Fuzzy dedup treats each document as a set of word n-gram "shingles" and compares sets by Jaccard similarity \(J(A,B)=|A\cap B|/|A\cup B|\). MinHash signatures with \(b\) bands of \(r\) rows make a pair a candidate with probability \(1-(1-J^{r})^{b}\) (an S-curve with threshold near \((1/b)^{1/r}\)); candidates are then removed as near duplicates. (The next data lecture covers dedup in more depth; this widget is a preview.)

9. Model-based quality filtering: Dolma, DCLM, Nemotron-CC

Dolma (AI2, 3T tokens, trained OLMo): sources are Common Crawl, C4, Reddit (Pushshift 2005-2023, submissions and comments separately), peS2o (40M academic papers from Semantic Scholar), Project Gutenberg, Wikipedia/Wikibooks. Common Crawl processing: fastText language ID (English), Gopher/C4 rule-based quality (explicitly avoiding model-based filtering), toxicity via rules and the Jigsaw classifier, Bloom-filter deduplication.

DataComp-LM (DCLM)

DCLM aims to be a standard dataset for trying out data-processing algorithms: extract DCLM-Pool (240T tokens) from Common Crawl with resiliparse, then filter it. DCLM-Baseline (3.8T tokens) is DCLM-Pool after heuristics (RefinedWeb reproduction), Bloom-filter dedup and a model-based quality classifier:

  • Positive examples (200K): OpenHermes-2.5 (mostly GPT-4-generated instruction data) and ELI5 (curiosity questions and answers).
  • Negative examples (200K): RefinedWeb.
  • Train a fastText classifier and run it over all of DCLM-Pool; keep the top fraction. Result 3.8T tokens.

The classifier beats alternatives (1B-1x scale; CORE / EXTENDED scores):

Lesson

A very simple classifier (fastText on bag-of-n-grams) trained on "instruction-like / explainer" text vs generic web beats fancier model-based signals (perplexity, LLM scoring, embedding classifiers, PageRank). What you choose as positive examples defines "quality".

Nemotron-CC: more tokens at preserved quality

Nemotron-CC observes that FineWeb-Edu and DCLM filter too aggressively (removing ~90% of data), so for longer training runs you need more tokens without giving up quality.

  • HTML-to-text with jusText (not trafilatura) because it returned more tokens.
  • Classifier ensembling: prompt Nemotron-340B-instruct to score FineWeb documents for educational value and distil into a faster model; combine with the DCLM classifier.
  • Synthetic rephrasing: for low-quality data, have an LM rephrase it; for high-quality data, have an LM generate tasks (QA pairs, key-information extraction, ...).

Result: 6.3T tokens (high-quality subset: 1.1T). For reference, Llama 3 trained on 15T and Qwen3 on 36T.

Interactive: data mixing across sources

Mixing = choosing what fraction of the training budget each source gets. Small, high-quality sources are repeated (multiple epochs) if you upsample them. Set shares for the non-web groups; web is the remainder; within each group tokens are split in proportion to the source's size. Defaults reproduce the OLMo 2 mix (every source seen ~1 epoch at 3.9T).

10. Code datasets: The Stack and Stack v2

The Stack (Kocetkov et al.): took repository names from GitHub Archive (2015-2022); git cloned 137M repositories, 51B files (only 5B unique!); kept only permissively licensed code (MIT, Apache) using go-license-detector; removed near-duplicates with MinHash and Jaccard similarity. Result: 3.1 TB of code.

Stack v2 (StarCoder 2) extends this:

  • Issues, comments and PRs from GitHub Archive; repositories from Software Heritage; documentation crawled from websites (PyPI, npm, devdocs.io).
  • Processing: remove binary files, malware and bot activity; deduplicate; PII redaction; subsample PRs.
  • Pair source code (especially low-resource languages such as Nim) with a shared low-level intermediate language (LLVM).
  • Include existing datasets (GSM8K, code contests, StackOverflow, arXiv, Wikipedia, OpenWebMath).

Pull requests: linearize the structured object into a token sequence, add some inline context (e.g. the file around the diff) and subsample.

11. CommonPile: only permissively licensed data

Recall: almost all data on the Internet is copyrighted; some is permissively licensed; fair use is unsettled. Key question: can you train a good model using only permissively licensed data? CommonPile collected an 8 TB dataset of permissively licensed data. The figure shows size per source (log axis) grouped by category; the category totals printed in the figure are charted below.

Subtleties
  • Licence laundering: someone redistributes a copyrighted work under a permissive licence (hard to detect).
  • Collection vs item licences: a collection licence (Dolma is ODC-By) does not extend to the individual items.
  • Synthetic data from LMs trained on unlicensed data has unclear status.

The Comma v0.1-1T model trained on CommonPile is compared with LLaMA, MPT and RPJ-INCITE at similar scale (Qwen3 is shown for reference). It does decently. The stars in the figure appear to mark benchmarks where Comma leads the non-Qwen3 models (the figure does not say so explicitly). As the lecture concludes, it is tough to compete without more tokens.

12. Summary and takeaways

Key takeaways
  • Data does not fall from the sky; you have to work to get it. Live service → raw data → processed data (transformation, filtering, deduplication).
  • Data is the key ingredient that differentiates language models, and it is the least disclosed part of the recipe.
  • Training goes from large amounts of lower-quality data (pre-training) to small amounts of high-quality data (mid-training, post-training).
  • Legal and ethical issues (copyright, privacy, consent) shape what can be used: everything is copyrighted by default; use licences or fair use; check ToS and robots.txt; piracy is separately illegal.
  • Most of the pipeline is heuristic — many opportunities to improve (extractors, classifiers, dedup, mixing, synthetic rephrasing).

13. Self-check quiz

Why can't you just train on "the Internet"? Name four kinds of barrier.
Dynamic content (apps whose URL does not change), authentication/paywalls (Facebook, NYTimes), technical restrictions (robots.txt, Cloudflare/CAPTCHAs, IP blocks, rate limits) and legal restrictions (ToS, no licence to copy). Also: you must crawl and download first; live servers cannot be trained on.
In DCLM, what fraction of original documents survive each stage, and what does that imply for token counts?
19.9% after heuristic cleaning (English filter alone drops 50.8%), 13.7% after Bloom-filter dedup, 1.4% after the fastText classifier. With 240T tokens in DCLM-Pool, 1.4% is ~3.4T, close to the 3.8T tokens of DCLM-Baseline (token-level survival is higher than document-level because filters favour longer documents).
From the OLMo 2 table, compute tokens per word and bytes per token for DCLM-Baseline and arXiv. Why do they differ?
DCLM: 3.71T/3.32T = 1.12 tokens/word, 21.32T/3.71T = 5.75 bytes/token. arXiv: 20.8B/19.3B = 1.08, 77.2B/20.8B = 3.71 bytes/token. LaTeX/math is symbol-heavy so it tokenizes into many short tokens (fewer bytes per token).
What did the Bartz v. Anthropic ruling say about training vs acquisition?
Training on the plaintiffs' books was held fair use, but pirating copies (from shadow libraries) was not, even without training. Buying and scanning books was also fair use but came too late; Anthropic paid $1.5B to settle. Kadrey v. Meta also found training on books fair use in that instance; the torrenting allegation was pending.
Fair use has four factors; which are most threatened by LM training, and why might ToS still bite?
Factor 1 (training can be transformative but is commercial) and factor 4 (LMs can substitute for writers/artists, hurting the market); factor 3 is weak since whole works are copied. ToS is a contract: it can forbid bot downloading even when a CC licence or fair use applies (e.g. YouTube).
Why did C4 filter lines ending without punctuation and drop pages containing "{"?
Common Crawl is mostly not natural language (menus, boilerplate, code); the heuristics keep well-formed sentences (≥5 words, terminal punctuation, ≥3 per page) and exclude code, lorem ipsum and "terms of use" pages. 1.4T tokens became 156B (806 GB).
What was surprising about DCLM's model-based filter, and how did Nemotron-CC change the trade-off?
A plain fastText classifier trained on OpenHermes-2.5 + ELI5 (positives) vs RefinedWeb (negatives) beat perplexity filtering, LLM scoring, embedding classifiers and PageRank (CORE 30.2 vs 27.5 baseline). But it discards ~90% of the data, so Nemotron-CC ensembled classifiers, used jusText for more tokens and rephrased low-quality text with an LM to get 6.3T tokens (1.1T HQ) with better accuracy (avg 60.1 for HQ vs 57.0 DCLM).
What is the central finding/limitation of CommonPile and the Comma model?
A competitive model can be trained on 8 TB of permissively licensed data (Comma v0.1-1T matches LLaMA/MPT on several benchmarks), but without more tokens it is hard to match models trained on larger unrestricted web data; licence laundering and collection-vs-item licences are residual risks.

Data II: filtering, deduplication, mixing

lecture_14.py data pipeline quality filtering fastText MinHash / LSH data mixing synthetic post-training data

TL;DR. Lecture 14 is the middle of the data pipeline. Raw dumps (HTML, PDF, code directories) are turned into text, then filtered with cheap classifiers that encode what "good" data looks like (language ID, quality, toxicity), then deduplicated with hashing (exact hashes, MinHash estimates of Jaccard similarity, banded LSH for linear-time candidate search), then mixed across sources using small proxy models, with the epoching trap as the main pitfall. It closes with synthetic post-training data (OpenThoughts, SWE-smith, SWE-Zero, SWE-rebench).

2021 Lee et al.: deduplicating training data makes LMs better
2023 LLaMA (RedPajama-style filter), UniMax (epoch caps), phi-1 (textbook-quality data)
2024 Dolma (toxicity and language ID), DCLM (fastText quality filter), RegMix (regression mixing)
2025 Simulated epoching; OpenThoughts; SWE-smith; SWE-rebench
2026 SWE-Zero: execution-free agent trajectories

1. Transformation: raw data to text

Raw data does not come as text. It is HTML (web crawls), PDF (for example arXiv), or directories (code repositories). Every conversion is a design decision, and conversions are lossy.

HTML to text (the main path)

  • Remove boilerplate (navigation, ads) and extract the content.
  • What about images, tables and other structure? The output has to linearize the page, so information is lost.
  • Tools are mostly rule-based: trafilatura, resiliparse, jusText, lynx, and others.
  • Accuracy matters. The DCLM paper compares extractors on its CORE and EXTENDED benchmark averages (1B-1x scale):
Text extractionCOREEXTENDED
resiliparse24.113.4
trafilatura24.512.5
WET files (CommonCrawl's pre-extracted text)20.712.2

PDFs: the FinePDFs pipeline

  • Source: Common Crawl. Truncated PDFs are recrawled because the truncated copies are big.
  • OCR with a vision-language model (RolmOCR) or with Docling. These must run fast, because they run at web scale.
  • Lots of cleanup and filtering afterwards.
  • A lot of layout information is missing from the result (reading order, tables, figures).

2. Filtering: the framework and the classifiers

The algorithmic building block is: given some target data T and lots of raw data R, find a subset T' of R that is similar to T. Filtering is therefore a form of sampling by example: T says what good looks like, and R is what you can afford to read.

Applications

  • Language identification (English versus the rest).
  • Quality filtering (high quality versus low quality).
  • Toxicity filtering (non-toxic versus toxic).

Desiderata

  • Generalize from the target. T' should be a different set from T, but still similar to it.
  • Extremely fast. The scorer runs on all of R, which is huge, so anything expensive is out.

The lecture points to a survey paper on data selection for language models (arXiv 2402.16827).

General framework

  1. Estimate a model based on R and T, and derive a scoring function s(x).
  2. Keep examples in R based on their score.

Generative scorer: a model of the target, \( s(x) = p_T(x) \). This is a language model trained on T (KenLM is the usual n-gram choice). Text that is likely under the target LM is kept; in practice this is perplexity filtering.

Discriminative scorer: a classifier, \( s(x) = p(T \mid x) \). This is a fastText-style linear model trained on positives (T) versus negatives (R). Text that the classifier believes is target-like is kept.

To use either one, keep an example x when its score passes a threshold, or keep it stochastically based on its score (GPT-3's rule, below).

Model-based filtering: a choice

Some pipelines deliberately avoid model-based filtering: C4, Gopher, RefinedWeb, FineWeb, Dolma. Others use it: GPT-3, LLaMA, DCLM. The lecture says model-based filtering is "becoming the norm".

The GPT-3 stochastic keep rule

GPT-3 trained a linear classifier on word features, with positives from {Wikipedia, WebText2, Books1, Books2} and negatives from CommonCrawl, and then kept documents stochastically based on their score. The lecture shows the rule as code:

def keep_document(score: float) -> bool:
    return np.random.pareto(9) > 1 - score

NumPy's pareto(9) is the Lomax (Pareto II) distribution, with \( P(X > x) = (1+x)^{-9} \). With \( x = 1 - s \), the keep probability is

\[ P(\text{keep} \mid s) = P(X > 1 - s) = (2 - s)^{-9}. \]

So a score of 1 is always kept, a score of 0.5 is kept about 2.6% of the time, and a score of 0 is kept about 0.2% of the time. The rule is a soft threshold, not a hard cut, and it keeps some low-scoring documents as diversity. The calculator below runs both the formula and a seeded Monte Carlo simulation of the same rule.

Language identification

  • Goal: find text in a specific language (for example English).
  • The off-the-shelf fastText language identification classifier (fasttext.cc) supports 176 languages.
  • It was trained on multilingual sites: Wikipedia, Tatoeba (a translation site) and SETimes (Southeast European news).
  • Dolma keeps pages with p(English) >= 0.5 (Dolma).

3. Model-based filtering in practice

The lecture walks through several real pipelines. Each one has a target (what good looks like), negatives (what to reject), and a scorer. Use the tabs.

OpenMathText (arXiv 2310.06786): curate a large mathematical corpus from CommonCrawl.

  • Rules first: for example, keep pages that contain LaTeX commands.
  • A KenLM model trained on ProofPile; keep if perplexity < 15000 (the threshold as stated in the source; KenLM perplexity units).
  • A fastText classifier predicts mathematical writing. The threshold is 0.17 for pages that are math and 0.8 for pages that are not.
  • Result: 14.7B tokens, used to train 1.4B models that do better than models trained on 20× more data.

GPT-3 (arXiv 2005.14165, Appendix A): positives are samples from {Wikipedia, WebText2, Books1, Books2}; negatives are samples from CommonCrawl. Train a linear classifier on word features (Spark's tokenizer and feature pipeline is linked in the source). Keep documents stochastically based on score (the rule above).

LLaMA / RedPajama (arXiv 2302.13971): positives are pages referenced by Wikipedia; negatives are CommonCrawl samples. Keep the documents that are classified positive. This is a hard threshold, not a stochastic keep.

phi-1 (arXiv 2306.11644): the philosophy is very high-quality data (textbooks) to train a small model (1.5B). It mixes synthetic data from GPT-3.5 (later GPT-4) with filtered real data.

  1. Raw data R: the Python subset of The Stack.
  2. Target T: use GPT-4 with the prompt "determine its educational value for a student whose goal is to learn basic coding concepts" to label a 100K subset of R.
  3. Train a random forest on T, using the output embeddings of a pretrained CodeGen model as features.
  4. Select the data in R that the classifier labels positive.

Result on HumanEval: a 1.3B LM trained on the Python subset of The Stack reaches 12.19% after 96K steps. A 1.3B LM trained on the new filtered subset reaches 17.68% after 36K steps. Better, and with fewer steps.

Toxicity filtering in Dolma (Dolma). The dataset is the Jigsaw Toxic Comments dataset (2018), a Kaggle competition whose stated goal is to help people have better discussions online. It contains comments on Wikipedia talk pages, annotated with six labels: toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity_hate.

The lecture does not show the thresholds used. Note that a multi-label toxicity classifier trained on this data inherits the annotators' judgments, so the keep/remove boundary is a policy decision as much as a statistical one.

DCLM: the funnel that produced DCLM-Baseline

The DCLM paper (arXiv 2406.11794) builds DCLM-Pool from CommonCrawl (extracted with resiliparse), then applies heuristic cleaning, deduplication, and a fastText model-based filter. Figure 4 of the paper tracks the share of original documents that survives each stage:

Repetition filter9.6

Other filters (word length, ellipsis count, stop words, ...)9.0

The bookkeeping: heuristic cleaning removes 80.1% and keeps 19.9%; deduplication removes 6.2 points and leaves 13.7%; the fastText filter removes 12.3 points and leaves 1.4%, which is DCLM-Baseline.

Which quality filter? (DCLM Table 4)

DCLM compares model-based quality filters at the 1B-1x scale. A fastText classifier using the OpenHermes 2.5 and ELI5 data (the table's "fastText OH-2.5 + ELI5" row) performs best on both averages.

4. Scale-dependent filtering

There is no single optimal threshold for filtering. The lecture's rule of thumb:

  • If you train for longer, you want more (lower-quality) data.
  • If you train for shorter, you want less (higher-quality) data.

The figure below (method comparison at d512, 157M parameters, N = 100 WARCs, loss against tokens trained) shows curves for several filter pools. The legend's dashed markers give the token count of one epoch for each pool. The lecture's reading is that the best pool depends on the budget: the curves cross, so a pool that wins at small token counts is not the one that wins at large ones.

Recipe

Define the target data (what good looks like), then extrapolate it to the raw data with a classifier. Filtering is critical for building a good model, and its threshold depends on your compute budget.

5. Deduplication

Two types of duplicates:

  • Exact duplicates: mirror sites, GitHub forks, copies of the same Project Gutenberg text (the lecture links the Gutenberg mirror list).
  • Near duplicates: the same text differing by a few tokens.

Near-duplicate sources the lecture lists: terms of service and licenses (for example the MIT license), formulaic writing (copy-pasted or generated from a template), and minor formatting differences from copy and paste. One example in the lecture: a single product description appears 61,036 times in C4.

Why deduplicate? Deduplication (Lee et al., 2021, "Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better") gives two benefits:

  • Efficiency: you train on fewer tokens.
  • Less memorization: duplicated text is memorized, which matters for copyright and privacy.

The design space

  1. What is an item? A sentence, a paragraph, or a whole document.
  2. How to match? Exact match, existence of a common subitem, or fraction of common subitems.
  3. What action? Remove all copies, or remove all but one.

The key challenge: deduplication is fundamentally about comparing items to other items, and you need linear-time algorithms to scale. Naive pairwise comparison is quadratic in the number of documents.

Hash functions

  • A hash function h maps an item to a hash value (an integer or string).
  • The hash value is much smaller than the item.
  • Hash collision: h(x) = h(y) for some x ≠ y.

There is a trade-off between efficiency and collision resistance:

  • Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, used in Bitcoin): collision resistant, slow.
  • DJB2, MurmurHash, CityHash: not collision resistant, fast (they are used for hash tables).

The lecture uses MurmurHash (mmh3):

h = mmh3.hash("hello")  # @inspect h
# h = 613153351

That value, 613153351, is the 32-bit MurmurHash3 (seed 0) of "hello". mmh3.hash returns a signed 32-bit integer. The JavaScript port used by the widgets in this section reproduces it.

Exact deduplication

The simple example: items are strings, the match is exact equality, and the action is "remove all but one".

items = ["Hello!", "hello", "hello there", "hello", "hi", "bye"]  # @inspect items

# Compute hash -> list of items with that hash
hash_items = itertools.groupby(sorted(items, key=mmh3.hash), key=mmh3.hash)

# Keep one item from each group
deduped_items = [next(group) for h, group in hash_items]  # @inspect deduped_items

The sort by hash puts equal hashes next to each other, so groupby can walk the groups in one pass. This is a MapReduce-style computation (hash, group by key, keep one per key), so it parallelizes and scales.

  • Pro: simple, clear semantics, high precision.
  • Con: it does not catch near duplicates.
Caveat: a hash collision is not a duplicate

The code above groups by the hash value alone. Two different strings with the same 32-bit hash would be merged and one would be silently dropped. With 32 bits this is rare, but it is not impossible, and it is exactly the case a real pipeline must check by comparing the strings in each group. The widget below flags such groups.

Running the lecture's code on its six items (the two "hello" strings are identical): the hash groups are sorted, and deduped_items keeps one item from each of the five distinct hash values. Since no two different strings collide here, the result is the same as a set of distinct strings.

C4 uses exact dedup on spans. Item: 3-sentence spans. Match: exact. Action: remove all but one. The lecture's warning: removing a 3-sentence span from the middle of a document can leave the rest of the document incoherent.

Jaccard similarity and MinHash

Exact hashing only finds identical items. For near duplicates we need a similarity measure:

\[ \operatorname{Jaccard}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}. \]

Worked example from the source: \(A = \{1,2,3,4\}\), \(B = \{1,2,3,5\}\). The intersection is \(\{1,2,3\}\) (size 3) and the union is \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) (size 5), so \( \operatorname{Jaccard}(A,B) = 3/5 = 0.6 \).

def compute_jaccard(A, B):
    intersection = len(A & B)  # @inspect intersection
    union = len(A | B)  # @inspect union
    return intersection / union
jaccard = compute_jaccard(A, B)  # @inspect jaccard

Definition used by the lecture: two documents are near duplicates if their Jaccard similarity is at least a threshold. The algorithmic challenge is to find such pairs in linear time.

MinHash is a random hash function \(h\) with \( \Pr[h(A) = h(B)] = \operatorname{Jaccard}(A,B) \). The argument uses a random permutation of the universe of items: the hash induces an order, and the minimum is the first item in that order.

  • For a random permutation of \(A \cup B\), the first item is equally likely to be any of the 5 items.
  • If the first item is in \(A \cap B\) (1, 2 or 3), then the first item of A equals the first item of B, so the minimum hashes agree.
  • If the first item is 4 or 5, the minimums differ.
\[ \Pr\big[\min_\pi A = \min_\pi B\big] = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|} = \operatorname{Jaccard}(A,B). \]

The lecture writes the sets as a characteristic matrix (one row per item, one column per set):

def minhash(S: set[str], seed: int):
    return min(mmh3.hash(x, seed) for x in S)

# Verify MinHash approximates Jaccard as advertised
n = 100  # Generate this many random hash functions
matches = [minhash(A, seed) == minhash(B, seed) for seed in range(n)]  # @stepover
estimated_jaccard = len([m for m in matches if m]) / len(matches)  # @inspect estimated_jaccard
assert abs(estimated_jaccard - jaccard) < 0.01

Each seed gives one hash function, so each seed gives one 0/1 "match" event. The estimate is the fraction of matches over 100 seeds. For these sets it comes out to exactly 60/100 = 0.60, so the assertion passes.

The assertion is luck, not a guarantee

Over n independent hash functions, the estimate is a binomial proportion with standard error \( \sqrt{J(1-J)/n} \). For J = 0.6 and n = 100 that is about 0.049, so a typical estimate is within ±0.05 of the truth, and the assertion's tolerance of 0.01 is far tighter than the method's typical error at this n. The check passes here because the seeds are fixed (0 to 99), not because MinHash is precise at n = 100. Precision grows with \( \sqrt{n} \).

Now we can hash all items. But a collision on one MinHash does not, by itself, tell us that \(\operatorname{Jaccard}(A,B) > \text{threshold}\). Sharpening the probabilities is what LSH does.

Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)

A single MinHash function gives \( \Pr[A \text{ and } B \text{ collide}] = \operatorname{Jaccard}(A,B) \). On average more similar items collide, but the signal is very noisy. The goal is for A and B to collide when \( \operatorname{Jaccard}(A,B) \) exceeds a threshold, and not otherwise. We have to sharpen the probabilities.

The solution: use \(n\) hash functions, split them into \(b\) bands of \(r\) hash functions each (\(n = b \cdot r\)). A and B collide if, for some band, all of its \(r\) hash functions agree. The and-or structure sharpens the threshold.

The probability that A and B collide is the function the code computes:

def get_prob_collision(sim, b, r):  # @inspect sim @inspect b @inspect r
    prob_match = sim ** r                        # Probability that a fixed band matches
    prob_collision = 1 - (1 - prob_match) ** b   # Probability that some band matches
    return prob_collision

prob_collision = get_prob_collision(sim=0.8, b=5, r=10)  # @inspect prob_collision

In formulas, with \(s\) the Jaccard similarity:

\[ P_{\text{collide}}(s) = 1 - \big(1 - s^{\,r}\big)^{b}. \]

For \(b = 5, r = 10, s = 0.8\), the source's example gives \(s^r = 0.1074\) and \(P = 1 - (0.8926)^5 \approx \mathbf{0.433}\).

The calculator below uses the same formula. Set \(b\) and \(r\), and watch the S-curve move. The dashed reference series is the paper's example setting, \(b = 20\), \(r = 450\).

What the knobs do

Increasing r sharpens the threshold and moves the curve to the right: harder to match. Increasing b moves the curve to the left: easier to match. The lecture's two charts show exactly this (r = 10 → 20, then b = 10 → 20).

Example setting from the paper (Lee et al.): \(n = 9000\), \(b = 20\), \(r = 450\) (indeed \(20 \cdot 450 = 9000\)).

  • Threshold (where the phase transition happens): \( t = (1/b)^{1/r} = (1/20)^{1/450} \approx \mathbf{0.9934} \). Only pairs with Jaccard above about 0.993 are likely to collide.
  • At that point, a fixed band matches with probability \(1/b\), so \( P(\text{collide}) = 1 - (1 - 1/b)^b = 1 - 0.95^{20} \approx \mathbf{0.6415} \).
  • The lecture says this is "a constant (≈ 1 - 1/e)". The exact value for b = 20 is 0.6415, and \(1 - 1/e \approx 0.632\) is the limit as \(b \to \infty\).
b = 20
r = 450
threshold = (1 / b) ** (1 / r)  # @inspect threshold          # 0.9934
prob_match = (1 / b)            # @inspect prob_match
prob_collision = 1 - (1 - 1 / b) ** b  # @inspect prob_collision  # 0.6415

Bloom filters (membership with false positives)

DCLM's deduplication uses a Bloom filter (see the Sankey figure above, "Bloom filter dedup"). A Bloom filter is a bit array of \(m\) bits with \(k\) hash functions. Inserting an item sets \(k\) bits; a query returns "seen" only if all \(k\) bits are set. A query can therefore give a false positive (an unseen item is reported as seen, and a new document is wrongly dropped as a duplicate) but never a false negative.

\[ p \approx \left(1 - e^{-kn/m}\right)^{k}, \qquad k_{\text{opt}} = \frac{m}{n}\ln 2. \]

The formula is the standard Bloom-filter approximation (it is not in the lecture code). With \(m/n\) bits per item, the optimal number of hash functions is \(k \approx 0.693\,(m/n)\).

Check it by hand

Default values: n = 109, 10 bits per item, k = 7. Then \(p = (1 - e^{-0.7})^7 = (0.5034)^7 \approx 0.0082\), so 0.82%. The optimum here is k = round(6.93) = 7, so the setting is already optimal. Memory is \(10 \cdot 10^9 / 8 = 1.25\) GB.

6. Data mixing

Recall that language models are trained on several data sources. The question is: what distribution over the sources should we use? The lecture shows Marin's token-count viewer as a starting point:

Dataset example from the lecture: The Pile (arXiv 2101.00027), an 825 GB collection of 22 subsets (CommonCrawl, PubMed, arXiv, GitHub, StackExchange, USPTO, OpenWebText2, Books3, and others).

Baselines

  • Vibes: set \(p(s)\) manually, based on intuition. Quite common in practice.
  • Uniform: sample sources uniformly, \(p(s) \propto 1\).
  • Proportional: sample in proportion to size, \(p(s) \propto \text{num\_tokens}(s)\).

The intuition is to upweight higher-quality sources. But there are two reasons not to upweight blindly:

  1. Diversity. You want coverage across incomparable sources: literature, code, papers.
  2. Finite sources. Each source is finite. If you put too much weight on a small source, you have to epoch over it (repeat it many times).

The epoching trap

The lecture's example uses two sources, one abundant and one scarce:

source_token_counts = {
    "low": trillion(10),  # 10T tokens (abundant)
    "high": billion(10),  # 10B tokens (scarce)
}
p = {"low": 0.5, "high": 0.5}  # Naive data mixture
train_tokens = trillion(1)  # Train for 1T tokens
low_num_epochs = (p["low"] * train_tokens) / source_token_counts["low"]    # @inspect low_num_epochs
high_num_epochs = (p["high"] * train_tokens) / source_token_counts["high"]  # @inspect high_num_epochs

The number of epochs over a source is \( \text{epochs}(s) = p(s) \cdot T / N(s) \), where \(T\) is the training tokens and \(N(s)\) the source size. With the naive 50/50 mixture: low gives \(0.5 \cdot 10^{12} / 10^{13} = 0.05\) epochs, and high gives \(0.5 \cdot 10^{12} / 10^{10} = \mathbf{50}\) epochs. The lecture's comment: "50x epochs on high quality data... can lead to overfitting!"

UniMax: cap the epochs

UniMax (arXiv 2304.09151) comes from multilingual models. Earlier work interpolated between uniform and proportional sampling: \( p(s) \propto \text{num\_tokens}(s)^{\alpha} \) for \( \alpha \in [0,1] \). UniMax instead samples sources uniformly, but with a hard cap \(C\) on the number of epochs for any source.

The lecture writes the constraint as \( p(s) \cdot \text{num\_training\_tokens} \le C \) for all sources \(s\). Read literally, \(C\) would be a token budget, not an epoch count, which is a mismatch with the "cap on the number of epochs" description. The dimensionally consistent form is \( p(s) \cdot T \le C \cdot N(s) \), that is \( \text{epochs}(s) \le C \). The explorer above uses that form.

Regression-based mixing

RegMix (arXiv 2407.01492; see also arXiv 2602.12237) treats mixture choice as a scaling-law problem. The four steps are shown below, with the example numbers from the figure.

The lecture's design choices for regression mixing (defined as a choice list): distribution over mixtures (Dirichlet, exponential grid, entropy-weighted, dynamic), regression family (LightGBM, log-linear, power law, Gaussian process), granularity (aggregated or per-task), and optimizer (search, gradient descent, exact solver). The table compares several published methods:

Simulated epoching

The lecture's warning: a scale-dependent effect breaks the naive transfer. At 10B tokens, a mixture with 90% high-quality data looks fine, because the high-quality source is seen only a few times. At 1T tokens, the same mixture epochs the high-quality source about 90 times, and overfits.

p = {"low": 0.1, "high": 0.9}  # More mass on high quality data
# At 1T training tokens: high epochs = 0.9 * 10^12 / 10^10 = 90  -> overfit

The fix (arXiv 2501.11747): make the small scale look like the large scale. The general theme of the course. The instantiation is to downsample all sources proportionally:

small_run_tokens = billion(10)
large_run_tokens = trillion(1)
ratio = small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens  # @inspect ratio          # 0.01
downsampled_source_token_counts = {s: count * ratio for s, count in source_token_counts.items()}  # @inspect downsampled_source_token_counts
# low: 10T -> 100B,  high: 10B -> 100M

In the downsampled mixture, a model that epochs too much will not look good, so the optimum is more balanced. The lecture's chosen mixture is \(p = \{\text{low}: 0.7, \text{high}: 0.3\}\).

The point: under proportional downsampling, \( \text{epochs}(s) = p(s) \cdot \frac{T_{\text{small}}}{N(s)\cdot(T_{\text{small}}/T)} = p(s) \cdot T / N(s) \). The ratio cancels, so the small run reproduces the epoch counts of the large run. That is what makes the small run a faithful proxy for the mixture choice.

Summary: data mixing

Problem: how to weight the sources (for example Wikipedia, general web, code). Regression-based mixing: estimate mixture to loss at small scale, then optimize, which is analogous to scaling laws. The important consideration is epoching and overfitting, with two remedies: a cap (UniMax) or a simulated small run (downsample proportionally).

7. Post-training data: synthetic prompts and teacher responses

The lecture's post-training recipe:

  1. Define a set of environments.
  2. Define a set of tasks and prompts.
  3. Collect responses from a strong model (the teacher).

OpenThoughts

OpenThoughts (arXiv 2506.04178): 1.2M examples using QwQ-32B as the teacher. The questions come from 27 human and synthetic sources (for example StackExchange, NuminaMath, chemistry).

Findings from the lecture:

  • Sampling multiple (16) responses per prompt is helpful.
  • Better models are not necessarily better teachers: QwQ-32B is a better teacher than DeepSeek-R1.
  • Answer filtering was not helpful.
  • Smaller high-quality sources (for example OpenMath-2-Math) beat large diverse sources.

SWE-smith

SWE-smith (arXiv 2504.21798): start from a real repository, install it with an agent (SWE-agent attempts setup; a developer writes a Dockerfile from that work), and then generate new tasks by four strategies: procedural modification, LM-generated bugs, combining bugs, and PR mirroring. The output is a generated issue, a bugged patch, and verified tests. The lecture's figures: 128 GitHub repositories yield 50K tasks.

SWE-rebench

SWE-rebench (arXiv 2505.20411): 21K interactive Python SWE tasks from 3.4K GitHub repositories, built from 450K PRs taken from GitHub and GitHub Archive. A Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct model installs dependencies and assesses PR quality.

SWE-Zero: no execution feedback

SWE tasks have heavy dependencies, unlike math or contest coding. Setting up thousands of Docker images is "an infrastructural nightmare". The observation of SWE-Zero (arXiv 2604.01496): strong models can solve many tasks without execution feedback, because they carry an internal "world model" of code semantics.

  • SWE-Zero: 300K agent trajectories that do not require repository-specific execution, drawn from 150K GitHub PRs.
  • The OpenHands scaffold is used, and future git commits are removed to prevent "git hacking" by the agent.
  • The prompt for the execution-free setup forbids running Python, pytest, mypy, pip, apt and apt-get, and asks the model to do static analysis.
  • Distilled from Qwen3-Coder-480B plus filtering ("try to execute anyway").
  • SWE-Hero: 13K agent trajectories that do require execution feedback.

SWE-ZERO-12M trajectories

  • Scale SWE-Zero up to 12M agent trajectories.
  • Used the SWE-rebench-v2 tasks: 32K executable tasks plus 120K non-executable tasks, that is 152K tasks in total. Spread evenly, that is about 79 trajectories per task (a derived figure, not stated in the lecture).
  • Ran mini-coder-1.7b (a very small model, 50.4 pass@100) with the mini-swe-agent scaffold.

Summary of the post-training data section: prompts can be fully synthetic, semi-synthetic (a real environment plus synthetic tasks), or real (GitHub PRs). Responses come from capable models that are also good teachers. Code environments are painful to build, which is what the execution-free approach avoids. And there are lots of filtering details.

8. Key takeaways

  • Filtering is about defining what good looks like: train a classifier (language ID, quality, toxicity) on target data and extrapolate to the raw pool. Generative (KenLM perplexity) and discriminative (fastText) scorers are both common.
  • The keep rule can be a hard threshold or stochastic (GPT-3's \((2-s)^{-9}\)). The threshold depends on the training budget: longer training wants more, lower-quality data.
  • Deduplication uses hashing to scale: exact hashing for identical items, MinHash to estimate Jaccard similarity in constant space, and banded LSH to find candidate pairs in roughly linear time. Always confirm candidates by comparing content.
  • LSH sharpens the collision curve: \( P = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b \). Increasing \(r\) raises the threshold, and increasing \(b\) lowers it. At the threshold \(t = (1/b)^{1/r}\), the collision probability is about \(1 - 1/e\).
  • Mixing is a scaling-law problem: estimate the loss of mixtures with small proxies, fit a regression, and optimize. The main trap is epoching; cap epochs (UniMax) or simulate the large run by downsampling proportionally.
  • Post-training data is synthetic: generate tasks from environments, collect responses from a strong teacher, and filter. Code environments are the bottleneck, which is why execution-free methods matter.

9. Self-check quiz

Why does the GPT-3 keep rule keep a document with score 0.5 only about 2.6% of the time?
The keep probability is \((2 - s)^{-9}\). With \(s = 0.5\), that is \(1.5^{-9} = 1/38.4 \approx 0.026\). The rule is a soft threshold based on a heavy-tailed draw, so even mid-scoring documents are sometimes kept, and very low scores are not kept at all.
Why does the exact-dedup code still need a string comparison inside each group?
Grouping by mmh3.hash merges any two items with the same 32-bit hash, even if the strings differ. A hash collision between different strings would silently drop one of them. Within each hash group, comparing the actual strings makes the removal exact.
Compute the Jaccard similarity of \(A = \{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(B = \{1,2,3,5\}\). What is the probability that a single MinHash agrees?
\(|A \cap B| = 3\) and \(|A \cup B| = 5\), so the Jaccard similarity is \(3/5 = 0.6\). A single MinHash agrees with probability equal to the Jaccard similarity, 0.6. The estimate over 100 seeds has standard error about \(\sqrt{0.6 \cdot 0.4/100} \approx 0.049\).
For \(b = 20\), \(r = 450\), what is the threshold, and why is the collision probability there about 0.64 rather than 0.5?
The threshold is \(t = (1/20)^{1/450} \approx 0.9934\). At \(t\), \(s^r = 1/b\), so a band matches with probability \(1/20\), and \(P(\text{collide}) = 1 - (1 - 1/20)^{20} \approx 0.6415\). The 50% point is lower than \(t\), so the threshold as defined is not the 50% crossing. The "≈ 1 - 1/e" in the lecture is the \(b \to \infty\) limit (0.632).
A 50/50 mixture of 10T low-quality and 10B high-quality tokens is trained for 1T tokens. How many epochs does each source get, and why is that a problem?
Low: \(0.5 \cdot 10^{12} / 10^{13} = 0.05\) epochs. High: \(0.5 \cdot 10^{12} / 10^{10} = 50\) epochs. The scarce source is repeated 50 times, which the lecture warns can overfit. The fix is a per-source epoch cap (UniMax) or a simulated small run.
Why does simulated epoching preserve the epoch count of each source?
Downsampling every source by the same ratio \(r = T_{\text{small}}/T_{\text{large}}\) scales both the source size and the token budget by \(r\). Epochs \(= p(s) \cdot T / N(s)\) is unchanged because the ratio cancels. The small run therefore overfits in the same way the large run would. Example: with 0.3 high-quality share, both runs give 30 epochs on the high source.
A Bloom filter has 10 bits per item and 7 hash functions. What is its false-positive rate, and is 7 optimal?
\(p = (1 - e^{-7/10})^7 = (0.5034)^7 \approx 0.0082\), about 0.82%. The optimal \(k = \text{round}(\ln 2 \cdot 10) = \text{round}(6.93) = 7\), so 7 is optimal at this size. The false positives drop a document; they never cause a duplicate to be missed.

Source notes and caveats
  • The lecture's Jaccard assertion (|estimate - 0.6| < 0.01 with 100 seeds) passes for these fixed seeds; the typical error at n = 100 is about 0.05 (see above).
  • The UniMax constraint as written, \(p(s) \cdot T \le C\), mixes units; the epoch form \(p(s) \cdot T \le C \cdot N(s)\) is the consistent one.
  • The OpenMathText "perplexity < 15000" threshold is quoted as in the source; KenLM perplexity units are not directly comparable to other tools.
  • Figures that exist only as images (the LSH plots from the remote CDN, the Pile figure, the FinePDFs diagram, the C4 table) are either reproduced by the calculators above or described in prose, not transcribed.
  • The widgets' MurmurHash3 is a JavaScript port of the x86_32 variant, seeded like mmh3.hash(x, seed). The hash value for "hello" matches the value the lecture prints (613153351).

To reproduce the lecture's sets, type 1 2 3 4 into A and 1 2 3 5 into B, set k = 1 and n = 100. The exact Jaccard is 0.6, and the seeds 0 to 99 give 60 agreements, so the estimate is exactly 0.60, matching the lecture's assertion.

After pretraining: mid-training, SFT, RLHF, PPO and DPO

lecture_15.pdf (65 slides) instruction tuning SFT data mid-training / annealing RLHF Bradley-Terry PPO DPO safety synthetic data chat templates evaluation

TL;DR. A pretrained model continues text; it does not follow instructions or prefer helpful answers. Post-training closes that gap in two stages. SFT fits the model to curated demonstrations (what the data looks like and how much of it matters). RLHF then optimises the model against a reward learned from pairwise preferences, either with PPO (a reward model plus an on-policy RL loop plus a KL leash to the SFT model) or with DPO, which solves the same KL-regularised problem in closed form and turns it into a classification-style log-loss with no reward model and no rollouts. The lecture also covers how the SFT data mix is built, why quality beats quantity, mid-training ("annealing") with high-quality data, synthetic and AI feedback, safety data, evaluation of post-trained models, and the side effects (length bias, over-optimisation, loss of calibration).

From GPT-3 to InstructGPT

The course so far ends with pretraining, which gives a model like GPT-3. Pretraining data is not what we want (it is the web as it is), but it scales. Lecture 15 asks how to get "better, tighter controls over LM output" by collecting data of the behaviours we do want and training on it. Three questions frame the rest of the lecture:

  1. What does that data look like?
  2. How do we best make use of it?
  3. Do we need scale for this?
Caveat: post-training information is sparse.

The richest public documents are from the pre-ChatGPT period: Stiennon et al. 2020 (the RLHF summarisation paper, with annotation guidelines) and Bai et al. 2022 (Anthropic HH, with safety annotation details). Modern practice is poorly documented: open-source releases mostly describe distillation from stronger models with little detail in the release notes, and closed labs treat their data as the "secret sauce". Treat specific recipes in this lecture as the best public evidence, not as a complete account.

2020 GPT-3: few-shot prompting from a pretrained model. Stiennon et al. apply RLHF to summarisation.
2022 InstructGPT (Ouyang et al.): SFT, then a reward model, then PPO. Bai et al.: Anthropic HH (helpfulness and harmlessness data).
2023 Open SFT datasets proliferate (FLAN, Alpaca, ShareGPT, OpenAssistant). DPO (Rafailov et al.) replaces PPO's loop with a closed-form loss.
2024 Tulu 3 and OLMo-style open recipes combine SFT, DPO and RL with public data; mid-training becomes standard.

The lecture's first goal is simple: "Instruction following is a remarkable form of control." Slide 3 shows an example from Bubeck et al. 2023 in which GPT-4 is asked, in one long natural-language request, for a plot with specific colours, labels, error bars and a pie chart. The model produces working code, which is a control interface that pretraining alone does not give.

Part 1, SFT: what is inside the instruction data

Standard practice is imitation first: fine-tune on demonstrations with the same next-token cross-entropy as pretraining. The "method" is just gradient descent on the demonstrations (slide 28). The "ingredients" are the datasets. The lecture asks two questions: what is actually inside them, and what matters for high-performance instruction data?

The slides show a progression of open SFT data: FLAN (collections of NLP tasks rephrased as instructions), Self-Instruct (generated by a GPT-3 model from a few seed tasks), Alpaca (52K examples generated by text-davinci-003), ShareGPT/Vicuna (user conversations shared with ChatGPT), OpenAssistant (human-written conversations), WizardLM, Tulu 3 and Nemotron (which includes tool use and agentic traces). Slide 7 also lists the collections that feed the FLAN-style mixes: T0-SF, Muffin, CoT (reasoning) and Natural Instructions v2.

Slide 10. FLAN is mostly classification and short-answer NLP tasks rewritten as instructions with a fixed template. Examples: "Write a subject line for this email" given an email; "What is this text about? OPTIONS: World, Sports, Business, Science/Tech" given a news article; "Write highlights for this article" given a travel article; and "Write a sentence that includes the following data about a restaurant" given a key-value record. Responses are short and correct, but they read like a benchmark, not a conversation.

Slide 11. Self-instruct style. "Give three tips for staying healthy" gets a numbered list of three. "What does 'algorithm' mean?" gets a two-paragraph definition. "Find the average number in a list" gets a Python function, avg_list, with a printed answer of 6.4. Medium-length, clean, fluent, and generated by a teacher model.

Slide 12. Human-written and long. The "monopsony" request asks for an introduction "with examples related to potential monopsonies in the labour market and cite relevant research". The answer is several paragraphs and cites Bivens & Mishel (2013). The science-project request gets eight numbered ideas (a lava lamp, a solar oven, magnets...). Detailed and chatty.

Slide 13. Agentic traces. An assistant message is followed by a tool_calls JSON object, for example a skill call with arguments {"name":"bash-skills"} or a todowrite call that plans steps. Recent SFT data increasingly contains this kind of structured tool use, which shows that "SFT data" now includes function-calling formats and not only chat text.

What varies across these datasets

  • Chattiness. FLAN is usually valid data, but people do not want to talk to an NLP benchmark. Later datasets move towards longer, more detailed responses.
  • Detail. OpenAssistant goes into much more factual detail. As the lecture says, this can be both a pro and a con (see the hallucination section below).
  • Tool use. In the last year or two SFT has shifted towards tool use and agentic downstream applications.
  • Length and bullet points (style variations).
  • References and other complex knowledge.
  • Less visible: scale and safety.

The question the lecture then asks: how do these factors affect the model?

Do the datasets change the model? Average benchmark score

The same paper fine-tunes LLaMA-13B on each dataset and evaluates on six benchmarks (MMLU, GSM, BBH, TydiQA, Codex-Eval, AlpacaEval win rate). The "Average" column is the mean of the six. The lecture's takeaway is that the score varies a lot with the dataset, and the best mixtures are the ones that combine sources. The chart below is computed from this table (I checked that the average column equals the mean of the six benchmark columns in every row).

Next, the SFT data curves: is longer or more detailed data better? The scatter plots average benchmark score against completion length for the twelve Table 1 datasets. The fit is computed in the script by least squares on log10 of the completion length. It is a correlation over twelve datasets that also differ in source and quality, so it is not a causal claim.

Question to think about

Why would a dataset with long completions score well on MMLU? The answer is not that long answers teach facts. The lecture's point is that style and length change how the model behaves, and that preference-style evaluations reward different things from knowledge benchmarks (see the evaluation section).

What matters in SFT data: style, facts, safety, quality

Style is measurable and it moves preference scores

Models vary a lot in response length. On slide 16 the average completion lengths differ by a factor of about 15, from 23.6 (Unnatural Instructions) to 357.8 (ShareGPT). When evaluating by preferences, style matters. Slide 17 (Dubois et al. 2023, AlpacaFarm) shows strong length effects for both human and GPT-based evaluators: in the bottom panel most annotator and model points sit above 50% preference for longer outputs. Slide 18 makes the contrast: these style factors are mostly not relevant to the other benchmarks, while the AlpacaEval column (a preference win rate) moves by up to about 70 points across datasets.

Factuality and "complex knowledge"

Take the OpenAssistant monopsony example again (slide 19). The answer cites "Bivens, J., & Mishel, L. (2013)". The lecture asks what this example teaches the model: (1) facts about Bivens and Mishel, or (2) to output citations when asked for research. The honest answer is that it is unclear. Does the model know about that paper at all? The alignment question is not whether the model can produce citations, but whether SFT is teaching a new fact or just a behaviour.

The folklore is that fine-tuning on "facts it doesn't know" makes the model hallucinate. Slide 20 shows the Schulman (2023) "hallucination and behavior cloning" argument and the Gekhman et al. (2024) experiment: as fine-tuning proceeds, training accuracy on known facts rises, while accuracy on unknown facts stays low and the dev accuracy eventually drops. The three takeaways on slide 21:

Takeaways on knowledge extraction and alignment (slide 21)
  1. You may not want to fine-tune on tail knowledge, even if that is the LM use case.
  2. In principle, RL-style correctness feedback could help: a reward that checks answers can train the model to use what it knows and avoid making things up.
  3. Knowledge storage and extraction in LMs is messy and nuanced.

Safety data

LMs are widely deployed to end users and need safety controls against misinformation (Goldstein et al. 2023) and scams and spam (Kang et al. 2023). Slide 22 shows the taxonomy from Goldstein et al. (scenario, actor, content, belief, impact) and a scam email example from Kang et al. The practical question is how much safety data SFT needs.

  • Llama 2: the safety SFT pipeline uses "a few thousand" examples (slide 23 note). The Llama 2 paper says that the design of safety training data has a profound impact on performance and that "the quality is more critical than the quantity". Adversarial "borderline" prompts are added so the model learns to be helpful on near-miss requests and reduce false refusals.
  • Extract scenarios from users: slide 25 describes mining real user logs (WildChat, 1M ChatGPT interaction logs) for adversarial scenarios, then composing jailbreaks from tactics.
  • A little data is enough: slide 26 shows that mean safety-violation scores on four datasets (I-MaliciousInstructions, I-CoNa, I-Controversial, Q-Harm) drop sharply as you add a few hundred safety examples to the Alpaca-style mix, and flatten after roughly 500. The slide's takeaway: significant improvements to safety with about 500 samples.

Slide 24 also gives a sense of the scale of modern safety mixes. Tulu 3 uses CoCoNot (non-compliance, 10,983 prompts), WildJailbreak (adversarial, 50,000 prompts in SFT) and WildGuardMix (50,000 prompts in SFT), with fewer in DPO (see the Tulu 3 table in the synthetic data section).

Putting it together: SFT data (slide 27)
  1. SFT works best when it is extracting behaviours the pretrained model already has, not adding new ones.
  2. Adding factually correct data can sometimes hurt, as the knowledge section above showed.
  3. Small amounts of the right kind of behaviour (safety, instruction-following, style) make a big difference, but there is a long tail that benefits from more data.

Quality over quantity: the LIMA paper (Zhou et al. 2023) is the classic demonstration that around 1,000 carefully curated examples can produce a strong assistant, and the Llama 2 quote above makes the same point for safety.

Fine-tuning mechanics and mid-training (annealing)

How to fine-tune: gradient descent

In many academic settings, SFT is basically just this loop (slide 28): iterate over batches, compute the loss, step the optimiser and the learning-rate scheduler. The loss is the same next-token cross-entropy as pretraining, usually computed only on the assistant tokens. A minimal masking sketch:

labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[prompt_mask] = -100            # no loss on system/user tokens
# (after the usual one-position shift of logits vs labels)
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, V), labels.view(-1), ignore_index=-100)
loss.backward(); optimizer.step(); lr_scheduler.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()

The one-line explanation: the prompt is conditioning, so only the response tokens are a training target. This is a sketch of the general technique, not code from the slides, and it assumes the one-token shift has already been applied.

The slide's reasoning is that this is enough when you are a research group with modest data. "But what if you have tons of compute and data and you want to scale up instruction tuning?"

Turning instruction tuning into pretraining

The increasingly popular idea on slide 29 is to treat instruction data as part of pretraining:

  1. Pre-train on web and pretraining data.
  2. Mix instruction-tuning data into pretraining.
  3. Do an actual (but short) instruction-tuning round.

This lets you scale instruction tuning without catastrophic forgetting, because the model never sees a long period of instruction-only updates. Slide 30 calls it mid-training or two-phase training. The recipe is common knowledge among many LLM companies but rarely documented, and it is used by most modern models and publicised in recent Chinese-derived LMs (MiniCPM, JetMoE). MiniCPM's WSD (warmup-stable-decay) learning-rate schedule is the best-known public version: a long stable phase at a constant learning rate, followed by a short decay.

A real mid-training mixture (OLMo 2 Dolmino)

The clearest public table of a mid-training mix is the Dolmino mix from OLMo 2 (embedded image images/olmo2-dolmino.png). The high-quality subset is web (DCLM-Baseline, filtered with FastText top 7%), instruction data (FLAN, decontaminated), academic papers (peS2o), Wikipedia and curated Stack Exchange. A separate math mix adds synthetic math and code. The chart uses the Token column of that table.

Synthetic data, distillation and the SFT mix

Open-source SFT increasingly uses data generated by other models. Two uses matter. Distillation means SFT on a stronger teacher's outputs (the lecture notes "lots of distillation" in open-source models). Synthetic preference data means a model labels which of two responses is better. The slides list several examples: Ultrafeedback, Zephyr 7B, Tulu 3, and the OLMo family, all using AI-generated feedback for RLHF.
