Self-training: the Constitutional AI loop (slide 47)

Slide 47 summarises the Constitutional AI pipeline (Bai et al. 2022). The idea is to replace human red-team labels with model critiques guided by a written set of principles (a "constitution"). The flow below follows the slide, simplified. The SL stage is supervised fine-tuning on self-revised responses; the RL stage trains a preference model on AI labels and uses it for RL from AI feedback (RLAIF).

Synthetic AI feedback works surprisingly well

Slide 45 (Dubois et al. 2023 and Zheng et al.) reports that GPT-4 is "a surprisingly good pairwise feedback system". Across systems, the GPT-4 win rate has a Spearman rank correlation of 0.98 with human win rates (R² = 0.87). At the level of individual examples, the agreement is near the level between humans. This is why AI feedback is now the default data source for many open RLHF pipelines.

Caveat: LM feedback has its own biases

AI judges reward the length and style of their own outputs. Slide 48 and the length section below show that RLHF itself drives length growth, so an AI judge will tend to amplify it. Also, a model trained on feedback from another model inherits that model's preferences, which is why the open-source distillation culture is worth reading critically.

Chat templates: the format the model actually sees

The lecture does not show a chat template slide, so this is general background. An instruction model expects its input in a specific format, with role markers and special tokens. Training and serving must use the same format, or the model will behave worse than it should. A ChatML-style template (used by several open models) looks like this:

messages = [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
  {"role": "user",   "content": "Write a subject line for this email."},
]
text = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
# <|im_start|>system
# You are a helpful assistant.<|im_end|>
# <|im_start|>user
# Write a subject line for this email.<|im_end|>
# <|im_start|>assistant

The template is a function from a list of messages to a token sequence. add_generation_prompt=True appends the assistant header so the model continues as the assistant. Templates differ between model families, and tool-call messages add another role. The safe rule is to use the tokenizer's own template for both SFT and inference.

Part 2, RLHF: from imitation to optimisation

Two objectives

Imitation (SFT) fits a model to a reference distribution: \(\hat p(y|x)\approx p^*(y|x)\). It is a pure generative-modelling view and it needs samples from the reference policy. Optimisation (RLHF) instead looks for a policy that maximises a reward we can measure:

\[\hat p(y|x)\ \text{such that}\ \max_{p}\ \mathbb{E}_{p}\big[R(y,x)\big]\]

The key shift is from "match the demonstrations" to "maximise a reward". LMs are policies, not models of a distribution. The lecture's motivation is the G-V gap: people do not always write the output they prefer. Slide 33 cites Zhang et al. 2023 (news summarisation): freelance writers' summaries and Instruct-Davinci summaries were judged almost equally often (50.4% vs 49.6% overall), with annotator agreement α = 0.07. Demonstrations are a noisy target, and comparisons can be easier to collect than ideal demonstrations.

The RLHF pipeline (step through)

Use the controls to step through the pipeline. Each step highlights the parts involved. Stages: demonstrations and SFT, sampling and ranking, reward model, PPO with a KL penalty to the SFT reference, and the final policy.

The reward model: Bradley-Terry

The reward model turns pairwise labels into a scalar score. The model of the labeller is the Bradley-Terry model: the probability that output \(y_w\) beats \(y_l\) for prompt \(x\) is a sigmoid of the reward gap.

\[P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x)=\frac{e^{r(x,y_w)}}{e^{r(x,y_w)}+e^{r(x,y_l)}}=\sigma\big(r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)\big),\qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\]

Fitting \(r_\phi\) by maximum likelihood on the labelled pairs (Stiennon et al. 2020) gives the reward-model loss:

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RM}}(\phi)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\log\sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l)\big)\Big]\]

def reward_model_loss(r_w, r_l):
    # r_w, r_l: scalar rewards for the chosen and rejected completions
    return -F.logsigmoid(r_w - r_l).mean()   # = -log sigma(r_w - r_l)

Only the reward gap matters, so the reward is defined up to an additive constant. Stiennon's paper normalises the reward model so that the SFT reference summaries score a mean of 0 on the dataset.

RLHF data: collecting pairwise feedback

The pairwise setup is standard: a prompt, several model outputs, and a labeller who ranks them or picks the better one. Slide 36 shows a typical annotation interface with an annotation guideline and a rating scale. Slide 37 quotes the InstructGPT labelling guideline, which defines three properties:

  • Helpful: the output should follow the user's intention and answer the question directly, with the user's implicit needs in mind.
  • Truthful: the output should contain accurate information and not mislead through overclaiming or fabrication.
  • Harmless: the output should not cause physical, psychological or social harm, and should refuse clearly harmful requests in a helpful way.

Slide 38 shows a similar set from Bard's annotation task: helpfulness (intent, accuracy, detail, and safety scales such as "Not at all helpful" to "Extremely helpful") and presentation (clarity, organisation, language quality).

Who labels, and how much do they matter?

  • Worker distribution. Slides 39 and 40 show the modern worker pool: many platforms cover only one kind of worker (Outlier and Scale AI are named), compensation varies enormously, and "expert annotation" is growing fast. Business Insider reports freelancers paid at least $50 an hour for expert data labelling, with about 3,000 to 4,000 freelancers on one project.
  • Crowdsourcing is hard. Slide 41: it is hard to find high-quality, verifiable annotators; hard to get them to check correctness; and annotators may use AI to write their labels.
  • Ethics. Slide 42 notes that data collection at scale can have significant issues, including very low pay for labelling toxic content.
  • Demographics. Santurkar et al. 2023 (slide 43) show that the annotator population shapes model opinions: the same model's answers shift with the demographic profile of the people who rated it.
  • Annotators matter a lot, but not for all errors. Hosking, Blunsom and Bartolo 2024 (slide 44) compare crowdsourced annotations with "expert" annotations. Crowd annotators under-detect inconsistency and factuality errors, and they miss them more often in model outputs. The effect is not uniform: the paper finds it for some error types, not all.
Pitfall: preferences are noisy

The G-V gap and the α = 0.07 agreement on slide 33 both show that pairwise human preference is a noisy signal. Preference evaluations also reward style (length, bullets), which the next sections show is a strong effect.

LM-generated feedback

The lecture's last data point is that AI feedback is now standard for frontier open models (Ultrafeedback, Zephyr 7B, Tulu 3, and the OLMo family). Slide 46 credits these as "AI feedback often used for RLHF". Section 5 above has the agreement numbers.

Length effects: RLHF makes outputs longer

Length is "a very significant outcome of RLHF" (slide 48). Chen et al. 2024 plot a Pareto front of win score against output length for several methods and find that the optimisers that score best do so by writing longer outputs. Singhal et al. 2024 show that the reward model's score correlates strongly with output length. The pattern repeats across the RL-based systems in the figure. The slide's example shows an SFT answer of 59 tokens and an RLHF answer of 243 tokens to "Why do I roll off the bed?", where the RLHF answer is longer but not more useful.

PPO: the original RLHF optimiser

The reward with a KL term

Stiennon et al. 2020 define the RL reward as the learned reward minus a KL penalty against the SFT model. The penalty does two things: it acts as an entropy bonus, which keeps the policy from collapsing onto a few outputs, and it keeps the policy from moving far from the SFT model, where the reward model is unreliable.

\[R(x,y)=r_\phi(x,y)-\beta\,\log\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}(y\mid x)}\]

InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022) uses the same penalty and adds a pretraining term. Slide 51 reproduces their objective (their Equation 2). The coefficient \(\gamma\) mixes in pretraining gradients; "PPO" models set \(\gamma=0\), and "PPO-ptx" models use the mixed objective, which the paper calls InstructGPT by default.

\[\mathrm{objective}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim D_{\pi^{\mathrm{RL}}_\phi}}\Big[r_\theta(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{\mathrm{RL}}_\phi(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}(y\mid x)}\Big]+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D_{\mathrm{pretrain}}}\big[\log\pi^{\mathrm{RL}}_\phi(x)\big]\]

From policy gradients to PPO (slide 53)

  • Attempt 1: policy gradients. \(\nabla_\theta\,\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[R(z)]=\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[R(z)\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(z)]\). Unbiased but the variance is too high for LMs.
  • Attempt 2: TRPO. Linearise around the current policy and keep the update inside a KL trust region: maximise an importance-weighted advantage subject to an average KL constraint \(\le\delta\).
  • Attempt 3: PPO. Replace the constraint with clipping of the probability ratio \(\rho_t=\pi_\theta/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\) at \(1\pm\epsilon\).

\[\mathrm{TRPO:}\quad \max_\theta\ \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\Big[\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t|s_t)}\hat A_t\Big]\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\big[\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot|s_t)\,\|\,\pi_\theta(\cdot|s_t)\big)\big]\le\delta\]

\[L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta)=\hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\Big[\min\big(\rho_t(\theta)\hat A_t,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\,\hat A_t\big)\Big],\qquad \rho_t(\theta)=\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t|s_t)}\]

The clipped objective removes the incentive to move the ratio beyond \(1+\epsilon\) for a positive advantage, or below \(1-\epsilon\) for a negative one. The calculator below shows the loss value and where the gradient is cut off.

def ppo_clip_loss(logp_new, logp_old, adv, eps=0.2):
    ratio = torch.exp(logp_new - logp_old)                  # rho_t
    clipped = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * adv
    return -torch.min(ratio * adv, clipped).mean()         # minimise -L^CLIP

The KL penalty is a trade-off knob

The closed-form answer below shows the trade-off the penalty controls. The toy problem has two responses: a "good" one with reward 1 and a "bad" one with reward 0. The reference model (SFT) gives the good response probability \(p_0\). The KL-regularised optimum for coefficient \(\beta\) is a Gibbs reweighting of the reference, \(\pi^*(y)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)e^{r(y)/\beta}\). This is my own illustrative toy, not an experiment from the lecture, so the numbers are not from the slides. It shows how reward, KL and the penalised objective move with \(\beta\).

Can we get rid of PPO?

The question for many practitioners (slide 54): can we avoid RL altogether, i.e., avoid on-policy algorithms? The alternatives people tried:

  • Train with a control token: SFT on the pairs, prepend [GOOD] to chosen and [BAD] to rejected responses.
  • Train only on the preferred output (rejection-sampling-style SFT).
  • Train a reward model, sample LM outputs, and train on the preferred one (best-of-n distillation).
  • Train a reward model, draw 1024 outputs, and take the best one at inference time (best-of-n).

DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) is the answer that worked best in practice.

DPO: RLHF without the reward model or rollouts

The pitch on slide 55: DPO "simplifies PPO" by removing the reward model and any on-policy stuff (rollouts, outer loops). Instead, take gradient steps on the log-loss of good outputs and negative gradient steps on bad outputs, weighted appropriately. The figure on the slide puts the two pipelines side by side: RLHF goes preference data → reward model → RL → LM, while DPO goes preference data → maximum likelihood → final LM.

Derivation (slides 56 and 57)

  1. The goal. Maximise expected reward minus a KL penalty against the reference model: \[\max_{\pi_\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal D,\ y\sim\pi_\theta(y|x)}\big[r_\phi(x,y)\big]-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[\pi_\theta(y|x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)\big]\]
  2. Nonparametric assumption. Assume \(\pi\) can be any distribution over outputs. Then the maximiser is the Gibbs form \[\pi_r(y|x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)\exp\!\Big(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\Big),\qquad Z(x)=\sum_y\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)\exp\!\Big(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\Big)\]
  3. Solve for the implied reward. Invert the Gibbs form: \[r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_r(y|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}+\beta\log Z(x)\] The slide notes that this same equivalence is used in the Kimi reasoning paper.
  4. Use the implied reward as a reward model. Plug it into the Bradley-Terry model. The partition term \(\beta\log Z(x)\) depends only on \(x\), so it cancels in the reward gap: \[P(y_w\succ y_l|x)=\sigma\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w|x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l|x)}\Big)\]
  5. Maximum likelihood on pairs. Maximise the log-likelihood of the observed labels. That is the DPO loss.
Full derivation of the DPO loss and its gradient

Steps 1 to 3 are the standard KL-regularised RL solution. Start from \(\max_\pi\ \mathbb E_\pi[r]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\) for a fixed \(x\). Write the objective as \(-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi^*)+\text{const}\), where \(\pi^*\) is the Gibbs distribution above, because \(\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})-\mathbb E_\pi[r]=\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi^*)-\beta\log Z\). The KL is non-negative and zero only at \(\pi=\pi^*\), which gives the optimum. Taking the log of the Gibbs form gives the implied reward.

Substituting into the Bradley-Terry likelihood and maximising over \(\theta\) gives \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\pi_\theta;\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\) below. Its gradient is

\[\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\beta\,\mathbb E_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\Big[\sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\big)\big(\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l|x)\big)\Big],\qquad \hat r_\theta=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\]

Check: with \(u=\hat r_\theta(y_w)-\hat r_\theta(y_l)\), \(\frac{d}{d\theta}(-\log\sigma(u))=-(1-\sigma(u))\,\frac{du}{d\theta}=-\sigma(-u)\frac{du}{d\theta}\), and \(\sigma(-u)=\sigma(\hat r_\theta(y_l)-\hat r_\theta(y_w))\). The weight is large when the current implicit reward ranks the rejected output above the chosen one.

The DPO loss

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\pi_\theta;\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=-\,\mathbb E_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\log\sigma\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w|x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l|x)}\Big)\Big]\]

Slide 58 states the gradient in words: the update is a positive gradient on the chosen output and a negative gradient on the rejected one, each scaled by the "prediction error" of the implicit reward model. The gradient weight is high when the reward estimate is wrong.

def dpo_loss(logp_w, logp_l, ref_logp_w, ref_logp_l, beta=0.1):
    # logp_*: sum of token log-probs of each completion under the policy
    # ref_logp_*: the same under the frozen reference model (no gradient)
    margin = beta * ((logp_w - ref_logp_w) - (logp_l - ref_logp_l))
    return -F.logsigmoid(margin).mean()

DPO calculator (β slider)

Choose the log-ratios of the chosen and rejected completions, \(\log\pi_\theta/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\), and the temperature \(\beta\). The margin is \(m=\beta(\Delta_w-\Delta_\ell)\). The loss is \(-\log\sigma(m)\), and the gradient weight is \(\sigma(-m)\), which multiplies the \(\beta\) factor for each gradient. The chart plots both against \(m\).

The key steps (slide 57)

  1. Make a nonparametric assumption that links \(\pi_\theta\) and \(r\) in closed form.
  2. Parametrise the reward through the policy (the implied reward).
  3. Optimise the reward with supervised losses, which in turn optimises the policy.

Conceptually, DPO is maximum likelihood on the pairwise rewards, under the nonparametric assumption and the alternative parametrisation. The "reward model" is never trained: it is the policy itself.

DPO in practice, its variants and PPO

A Llama-style post-training loop (expert iteration + DPO)

Slide 59 shows DPO used in an open model pipeline: "DPO + expert iteration for post-training". The flow below is my simplified reading of that figure. Collected prompts are sampled with several generations, rejection sampling (using a reward model) selects the best ones as SFT data, an SFT model is trained, and then DPO is applied on pairwise, per-capability preference data. The best model from each round feeds the next round.

Variants: SimPO and length-normalised DPO

The lecture mentions that there are too many DPO variants, and highlights two from the Tulu 3 paper (slide 60). SimPO removes the reference model and normalises by length, with a margin \(\gamma\):

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SimPO}}=-\mathbb E\Big[\log\sigma\Big(\frac{\beta}{|y_w|}\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)-\frac{\beta}{|y_l|}\log\pi_\theta(y_l|x)-\gamma\Big)\Big]\]

Length-normalised DPO keeps the reference model but divides each log-ratio by its length, \(\max\,\mathbb E\big[\log\sigma\big(\frac{\beta}{|y_w|}\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w|x)}-\frac{\beta}{|y_l|}\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l|x)}\big)\big]\). Length normalisation is a direct response to the length bias from the previous section.

But PPO does too (and sometimes better?)

Slide 61 stresses that RL results are highly contingent on the experimental setup. The Unpacking DPO and PPO paper (left chart, Ivison et al.) shows PPO runs with different reward models and prompt sets. The Tulu 3 table (right) shows the variance on one dataset. The table is reproduced below as a chart, using the Average Score column of the source table (the lecture's point is the spread, not a single winner).

Post-training changes what the model does, so evaluation has to measure the behaviour the training targeted. The lecture's table of benchmarks (slide 18, Table 3 of Wang et al.) shows the trade-off. Scores are percentages; AlpacaEval is a win rate against Davinci-003. AlpacaEval: length-controlled win rates

AlpacaEval 2.0 reports a length-controlled (LC) win rate against a baseline, judged by an LLM. The LC version exists because the raw win rate is biased toward longer outputs. The leaderboard states that LC win rates alleviate the length bias of GPT-4 but may favour models fine-tuned on its outputs, which is the synthetic-data caveat from above. The image below is the leaderboard snapshot from the repository.

Instruction following: IFEval

Some capabilities are checkable with code. IFEval (Zhou et al. 2023) gives prompts with verifiable constraints: include keywords, use a given number of paragraphs or words, wrap the title in double angular brackets, answer in JSON, and so on. The image below lists the instruction groups. Scores come from a checker, not a judge, which avoids the judge bias above.

How to read a post-training result
  • Is the win rate from a length-controlled judge, and is the judge from the same family as the training data?
  • Do capability benchmarks (MMLU, GSM, BBH) stay flat? A large drop means the post-training broke something.
  • Check the variance across hyperparameters, not just the best row (slide 61).

Side effects: over-optimisation, mode collapse and calibration

Over-optimisation (reward hacking)

Across many RLHF-style optimisers, optimising for reward overfits past a point. The slide 63 figure plots the proxy reward (the reward model) and the gold reward against the KL distance from the initial policy. The gold reward rises and then falls, while the proxy keeps rising. The pattern holds for human preferences (panel a) and for noisy LM preferences (panel b), but not for noiseless LM preferences (panel c). The lecture's takeaway is that the reward model is only reliable close to its training distribution, and KL is the leash that keeps the policy there.

Mode collapse, entropy and calibration

RLHF makes models no longer "probabilistic models": they are not calibrated by default. Slide 64 shows calibration curves on MMLU (5-shot): the RLHF model's confidence is misaligned with its accuracy (the blue curve sits below the diagonal at high probability). Raising the sampling temperature to T = 2.5 moves the curve back towards the diagonal in the figure. The histogram shows that the entropy of the RLHF model's outputs is much lower than that of the reference models, so the model commits to few outputs. That is mode collapse: RLHF narrows the output distribution.

Length, again

Length growth is a side effect too: longer answers score higher on preference evaluations, so the optimiser learns to produce them (slide 48, the section above). Length normalisation and length-controlled evaluation are both direct responses.

RLHF recap (slide 65)
  1. RLHF data collection is hard. There are many confounding factors: annotator demographics, expertise, pay, AI assistance, and style.
  2. RLHF algorithms are more complex than SFT, especially PPO. DPO is simpler but has its own variants and sensitivities.
  3. Be mindful of over-optimising rewards: reward goes up while quality goes down past a point, and outputs get longer and less calibrated.

Key takeaways

  • Pretraining is not the product. Instruction following is a control interface learned from demonstrations and preferences on top of pretraining.
  • SFT extracts behaviours; it rarely adds knowledge. Fine-tuning on facts the model does not know tends to encourage hallucination. Correctness feedback (RL-style) is a better route.
  • Quality beats quantity, and a few hundred examples can matter. Safety gains came from about 500 samples; LIMA and the Llama 2 ablation make the same point.
  • Mid-training (annealing) lets you scale instruction data without catastrophic forgetting. Pretrain, mix in instruction and high-quality data, then do a short instruction round with a decaying learning rate.
  • Style is a confounder. Length and bullet points move preference scores far more than benchmark scores.
  • Pairwise preferences are noisy and biased. Annotator populations, expertise and AI feedback all change the learned behaviour.
  • PPO is the original RLHF optimiser; it needs a reward model, rollouts and a KL penalty, and is sensitive to setup.
  • DPO optimises the same objective in closed form. The implied reward is the policy's log-ratio to the reference; the loss is a logistic classification loss on pairs.
  • Over-optimisation, mode collapse and length growth are the standing risks. Evaluate with length-controlled judges and capability benchmarks.

Self-check quiz

Why does the lecture say SFT works best when it extracts behaviours rather than adding new ones?
Because the pretrained model already has most of the capabilities; SFT mainly selects and shapes them into the instruction format and style (slide 27). Adding facts the model does not know tends to teach it to produce plausible but unsupported answers (the Gekhman et al. result on slide 20), so fine-tuning on tail knowledge can hurt.
Write the Bradley-Terry probability that the chosen output beats the rejected one, and the reward-model loss.
\(P(y_w\succ y_l|x)=\sigma(r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l))\) with \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\). The reward-model loss is \(-\mathbb E[\log\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l))]\). With a reward gap of 0, P = 0.5 and the loss is \(\ln 2\approx 0.693\).
What is the KL-regularised optimum, and what is the implied reward used by DPO?
The maximiser of \(\mathbb E_\pi[r]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\) is \(\pi^*(y|x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)\). Inverting gives the implied reward \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi^*(y|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}+\beta\log Z(x)\). The \(\beta\log Z(x)\) term cancels in a reward gap, which is what lets DPO skip the reward model.
Derive the sign of the DPO gradient: why does it push up the chosen output and push down the rejected one?
Let \(u=\hat r_\theta(y_w)-\hat r_\theta(y_l)\) with \(\hat r_\theta=\beta\log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\). The loss is \(-\log\sigma(u)\), so its derivative is \(-\sigma(-u)\,\nabla_\theta u\). Since \(\nabla_\theta u=\beta(\nabla\log\pi_\theta(y_w)-\nabla\log\pi_\theta(y_l))\), the descent step increases \(\log\pi_\theta(y_w)\) and decreases \(\log\pi_\theta(y_l)\). The weight \(\sigma(-u)\) is close to 1 when the implicit reward ranks the rejected output higher (a wrong ranking), and close to 0 when the pair is already correct.
In the PPO clipped objective with a positive advantage, what happens when the ratio rises above 1+ε?
The term \(\min(\rho\hat A,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho)\hat A)\) equals \((1+\epsilon)\hat A\), which does not depend on \(\rho\), so the gradient through \(\rho\) is zero. This removes the incentive to move the policy further in the same direction in a single update. With a negative advantage the mirror case happens below \(1-\epsilon\). Try it in the PPO calculator with \(\hat A>0\) and \(\rho=1.5\).
Using the Tulu 3 table: why is it misleading to pick a single "best" method from this table?
The DPO-norm rows span 46.8 to 57.3 in average score on the same benchmark suite, a spread of about 10 points, driven by β, learning rate and epochs. Plain DPO (55.2) and PPO (54.5 and 55.5) are within a few points of each other and of the SFT base (55.7). The lecture's point (slide 61) is that results are contingent on the setup, so compare methods with matched tuning budgets and report the variance.
Name the three forms of "quality over quantity" evidence in the lecture and what each one showed.
(1) Llama 2 safety SFT: "the quality is more critical than the quantity", with a few thousand examples and a strong effect from careful borderline data (slide 23). (2) Safety tuning with about 500 samples improves safety scores substantially (slide 26). (3) Dataset mixing: the best row in the Table 3 comparison is a mixture of human and GPT data (45.2), not the largest single dataset. LIMA (about 1,000 curated examples) is the standard outside reference for the same claim.

Post-training 2: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)

lecture_16.pdf PPO GRPO Dr. GRPO RLVR DeepSeek-R1 Kimi k1.5 Qwen3 test-time scaling RL infrastructure

TL;DR. Pre-training + RLHF gets you to roughly GPT-3.5; RLHF cannot be scaled much further because a learned reward model is over-optimised. RLVR swaps the learned reward for a verifier (a unit test, an answer checker) so we optimise exactly what we want. The workhorse algorithm is GRPO: PPO with the value network deleted and the advantage replaced by a z-score within a group of samples of the same prompt. DeepSeek-R1, Kimi k1.5 and Qwen3 are three open recipes built on it; they all (i) filter prompts by difficulty, (ii) warm up with a small amount of long-CoT SFT, (iii) run RL on verifiable (accuracy) rewards, often with a format or length term, and (iv) add general RLHF and/or distillation afterwards. Theory warns that GRPO's std-division and length-normalisation are biased (Dr. GRPO), and systems work (rollout vs. training frameworks, long-tail sequences) is half the battle.

1. Where we are: from RLHF to RLVR

Lecture 15 ended with RLHF/DPO: pairwise preference data, a Bradley–Terry reward model, PPO or DPO. That recipe takes a base model to roughly GPT-3.5 level (the “ChatGPT: Optimizing Language Models for Dialogue” era). Today's goal is to go “all the way to o1 / R1”. The slide's motivating picture is o1's AIME accuracy rising roughly log-linearly with test-time compute (the slide plots pass@1 from ~20% to ~75% on a log-scale x-axis; it carries no numbers I can quote, so I do not redraw it).

Why RLHF does not scale, and why RLVR does

With a learned proxy reward \(\hat r_\phi\), optimisation pressure eventually exploits its errors (reward hacking / overoptimisation): proxy reward goes up while the true preference goes down. If instead the reward is a programmatic verifier (does the final answer equal the ground truth? do all unit tests pass?), there is nothing to over-fit: reward = what we want. The price is that this only works in domains where correctness is checkable (math, code, logic puzzles, some tool-use), and we must still make sure the verifier itself cannot be gamed (§9).

Lecture outline

  1. Core algorithms: PPO → GRPO, and GRPO variants / critiques (Dr. GRPO).
  2. Case studies of open RLVR recipes: DeepSeek-R1 (central to most recent RLVR efforts), Kimi k1.5 (contemporaneous, complementary details), Qwen3 (low-data RLVR, thinking-mode fusion) and its coder/agent descendant.
2017 PPO (Schulman et al.), the policy-gradient method used for RL tasks
2019 OpenAI Five: PPO at large scale (slide 6)
2023 DPO and AlpacaFarm, an open PPO implementation for LM alignment
2024 GRPO introduced in DeepSeekMath (the slides give no month)
Jan 2025 DeepSeek-R1 paper submitted (22 Jan, per the slide's arXiv stamp); Kimi k1.5 released at about the same time

The RLVR training loop (step-through)

Everything in this lecture is a variation of one loop. Click through it; each later section zooms into one box.

2. Policy-gradient background: REINFORCE, baselines, importance sampling

The slide gives the “three attempts” narrative that leads to PPO. Expanded into the maths below, because GRPO's critique (§5) depends on it.

Attempt 1 – the policy gradient (REINFORCE)

For a prompt \(q\), the policy \(p_\theta\) generates a sequence \(z\) (the tokens of the response) and receives a scalar reward \(R(z)\). We want to maximise \(J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_\theta}[R(z)]\). The log-derivative trick gives

\[ \nabla_\theta\, \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_\theta}[R(z)] \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_\theta}\big[R(z)\,\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(z)\big],\qquad \log p_\theta(z)=\sum_t \log \pi_\theta(z_t\mid q,z_{\lt t}). \]

This is unbiased but has very high variance (“variances are too high” on the slide): if all rewards are positive, every sampled sequence is pushed up, only by different amounts.

Baselines (Sutton & Barto §13.4)

You may subtract any term that does not depend on the action: \(\nabla J=\mathbb{E}[(R-b)\nabla\log p_\theta(z)]\), because

\[ \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_\theta}[b\,\nabla\log p_\theta(z)] = b\sum_z \nabla p_\theta(z)=b\,\nabla\!\sum_z p_\theta(z)=b\,\nabla 1=0. \]

A natural, variance-reducing choice is \(b\approx V(q)=\mathbb{E}[R]\), the expected reward under the current policy. The weight \(A=R-V\) is then an advantage: positive if the sample was better than average. PPO learns \(V\) with a separate network; GRPO estimates \(b\) from the other samples of the same prompt.

Condition for unbiasedness

\(b\) must not depend on the sampled action \(z\) itself. A baseline that includes the sample's own reward (the group mean in GRPO!) or that rescales the advantage (dividing by a std) violates this: see §5 and the Monte-Carlo widget there.

Attempt 2 – TRPO: stay close to the current policy

Large steps on a high-variance gradient can wreck the policy. TRPO linearises around the current policy \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) and constrains the step in KL:

\[ \max_\theta\; \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\Big[\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t\mid s_t)}\hat A_t\Big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\big[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot\mid s_t)\,\|\,\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_t))\big]\le\delta. \]

The ratio is an importance weight: data was sampled from \(\pi_{old}\) but we evaluate the objective of \(\pi_\theta\). It is only trustworthy while the two stay close; the constraint enforces that, but a hard constraint needs second-order machinery (conjugate gradient, line search).

Attempt 3 – PPO: clip the ratio

PPO replaces the hard KL constraint by a clipped surrogate, with \(\rho=\pi_\theta/\pi_{\theta_k}\):

\[ L(s,a,\theta_k,\theta)=\min\Big(\rho\,A^{\pi_{\theta_k}}(s,a),\;\operatorname{clip}(\rho,\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon)\,A^{\pi_{\theta_k}}(s,a)\Big). \]

For \(A\gt 0\) the objective stops rewarding increases of \(\rho\) beyond \(1+\epsilon\); for \(A\lt 0\) it stops rewarding decreases below \(1-\epsilon\). The “min” keeps the pessimistic bound: if the update has already moved \(\rho\) the “wrong” way, the unclipped (larger-magnitude) term is used and the gradient is non-zero, so the policy can correct itself. Play with it:

3. PPO for language models: what it looks like in code (AlpacaFarm)

“The objective is basically all there is to it at a conceptual level”, but PPO is notorious for implementation details (the slide shows the paper Implementation Matters in Deep Policy Gradients). So the lecture reads a live implementation: AlpacaFarm's ppo_trainer.py, which the slides note was used by other projects to reasonable success (SALMON; Aligning Large Multimodal Models with Factually Augmented RLHF). In the LM setting actions are tokens, and there is one big dense-ish reward at the very end of the sequence.

AlpacaFarm's results table (slide 10) shows PPO implemented this way is competitive: it beats SFT, expert iteration and best-of-1024 on both simulated and human win-rate, and ties DPO on simulated win-rate (46.8 each). It is below GPT-4 and ChatGPT on the simulated metric.

3.1 Outer loop and inner loop

PPO has an outer loop (collect rollouts with the current policy) and an inner loop (several epochs of minibatch gradient steps on that fixed buffer). The second and later steps are off-policy, which is exactly why the ratio and clipping exist.

# Simplified rewrite of the outer/inner loop shown on slide 11 (AlpacaFarm PPOTrainer)
def step_with_rollouts(self, rollouts):
    loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(*rollouts.values()), batch_size=self.args.per_device_batch_size, shuffle=True)
    for epoch_idx in range(self.args.noptepochs):          # inner loop over the SAME rollouts
        for batch in loader:
            with self.accelerator.accumulate(self.policy):
                ppo_loss, stats = self.compute_loss(batch)  # see 3.2
                self.accelerator.backward(ppo_loss)
                if self.accelerator.sync_gradients:
                    # gradient can blow up at some point; clipping the norm stabilises it eventually
                    if self.args.max_grad_norm is not None:
                        self.accelerator.clip_grad_norm_(self.policy.parameters(), self.args.max_grad_norm)
                self.optimizer.step()
                self.optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

3.2 Loss computation: clipped policy loss + clipped value loss

def compute_loss(self, rollouts):
    values, old_logprob, returns, advantages, queries, query_attn_masks, responses = prepare_inputs(
        unpack_dict(rollouts, keys=("values", "logprobs", "returns", "advantages",
                                    "queries", "query_attn_masks", "responses")))
    outputs = self.policy(queries, query_attn_masks, responses, temperature=self.args.temperature)

    # --- value (critic) loss, also clipped around the OLD value prediction
    vpred = outputs["values"]
    vpredclipped = torch.clamp(vpred, min=values - self.args.cliprange_value,
                                      max=values + self.args.cliprange_value)
    vf_losses1 = (vpred - returns) ** 2.0
    vf_losses2 = (vpredclipped - returns) ** 2.0
    vf_loss = 0.5 * torch.maximum(vf_losses1, vf_losses2).mean()

    # --- policy loss: PPO clipped surrogate on the token ratio
    logprob = outputs["logprobs"]
    ratio = torch.exp(logprob - old_logprob)
    pg_losses  = -advantages * ratio
    pg_losses2 = -advantages * torch.clamp(ratio, min=1.0 - self.args.cliprange,   # cliprange = 0.2
                                                  max=1.0 + self.args.cliprange)
    pg_loss = torch.maximum(pg_losses, pg_losses2).mean()   # max of negatives == min of objectives
    loss = pg_loss + self.args.vf_coef * vf_loss

Notes: (i) torch.maximum(-A·ρ, -A·clip(ρ)) is the same as \(-\min(\rho A,\operatorname{clip}(\rho)A)\); (ii) the value loss is clipped in the same spirit (the “max” of the clipped and unclipped squared errors); (iii) the logged pg_clipfrac / vf_clipfrac tell you what fraction of tokens were clipped, a standard health metric; (iv) cliprange = 0.2.

3.3 Rollouts (what is stored)

# Simplified paraphrase of AlpacaFarm's rollout() (slide 13); the real function also
# handles FSDP, autocast wrappers, and tokenizer/padding details that are omitted here.
def rollout(self, queries_data):
    self.policy.eval(); self.ref_policy.eval(); self.reward_model.eval()      # "give up dropout throughout"
    rollouts = []
    for batch in queries_data:
        queries, query_attn_masks = unpack(batch)
        responses = unwrapped_policy.respond(queries, query_attn_masks, temperature=self.args.temperature)
        # log-probs / values / entropies of the sampled tokens under policy AND reference
        policy_out = self.policy(queries, query_attn_masks, responses, temperature=...)       # logprobs, values, entropies
        ref_out    = self.ref_policy(queries, query_attn_masks, responses, temperature=...)   # logprobs, entropies
        # reward model may use a different tokenizer, so decode and re-tokenise the text
        text = [q + r for q, r in zip(tokenizer.batch_decode(queries), tokenizer.batch_decode(responses))]
        reward_out = self.reward_model(**tokenize(text))                  # sequence-level score
        shaped = self._shape_reward(rewards=reward_out["rewards"], responses=responses,
                                    logprobs=policy_out["logprobs"], ref_logprobs=ref_out["logprobs"])
        rollouts.append({**batch, "responses": responses, **policy_out, **ref_out, **reward_out, **shaped})
    rollouts = merge_dict(rollouts, merge_fn=torch.cat)
    # estimating advantages OUTSIDE the loop gives more samples for reward normalisation
    advantages = self._estimate_advantage(rollouts["shaped_rewards"], rollouts["values"])
    return {**rollouts, **advantages}

3.4 Reward shaping: per-token KL, full reward on the last token

High level: per-token KL penalty against the reference model, and the full reward-model score added on the last token. In practice AlpacaFarm clamps the KL at zero: only positions where the new policy's log-prob is higher than the reference's are penalised. The slide's comment: it “helps with stability” – if the model blows up, this stops the KL term from diverging.

Caveat: the slide text says “clip KL for sequences where new policy logp < reference logp”, which does not match the code: clamp(min=0) zeroes the penalty exactly when the policy's log-prob is below the reference's, so the penalty acts where logp > ref. The code is what I have followed above.

def _shape_reward(self, rewards, responses, logprobs, ref_logprobs):
    # The source keeps a commented-out full-distribution KL ("For some reason, line below doesn't work");
    # it uses this per-sampled-token estimate instead (the slide's "clip KL" rule).
    kl = torch.clamp(logprobs - ref_logprobs, min=0.0)             # sampled-token KL estimate, clipped at 0
    non_score_rewards = -self.kl_ctl.value * kl                    # dense per-token penalty
    shaped_rewards = non_score_rewards.clone()
    # (comment in source: small off-by-one bug if pad_token_id == eos_token_id)
    terminal_positions = (responses != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id).sum(dim=1) - 1
    shaped_rewards[list(range(rewards.size(0))), terminal_positions] += rewards   # RM score on last token
    return dict(shaped_rewards=shaped_rewards, non_score_rewards=non_score_rewards, kl=kl)

3.5 Generalised Advantage Estimation and the value network

PPO uses a learned value function \(V_\phi(s_t)\) to build advantages. The slide-9 diagram draws it as a separate network; the AlpacaFarm code instead reads a values head off the policy LM. With TD residual \(\delta_t^V=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\):

\[ \hat A_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(\gamma\lambda)^l\,\delta^V_{t+l}. \]

\(\lambda=0\) gives the one-step TD error (low variance, biased by the value net); \(\lambda=1\) gives (reward-to-go) \(-V(s_t)\) (unbiased, high variance). The recursion is computed backwards:

def _estimate_advantage(self, rewards, values):
    """Generalized advantage estimation  (https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02438)"""
    if self.args.whiten_rewards:
        rewards = torch_ops.whiten(rewards, shift_mean=False)
    lastgaelam = 0
    advantages_reversed = []
    gen_length = self.args.response_len
    for t in reversed(range(gen_length)):
        nextvalues = values[:, t + 1] if t < gen_length - 1 else 0.0
        delta = rewards[:, t] + self.args.gamma * nextvalues - values[:, t]
        lastgaelam = delta + self.args.gamma * self.args.lam * lastgaelam
        advantages_reversed.append(lastgaelam)
    advantages = torch.stack(advantages_reversed[::-1], dim=1)
    returns = advantages + values                                   # regression target for the value net
    advantages = torch_ops.whiten(advantages, shift_mean=True)      # normalise over the batch
    return dict(returns=returns, advantages=advantages)
“Funny detail”

LM-RLHF is really a bandit problem (one reward at the end), and in practice gamma = lambda = 1 works: GAE collapses to reward-to-go minus value. The critic is then just a learned, token-dependent baseline. This is the observation GRPO exploits: if you have many samples per prompt you can build the baseline without a critic.

3.6 What healthy PPO training looks like

The slide shows three W&B curves from a run that works: (1) KL-penalised sequence reward rises, (2) the reward model's raw score rises, (3) the “non-score rewards” (i.e. \(-\beta\cdot\)KL) go increasingly negative as the policy moves away from the reference. Because this is effectively a bandit, you should see reasonably smooth, boring training curves; wild curves point to an implementation bug.

3.7 Why look for yet another algorithm?

Why not PPO?

  • Complicated implementation (rollouts, GAE, whitening, two clipped losses, KL controller…).
  • Value model: memory-hungry (another full-size network + optimiser state) and needs its own tuning.

Why not DPO?

  • Verifiable data is not inherently pairwise / Bradley–Terry; you have a 0/1 outcome per sample.
  • DPO is offline (can be made online by iterating).

4. GRPO: PPO without the value network

Group Relative Policy Optimisation (Shao et al., DeepSeekMath 2024) is, in the slide's words: start with PPO, remove the value function / advantage computation, and compute the advantage as the z-score within a group. For each prompt \(q\) sample a group of \(G\) outputs \(\{o_i\}\) from \(\pi_{old}\), score each with the reward, and optimise

\[ \mathcal J_{GRPO}(\theta)=\mathbb E_{q,\{o_i\}\sim\pi_{old}}\Big[\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac1{|o_i|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_i|}\Big(\min\big(\rho_{i,t}\hat A_{i},\;\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat A_{i}\big)-\beta\,\mathbb D_{KL}[\pi_\theta\|\pi_{ref}]\Big)\Big],\quad \rho_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_\theta(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,\lt t})}{\pi_{old}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,\lt t})}, \] \[ \hat A_i=\frac{r_i-\operatorname{mean}(\{r_1,\dots,r_G\})}{\operatorname{std}(\{r_1,\dots,r_G\})},\qquad \mathbb D_{KL}[\pi_\theta\|\pi_{ref}]=\frac{\pi_{ref}}{\pi_\theta}-\log\frac{\pi_{ref}}{\pi_\theta}-1 . \]

Three things differ from PPO: (1) no critic, so the advantage is the same scalar for every token of response \(i\); (2) the KL to the reference policy is a separate term in the loss rather than folded into the reward; (3) a per-sequence \(1/|o_i|\) length normaliser (this one matters, see §5). In the strictly online case (rollout, then one immediate gradient step) \(\rho=1\), clipping never triggers, and the update is just policy gradient with group-normalised rewards.

4.1 Worked example: group advantages with editable rewards

Set the reward of each of the \(G=8\) samples of one prompt. The calculator computes the vanilla GRPO advantage exactly as in the lecture code ((r - mean) / (std + 1e-4), population std), and for comparison the two “fixed” variants discussed in §5: mean-only (Dr. GRPO) and leave-one-out (RLOO). Try making all rewards equal: the advantage is exactly zero, i.e. the prompt gives no gradient (and an all-correct group still costs a full rollout).

4.2 A tiny GRPO implementation (McGill-NLP nano-aha-moment)

The lecture walks through github.com/McGill-NLP/nano-aha-moment: “you can (and people do) write tiny GRPO implementations”. The recipe: compute a reward for each rollout, normalise per group, compute the KL term, take gradient steps. First the advantage code (slide 20), “basically just the vanilla GRPO setup” – the one difference to the paper is a 1e-4 stability term in the std:

def compute_advantages(samples, all_generations, all_finish_reasons, GENERATIONS_PER_SAMPLE):
    assert len(all_generations) == len(all_finish_reasons)
    assert len(all_generations) == len(samples) * GENERATIONS_PER_SAMPLE
    groups = [list(range(i, i + GENERATIONS_PER_SAMPLE))          # e.g. [[0,1,2],[3,4,5],[6,7,8]]
              for i in range(0, len(all_generations), GENERATIONS_PER_SAMPLE)]
    for sample, group_indices in zip(samples, groups):
        responses = tokenizer.batch_decode([all_generations[i] for i in group_indices],
                                           skip_special_tokens=False)
        rewards_and_metrics = [compute_reward(resp, sample) for resp in responses]
        rewards, reward_metrics = zip(*rewards_and_metrics)
        rewards = np.array(rewards)                                # [group_size]
        response_advantages = (rewards - rewards.mean()) / (rewards.std() + 1e-4)
        # the SAME scalar advantage is copied onto every token of each response
        advantages = [[resp_adv] * len(resp)
                      for resp_adv, resp in zip(response_advantages, response_token_ids)]
        ...   # extend all_query_token_ids / all_response_token_ids / all_advantages and log stats
                # (rewards, response_lengths, non_stop_rate = fraction whose finish_reason != "stop")

Then the loss (slide 19). Note the very simple on-policy form: no ratio, no clipping – one gradient step per batch, so \(\rho=1\) and the clipped surrogate reduces to the plain term.

def compute_pg_loss(policy_model, reference_model, batch, total_response_len):
    input_ids, attention_mask = batch["input_ids"], batch["attention_mask"]   # [B, T]
    labels, advantages = batch["labels"], batch["advantages"]                  # labels: -100 on prompt tokens
    labels_mask = (labels[..., 1:] != -100).float()                            # only response tokens count

    with torch.no_grad():                                                      # frozen reference policy
        ref_logps = compute_token_log_probs(reference_model, model_inputs, TEMPERATURE)
    logps = compute_token_log_probs(policy_model, model_inputs, TEMPERATURE)   # [B, T-1]

    kl_penalty = torch.exp(ref_logps - logps) - (ref_logps - logps) - 1        # k3 estimator, per token
    kl_penalty = kl_penalty * labels_mask

    entropy = -logps.sum() / labels_mask.sum()                                 # monitoring metric (see 4.4)

    policy_loss = -logps * advantages[..., 1:]                                 # REINFORCE with group advantage
    policy_loss = policy_loss * labels_mask

    loss = (policy_loss + KL_COEFFICIENT * kl_penalty).sum() / total_response_len   # token-level normaliser
An observation worth making

The paper's objective divides each sequence by its own \(|o_i|\) (“mean over tokens of each sequence, then mean over sequences”). This implementation instead divides the sum over all tokens in the batch by total_response_len, i.e. every token has equal weight regardless of which response it belongs to. That is exactly the kind of choice that §5 shows to matter. (My comment, not a statement on the slides.)

4.3 The KL term: why the k3 estimator

The KL penalty keeps the policy near the reference. It is estimated from one sampled token. With \(d=\log\pi_{ref}-\log\pi_\theta\) on that token, the lecture code uses \(\mathrm{k3}=e^{d}-d-1\). Because \(\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}[e^{d}]=\sum\pi_{ref}=1\), \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{k3}]=-\mathbb E[d]=\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{ref})\): it is unbiased, and (because \(e^{d}\ge 1+d\)) always non-negative, unlike the naive estimate \(-d\) (k1, unbiased but noisy and often negative). The labels k1/k2/k3 come from Schulman's well-known note on KL approximators; they are not on the slides.

4.4 Entropy and the other training diagnostics

The nano-aha-moment loss also returns entropy = -logps.sum()/labels_mask.sum(): the negative mean log-probability of the sampled tokens, a single-sample estimate of the policy's per-token entropy. Together with the reward, response length, non_stop_rate, KL and the clip fraction it is the standard dashboard of an RLVR run. Typical readings: mean reward rising; entropy falling (the policy sharpens as it commits to strategies); a collapse of entropy to near zero means exploration has died and groups will increasingly be all-correct or all-wrong (no signal); response length drifting up (§5, §7) is a thing to check, not automatically a sign of progress.

Not on the slides

DAPO (Yu et al. 2025) is a well-known follow-up that targets exactly these diagnostics: asymmetric clip bounds (“clip-higher”) to keep entropy up, dynamic sampling that drops groups with zero advantage, token-level loss normalisation, and soft over-length penalties. The lecture does not cover it; I mention it only to place Dr. GRPO in context.

5. Is the GRPO advantage “valid”? Baselines, std and length biases

The slide's detour: baselining (Sutton & Barto §13.4, shown on the slide) says we may subtract any term from the reward that does not vary with the action. Then asks: is the GRPO advantage a valid baseline? The answer on slide 23: the division by the stdev is not a valid baseline that preserves unbiasedness. Following Liu et al. 2025 (“Dr. GRPO”, Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training), the unbiased version removes both the std and the \(1/|o_i|\) length normaliser.

5.1 Three separate issues

Component in GRPOWhat it doesProblemDr. GRPO fix
mean over the group, includes sample \(i\) itselfbaseline \(b=\bar r\)\(b\) depends on \(r_i\): slightly biased, but only by a positive factor \((G-1)/G\) (widget below), so the update direction is rightkeep (or use leave-one-out)
division by stdrescales each prompt's gradient by \(1/\sigma_q\)Not a baseline. For 0/1 rewards \(\sigma=\sqrt{p(1-p)}\), so prompts that are too easy or too hard (small \(\sigma\)) are up-weighted: a question-level difficulty biasremove
\(1/|o_i|\) per sequencemakes every response contribute the same total weightResponse-level length bias (quote from slide 24): for \(A\gt0\), shorter responses get larger per-token updates, so the policy favours brevity among correct answers; for \(A\lt0\) longer responses are penalised less per token, so the policy prefers lengthy incorrect ones. Net effect: wrong answers grow longerremove (divide by a constant, e.g. max length)

5.2 Monte-Carlo-free check: expected gradient of each estimator

Use the simplest model that shows it: one prompt whose answer is correct with probability \(p=\sigma(\theta)\) (a Bernoulli policy; the score of a sample is \(r-p\) w.r.t. the logit \(\theta\)). The true gradient is \(\nabla_\theta\mathbb E[r]=p(1-p)\). For a group of \(G\) samples the estimator is \(\frac1G\sum_i A_i\,(r_i-p)\); I enumerate all \(k\in\{0..G\}\) successes with their binomial probabilities, so the curves below are exact expectations, not noisy simulations. Observe: mean-baseline = exactly \((G-1)/G\) times the truth (right direction, slightly shrunk); leave-one-out = the truth; GRPO (std) has a different shape: relative to the true gradient it amplifies the tails (very easy and very hard prompts, factor about 1/σ), which changes which prompts the model learns from.

5.3 The length bias, quantified

Under \(1/|o_i|\) normalisation a response of length \(L\) and advantage \(A\) puts weight \(A/L\) on each of its tokens. Plot that weight against length, next to the Dr. GRPO version that divides by a constant (e.g. the maximum generation length) for every response.

The punchline for R1

The famous “response length grows during RL” curve of R1-Zero is therefore partly an artifact of the biased objective. Dr. GRPO matches accuracy with far shorter chains of thought. See §6 for the same point about the “aha moment”.

6. DeepSeek-R1-Zero: pure RL from a base model

Why R1 matters (slide 26): performance exceeding OpenAI o1; an open and fairly simple RL recipe; it ended speculation that MCTS or process reward models are necessary; and SFT insights (both R1-Zero and the distilled models). R1 builds directly on GRPO from DeepSeekMath but does not use process supervision.

Controlled setting: R1-Zero

  • Base model: DeepSeek-V3 (671B total / 37B activated MoE). Data: not public.
  • Rewards, only two: an accuracy reward (is the final answer correct?) and a format reward (put the reasoning inside thinking tags).
  • Algorithm: GRPO, no SFT, no process reward, no search.

Results, as the slide puts it, “a bit worse than OpenAI o1”:

The “aha moment” and growing chains of thought, and why to be sceptical

7. DeepSeek-R1: the full recipe

R1 vs R1-Zero, key differences (slide 31): (i) SFT initialisation, (ii) a language-consistency reward for the CoT, (iii) non-verifiable rewards in a later stage. Pipeline: DeepSeek-V3 → reasoning SFT → RL (GRPO) → SFT/RLHF. Step through it:

R1's quote: to prevent the early unstable cold-start phase of RL, they collect a small amount of long-CoT data. 7.2 The RL step and the language-consistency reward

From the R1 paper (slide 34): during RL they observe language mixing in the CoT, particularly when prompts involve several languages. To mitigate, they add a language-consistency reward computed as the proportion of target-language words in the CoT. Ablations show this alignment slightly degrades raw accuracy, but it matches human preference and readability, so the final reward directly sums accuracy and language consistency. The slide's aside: “RL naturally leads to mixed languages?”.

7.3 Final stages, results, and distillation

After reasoning RL, “the usual post-training process happens”: SFT for 2 epochs with 600k reasoning samples for non-verifiable tasks (V3 as judge) and 200k non-reasoning samples, then RLHF re-using the R1-Zero-style reasoning RL for verifiable prompts and V3's RLHF pipeline for the rest (still GRPO). 7.4 What did not work (the “unsuccessful attempts” section)

8. Kimi k1.5: a contemporaneous recipe

Why study it (slide 39): released at the same time as R1 and also beats o1 using RL, with complementary details. Key steps (slide 40): dataset construction with difficulty filtering, SFT for long CoT, RL with their own policy-gradient loss.

8.1 Data curation and SFT

  • Standard curation across math-style settings, balancing topics with a tagging system; includes STEM, competitions and general reasoning, text-only and image-text.
  • Exclude multiple-choice and true/false questions (guessable ⇒ false positives).
  • Difficulty by pass rate: an SFT model samples answers 10 times at high temperature; the lower the pass rate, the higher the difficulty. Keep only examples the model fails on best-of-8.
  • SFT: very little description, just “prompt engineering” (distillation?).

8.2 The Kimi RL objective

With a reference-based reward \(r(x,y,y^*)\) (compare answer \(y\) to ground truth \(y^*\); \(z\) is the CoT), the problem is a KL-regularised policy improvement step relative to the current iterate \(\pi_{\theta_i}\):

\[ \max_\theta\;\mathbb E_{(x,y^*)\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\mathbb E_{(y,z)\sim\pi_\theta}[r(x,y,y^*)]-\tau\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta(x)\,\|\,\pi_{\theta_i}(x)\big)\Big]. \]

The algorithm is “inspired by a DPO-type derivation”: under a non-parametric assumption the optimum satisfies \(\pi^*\propto\pi_{\theta_i}e^{r/\tau}\), i.e. \(r-\tau\log Z=\tau\log\frac{\pi^*(y,z|x)}{\pi_{\theta_i}(y,z|x)}\). Solve for \(r\) and use a squared loss as a surrogate:

\[ L(\theta)=\mathbb E\Big[\mathbb E_{(y,z)\sim\pi_{\theta_i}}\Big(r-\tau\log Z-\tau\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y,z|x)}{\pi_{\theta_i}(y,z|x)}\Big)^2\Big]. \]

Replacing the unknown \(\tau\log Z\) by the empirical mean reward \(\bar r\) of \(k\) samples and differentiating (using \(\nabla\ell^2=2\ell\nabla\log\pi_\theta\) with \(\ell=\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\theta_i}}\)) gives the baselined policy gradient with regularisation shown on the slide:

\[ \frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Big(\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_j,z_j|x)\,\big(r(x,y_j,y^*)-\bar r\big)-\frac\tau2\nabla_\theta\Big(\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_j,z_j|x)}{\pi_{\theta_i}(y_j,z_j|x)}\Big)^2\Big). \]

Compared with GRPO: the baseline is the group mean only (no std division, no per-sequence length division), the regulariser is a squared log-ratio to the previous iterate (not the fixed SFT reference), and there is no clipping and no value network. The slide notes this objective does not have GRPO's length-bias problem.

8.3 Length control: a length reward

Kimi nevertheless wants to compress CoTs, so within each group of rollouts they add a length reward, with \(\lambda=0.5-\frac{\mathrm{len}(i)-\min\_len}{\max\_len-\min\_len}\):

\[ \mathrm{len\_reward}(i)=\begin{cases}\lambda & r(x,y_i,y^*)=1\\ \min(0,\lambda) & r(x,y_i,y^*)=0.\end{cases} \]

\(\lambda\in[-0.5,0.5]\) with longer sequences more negative: correct answers are incentivised to be short; incorrect answers are incentivised to be shorter than the centre of the range of rollouts (long wrong answers are penalised, short wrong ones are not rewarded). It is switched on only later in training, because it hurts performance early.

8.4 Curriculum, rewards, ablations

  • Curriculum: assign difficulty labels, go easy → hard; sample problems proportional to \((1-\text{success\_rate})\) so solved prompts are not repeated.
  • Code rewards: take problems with ground-truth solutions and generate new test cases.
  • Math rewards: 800k samples to train a chain-of-thought reward model for answer-equivalence checks. Manual spot-check: the classic RM reached about 84.4% accuracy, the CoT RM 98.5%; RL uses the CoT RM for more correct feedback. (So “verifier” can itself be a small model; see reward hacking in §13.)

9. RL infrastructure: why efficiency is its own problem

The slide's three reasons RL is hard to make efficient: (1) on-policy means rollouts, i.e. slow inference; (2) switching from training to rollouts often means different frameworks (a training stack such as Megatron and an inference engine such as vLLM with different parallelism and weight layouts); (3) long CoTs make batches very uneven (a few 30k-token rollouts hold up a batch of 2k-token ones).

9.1 The long-tail problem, quantified (my model, not from the slides)

Assume rollout lengths are log-normal around a median length with spread \(\sigma\) (long tails are typical of CoT). In a synchronous iteration with static batching every sequence slot is busy until the longest one ends, so average utilisation is \(\bar L/L_{max}\). Partial rollout caps the per-iteration generation at \(C\) tokens (the rest continues next iteration), so utilisation becomes \(\overline{\min(L,C)}/\min(L_{max},C)\). The lengths are the deterministic quantiles of the distribution, so there is no sampling noise.

  • Filter for difficulty by best-of-n, like Kimi; remove prompts the model gets right without CoT; remove prompts too similar to validation data.
  • Manual filtering of CoT quality (guessing vs. getting it right).
  • RL with GRPO on only 3,995 examples: low-data RLVR.

11. Qwen3-Coder-Next: from RLVR to agentic RL

Built on Qwen3-Next and post-trained for agentic abilities (technical report linked in the papers list). The slides sketch the whole stack:

  • Mid-training data: GitHub long-context “repository-level” data (concatenated files, 600B tokens) and pull requests with RAG-retrieved repository-state context; Common Crawl with joint text+code documents and LLM-based HTML parsing; synthetic data (LM-prompted QA about coding web documents, and trajectories from running coding agents in various environments); instruction-following and fill-in-the-middle data.
  • Expert models trained separately from Qwen3-Next: a web-dev expert (SFT on “valid web code” checked by a VLM and agent actions), a UX expert (trained on many tool-call formats), a single-turn QA expert (standard code synthesis, just more data), and an SWE expert; then distilled into Qwen3-Coder-Next.
  • Environment construction: automated SWE-bench-style environments, 800k tasks.

12. Test-time scaling, pass@k and why group size and difficulty matter

The motivating plot (o1's AIME accuracy rising with test-time compute; Qwen3's budget curve above) says: if a model can spend more tokens thinking, accuracy follows. Two numbers on the R1 slides quantify the other kind of test-time compute, sampling many answers: pass@1 (a single sample) versus cons@64 (majority vote of 64): e.g. R1-Zero 71.0 → 86.7 on AIME, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 55.5 → 83.3. For an idealised prompt with per-sample success probability \(p\), \(\text{pass@}k=1-(1-p)^k\). Real prompts have different \(p\), so the benchmark curve is a mixture; the calculator shows the i.i.d. ideal.

Why this matters for RLVR training itself: GRPO only learns from groups with mixed outcomes. With \(G\) samples and success rate \(p\), the probability a group has non-zero advantage is \(1-p^G-(1-p)^G\). This is the quantitative reason Kimi keeps only prompts the model fails best-of-8, Qwen3 removes prompts it answers right without CoT, and Kimi's curriculum samples \(\propto 1-\text{success rate}\).

13. Reward design and its failure modes

SystemRewards used (from the slides)Caveat flagged
R1-Zeroaccuracy (correct?) + format (thinking tags)unreadable, language-mixed CoT
R1same + language consistency (fraction of target-language words) + V3-as-judge / RLHF reward for non-verifiableconsistency costs a little accuracy; judge-based rewards are learned, so over-optimisable
Kimi k1.5binary correctness (reference-based); code: generated test cases; math: CoT reward model (98.5% vs 84.4% for a classic RM); + length rewardexclude multiple-choice/true-false (false positives); length reward only later in training
Qwen3query-verifier pairs (3,995); general RL stage with rule-based and model-based rewards across many tasksgeneral RL slightly lowers math/STEM
Qwen3-Coder-Nextunit tests / SWE-bench-style environmentsagent learns to exploit git history unless blocked
Verifiers can be hacked too

RLVR removes learned reward-model over-optimisation only to the degree the verifier is exact. A CoT reward model for answer equivalence (Kimi) is 98.5% accurate, not 100%; a test suite can be satisfied by reading the answer out of the environment (Qwen3-Coder-Next's git exploit, which got more likely as capability increased). Practical rules from these case studies: filter guessable formats, generate extra test cases, block information leaks in the environment, and monitor train-vs-held-out reward.

Self-check quiz

1. Four samples of a prompt receive rewards [1, 0, 0, 0]. Compute the vanilla GRPO advantages and the Dr. GRPO advantages.
Mean = 0.25; population std = √(0.25·0.75) = 0.433. Vanilla: correct sample (1 − 0.25)/0.433 = +1.73; each wrong sample −0.25/0.433 = −0.577 (they sum to 0: 1.73 − 3·0.577 = 0). Dr. GRPO (mean only): +0.75 and −0.25. If the rewards were all equal the advantages would all be 0 and the group gives no gradient.
2. What exactly does GRPO remove from PPO, and why can it get away with it for LLM RLVR?
It removes the value network (critic) and GAE. For LM tasks the reward is a single terminal scalar, so the problem is a bandit; with \(\gamma=\lambda=1\) the GAE advantage is just reward-to-go minus a learned baseline. GRPO replaces the learned baseline by the mean reward of other samples of the same prompt, saving the memory/tuning of a critic. This only works if you can afford several samples per prompt, which RLVR does anyway.
3. Which parts of the GRPO advantage are biased, and what does each do to learning?
(a) Dividing by std is not a baseline: for 0/1 rewards it multiplies each prompt's gradient by about \(1/\sqrt{p(1-p)}\), up-weighting very easy and very hard questions (difficulty bias). (b) Dividing each response by \(|o_i|\) gives per-token weight \(A/|o_i|\): short correct answers are reinforced more per token (brevity) and long wrong answers are penalised less per token (verbosity when wrong). (c) The mean including the sample itself shrinks the gradient by \((G-1)/G\) but keeps its direction; leave-one-out removes that. Dr. GRPO drops (a) and (b).
4. How does R1 differ from R1-Zero, and what are the stages of R1?
R1-Zero: GRPO on V3 with accuracy and format rewards only. R1 adds (i) a cold-start long-CoT SFT, (ii) a language-consistency reward summed into the RL reward, (iii) a later SFT (600k reasoning samples with V3 as judge for non-verifiable tasks + 200k non-reasoning) and RL/RLHF for all tasks (still GRPO). Separately, 800k R1-generated CoTs distil into Qwen2.5/Llama.
5. Kimi's length reward with min_len = 1000 and max_len = 5000: give the reward of (a) a correct 3000-token answer, (b) a correct 1000-token answer, (c) an incorrect 1000-token answer, (d) an incorrect 5000-token answer.
λ = 0.5 − (len − 1000)/4000. (a) λ = 0 ⇒ 0. (b) λ = 0.5 ⇒ +0.5. (c) λ = 0.5, reward min(0, 0.5) = 0. (d) λ = −0.5, reward min(0, −0.5) = −0.5. So short correct answers are favoured, and incorrect answers are punished only if they are longer than the middle of the range.
6. Why is RL infrastructure hard, and what is partial rollout?
On-policy RL needs fresh rollouts (slow autoregressive inference) from the current weights; training and inference often use different frameworks with different parallelism, so weights must be moved (Kimi: Megatron ↔ vLLM time-sharing GPUs via a checkpoint engine); and long-CoT lengths are heavy-tailed so a synchronous batch waits for its longest sample. Partial rollout caps the tokens generated per iteration and stores the unfinished prefixes in the replay buffer to resume later.
7. Qwen3 trains reasoning RL on only 3,995 examples. How can that suffice, and what happens in the general RL stage?
The data are heavily filtered: difficulty-filtered by best-of-n, prompts answerable without CoT removed, validation-similar prompts removed, CoT quality manually checked, after a long-CoT cold start. Since an informative GRPO group needs mixed outcomes, a small set of well-calibrated prompts is data-efficient. General RL (stage 4) boosts instruction following, agent and general scores but slightly lowers math/STEM (AIME’24 83.8 → 81.9 → 81.4).

Key takeaways

  • RLVR = RL with a programmatic verifier. It scales where RLHF over-optimises because the reward is the thing you want, as long as the verifier is hard to game.
  • GRPO = PPO clipped surrogate + KL, with the critic replaced by within-group z-scored rewards. Online it is just policy gradient with normalised rewards; a working version is a few dozen lines.
  • The std division and per-sequence length division are biased (difficulty and length biases). Dr. GRPO removes them; part of R1-Zero's growing response length is an artifact, and the base model already shows “aha” behaviour.
  • R1 recipe: small long-CoT SFT → GRPO on accuracy+format(+language) rewards → SFT with judge-selected data → RLHF; then distil 800k traces into smaller models. No PRM, no MCTS.
  • Kimi k1.5: difficulty-filtered data (fails best-of-8), a baselined policy gradient with a squared-log-ratio regulariser, a length reward for shorter CoT, curriculum, CoT answer-checker RM, and an RL system with partial rollouts and Megatron/vLLM time-sharing.
  • Qwen3: 3,995 GRPO prompts, thinking-mode fusion with a controllable thinking budget, general RL afterwards (small math/STEM cost), distillation for small models. Qwen3-Coder-Next extends RLVR to long-horizon agentic coding with 800k auto-constructed tasks and must fight reward hacking.
  • Rollouts dominate RL cost: keep groups informative (difficulty filtering), and engineer for long tails.
