Multimodal Models: ViT, CLIP/SigLIP, LLaVA, Qwen-VL, Chameleon

lecture_17.py ViT CLIP SigLIP VQ-VAE LLaVA AnyRes M-RoPE Chameleon

TL;DR. Transformers only speak tokens, so every new modality must become tokens. For understanding images the dominant recipe is: a vision transformer (ViT) pretrained contrastively (CLIP, then SigLIP) turns an image into a grid of patch embeddings; a small projector (linear or MLP) maps them into the LLM's embedding space; the LLM is then tuned on synthetic multimodal instruction data (LLaVA, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen-VL / Qwen2-VL / Qwen3-VL). The hard engineering questions are how many tokens an image costs (AnyRes, dynamic resolution, video), how positions are encoded (M-RoPE), and what data to train on. For generation inside the same model, images must be discretised (VQ-VAE) and everything modelled as next-token prediction (Chameleon): elegant, but lossy and unstable to train.

1. Why multimodal, and the token problem

So far in the course: text ⇒ text. The world is not text-only: images, audio and video carry most of the information humans use. The long-term goal is an omni model: input any combination of modalities (understanding) and output any combination (generation).

Reasoning chain of the lecture

Transformers work really well, so we keep them. Transformers speak tokens (discrete ids or continuous vectors), where a token stands for a roughly semantic unit of information. Therefore everything must be converted into tokens. We already had to do this for text (the tokenization lecture); for non-text modalities it is much harder.

Question 1: input

How do we input non-text data, e.g. understand an image?

Question 2: output

How do we output non-text data, e.g. generate an image or audio?

Timeline of the models covered in this lecture:

2020 ViT: split the image into patches and run a Transformer over them (Dosovitskiy et al.).
2021 CLIP: contrastive image-text pretraining on 400M pairs; zero-shot classification.
Mar 2023 SigLIP: replace the batch-wide softmax by an independent sigmoid per pair.
Apr 2023 LLaVA: CLIP encoder + linear projection + Vicuna.
Aug 2023 Qwen-VL: cross-attention adapter with 256 visual tokens; grounding tokens.
May 2024 Chameleon: everything is a discrete token, one autoregressive model.
Aug 2024 LLaVA-OneVision: SigLIP + AnyRes; single image, multi-image and video.
Sep 2024 Qwen2-VL: dynamic (native) resolution, M-RoPE.
Nov 2025 Qwen3-VL: SigLIP-2, interleaved M-RoPE, DeepStack, 256K context.

2. Vision Transformer (ViT): images as sequences of patches

CLIP's best image encoder, and most later VLMs, use a Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). The recipe is a direct port of the text Transformer:

  1. Cut the \(H\times W\times 3\) image into non-overlapping \(P\times P\) patches: \(N=\lfloor H/P\rfloor\cdot\lfloor W/P\rfloor\) patches.
  2. Flatten each patch into a vector of length \(P^2\cdot 3\) and apply one shared linear map to \(d\) dimensions. (Equivalently, a convolution with kernel = stride = \(P\).)
  3. Add position embeddings, and optionally prepend a learnable [class] token.
  4. Run \(L\) standard encoder blocks (LayerNorm, multi-head self-attention, residual, LayerNorm, MLP, residual). Attention is bidirectional: there is no causal mask.

CLIP's name ViT-L/14@336px reads: L = Large, 14 = 14x14 patches with 3 channels, @336px = trained on 336x336 images. With \(P=14\) and \(336\) px, \(N=(336/14)^2=24^2=576\) patch tokens. CLIP's "attention pooling" replaces the class-token read-out: a QKV attention whose query is the global average of the final activations.

Code: patchify and embed (illustrative PyTorch, not in the lecture file) 
def patchify(img, P):                       # img: [B, 3, H, W] -> [B, N, P*P*3]
    B, C, H, W = img.shape
    x = img.unfold(2, P, P).unfold(3, P, P)                  # [B, C, H/P, W/P, P, P]
    return x.permute(0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1).reshape(B, (H//P)*(W//P), P*P*C)

patch_embed = nn.Linear(14*14*3, 1024)                       # same as Conv2d(3, 1024, kernel=14, stride=14)
tokens = patch_embed(patchify(img, 14)) + pos_emb            # [B, 576, 1024] for ViT-L/14@336
tokens = torch.cat([cls_token.expand(B, -1, -1), tokens], 1) # [B, 577, 1024]
for blk in blocks:
    tokens = blk(tokens)                                     # bidirectional self-attention

3. CLIP: contrastive language-image pretraining

CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). Context: vision models were trained on human-annotated images (ImageNet-style labels). Can we use the far larger supply of noisy (image, caption) pairs from the web instead?

Method

  • Take a batch of \(n\) (image, text) pairs (32,768 in CLIP).
  • Encode every image and every text into a shared \(d_e\)-dimensional space, and \(\ell_2\)-normalise.
  • For each image prefer its aligned text over the other \(n-1\) texts; for each text prefer its aligned image over the other images. This is a symmetric InfoNCE (cross-entropy over the \(n\times n\) cosine-similarity matrix, in both directions).
\[ \mathcal L_{\text{CLIP}}=\tfrac12\Big[\underbrace{-\tfrac1n\sum_i \log\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{s_{ij}/\tau}}}_{\text{image}\to\text{text}}+\underbrace{-\tfrac1n\sum_j \log\frac{e^{s_{jj}/\tau}}{\sum_i e^{s_{ij}/\tau}}}_{\text{text}\to\text{image}}\Big],\qquad s_{ij}=\frac{I_i\cdot T_j}{\lVert I_i\rVert\,\lVert T_j\rVert} \]

The lecture's code scales the cosine by \(e^{t}\), where \(t\) is a learned scalar; so \(1/\tau=e^{t}\). The CLIP paper initialises \(\tau=0.07\) and clips the scale at 100.

# image_encoder - ResNet or Vision Transformer
# text_encoder  - CBOW or Text Transformer
# I[n, h, w, c] - minibatch of aligned images
# T[n, l]       - minibatch of aligned texts
# W_i[d_i, d_e] - learned proj of image to embed
# W_t[d_t, d_e] - learned proj of text to embed
# t             - learned temperature parameter

I_f = image_encoder(I)  #[n, d_i]
T_f = text_encoder(T)   #[n, d_t]

# joint multimodal embedding [n, d_e]
I_e = l2_normalize(np.dot(I_f, W_i), axis=1)
T_e = l2_normalize(np.dot(T_f, W_t), axis=1)

# scaled pairwise cosine similarities [n, n]
logits = np.dot(I_e, T_e.T) * np.exp(t)

# symmetric loss function
labels = np.arange(n)
loss_i = cross_entropy_loss(logits, labels, axis=0)
loss_t = cross_entropy_loss(logits, labels, axis=1)
loss   = (loss_i + loss_t)/2
def clip_loss(img_f, txt_f, W_i, W_t, t):            # t: learnable log-scale
    I = F.normalize(img_f @ W_i, dim=-1)               # [n, d_e]
    T = F.normalize(txt_f @ W_t, dim=-1)               # [n, d_e]
    logits = I @ T.T * t.exp().clamp(max=100)          # [n, n]; logits[i, j] = scaled cos(I_i, T_j)
    y = torch.arange(len(I), device=I.device)
    return (F.cross_entropy(logits, y) + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, y)) / 2   # rows: image to text, cols: text to image

# zero-shot classification: class names become the classifier weights
T = F.normalize(text_enc(tok([f"a photo of a {c}." for c in classes])), dim=-1)
pred = (F.normalize(img_enc(img), dim=-1) @ T.T).argmax(-1)
Reading the pseudo-code

The two cross-entropies normalise over different axes: loss_i over images for each text, loss_t over texts for each image. Their average is symmetric, so the naming does not matter. The cost to remember: every example's loss needs a softmax over the whole batch, so large batches and cross-device communication are required.

Data, preprocessing and encoders

ComponentDetail (from the lecture)
DataSearched for 500K queries, got ~20K (image, text) pairs per query: 400M pairs. The dataset was not released.
Open reproductionOpenCLIP on LAION-5B (itself filtered with CLIP).
PreprocessingImages come in arbitrary W x H. Bicubic-resize so the shorter side = 336, then centre-crop to 336 x 336 (code). Borders, and detail, are thrown away.
Image encoderResNet-50 or ViT. Best: ViT-L/14@336px with attention pooling.
Text encoderGPT-2-style Transformer, 63M parameters, 12 layers. Encode [BOS] ... [EOS] and return the top-layer activation at [EOS].
HeadlineZero-shot CLIP on ImageNet beats a ResNet-50 trained on the 1.2M ImageNet training images.

Ablation: contrastive beats generative

The alternative is to predict the caption text from the image (with a Transformer language model, or with a bag-of-words predictor). The lecture's efficiency figure annotates two gaps: 4X between bag-of-words contrastive (CLIP) and bag-of-words prediction, and 3X between bag-of-words prediction and the Transformer LM. CLIP-style ranking is clearly the more compute-efficient objective. Intuition: predicting every word of a noisy caption exactly is a harder, higher-entropy task than telling which of \(n\) captions fits the image.

Take-away on CLIP

The image encoding captures the semantics expressed by (noisy) text. The design choices were tuned on image classification, which is not very fine-grained. Technical cost: large batches and a softmax over the full batch.

4. Contrastive loss lab: similarity matrix, temperature, batch

The widget builds a mini-batch of \(n\) text embeddings (random unit vectors in 16-D). Image embeddings are a mixture of the paired text vector and noise, controlled by the alignment slider. It then computes the CLIP loss exactly as in the pseudo-code: \(\ell_2\)-normalise, logits \(= s/\tau\), softmax along rows or columns, cross-entropy against the diagonal. Cell numbers are softmax probabilities in percent.

5. SigLIP: sigmoid loss for language-image pretraining

SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) changes the objective. CLIP is a multiclass problem per row and column (which of the n texts matches this image?), so every pair is coupled to the whole batch through the softmax normaliser. SigLIP makes each (image, text) pair an independent binary classification: aligned or not? Diagonal pairs get label +1; all \(n^2-n\) other pairs get −1.

\[ \mathcal L_{\text{SigLIP}}=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n \log\sigma\big(z_{ij}\,(t\,\hat I_i\!\cdot\!\hat T_j+b)\big),\qquad z_{ij}=\begin{cases}+1&i=j\\-1&i\neq j\end{cases} \]

with a learnable scale \(t=e^{t'}\) and a learnable bias \(b\). Negatives outnumber positives \(n-1\) to 1, so a strongly negative initial bias prevents the negatives from dominating the loss at the start. The SigLIP paper initialises \(t'=\log 10\) and \(b=-10\).

# img_emb : image model embedding [n, dim]
# txt_emb : text model embedding  [n, dim]
# t_prime, b : learnable temperature and bias
# n : mini-batch size

t = exp(t_prime)
zimg = l2_normalize(img_emb)
ztxt = l2_normalize(txt_emb)
logits = dot(zimg, ztxt.T) * t + b
labels = 2 * eye(n) - ones(n)        # -1 with diagonal 1
l = -sum(log_sigmoid(labels * logits)) / n

Data, efficiency and batch size

  • Data: WebLI (PaLI paper): O(billion) image-text pairs scraped from the web; OCR extracts text from images; keep the highest-quality 10%; supports 100 languages.
  • Efficiency: CLIP took ~10 days on 256 TPUv3. SigLIP took ~5 days on 32 TPUv4 (the lecture notes TPUv4 has lower FLOP/s than TPUv3), so it is much faster.
  • Batch size: the loss no longer needs a global softmax, so batch size is decoupled from the loss. SigLIP beats CLIP for batches below ~16K, scales up to 1M, and ~32K is already enough.

With a softmax, every row needs its entire row of logits, so embeddings must be all-gathered. With independent pairs each of \(D\) devices handles an \((n/D)\times(n/D)\) block, sums its partial loss, and the text embeddings rotate around a ring; the final loss is a cross-device sum.

6. LLaVA: plugging a vision encoder into an LLM

LLaVA (Large Language and Vision Assistant, Liu et al., 2023) is the template most open VLMs still follow. Vision encoder: CLIP ViT-L/14. Text decoder: Vicuna (LLaMA fine-tuned on ShareGPT conversations, blog). The two are glued by a single linear projection \(W\). Flamingo's cross-attention and Q-former are more complex alternatives.

\[ \mathbf Z_v=g(\mathbf X_v),\qquad \mathbf H_v=\mathbf W\mathbf Z_v,\qquad p(\mathbf X_a\mid \mathbf X_v,\mathbf X_q)=\prod_{k=1}^{L}p_\phi\big(x_k\mid \mathbf H_v,\mathbf H_q,\mathbf X_{a,\lt k}\big) \]

The loss is the usual next-token cross-entropy on the answer tokens; the image tokens are simply a prefix in the LM's context.

Zv = clip_vit(images)                     # [B, N, 1024] patch (grid) features of the ViT
Hv = W(Zv)                                # nn.Linear(1024, d_llm) -> [B, N, d_llm]
Hq = llm.embed_tokens(question_ids)       # [B, Lq, d_llm]
Ha = llm.embed_tokens(answer_ids)         # teacher forcing
x  = torch.cat([Hv, Hq, Ha], dim=1)       # the image is just a prefix of embeddings
logits = llm(inputs_embeds=x).logits
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[:, -len_a-1:-1].flatten(0, 1), answer_ids.flatten())   # answer tokens only

Data: let GPT-4 write the instruction data (158K examples)

Image-instruction data did not exist at scale. LLaVA's trick: take MS COCO, which has Mechanical-Turk captions and object bounding boxes, and prompt text-only GPT-4 with the captions (context type 1) and boxes (context type 2) to write questions and conversations. The generations are paired with the original image. The LLaVA paper's split is 58K conversations, 23K detailed descriptions and 77K complex-reasoning examples, 158K in total.

Two-stage recipe

Stage 1 (alignment): freeze the vision encoder and the LM, train only \(W\) on image-caption pairs. Stage 2 (fine-tuning): freeze the vision encoder, train \(W\) and the LM on the instruction data.

7. LLaVA-OneVision: AnyRes, three input types, staged training

LLaVA-OneVision (Li et al., 2024) is the latest in the LLaVA series (after LLaVA 1.5 and LLaVA-NeXT). It handles multiple images and video as well as single images, keeps the standard template (vision encoder, projector, LM), and puts most of the work into data.

High resolution: AnyRes

CLIP resizes and crops to 336 x 336, which loses information (bad for OCR). AnyRes (from LLaVA 1.5): break the image into an \(a\times b\) grid of pieces matching the encoder's resolution (384 px for SigLIP), encode each piece, and concatenate the token grids. Each 384 px tile gives \(\lfloor 384/14\rfloor^2 = 27^2 = \mathbf{729}\) tokens. If the total becomes too long (the original is very high resolution), the tile grids are shrunk by bilinear interpolation.

Three input types, roughly equal sequence length

Design goal: all modalities should produce roughly the same number of tokens, so that capacity transfers between them.

Code: best-resolution tile selection (LLaVA-NeXT style, simplified) 
def select_best_grid(W, H, tile=384, max_side=6):
    best, best_eff, best_waste = (1, 1), -1, float("inf")
    for a in range(1, max_side + 1):              # tiles across
        for b in range(1, max_side + 1):          # tiles down
            scale = min(a * tile / W, b * tile / H)
            eff   = min(W * scale * H * scale, W * H)        # pixels actually usable
            waste = a * b * tile**2 - eff                     # padded area
            if eff > best_eff or (eff == best_eff and waste < best_waste):
                best, best_eff, best_waste = (a, b), eff, waste
    return best

def anyres_tokens(W, H, tile_tokens=27*27, cap=10*729):
    a, b = select_best_grid(W, H);  k = a * b
    side = 27
    if tile_tokens * (1 + k) > cap:                 # too long: bilinearly shrink each tile grid
        side = int(((cap - tile_tokens) / k) ** 0.5)
    return tile_tokens + k * side * side              # 1920 x 1080 -> 5 x 3 tiles, 729 + 15*20*20 = 6729

Data: quality over quantity, and easy-to-hard training

The philosophy is quality over quantity, with heavy use of synthesised, task-specific data. The single-image set has 3.2M samples and the OneVision (multi-image + video) set 1.6M. Their composition, as the paper's sunburst charts show:

Training: easier to harder. Three stages, from the paper's recipe table:

Stage-1Stage-1.5Stage-2 single-imageStage-2 OneVision
Resolution384384 x {2x2, 1x{2,3}, {2,3}x1}384 x {1x1 ... 6x6}384 x {1x1 ... 6x6}
Max tokens729729 x 5729 x 10729 x 10
DataLCS, 558Kimage, 4Mimage, 3.2Mmulti-image + video, 1.6M
Trainableprojector only (72.0M for the 72.7B LLM)full model (73.2B)full model (73.2B)full model (73.2B)

Transfer between modalities

Because the three modes share one token budget and one model, skills learned on one input type transfer to the others:

Summary

Standard VLM template (vision encoder + projector + LM). Most of the effort goes into data curation, which is heavily synthesised and task-specific. Model weights and data are released openly.

8. Qwen-VL: a cross-attention adapter with 256 visual tokens

Qwen-VL (Bai et al., 2023) adds explicit grounding abilities.

  • Vision encoder: OpenCLIP's ViT-bigC with 14 x 14 patches (OpenCLIP).
  • Adaptor: one layer of cross-attention with 2-D positional encodings. It maps any number of patch features to a fixed length of 256 visual tokens.
  • Special tokens: <img>, <box>, <ref>, used for grounding (boxes are written as text).

Three-stage training

Stage 1: large-scale, low-quality data. The slide's table (qwen-vl-stage1.png) shows 5B image-text pairs before cleaning and 1.4B after (28% kept).

Stage 2: higher-quality task data at higher resolution, all parameters trained. The stage-2 table (qwen-vl-stage2.png) totals 76.8M samples:

Stage-2 sources: captioning (LAION, DataComp, Coyo, CC, SBU, COCO), VQA (GQA, VGQA, VQAv2, DVQA, OCR-VQA, DocVQA, TextVQA, ChartQA, AI2D), grounding (GRIT, Visual Genome, RefCOCO/+/g), OCR (SynthDoG-en/zh, Common Crawl PDF and HTML), and in-house pure text. Stage 3: instruction tuning with the ViT frozen.

9. Qwen2-VL: dynamic resolution and multimodal RoPE

Qwen2-VL (Wang et al., 2024) uses a larger ViT (675M parameters, initialised from DFN) and an LM initialised from Qwen2. The key idea is dynamic (native) resolution: no resize to a fixed square. The number of visual tokens follows the image size.

Token arithmetic. The ViT uses 14 x 14 patches. A 2 x 2 merge combines each block of four neighbouring patch tokens into one LM token, so one LM token covers a \(28\times28\) px area. The lecture's example: a \(224\times224\) region gives \(16\times16=256\) patches, which is \(256/4=64\) tokens. The lecture says 66; the two extra tokens are most likely the vision start and end markers (my reading, not stated in the lecture). Video: 2 frames per second, with pairs of frames fused by the patch embedding, and at most 16,384 tokens per video.

Code: smart_resize (paraphrased from the Qwen2-VL reference preprocessing) 
import math
def smart_resize(h, w, factor=28, min_pixels=56*56, max_pixels=16384*28*28):
    h2, w2 = round(h / factor) * factor, round(w / factor) * factor
    if h2 * w2 > max_pixels:                        # too big: scale down, keep aspect ratio
        beta = math.sqrt(h * w / max_pixels)
        h2, w2 = math.floor(h / beta / factor) * factor, math.floor(w / beta / factor) * factor
    elif h2 * w2 < min_pixels:                      # too small: scale up
        beta = math.sqrt(min_pixels / (h * w))
        h2, w2 = math.ceil(h * beta / factor) * factor, math.ceil(w * beta / factor) * factor
    return h2, w2     # tokens = (h2 // factor) * (w2 // factor): 224 x 28 -> 8, 1260 x 700 -> 1125

Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (M-RoPE)

RoPE rotates query and key pairs by an angle proportional to the position. For text one index per token is enough. For an image a flat 1-D index destroys the 2-D structure, and a video also has time. M-RoPE gives every token a triple \((t,h,w)\) and assigns the rotary frequency pairs of each head to three groups, rotated by \(t\), \(h\) and \(w\) respectively. Text tokens use \(t=h=w=\) the ordinary 1-D index, so text reduces to ordinary RoPE. The text after a visual segment continues from the largest id used so far, plus one. Positions therefore grow like \(\max(T,h,w)\), not \(T\cdot h\cdot w\).

def mrope_position_ids(segments):
    """segments: [('text', n) | ('vision', T, h, w), ...] -> position ids of shape [3, L] = (t, h, w)."""
    pos, start = [], 0
    for seg in segments:
        if seg[0] == 'text':
            r = torch.arange(seg[1]) + start
            pos.append(torch.stack([r, r, r]))                      # equal axes: plain 1-D RoPE
            start += seg[1]
        else:
            _, T, h, w = seg
            t = torch.arange(T).view(T, 1, 1).expand(T, h, w).flatten()
            y = torch.arange(h).view(1, h, 1).expand(T, h, w).flatten()
            x = torch.arange(w).view(1, 1, w).expand(T, h, w).flatten()
            pos.append(torch.stack([t, y, x]) + start)
            start = int(pos[-1].max()) + 1                           # continue after the largest id used
    return torch.cat(pos, dim=1)

# check against the figure: mrope_position_ids([('vision', 3, 3, 4), ('text', 4)])[:, -4:]  ->  starts at (4,4,4)

Training and capabilities

Similar to Qwen-VL: Stage 1 trains only the visual encoder (LM frozen, image-text data); Stage 2 trains all parameters on mixed multimodal data; Stage 3 trains the language model on instruction-following data.

10. Qwen3-VL: interleaved M-RoPE, timestamps, DeepStack, 256K context

Qwen3-VL (Qwen team, 2025) scales the same recipe: a Qwen3 language model (dense and MoE, up to 235B-A22B), 256K context, and the vision encoder SigLIP-2 (same architecture as SigLIP).

Interleaved M-RoPE

In chunked M-RoPE the frequency pairs of a head form blocks [t t t t ... h h h h ... w w w w]. Low pair indices rotate fast (high frequency) and high indices slowly, so time gets only the fast bands and width only the slow ones. Qwen3-VL interleaves the axes: [t w h t w h ...], so every axis spans the full frequency range. This helps long-range and long-video behaviour.

Other changes

  • Explicit video timestamps: given as text tokens (for example <0.0 seconds> before the frame embeddings) rather than baked into the positional embeddings.
  • Square-root-normalised per-token loss: balances text against multimodal data, since video examples are long and should not dominate.
  • DeepStack (paper): cross-layer fusion. Visual features from several ViT levels are injected into several early LM blocks, not only at the input.

Training

Pre-training has 4 stages (S0 to S3). S0 trains only the vision-language merger on 67B tokens. S1 trains everything on about 1T multimodal tokens at sequence length 8,192. S2 is long-context pre-training on about 1T tokens at 32,768. S3 is ultra-long-context adaptation on 100B tokens at 262,144. Post-training: SFT on long chain-of-thought data, knowledge distillation, and RL.

Summary of Qwen3-VL (lecture)

State-of-the-art performance. Lots of data work, but few details. Minor yet potentially important architectural changes. Scale up.

11. Towards omni models: Chameleon and discrete image tokens

The VLMs so far encode images with a continuous encoder (CLIP, SigLIP) and inject them into the LM. Their disadvantage: they cannot generate images (that needs an extra diffusion model). Chameleon (Meta, 2024) maps everything into discrete tokens: one vocabulary, one autoregressive Transformer, and uniform analysis and generation of text and images (early fusion).

Vision tokenizer: VQ-VAE

Chameleon's image tokenizer builds on Make-A-Scene and the VQ-VAE of van den Oord et al. The encoder must output discrete tokens so the LM can also generate them. The idea: an encoder produces a grid of continuous latents \(z_e\); each latent is replaced by its nearest entry in a learned codebook \(E\in\mathbb R^{K\times D}\); a decoder reconstructs the image from the quantised latents; everything is trained to minimise reconstruction error.

\[ z_q = e_k,\quad k=\arg\min_j\lVert z_e-e_j\rVert_2,\qquad \mathcal L=\underbrace{\lVert x-\hat x\rVert^2}_{\text{reconstruction}}+\underbrace{\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e]-e\rVert^2}_{\text{codebook}}+\beta\underbrace{\lVert z_e-\mathrm{sg}[e]\rVert^2}_{\text{commitment}} \]

The argmin is not differentiable, so the straight-through estimator copies the decoder's gradient from \(z_q\) back to \(z_e\). The stop-gradient (sg) terms pull codes towards encoder outputs and keep the encoder from drifting away from the codebook (\(\beta=0.25\) in the VQ-VAE paper).

class VectorQuantizer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, K=8192, D=256, beta=0.25):
        super().__init__(); self.codebook = nn.Embedding(K, D); self.beta = beta
    def forward(self, z_e):                                  # z_e: [B, h, w, D] continuous latents
        flat = z_e.reshape(-1, z_e.size(-1))
        E = self.codebook.weight                               # [K, D]
        d = flat.pow(2).sum(1, keepdim=True) - 2 * flat @ E.T + E.pow(2).sum(1)   # ||z - e_k||^2
        idx = d.argmin(1)                                      # nearest code = the discrete token
        z_q = self.codebook(idx).view_as(z_e)
        vq_loss = F.mse_loss(z_q, z_e.detach()) + self.beta * F.mse_loss(z_e, z_q.detach())
        z_q = z_e + (z_q - z_e).detach()                       # straight-through estimator
        return z_q, idx.view(z_e.shape[:-1]), vq_loss

How many tokens, how many bits? Chameleon encodes a \(512\times512\) image into 1024 tokens with a codebook of 8192 entries: a downsampling factor of 16 gives a \(32\times32\) grid, and each token carries 13 bits. A new BPE tokenizer is trained over text and image codes together.

Training Chameleon

  • Stage 1 (80% of training): large-scale unsupervised data: 2.9T text tokens, 1.5T text/image tokens, 400B interleaved text/image tokens.
  • Stage 2 (20%): 50% of the stage-1 mixture and 50% high-quality data.

Training stability: modality entropy and logit drift

Text tokens have low entropy (grammar constrains the next token), while image tokens have high entropy (many codes are plausible at each position). Mixing both in one softmax causes norm growth and a logit drift problem. The softmax is invariant to a constant shift of all logits, so nothing stops the common shift from growing. Chameleon's fixes:

  • QK-norm: normalise queries and keys before the dot product, which bounds the attention logits.
  • z-loss: penalise \(\log^2 Z\), where \(Z=\sum_v e^{\ell_v}\), with a small coefficient (about \(10^{-5}\) in the Chameleon paper): \(\mathcal L=\mathrm{CE}+10^{-5}(\log Z)^2\).
logits = model(x)                                           # [B, L, V]
ce     = F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), y.flatten())
z_loss = 1e-5 * torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1).pow(2).mean()   # keeps the log-partition near 0
loss   = ce + z_loss
Chameleon summary

Elegant: just autoregressive modelling of discrete tokens. Not as performant: discretisation loses information (think OCR). Training with multiple modalities is tricky.

Which parts train when?

Comprehension vs generation

Understanding wants semantic features (what is in the image: CLIP/SigLIP-style, continuous, fewer tokens). Generation needs fine-grained, reconstructable detail (VQ-style tokens or diffusion latents). The two may demand different encoders; unifying them in one tokenizer (Chameleon) trades quality for elegance. Also balance images and video (lower information density per token) with text, for training stability.

13. Efficiency: what a visual token costs

Every visual token is context the LLM must prefill, costing roughly \(2\,P_{\text{LM}}\) FLOPs per token, plus quadratic attention and KV-cache memory. A 1920 x 1080 frame costs 576 tokens in CLIP-336 (after cropping) and 6,729 with AnyRes. A one-minute video at 2 fps is 120 frames, or 60 temporal groups; at 644 x 336 that is \(60\times276=16{,}560\) tokens, already above Qwen2-VL's 16,384 cap. Levers used by the models in this lecture:

  • Fewer tokens per pixel: the 2 x 2 merger (Qwen2-VL and Qwen3-VL: 4x fewer), 256 learned queries (Qwen-VL), bilinear shrinking (OneVision).
  • Per-modality budgets: lower resolution per video frame (196 tokens instead of 729), and a cap per input type (7290, 8748, 6272).
  • Pretraining cost: SigLIP's chunked sigmoid loss (about 5 days on 32 TPUv4, against about 10 days on 256 TPUv3 for CLIP) and the decoupled batch size.
  • Stage-wise training: train only the connector first (the 72.0M-parameter projector of the 72.7B model in OneVision stage 1), and the long-context stages last (Qwen3-VL: 8K, then 32K, then 256K).

Summary of the lecture

  • Frontier models are expected to be multimodal (natively multimodal, omni).
  • Fundamental challenge: how to encode non-text modalities.
  • Comprehension and generation may demand different things (semantics versus fine-grained detail).
  • Balance images and video (lower information density) with text, for training stability.
  • Continuous encoders plus a Transformer, with diffusion models for generation.

14. Self-check quiz

1. CLIP ViT-L/14@336: how many patch tokens does an image give, and what happens to a 1920 x 1080 photo?
\(336/14=24\), so \(24^2=576\) patch tokens (plus one class token). The photo is bicubic-resized so the shorter side is 336: width \(1920\cdot336/1080\approx597\), so it becomes 597 x 336. The centre crop keeps 336 of those 597 columns (56%) and discards 44%. The 336 x 336 input holds only 5.4% of the original pixels, at 31% of the original linear resolution.
2. Write the CLIP loss for a batch and say what sets its minimum.
Logits \(=\hat I\hat T^\top e^{t}\); cross-entropy with labels \(0,\dots,n-1\) along both axes, averaged. For uninformative embeddings the loss is \(\ln n\) (uniform softmax). It approaches 0 only when each diagonal logit beats all off-diagonal logits by a margin that is large relative to the temperature. That is why the temperature is learned (the paper initialises \(\tau=0.07\)).
3. How does SigLIP differ from CLIP, and why does it scale batch size better? Compute the logit memory for n = 32,768 on 32 devices.
SigLIP treats each of the \(n^2\) pairs as an independent binary problem, \(-\log\sigma(z_{ij}(t\,\cos_{ij}+b))\) with \(z=+1\) on the diagonal. No softmax over the batch is needed, so devices can process \((n/D)\times(n/D)\) blocks and pass texts around a ring. In fp32: the full matrix is \(32768^2\cdot4\approx4.3\) GB; a CLIP per-device slab \((1024)\cdot32768\cdot4\approx134\) MB; a SigLIP block \(1024^2\cdot4\approx4.2\) MB.
4. What are the two LLaVA training stages and which parameters train in each?
Stage 1 (alignment): the vision encoder and the LM are frozen, and only the linear projection \(W\) is trained, on image-caption pairs. Stage 2 (fine-tuning): the vision encoder stays frozen, while \(W\) and the LM are trained on the 158K GPT-4-generated instruction examples (conversations, detailed descriptions, complex reasoning) built from COCO captions and boxes.
5. How many tokens does AnyRes give for a 1920 x 1080 image in OneVision, and what happens when that is too many?
The best tile grid is 5 x 3 (15 tiles of 384 px, no wasted area beyond the image border): \(16\times729=11{,}664\) tokens with the base view, which exceeds the \((1+9)\times729=7290\) cap. Shrinking each 27 x 27 tile grid bilinearly to 20 x 20 gives \(729+15\cdot400=6729\) tokens. The tile choice follows the LLaVA-NeXT rule; the exact shrink schedule is a simplification.
6. Qwen2-VL: how many tokens for a 1092 x 8204 page, and for a 224 x 224 region? Where does 66 come from?
One token covers 28 x 28 px (patch 14 with a 2 x 2 merge). The page gives \(39\times293=11{,}427\) tokens. The 224 x 224 region gives \(16\times16=256\) patches, \(256/4=64\) tokens, plus 2 start and end markers, which I read as the source of the 66.
7. What is M-RoPE, and what position does the text after a 3 x 3 x 4 video (3 frames, 3 x 4 patches) receive?
Each visual token gets a (t,h,w) triple, and the rotary frequency pairs are split into three groups rotated by t, h and w. Text tokens use equal ids, so they reduce to ordinary RoPE. Visual ids reach 2 on t, 2 on h and 3 on w; the following text starts at max + 1 = 4, i.e. (4,4,4). Flat 1-D ids would advance by \(3\cdot3\cdot4=36\) positions instead. Qwen3-VL interleaves the axes across the frequency bands instead of chunking them.
8. Why does Chameleon need a VQ-VAE, and what does it cost? Compute the tokens and the compression for 512 x 512.
To generate images with the same next-token objective, the image must be discrete. The VQ-VAE maps each latent to its nearest codebook entry (8192 codes, 13 bits) and trains encoder, codebook and decoder with reconstruction, codebook and commitment losses, using a straight-through gradient. With downsampling 16 you get a 32 x 32 grid = 1024 tokens = 13,312 bits, against 6.29 Mbit of raw 8-bit RGB (about 472x). Costs: the representation is lossy (OCR, fine text), and training is unstable because image tokens have high entropy, which needs QK-norm and z-loss.

15. Key takeaways

  • Everything must become tokens: images become patch tokens (ViT) or code indices (VQ-VAE).
  • CLIP: a symmetric InfoNCE over an n x n similarity matrix gives semantic image embeddings from noisy captions. SigLIP's per-pair sigmoid removes the global softmax and the coupling to batch size.
  • The standard VLM is vision encoder + projector + LLM. Stage-wise training (align the connector first, then unfreeze) and synthetic instruction data matter as much as the architecture.
  • Token count is the cost lever: AnyRes (729 per tile, 7290 cap), 2 x 2 merging, dynamic resolution (28 or 32 px per token), 196-token video frames.
  • M-RoPE gives vision tokens (t,h,w) positions. Qwen3-VL interleaves the axes across frequencies and adds text timestamps, DeepStack and a square-root-normalised loss.
  • Chameleon shows that early fusion with discrete tokens works, at a cost in fidelity and stability.

Cheat sheet & glossary

Every back-of-the-envelope formula used across the course, in one place, with a live calculator for the ones you will reach for most often.

Formulas to memorise

QuantityFormulaWhere
Matmul FLOPs \((m\times k)\cdot(k\times n)\)\(2mkn\)L2, L5
Training FLOPs, dense transformer\(\approx 6\,N D\) (2 forward + 4 backward per param per token)L2, L9
Inference FLOPs per token\(\approx 2N\) (active params for MoE)L10
Training memory / param (AdamW, bf16 params + fp32 states)\(\approx 16\) bytes: 2 (param) + 2 (grad) + 4 (master) + 4 + 4 (Adam \(m,v\)); activations extraL2, L8
Model FLOPs utilisation\(\mathrm{MFU}=\dfrac{\text{useful FLOP/s}}{\text{peak FLOP/s}}\)L2
Arithmetic intensity\(I=\dfrac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}\); compute-bound iff \(I > \dfrac{\text{peak FLOP/s}}{\text{bandwidth}}\) (H100 bf16: \(989\text{T}/3.35\text{T}\approx 295\))L5, L10
Roofline\(\text{attainable}=\min(\text{peak},\; I\cdot \text{BW})\)L5
Chinchilla\(L(N,D)=E+\dfrac{A}{N^{\alpha}}+\dfrac{B}{D^{\beta}}\); compute-optimal \(D\approx 20N\) with \(C\approx 6ND\)L9, L11
KV cache bytes\(2\cdot \text{bytes}\cdot L\cdot n_{kv}\cdot d_{head}\cdot S\cdot B\)L10
Ring all-reduce (per GPU traffic)\(2\dfrac{p-1}{p}\,M \approx 2M\)L7, L8
Pipeline bubble fraction (GPipe)\(\dfrac{p-1}{m+p-1}\) for \(p\) stages, \(m\) micro-batchesL7, L8
Speculative decoding speed-upexpected tokens/step \(=\dfrac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}\) for acceptance \(\alpha\), draft length \(\gamma\)L10
Bradley–Terry / reward model\(P(y_w\succ y_l)=\sigma\big(r(y_w)-r(y_l)\big)\)L12, L15
DPO loss\(-\log\sigma\!\Big(\beta\big[\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w)}{\pi_{ref}(y_w)}-\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l)}{\pi_{ref}(y_l)}\big]\Big)\)L15
GRPO advantage\(A_i=\dfrac{r_i-\operatorname{mean}(r_{1..G})}{\operatorname{std}(r_{1..G})}\)L16
MinHash / LSH candidate probability\(P=1-(1-s^{r})^{b}\) (b bands of r rows)L14
CLIP / InfoNCE\(\mathcal L=-\tfrac1n\sum_i\log\dfrac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{s_{ij}/\tau}}\) (symmetrised over rows and columns)L17

Calculator: how big a run can I afford?

Combines the \(6ND\) rule, hardware peak, MFU and the Chinchilla ratio. Defaults: an H100 at its bf16 dense peak of 989 TFLOP/s.

Calculator: compute- or memory-bound?

Glossary

TermMeaning
BPEByte-pair encoding: iteratively merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
bf16 / fp16 / fp816-/8-bit floating formats; bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits (range) but only 7 mantissa bits.
MFUModel FLOPs utilisation – fraction of hardware peak spent on useful model FLOPs.
HBM / SRAMOff-chip high-bandwidth memory (GBs, ~3 TB/s) vs. on-chip shared memory/registers (MBs, ~10× faster).
RooflinePerformance bound = min(peak compute, intensity × memory bandwidth).
Fusion / tilingCombine ops to avoid HBM round-trips / process blocks that fit in fast memory.
FlashAttentionExact attention computed in tiles with an online softmax so the \(S\times S\) matrix is never materialised.
RoPERotary position embedding – rotate query/key pairs by position-dependent angles so dot products depend on relative offset.
RMSNormLayerNorm without mean-subtraction or bias: \(x/\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(x^2)+\epsilon}\cdot g\).
SwiGLUGated MLP: \(W_{down}(\operatorname{SiLU}(W_{gate}x)\odot W_{up}x)\).
GQA / MQA / MLAShare K/V heads across query heads (GQA/MQA) or compress K/V into a low-rank latent (MLA) to shrink the KV cache.
MoEMixture of experts: a router sends each token to top-k of many FFN experts; total ≫ active parameters.
DP / TP / PP / SP / EPData / tensor / pipeline / sequence / expert parallelism.
ZeRO / FSDPShard optimizer states (1), gradients (2), parameters (3) across data-parallel ranks.
All-reduceEvery rank ends with the sum of all ranks' tensors = reduce-scatter + all-gather.
Scaling lawSmooth power-law relation between loss and compute / params / data.
muPMaximal-update parametrisation – scale init/LR with width so optimal hyper-parameters transfer.
WSDWarmup–stable–decay learning-rate schedule (flat plateau + short decay), reusable across token budgets.
KV cacheStored keys/values of past tokens so decoding costs O(S) rather than O(S²) per step.
Speculative decodingA cheap draft model proposes tokens; the large model verifies them in one pass – lossless.
PagedAttentionKV cache split into fixed blocks with a block table (virtual-memory style) to kill fragmentation.
pass@kProbability at least one of k samples solves the task.
Elo / Bradley–TerryRatings from pairwise preferences: \(P(A\succ B)=1/(1+10^{(R_B-R_A)/400})\).
MinHash / LSHSketch sets so that signature agreement estimates Jaccard similarity; banding finds near-duplicates sub-quadratically.
SFT / RLHF / DPOSupervised fine-tuning / RL from human feedback via a reward model / direct preference optimisation without one.
RLVR / GRPORL with programmatically verifiable rewards / group-relative policy optimisation (no value network).
ViT / CLIP / SigLIPPatch-token vision transformer / contrastive image–text pre-training with softmax / sigmoid loss.
